output: A very worthy person, a true lover of his country, and whose virtues I highly esteem, was lately pleased in discoursing on this matter, to offer a refinement upon my scheme. He said, that many gentlemen of this kingdom, having of late destroyed their deer, he conceived that the want of venison might be well supplied by the bodies of young lads and maidens, not exceeding fourteen years of age, nor under twelve; so great a number of both sexes in every county being now ready to starve for want of work and service: and these to be disposed of by their parents if alive, or otherwise by their nearest relations. But with due deference to so excellent a friend, and so deserving a patriot, I cannot be altogether in his sentiments; for as to the males, my American acquaintance assured me from frequent experience, that their flesh was generally tough and lean, like that of our schoolboys, by continual exercise, and their taste disagreeable, and to fatten them would not answer the charge. Then as to the females, it would, I think, with humble submission, be a loss to the publick, because they soon would become breeders themselves: and besides, it is not improbable that some scrupulous people might be apt to censure such a practice, (although indeed very unjustly) as a little bordering upon cruelty, which, I confess, hath always been with me the strongest objection against any project, how well soever intended.

input: The population of this kingdom is usually estimated at one and a half million. I estimate that there are approximately two hundred thousand couples with wives who are capable of bearing children. From this number, I deduct thirty thousand couples who can support their own children. I suspect, however, that the actual number might be lower due to the current hardships facing the kingdom. If we accept this figure, we are left with one hundred and seventy thousand potential breeders. Next, I subtract fifty thousand for women who experience miscarriages or whose children die from accidents or diseases within the first year. Consequently, we find there are only one hundred and twenty thousand children born annually to poor parents. The pressing question is how to rear and provide for this number. As I have previously mentioned, given the current circumstances, it is entirely untenable to implement any of the proposed solutions. We cannot employ these children in crafts or agriculture. They do not construct houses, especially in rural areas, nor do they farm the land. They rarely manage to survive by stealing until they reach six years of age, unless they are exceptionally gifted. I acknowledge that they learn the basics of survival earlier, but during this formative period, they should be seen only as learners. A prominent gentleman from the county of Cavan informed me that he has never encountered more than one or two cases of children under six who were adept at this skill, even in a region noted for its rapid learning.
output: The number of souls in this kingdom being usually reckoned one million and a half, of these I calculate there may be about two hundred thousand couple, whose wives are breeders; from which number I subtract thirty thousand couple, who are able to maintain their own children, (although I apprehend there cannot be so many under the present distresses of the kingdom) but this being granted, there will remain a hundred and seventy thousand breeders. I again subtract fifty thousand, for those women who miscarry, or whose children die by accident or disease within the year. There only remain a hundred and twenty thousand children of poor parents annually born. The question therefore is, How this number shall be reared and provided for? which, as I have already said, under the present situation of affairs, is utterly impossible by all the methods hitherto proposed. For we can neither employ them in handicraft or agriculture; they neither build houses, (I mean in the country) nor cultivate land: they can very seldom pick up a livelihood by stealing till they arrive at six years old; except where they are of towardly parts, although I confess they learn the rudiments much earlier; during which time they can however be properly looked upon only as probationers; as I have been informed by a principal gentleman in the county of Cavan, who protested to me, that he never knew above one or two instances under the age of six, even in a part of the kingdom so renowned for the quickest proficiency in that art.

input: Some people of a despondent disposition are deeply concerned about the large number of poor people who are aged, diseased, or maimed, and I have been asked to consider what measures might be taken to relieve the nation of such a burdensome problem. However, I feel no unease about the matter, since it is well known that these people are dying and decaying every day from cold, famine, filth, and vermin as quickly as could reasonably be expected. This suggests that the problem is, in practice, resolving itself. As for the young laborers, they are now in an almost equally promising condition. They cannot find work, and consequently waste away from lack of nourishment to such a degree that if they are ever accidentally hired for common labor, they lack the strength to perform it. Ultimately, in this way both the country and themselves are conveniently delivered from the evils to come.
output: Some persons of a desponding spirit are in great concern about that vast number of poor people, who are aged, diseased, or maimed; and I have been desired to employ my thoughts what course may be taken, to ease the nation of so grievous an incumbrance. But I am not in the least pain upon that matter, because it is very well known, that they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected. And as to the young labourers, they are now in almost as hopeful a condition. They cannot get work, and consequently pine away from want of nourishment, to a degree, that if at any time they are accidentally hired to common labour, they have not strength to perform it, and thus the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come.

input: In essence, I do not hold my own opinion with such fervor as to dismiss any proposal put forth by wise individuals, provided that such proposals are found to be equally innocent, economical, straightforward, and effective. However, before any alternative to my scheme is presented, along with an assertion of superiority, I request that the author or authors carefully consider two critical points. First, given the current circumstances, I would like to know how they plan to secure food and clothing for a hundred thousand individuals who contribute little to society. Furthermore, considering that there exists a total of one million individuals in human form within this kingdom, if their collective means of subsistence were to be pooled together, they would find themselves in debt to the tune of two million pounds sterling. This figure includes not only professional beggars but also those who, though engaged in farming, cottage industries, or labor, find themselves in a state of perpetual need alongside their families. I urge those politicians who oppose my proposal and may dare to respond to first consult with the parents of these individuals. They should inquire whether, at this moment, those parents would perceive it as a significant fortune to have been sold for sustenance at the tender age of one, as I suggest, thereby escaping the relentless cycle of misfortune that they have endured due to the tyranny of landlords, the inability to pay rent in the absence of money or trade, the lack of basic necessities, and the absence of shelter or clothing to protect them from the harshness of the elements. Additionally, they should consider the grim prospect of perpetuating similar, if not greater, miseries for future generations.
output: After all, I am not so violently bent upon my own opinion, as to reject any offer, proposed by wise men, which shall be found equally innocent, cheap, easy, and effectual. But before something of that kind shall be advanced in contradiction to my scheme, and offering a better, I desire the author or authors will be pleased maturely to consider two points. First, As things now stand, how they will be able to find food and raiment for a hundred thousand useless mouths and backs. And secondly, There being a round million of creatures in humane figure throughout this kingdom, whose whole subsistence put into a common stock, would leave them in debt two million of pounds sterling, adding those who are beggars by profession, to the bulk of farmers, cottagers and labourers, with their wives and children, who are beggars in effect; I desire those politicians who dislike my overture, and may perhaps be so bold to attempt an answer, that they will first ask the parents of these mortals, whether they would not at this day think it a great happiness to have been sold for food at a year old, in the manner I prescribe, and thereby have avoided such a perpetual scene of misfortunes, as they have since gone through, by the oppression of landlords, the impossibility of paying rent without money or trade, the want of common sustenance, with neither house nor clothes to cover them from the inclemencies of the weather, and the most inevitable prospect of intailing the like, or greater miseries, upon their breed for ever.
title: A Modest Proposal
author: Jonathan Swift

My intention may not be limited to assisting only the children of known beggars; it can often extend to include all infants of a certain age who are born to parents who may be equally unable to support them, much like those who seek our help on the streets. 

Reflecting on this important issue over many years and carefully considering various proposals, I have found that many of these ideas may be fundamentally flawed in their calculations. It is true that a newborn may survive on its mother's milk for about a year with minimal additional nourishment, typically costing around two shillings, which the mother can often earn through her legal begging activities. It is precisely at the age of one year that I plan to ensure their care in a way that not only relieves their parents and the community from financial burden but also enables these children to eventually contribute to the sustenance and clothing of many others. In summary, my aim is to create a system that benefits both the children in need and the wider community.
output:
But my intention is very far from being confined to provide only for the children of professed beggars: it is of a much greater extent, and shall take in the whole number of infants at a certain age, who are born of parents in effect as little able to support them, as those who demand our charity in the streets.

As to my own part, having turned my thoughts for many years upon this important subject, and maturely weighed the several schemes of our projectors, I have always found them grossly mistaken in their computation. It is true, a child just dropt from its dam, may be supported by her milk, for a solar year, with little other nourishment: at most not above the value of two shillings, which the mother may certainly get, or the value in scraps, by her lawful occupation of begging; and it is exactly at one year old that I propose to provide for them in such a manner, as, instead of being a charge upon their parents, or the parish, or wanting food and raiment for the rest of their lives, they shall, on the contrary, contribute to the feeding, and partly to the clothing of many thousands.

output: Many other advantages might be enumerated. input: I can think of no objection that might possibly be raised against this proposal, unless it should be argued that the number of people in the kingdom would be greatly reduced. This I freely admit, and indeed it was one principal design in offering it to the world. I wish the reader to observe that I calculate my remedy for this one individual Kingdom of Ireland, and for no other that ever was, is, or, I believe, ever can be upon Earth. Therefore, let no man speak to me of other expedients: of taxing our absentees at five shillings a pound; of using neither clothes nor household furniture except what is of our own growth and manufacture; of utterly rejecting the materials and instruments that promote foreign luxury; of curing the expensiveness of pride, vanity, idleness, and gaming in our women; of introducing a vein of parsimony, prudence, and temperance; of learning to love our country, in which we differ even from Laplanders and the inhabitants of Topinamboo; of quitting our animosities and factions, and no longer acting like the Jews, who were murdering one another at the very moment their city was taken; of being a little cautious not to sell our country and consciences for nothing; of teaching landlords to have at least one degree of mercy toward their tenants. Lastly, of putting a spirit of honesty, industry, and skill into our shopkeepers, who, if a resolution could now be taken to buy only our native goods, would immediately unite to cheat and exact upon us in the price, the measure, and the goodness, nor could ever yet be brought to make one fair proposal of just dealing, though often and earnestly invited to do so.

The March Hare examined the watch, initially with a gloomy expression, and then attempted to troubleshoot the problem by submerging it in his tea. However, this effort did not yield any new insights, and he simply reiterated his earlier claim that the butter used was of high quality. 

Alice had been observing the March Hare's actions with interest and commented on the unusual design of the watch. This highlights its unique feature of displaying the day of the month, while omitting the current time. Ultimately, this design aspect struck Alice as noteworthy and amusing.
output:
“Two days wrong!” sighed the Hatter. “I told you butter wouldn’t suit the works!” he added looking angrily at the March Hare.

The March Hare took the watch and looked at it gloomily: then he dipped it into his cup of tea, and looked at it again: but he could think of nothing better to say than his first remark, “It was the best butter, you know.”

Alice had been looking over his shoulder with some curiosity. “What a funny watch!” she remarked. “It tells the day of the month, and doesn’t tell what o’clock it is!”

Upon approaching, Alice discerned his sorrowful sighs, as if his heart were shattered. She felt a profound sense of sympathy for him. "What is his sorrow?" she inquired of the Gryphon. In response, the Gryphon articulated, nearly echoing its previous sentiments, "It is merely a product of his imagination; he does not possess any sorrow, you see. Let us proceed!"
output:
The Gryphon sat up and rubbed its eyes: then it watched the Queen till she was out of sight: then it chuckled. “What fun!” said the Gryphon, half to itself, half to Alice.

They had not gone far before they saw the Mock Turtle in the distance, sitting sad and lonely on a little ledge of rock, and, as they came nearer, Alice could hear him sighing as if his heart would break. She pitied him deeply. “What is his sorrow?” she asked the Gryphon, and the Gryphon answered, very nearly in the same words as before, “It’s all his fancy, that: he hasn’t got no sorrow, you know. “I mean what I say,” the Mock Turtle responded, sounding offended. The Gryphon then urged, “Come, let us hear some of your adventures.”

Alice spoke timidly, “I could share my adventures starting from this morning, but it would be pointless to go back to yesterday, as I was a different person then.”

“No, no! We want the adventures first,” the Gryphon said impatiently. “Explanations take such an excessive amount of time.”

With that, Alice began recounting her adventures from the moment she first encountered the White Rabbit. Initially, she felt nervous as the two creatures positioned themselves closely beside her, their eyes and mouths wide open. However, she gradually gained confidence as she continued. Her audience remained perfectly still until she described the moment she recited “You are old, Father William,” to the Caterpillar, noting how the words came out differently. At that point, the Mock Turtle inhaled deeply and remarked, “That is very curious.”
output:

“I could tell you my adventures - beginning from this morning,” said Alice a little timidly: “but it’s no use going back to yesterday, because I was a different person then.”

So Alice began telling them her adventures from the time when she first saw the White Rabbit. "Then, doctor," said Silver, "you just step outside of that stockade, and once you are there I will bring the boy down on the inside, and I reckon you can yarn through the spars. Good day to you, sir, and all our duties to the squire and Captain Smollett."

The explosion of disapproval, which nothing but Silver's black looks had restrained, broke out immediately after the doctor had left the house. Silver was roundly accused of playing double - of attempting to make a separate peace for himself, of sacrificing the interests of his accomplices and victims, and, in one word, of the identical, exact thing that he was doing. It appeared to me so obvious, in this case, that I could not imagine how he was to turn their anger. However, he was twice the man the rest were, and his last night's victory had given him a huge preponderance over their minds. He called them all the fools and dolts you can imagine, said it was necessary I should talk to the doctor, fluttered the chart in their faces, asked them if they could afford to break the treaty the very day they were bound a-treasure-hunting.

input: As I approached the location where I had previously met Ben Gunn, I became more cautious, remaining vigilant of my surroundings. The evening was approaching quickly, and when I opened the gap between the two peaks, I noticed a flickering light against the sky, which I assumed indicated that the man from the island was preparing his dinner over an open fire. This situation raised concerns for me, as it seemed reckless for him to be so exposed. If I could perceive this light, it was possible that Silver, who was encamped nearby on the shore, might also see it.
output: This brought me near to where I had encountered Ben Gunn, the maroon; and I walked more circumspectly, keeping an eye on every side. The dusk had come nigh hand completely, and as I opened out the cleft between the two peaks, I became aware of a wavering glow against the sky, where, as I judged, the man of the island was cooking his supper before a roaring fire. And yet I wondered, in my heart, that he should show himself so careless. For if I could see this radiance, might it not reach the eyes of Silver himself where he camped upon the shore among the marshes?

input:
Merry expressed his disbelief by shaking the two guineas at Silver, mocking him about the supposed value of seven hundred thousand pounds. He characterized Silver as someone who is good at making deals and implied that Silver's competence was questionable. In response, Silver maintained a calm demeanor, telling his crew to continue digging, suggesting that they might uncover something insignificant. 

At this moment, it became clear that the group was largely in support of Merry. They quickly exited the excavation site, casting angry looks back at Silver. An important observation was made: they all chose to leave the site by the side opposite to where Silver was standing.
output:
“Two guineas!” roared Merry, shaking it at Silver. “That’s your seven hundred thousand pounds, is it? You’re the man for bargains, ain’t you? You’re him that never bungled nothing, you wooden-headed lubber!”

“Dig away, boys,” said Silver with the coolest insolence; “you’ll find some pig-nuts and I shouldn’t wonder.”

But this time everyone was entirely in Merry’s favour. They began to scramble out of the excavation, darting furious glances behind them. One thing I observed, which looked well for us: they all got out upon the opposite side from Silver.

I navigated through the woods until I reached the back, or shoreward side, of the stockade, where I was warmly welcomed by my loyal companions. 

After sharing my story, I began to observe my surroundings. The log house was constructed from unrefined pine trunks, forming the roof, walls, and floor. In several areas, the floor rose as much as one to one and a half feet above the sand. There was a porch at the entrance, and beneath this porch, a small spring flowed into an unusual artificial basin. This basin was nothing more than a large iron ship’s kettle, its bottom removed and positioned firmly in the sand, as the captain would describe it.
output:
Then I skirted among the woods until I had regained the rear, or shoreward side, of the stockade, and was soon warmly welcomed by the faithful party.

I had soon told my story and began to look about me. The log-house was made of unsquared trunks of pine - roof, walls, and floor. The latter stood in several places as much as a foot or a foot and a half above the surface of the sand. There was a porch at the door, and under this porch the little spring welled up into an artificial basin of a rather odd kind - no other than a great ship’s kettle of iron, with the bottom knocked out, and sunk “to her bearings,” as the captain said, among the sand.

input:
Eventually, the group was assembled. Six men were to remain on board, while the other thirteen, including Silver, began to disembark.

At that moment, the first of the wild ideas that would later help save our lives came to me. If Silver left six men behind, it was clear that our group could not seize and fight the ship. Since only six remained, it was equally clear that the cabin group had no immediate need of my help. I immediately decided to go ashore. In an instant, I slipped over the side and curled up in the fore-sheets of the nearest boat, and almost at the same moment, it pushed off.
output:

Then it was that there came into my head the first of the mad notions that contributed so much to save our lives. If six men were left by Silver, it was plain our party could not take and fight the ship; and since only six were left, it was equally plain that the cabin party had no present need of my assistance. input:
We were all engaged in our tasks, modifying the powder and the berths, when the remaining individuals, including Long John, arrived in a shore-boat. Meanwhile, the cook responded to a command and promptly disappeared in the direction of his galley. 

Subsequently, it became clear that the squire and I shared similar sentiments, and we both harbored strong negative feelings towards the captain. 

Throughout the night, the crew was extremely busy, as we worked to store items in their designated locations. Furthermore, numerous boatloads of the squire's acquaintances, such as Mr. Blandly, arrived to extend their well wishes for a successful voyage and a safe return. Notably, the level of activity on this occasion surpassed that of any night I had previously experienced at the Admiral Benbow, and I was thoroughly exhausted by the time the boatswain sounded his pipe, shortly before dawn, and the crew began to prepare the capstan-bars. Nevertheless, despite my fatigue, I remained on deck, as every aspect of the scene was novel and fascinating to me, including the concise commands, the high-pitched sound of the whistle, and the men rapidly taking their positions in the faint light of the ship's lanterns.
output:
We were all hard at work, changing the powder and the berths, when the last man or two, and Long John along with them, came off in a shore-boat.

“Aye, aye, sir,” answered the cook, and touching his forelock, he disappeared at once in the direction of his galley.

I assure you I was quite of the squire’s way of thinking, and hated the captain deeply.

All that night we were in a great bustle getting things stowed in their place, and boatfuls of the squire’s friends, Mr. Blandly and the like, coming off to wish him a good voyage and a safe return. We never had a night at the Admiral Benbow when I had half the work; and I was dog-tired when, a little before dawn, the boatswain sounded his pipe and the crew began to man the capstan-bars. I might have been twice as weary, yet I would not have left the deck, all was so new and interesting to me - the brief commands, the shrill note of the whistle, the men bustling to their places in the glimmer of the ship’s lanterns.

It was uplifting for all of us to witness him spit into his hand, furrow his brow, and make the blade whistle through the air. output:

output:

input: He had been positioned against the bulwarks, resembling a grotesque puppet, life-size but starkly lacking the vibrancy and beauty of true life. In that moment, I felt empowered to act, and since my previous fear of the deceased had diminished due to my experiences with tragic events, I grasped him by the waist as if he were merely a sack of flour. With a decisive heave, I tossed him overboard. He splashed into the water with a loud sound, and his red cap detached, bobbing on the surface. Once the splash settled, I observed him and Israel lying side by side, both swaying gently in the undulating water. O'Brien, although still relatively young, had a completely bald head. There he rested, his baldness positioned across the knees of the man who had caused his demise, while the swift fish moved to and fro above them both.
output: He had pitched, as I have said, against the bulwarks, where he lay like some horrible, ungainly sort of puppet, life-size, indeed, but how different from life’s colour or life’s comeliness! In that position I could easily have my way with him, and as the habit of tragical adventures had worn off almost all my terror for the dead, I took him by the waist as if he had been a sack of bran and with one good heave, tumbled him overboard. He went in with a sounding plunge; the red cap came off and remained floating on the surface; and as soon as the splash subsided, I could see him and Israel lying side by side, both wavering with the tremulous movement of the water. O’Brien, though still quite a young man, was very bald. There he lay, with that bald head across the knees of the man who had killed him and the quick fishes steering to and fro over both.

input: As we passed the two-pointed hill, we were able to observe the black mouth of Ben Gunn’s cave and a figure standing beside it, leaning upon a musket. It was the squire, and we waved a handkerchief and gave him three cheers, in which the voice of Silver joined as heartily as any. Three miles farther, just inside the mouth of North Inlet, we encountered the HISPANIOLA, cruising by herself. The last flood had lifted her, and had there been much wind or a strong tide current, as in the southern anchorage, we should never have found her more, or found her stranded beyond help. As it was, there was little amiss beyond the wreck of the main-sail. Another anchor was got ready and dropped in a fathom and a half of water. We all pulled round again to Rum Cove, the nearest point for Ben Gunn’s treasure-house; and then Gray, single-handed, returned with the gig to the HISPANIOLA, where he was to pass the night on guard.

input: The mail coach collected passengers at dusk from the Royal George located on the heath. The narrator was seated between Redruth and an elderly man of considerable size. Despite the rapid movement and chilly night air, the narrator likely dozed off early in the journey and continued to sleep soundly through various stages of travel. Eventually, the narrator was roused by a jab in the ribs and, upon waking, noticed that the coach had stopped in front of a large building on a city street, with daylight already prevailing.
output: The mail picked us up about dusk at the Royal George on the heath. I was wedged in between Redruth and a stout old gentleman, and in spite of the swift motion and the cold night air, I must have dozed a great deal from the very first, and then slept like a log up hill and down dale through stage after stage, for when I was awakened at last it was by a punch in the ribs, and I opened my eyes to find that we were standing still before a large building in a city street and that the day had already broken a long time.

input: Silver faced quite a challenging task as he attempted to ascend the knoll. The steep incline, the presence of thick tree stumps, and the soft sand may have made him and his crutch feel somewhat unsteady. However, he persevered quietly and eventually reached the captain, whom he greeted with great respect. He was dressed in his finest attire; a large blue coat, adorned with brass buttons, reached down to his knees, and a stylish laced hat perched on the back of his head. Overall, Silver demonstrated determination and readiness in his appearance and demeanor.
output: Silver had terrible hard work getting up the knoll. What with the steepness of the incline, the thick tree stumps, and the soft sand, he and his crutch were as helpless as a ship in stays. But he stuck to it like a man in silence, and at last arrived before the captain, whom he saluted in the handsomest style. He was tricked out in his best; an immense blue coat, thick with brass buttons, hung as low as to his knees, and a fine laced hat was set on the back of his head.

input: It is worth noting that, at that moment, although the sun had still an hour or two remaining in its descent, the resonances of the island stirred and resonated in response to the thunderous sound of a cannon. Furthermore, I commenced to run toward the anchorage, my fears entirely forgotten, while the marooned man, clad in goatskins, moved effortlessly and lightly alongside me. Additionally, after a brief pause, I observed, not a quarter of a mile ahead, the Union Jack waving in the air above a wooded area.
output:
For just then, although the sun had still an hour or two to run, all the echoes of the island awoke and bellowed to the thunder of a cannon.

And I began to run towards the anchorage, my terrors all forgotten, while close at my side the marooned man in his goatskins trotted easily and lightly.

Another pause, and then, not a quarter of a mile in front of me, I beheld the Union Jack flutter in the air above a wood.

His eyes remained fixed on the water as it bubbled from the old iron kettle in the sand. Meanwhile, he was whistling "Come, Lasses and Lads."
output: I will confess that I was far too much taken up with what was going on to be of the slightest use as sentry; indeed, I had already deserted my eastern loophole and crept up behind the captain, who had now seated himself on the threshold, with his elbows on his knees, his head in his hands, and his eyes fixed on the water as it bubbled out of the old iron kettle in the sand. The four who had breached our defenses made a beeline for the building, shouting as they approached, and the men positioned among the trees responded with shouts of encouragement. output:

The four who had boarded made straight before them for the building, shouting as they ran, and the men among the trees shouted back to encourage them. Several shots were fired, but such was the hurry of the marksmen that not one appears to have taken effect. In a moment, the four pirates had swarmed up the mound and were upon us.

Captain Smollett pointed out a man, noting that he was new to this line of work and seemed to nearly faint upon hearing the cry. With just a slight shift of the rudder, that man might have found himself in our situation.

I shared my plan with the captain, and together we worked out the specifics for how to implement it.

We positioned old Redruth in the gallery between the cabin and the forecastle, equipping him with three or four loaded muskets and a mattress for some protection. Hunter maneuvered the boat to the stern-port, while Joyce and I began loading it with powder tins, muskets, bags of biscuits, kegs of pork, a cask of cognac, and my essential medicine chest. output:

We put old Redruth in the gallery between the cabin and the forecastle, with three or four loaded muskets and a mattress for protection. input: Scarcely had we navigated past the heads when the land enveloped us. The shores of North Inlet were as densely forested as those of the southern anchorage; however, the area was longer and narrower, resembling, in truth, the estuary of a river. Directly ahead, at the southern terminus, we observed the wreck of a ship in the advanced stages of decay. This vessel, once a magnificent three-masted ship, had endured prolonged exposure to the elements, resulting in its being enveloped by extensive strands of dripping seaweed. Additionally, shrubs from the shore had taken root on its deck, flourishing abundantly with flowers. Although it presented a melancholic view, it indicated that the anchorage was calm.
output: Scarcely had we passed the heads before the land closed around us. The shores of North Inlet were as thickly wooded as those of the southern anchorage, but the space was longer and narrower and more like, what in truth it was, the estuary of a river. Right before us, at the southern end, we saw the wreck of a ship in the last stages of dilapidation. It had been a great vessel of three masts but had lain so long exposed to the injuries of the weather that it was hung about with great webs of dripping seaweed, and on the deck of it shore bushes had taken root and now flourished thick with flowers. It was a sad sight, but it showed us that the anchorage was calm.

author: Robert Louis Stevenson

input: I was now alone upon the vessel; the tide had just turned. Furthermore, the evening breeze had arisen, and though it was well warded off by the hill with the two peaks upon the east, the cordage had begun to emit a little soft sound to itself and the idle sails to move to and fro.

input: Nearby, one of the boats lay idle, with Silver sitting in the stern-sheets—his presence was always unmistakable. A couple of men leaned over the stern bulwarks, one wearing a red cap. Suddenly, a terrible, otherworldly screaming erupted, which startled me at first. However, I quickly recalled the voice of Captain Flint and thought I could identify the bird by its vibrant plumage as it perched on its master’s wrist.
output: Alongside lay one of the gigs, Silver in the stern-sheets - him I could always recognize - while a couple of men were leaning over the stern bulwarks, one of them with a red cap - the very rogue that I had seen some hours before stride-legs upon the palisade. input: The captain and Gray were already examining him, and I could see at a glance that all was over. I believe the readiness of our return volley had scattered the mutineers once more, for we were allowed without further molestation to get the poor old gamekeeper hoisted over the stockade and carried, groaning and bleeding, into the log-house. Poor old fellow, he had not uttered one word of surprise, complaint, fear, or even acquiescence from the very beginning of our troubles until now, when we had laid him down in the log-house to die. He had lain like a Trojan behind his mattress in the gallery; he had followed every order silently, doggedly, and well; he was the oldest of our party by a score of years; and now, sullen, old, serviceable servant, it was he who was to die.

Gradually, the night became darker. It was all I could do to guide myself even roughly toward my destination. The double hill behind me and the Spy-glass on my right hand loomed faint and fainter. The stars were few and pale. In the low ground where I wandered, I kept tripping among bushes and rolling into sandy pits.

Suddenly, a kind of brightness fell about me. I looked up. A pale glimmer of moonbeams had alighted on the summit of the Spy-glass. Soon after, I saw something broad and silvery moving low down behind the trees, and I knew the moon had risen.

input: Suddenly, a commotion emerged among the bulrushes. A wild duck took flight with a quack, followed by another. Soon, a large cloud of birds filled the sky, screaming and circling above the marsh. I realized that some of my shipmates must be approaching along the edges of the fen. My assessment was accurate. I soon heard the faint sound of a human voice, which gradually became louder and approached closer.
output: All at once there began to go a sort of bustle among the bulrushes; a wild duck flew up with a quack, another followed, and soon over the whole surface of the marsh a great cloud of birds hung screaming and circling in the air. I judged at once that some of my shipmates must be drawing near along the borders of the fen. Nor was I deceived, for soon I heard the very distant and low tones of a human voice, which, as I continued to give ear, grew steadily louder and nearer.

author: Robert Louis Stevenson

input:
After administering the medications and providing prescriptions, the doctor observed that the individuals had accepted his instructions with a humility that was almost amusing, resembling that of charity schoolchildren rather than individuals guilty of mutiny and piracy. The doctor then expressed a desire to speak with a particular young person. 

Meanwhile, George Merry was standing near the door, experiencing difficulty with a medication that had an unpleasant taste. However, upon hearing the doctor's proposal, he immediately turned around, his face reddening noticeably, and vehemently refused, using strong language to emphasize his objection.
output:
“Well,” he added after he had dosed them round and they had taken his prescriptions, with really laughable humility, more like charity schoolchildren than blood-guilty mutineers and pirates - “well, that’s done for today. And now I should wish to have a talk with that boy, please.”

George Merry was at the door, spitting and spluttering over some bad-tasted medicine; but at the first word of the doctor’s proposal he swung round with a deep flush and cried “No!” and swore.

author: Robert Louis Stevenson

input:
Finally, as the ship continued on its path and gradually faded from hearing range, one of the individuals—though I cannot recall which one—stood up with a loud shout, raised his musket, and fired a shot that went over Silver's head and pierced the main-sail. 

After this incident, we sought refuge behind the bulwarks, and when I looked out again, they had vanished from the spit, which itself seemed to blend into the distance. This signaled a conclusion to the matter, and by noon, to my immense relief, the tallest rock of Treasure Island had disappeared into the vast blue sea.
output:
At last, seeing the ship still bore on her course and was now swiftly drawing out of earshot, one of them - I know not which it was - leapt to his feet with a hoarse cry, whipped his musket to his shoulder, and sent a shot whistling over Silver’s head and through the main-sail.

After that, we kept under cover of the bulwarks, and when next I looked out they had disappeared from the spit, and the spit itself had almost melted out of sight in the growing distance. That was, at least, the end of that; and before noon, to my inexpressible joy, the highest rock of Treasure Island had sunk into the blue round of sea.

author: Robert Louis Stevenson

input: I felt shaken by the alarms, making it difficult to keep pace with the treasure-hunters. Occasionally, I stumbled, and during those moments, Silver would roughly tug at the rope and shoot me threatening glances. Dick, who had fallen behind and was now trailing us, muttered a mix of prayers and curses as his fever intensified. This only deepened my distress. To make matters worse, I was plagued by the memory of the tragedy that had unfolded on that plateau. I recalled the notorious buccaneer with the blue face, who had met his end in Savannah, singing and shouting for drink. He had brutally executed his six accomplices right there. I could not help but imagine that this tranquil grove had once been filled with their cries, and with that thought, it felt as if I still heard those echoes.
output: Shaken as I was with these alarms, it was hard for me to keep up with the rapid pace of the treasure-hunters. Now and again I stumbled, and it was then that Silver plucked so roughly at the rope and launched at me his murderous glances. Dick, who had dropped behind us and now brought up the rear, was babbling to himself both prayers and curses as his fever kept rising. This also added to my wretchedness, and to crown all, I was haunted by the thought of the tragedy that had once been acted on that plateau, when that ungodly buccaneer with the blue face - he who died at Savannah, singing and shouting for drink - had there, with his own hand, cut down his six accomplices. This grove that was now so peaceful must then have rung with cries, I thought; and even with the thought I could believe I heard it ringing still.

Tired though we all were, two were sent out for firewood; two more were set to dig a grave for Redruth; the doctor was named cook; I was put sentry at the door; and the captain himself went from one to another, keeping up our spirits and lending a hand wherever it was wanted.

input: Mr. Trelawney had established his residence at an inn located at a considerable distance down the docks in order to oversee the work being done on the schooner. Consequently, we were now required to walk to this location, and our route, which brought me a great deal of pleasure, took us along the quays and adjacent to a large number of ships of various sizes and rigs, representing different nations. Meanwhile, the activity on these ships was a source of fascination for me, as in one vessel, sailors were singing while they worked, and in another, men were positioned high above my head, clinging to ropes that appeared to be remarkably thin. Although I had spent my entire life in a coastal area, I felt as though I was experiencing the sea for the first time. Furthermore, the smell of tar and salt was a novel sensation for me. As I walked, I observed a number of impressive figureheads, which had apparently traveled extensively across the ocean. Additionally, I saw many older sailors, who were distinguishable by their earrings, curly whiskers, and pigtails, as well as their distinctive gait, which was both awkward and confident. Moreover, I was thoroughly delighted by these sights, and I would have been equally impressed if I had seen a similar number of high-ranking officials or dignitaries.
output: Mr. Trelawney had taken up his residence at an inn far down the docks to superintend the work upon the schooner. Thither we had now to walk, and our way, to my great delight, lay along the quays and beside the great multitude of ships of all sizes and rigs and nations. In one, sailors were singing at their work, in another there were men aloft, high over my head, hanging to threads that seemed no thicker than a spider’s. Though I had lived by the shore all my life, I seemed never to have been near the sea till then. The smell of tar and salt was something new. I saw the most wonderful figureheads, that had all been far over the ocean. I saw, besides, many old sailors, with rings in their ears, and whiskers curled in ringlets, and tarry pigtails, and their swaggering, clumsy sea-walk; and if I had seen as many kings or archbishops I could not have been more delighted.

author: Robert Louis Stevenson

input:
That marked the conclusion of the evening's activities. Subsequently, after sharing a drink, we settled down to rest, while the external manifestation of Silver’s wrath involved appointing George Merry as the sentinel and threatening him with death should he prove disloyal. 

It was some time before I could close my eyes, and it is worth noting that I had ample matters occupying my thoughts: the man I had killed that afternoon, my own precarious circumstances, and, most significantly, the extraordinary strategy Silver appeared to be executing—maintaining cohesion among the mutineers with one hand while simultaneously seeking every conceivable means, both reasonable and unreasonable, to negotiate his safety and preserve his wretched existence. He himself slept soundly and snored loudly, yet my heart ached for him, despite his malevolence, when I considered the ominous dangers surrounding him and the disgraceful gallows that awaited him.
output:
That was the end of the night’s business. Soon after, with a drink all round, we lay down to sleep, and the outside of Silver’s vengeance was to put George Merry up for sentinel and threaten him with death if he should prove unfaithful.

It was long ere I could close an eye, and heaven knows I had matter enough for thought in the man whom I had slain that afternoon, in my own most perilous position, and above all, in the remarkable game that I saw Silver now engaged upon - keeping the mutineers together with one hand and grasping with the other after every means, possible and impossible, to make his peace and save his miserable life. He himself slept peacefully and snored aloud, yet my heart was sore for him, wicked as he was, to think on the dark perils that environed and the shameful gibbet that awaited him.

input:
No one paid any attention to me, except for the bow oar, who said, "Is that you, Jim? Keep your head down." However, Silver, from the other boat, looked sharply in my direction and called out to ask if it was me. From that moment, I began to regret what I had done.

The crews raced toward the beach, but the boat I was in had a slight head start and was both lighter and better manned, so it quickly shot far ahead of its companion. The bow struck among the trees along the shore, and I caught a branch and swung myself out, then plunged into the nearest thicket while Silver and the others were still a hundred yards behind.
output:
No one took notice of me, only the bow oar saying, “Is that you, Jim? Keep your head down.” But Silver, from the other boat, looked sharply over and called out to know if that were me; and from that moment I began to regret what I had done.

The crews raced for the beach, but the boat I was in, having some start and being at once the lighter and the better manned, shot far ahead of her consort, and the bow had struck among the shore-side trees and I had caught a branch and swung myself out and plunged into the nearest thicket while Silver and the rest were still a hundred yards behind.
