input: There is a fundamental difference between the mere adhesion of grafted stocks and the union of male and female elements in reproduction. However, similarities exist in the outcomes of grafting and crossing distinct species. The complex laws that govern the ease with which trees can be grafted onto one another appear to stem from unknown differences in their vegetative systems. Similarly, I propose that the intricate laws related to the ease of first crosses are influenced by unknown differences, primarily in their reproductive systems. These differences, in both scenarios, tend to reflect systematic affinities, which seek to express the various resemblances and dissimilarities among organic beings. The evidence does not suggest that the varying degrees of difficulty in grafting or crossing species are simply special traits. In the case of crossing, this difficulty significantly impacts the endurance and stability of specific forms, while in grafting, it does not affect their well-being.
output: We thus see, that although there is a clear and fundamental difference between the mere adhesion of grafted stocks, and the union of the male and female elements in the act of reproduction, yet that there is a rude degree of parallelism in the results of grafting and of crossing distinct species. And as we must look at the curious and complex laws governing the facility with which trees can be grafted on each other as incidental on unknown differences in their vegetative systems, so I believe that the still more complex laws governing the facility of first crosses, are incidental on unknown differences, chiefly in their reproductive systems. These differences, in both cases, follow to a certain extent, as might have been expected, systematic affinity, by which every kind of resemblance and dissimilarity between organic beings is attempted to be expressed. The facts by no means seem to me to indicate that the greater or lesser difficulty of either grafting or crossing together various species has been a special endowment; although in the case of crossing, the difficulty is as important for the endurance and stability of specific forms, as in the case of grafting it is unimportant for their welfare.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: It's possible that experienced naturalists, who have spent many years studying a wide range of facts from a different perspective, may not be convinced by the views presented in this volume, despite my own confidence in their accuracy. It can often be the case that we unintentionally obscure our lack of understanding by using phrases such as "the plan of creation" or "unity of design", which may give the impression that we are providing an explanation when, in fact, we are simply restating a fact. Individuals who tend to prioritize unexplained difficulties over the explanation of certain facts may likely reject my theory. However, some naturalists, who are open to new ideas and have already begun to question the idea that species are immutable, may be influenced by this volume. I am hopeful that younger naturalists, who can approach the topic with an impartial mindset, will consider my views in the future. Anyone who comes to believe that species can change may be able to make a positive contribution by sharing their thoughts, as this can help to gradually reduce the prejudice that surrounds this subject. In summary, this volume aims to present a new perspective on the topic, and it is hoped that it will contribute to a more nuanced and open-minded discussion about the nature of species.
output: Although I am fully convinced of the truth of the views given in this volume under the form of an abstract, I by no means expect to convince experienced naturalists whose minds are stocked with a multitude of facts all viewed, during a long course of years, from a point of view directly opposite to mine. It is so easy to hide our ignorance under such expressions as the “plan of creation,” “unity of design,” etc., and to think that we give an explanation when we only restate a fact. Any one whose disposition leads him to attach more weight to unexplained difficulties than to the explanation of a certain number of facts will certainly reject my theory. A few naturalists, endowed with much flexibility of mind, and who have already begun to doubt on the immutability of species, may be influenced by this volume; but I look with confidence to the future, to young and rising naturalists, who will be able to view both sides of the question with impartiality. Whoever is led to believe that species are mutable will do good service by conscientiously expressing his conviction; for only thus can the load of prejudice by which this subject is overwhelmed be removed.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input:
Long before reaching this stage of my work, a variety of difficulties will have presented themselves to the reader. Some of these difficulties are of such a serious nature that I find myself astonished upon reflecting on them even to this day; however, to the best of my judgment, I believe that the majority are merely apparent, and those that are genuine do not, in my opinion, pose a fatal threat to my theory. 

Furthermore, one might ask why, if species have indeed descended from other species through imperceptibly fine gradations, we do not observe countless transitional forms throughout nature. Additionally, why does nature not appear in disarray, instead of the species being distinctly defined, as we perceive them?
output:
Long before having arrived at this part of my work, a crowd of difficulties will have occurred to the reader. Some of them are so grave that to this day I can never reflect on them without being staggered; but, to the best of my judgment, the greater number are only apparent, and those that are real are not, I think, fatal to my theory.

Firstly, why, if species have descended from other species by insensibly fine gradations, do we not everywhere see innumerable transitional forms? Why is not all nature in confusion instead of the species being, as we see them, well defined?
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: One noteworthy observation from our comprehensive review is that barriers or obstacles to free migration tend to be closely related to the differences in the various products of different regions. This can often be seen in the significant disparities among many terrestrial products between the New and Old Worlds, particularly in areas where land is nearly connected, such as the northern regions. In these areas, a slightly different climate may allow for more free movement of northern temperate species, similar to what occurs with strictly arctic products. We can also observe similar patterns when comparing the inhabitants of Australia, Africa, and South America, which, despite being situated at the same latitude, are largely isolated from one another. Within individual continents, we find this phenomenon as well; for example, on opposite sides of high mountain ranges, vast deserts, and even large rivers, we observe differing products. However, since these geographical features are generally not as insurmountable or enduring as the oceans that separate continents, the resulting disparities tend to be less pronounced than those found between entirely distinct continents. In summary, the interplay between geographical barriers and regional production differences highlights the complexities of migration and biodiversity.
output: A second great fact which strikes us in our general review is, that barriers of any kind, or obstacles to free migration, are related in a close and important manner to the differences between the productions of various regions. We see this in the great difference of nearly all the terrestrial productions of the New and Old Worlds, excepting in the northern parts, where the land almost joins, and where, under a slightly different climate, there might have been free migration for the northern temperate forms, as there now is for the strictly arctic productions. We see the same fact in the great difference between the inhabitants of Australia, Africa, and South America under the same latitude: for these countries are almost as much isolated from each other as is possible. On each continent, also, we see the same fact; for on the opposite sides of lofty and continuous mountain-ranges, and of great deserts, and sometimes even of large rivers, we find different productions; though as mountain chains, deserts, etc., are not as impassable, or likely to have endured so long as the oceans separating continents, the differences are very inferior in degree to those characteristic of distinct continents.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: Those who believe that each creature has been created in its current form may occasionally feel surprised upon encountering animals with habits and anatomical features that do not align. For instance, it is evident that the webbed feet of ducks and geese are adapted for swimming. However, there are upland geese with webbed feet that seldom approach water, and it is noted that only Audubon has observed the frigate-bird, which possesses webbed toes, land on the ocean's surface. Conversely, grebes and coots are highly aquatic, despite having toes that are merely bordered by membrane. Additionally, the long toes of grallatores appear to be designed for traversing swamps and floating vegetation, yet the water-hen exhibits behaviors similar to the coot, and the landrail is nearly as terrestrial as the quail or partridge. These examples, along with many others, highlight that behaviors can evolve without a corresponding alteration in physical structure. The webbed feet of the upland goose may be considered rudimentary in function but not in form, while the frigate-bird’s distinctly shaped membrane between its toes indicates that structural changes may be underway.
output: He who believes that each being has been created as we now see it, must occasionally have felt surprise when he has met with an animal having habits and structure not at all in agreement. What can be plainer than that the webbed feet of ducks and geese are formed for swimming? yet there are upland geese with webbed feet which rarely or never go near the water; and no one except Audubon has seen the frigate-bird, which has all its four toes webbed, alight on the surface of the sea. On the other hand, grebes and coots are eminently aquatic, although their toes are only bordered by membrane. What seems plainer than that the long toes of grallatores are formed for walking over swamps and floating plants, yet the water-hen is nearly as aquatic as the coot; and the landrail nearly as terrestrial as the quail or partridge. In such cases, and many others could be given, habits have changed without a corresponding change of structure. The webbed feet of the upland goose may be said to have become rudimentary in function, though not in structure. In the frigate-bird, the deeply-scooped membrane between the toes shows that structure has begun to change.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: In many situations, a substantial population of individuals of the same species is essential for their survival, particularly when considering the number of their natural enemies. This highlights that we can successfully cultivate crops like corn and rapeseed in our fields because the seeds are abundant compared to the number of birds that consume them. Despite the availability of food during a specific season, the bird population does not increase proportionally due to factors such as winter conditions limiting their numbers. Conversely, obtaining seeds from a small number of wheat or similar plants in a garden can be quite challenging; often, all seeds may be lost. This perspective on the necessity of a large population for survival helps to explain certain peculiarities in nature, such as the occurrence of very rare plants being plentiful in the limited areas where they grow, or the abundance of social plants even at the edges of their distribution. This suggests that these plants thrive in environments where the conditions are favorable enough to support large populations, thereby providing mutual protection against extinction. Additionally, the benefits of frequent intercrossing and the drawbacks of close inbreeding may also be relevant in these contexts, although this topic is complex and requires further exploration.
output: On the other hand, in many cases, a large stock of individuals of the same species, relatively to the numbers of its enemies, is absolutely necessary for its preservation. Thus we can easily raise plenty of corn and rape-seed, etc., in our fields, because the seeds are in great excess compared with the number of birds which feed on them; nor can the birds, though having a superabundance of food at this one season, increase in number proportionally to the supply of seed, as their numbers are checked during winter: but any one who has tried, knows how troublesome it is to get seed from a few wheat or other such plants in a garden; I have in this case lost every single seed. This view of the necessity of a large stock of the same species for its preservation, explains, I believe, some singular facts in nature, such as that of very rare plants being sometimes extremely abundant in the few spots where they do occur; and that of some social plants being social, that is, abounding in individuals, even on the extreme confines of their range. For in such cases, we may believe, that a plant could exist only where the conditions of its life were so favourable that many could exist together, and thus save each other from utter destruction. I should add that the good effects of frequent intercrossing, and the ill effects of close interbreeding, probably come into play in some of these cases; but on this intricate subject I will not here enlarge.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input:
It is worth noting that a certain degree of variation in instincts, within a state of nature, as well as the inheritance of such variations, is essential for the process of natural selection. Although numerous examples could be provided in this context, limitations of space restrict my ability to do so. I can only assert that instincts do indeed exhibit variation; for instance, the migratory instinct varies in both its extent and direction, and it may also be entirely lost in some instances. Similarly, the nests of birds demonstrate variability that is influenced in part by the locations they select and the environmental conditions of the regions they inhabit, although many factors remain unknown to us. Audubon has documented several striking examples of differences in the nests of the same species across the northern and southern regions of the United States. 

Furthermore, fear of specific predators is an instinctive trait, as evidenced in nestling birds; however, this instinct is enhanced by experience and by the observation of other animals exhibiting fear of the same predator. In contrast, the fear of humans is gradually acquired, as I have previously illustrated, among various animals residing on deserted islands. This phenomenon can also be observed in England, where larger birds tend to be more wary than smaller birds, likely due to the greater persecution they have faced from humans. We can confidently attribute the heightened wariness of our larger birds to this factor; in uninhabited islands, there is no significant difference in the fear exhibited by larger and smaller birds. For example, the magpie, which is quite cautious in England, is relatively tame in Norway, just as the hooded crow is in Egypt.
output: As some degree of variation in instincts under a state of nature, and the inheritance of such variations, are indispensable for the action of natural selection, as many instances as possible ought to have been here given; but want of space prevents me. I can only assert, that instincts certainly do vary - for instance, the migratory instinct, both in extent and direction, and in its total loss. So it is with the nests of birds, which vary partly in dependence on the situations chosen, and on the nature and temperature of the country inhabited, but often from causes wholly unknown to us: Audubon has given several remarkable cases of differences in nests of the same species in the northern and southern United States. Fear of any particular enemy is certainly an instinctive quality, as may be seen in nestling birds, though it is strengthened by experience, and by the sight of fear of the same enemy in other animals. But fear of man is slowly acquired, as I have elsewhere shown, by various animals inhabiting desert islands; and we may see an instance of this, even in England, in the greater wildness of all our large birds than of our small birds; for the large birds have been most persecuted by man. We may safely attribute the greater wildness of our large birds to this cause; for in uninhabited islands large birds are not more fearful than small; and the magpie, so wary in England, is tame in Norway, as is the hooded crow in Egypt.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input:
When dividing the plant species of a country, as detailed in any Flora, into two equal groups—placing the larger genera on one side and the smaller genera on the other—it becomes evident that a greater number of common and widely distributed species typically appears in the larger genera. This observation aligns with expectations; the presence of multiple species from the same genus within a country suggests that both organic and inorganic conditions of that country are favorable to that genus. Therefore, it follows that larger genera, which encompass several species, would likely include a higher proportion of dominant species. However, various factors complicate this outcome, so it is surprising that my data reveals even a slight majority for the larger genera. 

I will mention only two factors that contribute to this complexity. First, freshwater and salt-tolerant plants usually have extensive ranges and are widely distributed. This distribution seems more related to the nature of their habitats rather than the size of the genera they belong to. Second, plants that are lower on the organizational scale tend to be more widely distributed than their higher-organized counterparts, and again, this distribution does not correlate closely with the size of the genera. The reasons why lower-organized plants have such wide distribution will be explored in the chapter on geographical distribution.
output: If the plants inhabiting a country and described in any Flora be divided into two equal masses, all those in the larger genera being placed on one side, and all those in the smaller genera on the other side, a somewhat larger number of the very common and much diffused or dominant species will be found on the side of the larger genera. This, again, might have been anticipated; for the mere fact of many species of the same genus inhabiting any country, shows that there is something in the organic or inorganic conditions of that country favourable to the genus; and, consequently, we might have expected to have found in the larger genera, or those including many species, a large proportional number of dominant species. But so many causes tend to obscure this result, that I am surprised that my tables show even a small majority on the side of the larger genera. I will here allude to only two causes of obscurity. Fresh-water and salt-loving plants have generally very wide ranges and are much diffused, but this seems to be connected with the nature of the stations inhabited by them, and has little or no relation to the size of the genera to which the species belong. Again, plants low in the scale of organisation are generally much more widely diffused than plants higher in the scale; and here again there is no close relation to the size of the genera. The cause of lowly-organised plants ranging widely will be discussed in our chapter on geographical distribution.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: Additionally, the principles outlined in this brief abstract are applicable to plants exclusively, whereas similar phenomena can be observed in the distribution of terrestrial animals. Furthermore, analogous cases can be found in marine productions, as evidenced by a remark made by the esteemed Professor Dana, who notes that it is a remarkable fact that New Zealand exhibits a greater resemblance to Great Britain, its antipode, in terms of its crustacea than to any other region. Moreover, Sir J. Richardson has also observed the recurrence of northern forms of fish on the shores of New Zealand, Tasmania, and other locations. It is worth noting that Dr. Hooker has informed me that twenty-five species of Algæ are common to both New Zealand and Europe, yet these species haven not been discovered in the intervening tropical seas.
output: This brief abstract applies to plants alone: some strictly analogous facts could be given on the distribution of terrestrial animals. In marine productions, similar cases occur; as an example, I may quote a remark by the highest authority, Professor Dana, that “it is certainly a wonderful fact that New Zealand should have a closer resemblance in its crustacea to Great Britain, its antipode, than to any other part of the world.” Sir J. Richardson, also, speaks of the reappearance on the shores of New Zealand, Tasmania, etc., of northern forms of fish. Dr. Hooker informs me that twenty-five species of Algæ are common to New Zealand and to Europe, but have not been found in the intermediate tropical seas.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: Subsequently to my experiments, Monsieur Martens conducted similar investigations, albeit in a more refined manner. He placed the seeds in a box situated in the sea itself, allowing them to experience alternating periods of submersion and exposure to the air, akin to naturally floating plants. He experimented with 98 seeds, primarily distinct from my own; notably, he selected many large fruits and also seeds from species that thrive in coastal environments. This selection likely enhanced the average duration of their flotation and their resilience against the detrimental effects of saltwater. However, it is important to note that he did not dry the plants or branches containing the fruit beforehand; as previously indicated, this could have resulted in a significantly extended flotation time for some of them. Consequently, the outcome was that 18 out of 98 of his seeds remained buoyant for 42 days and subsequently demonstrated the capacity for germination. Nonetheless, I maintain that plants subjected to wave action would likely remain afloat for a shorter duration than those shielded from turbulent movements, as observed in our experiments. Therefore, it may be prudent to estimate that approximately 10 out of 100 seeds from a given flora, after undergoing the drying process, could be transported across a marine expanse of 900 miles and still retain the ability to germinate. The observation that larger fruits tend to float for longer periods than smaller ones is particularly noteworthy, as plants bearing sizeable seeds or fruits would struggle to be dispersed by alternative means. Furthermore, Alph. de Candolle has demonstrated that such plants typically inhabit restricted geographical ranges.
output: Subsequently to my experiments, M. Martens tried similar ones, but in a much better manner, for he placed the seeds in a box in the actual sea, so that they were alternately wet and exposed to the air like really floating plants. He tried 98 seeds, mostly different from mine; but he chose many large fruits and likewise seeds from plants which live near the sea; and this would have favoured the average length of their flotation and of their resistance to the injurious action of the salt-water. On the other hand he did not previously dry the plants or branches with the fruit; and this, as we have seen, would have caused some of them to have floated much longer. The result was that 18/98 of his seeds floated for 42 days, and were then capable of germination. But I do not doubt that plants exposed to the waves would float for a less time than those protected from violent movement as in our experiments. Therefore it would perhaps be safer to assume that the seeds of about 10/100 plants of a flora, after having been dried, could be floated across a space of sea 900 miles in width, and would then germinate. The fact of the larger fruits often floating longer than the small, is interesting; as plants with large seeds or fruit could hardly be transported by any other means; and Alph. de Candolle has shown that such plants generally have restricted ranges.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: With respect to the nearly universal sterility observed in species when they are initially crossed, which presents a striking contrast to the almost universal fertility exhibited by varieties when subjected to crossing, it is worth noting that I must direct the reader to the summary of facts presented at the conclusion of the eighth chapter. These facts, in my view, provide conclusive evidence that this sterility is not a unique characteristic, much like the inability of two trees to be grafted together. Rather, it arises as a consequence of the constitutional differences present in the reproductive systems of the species involved in the intercrossing. Furthermore, the validity of this conclusion is evident in the significant disparity in outcomes when the same two species are crossed in a reciprocal manner; that is, when one species is utilized as the male parent and subsequently as the female parent.
output: With respect to the almost universal sterility of species when first crossed, which forms so remarkable a contrast with the almost universal fertility of varieties when crossed, I must refer the reader to the recapitulation of the facts given at the end of the eighth chapter, which seem to me conclusively to show that this sterility is no more a special endowment than is the incapacity of two trees to be grafted together, but that it is incidental on constitutional differences in the reproductive systems of the intercrossed species. We see the truth of this conclusion in the vast difference in the result, when the same two species are crossed reciprocally; that is, when one species is first used as the father and then as the mother.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: The slave-making instinct presents a remarkable phenomenon that was first identified in the species Formica (Polyerges) rufescens by Pierre Huber, who was an astute observer, surpassing even his renowned father. This particular ant species relies entirely on its slaves; without their assistance, it would undoubtedly face extinction within the span of a year. The males and fertile females do not engage in any labor. Furthermore, while the workers, or sterile females, exhibit considerable energy and bravery in the pursuit of capturing slaves, they fail to perform any other tasks. They lack the capacity to construct their own nests or to nourish their own larvae. Additionally, when the existing nest becomes unsuitable, it is the slaves who facilitate migration, physically transporting their masters in their mandibles. The helplessness of the masters is further illustrated by Huber's experiment in which he confined thirty of them without a slave, providing them with an abundance of their preferred food and their larvae and pupae to stimulate activity; they remained inactive, unable even to feed themselves, leading to the demise of many from starvation. Upon the introduction of a single slave (F. fusca), she promptly initiated work, attending to the feeding and rescue of the survivors, constructing cells, tending to the larvae, and restoring order. What could be more extraordinary than these well-documented observations? If we had not been aware of any other slave-making ant, speculating on how such a remarkable instinct could have evolved would have been an exercise in futility.
output: Slave-making instinct. - This remarkable instinct was first discovered in the Formica (Polyerges) rufescens by Pierre Huber, a better observer even than his celebrated father. This ant is absolutely dependent on its slaves; without their aid, the species would certainly become extinct in a single year. The males and fertile females do no work. The workers or sterile females, though most energetic and courageous in capturing slaves, do no other work. They are incapable of making their own nests, or of feeding their own larvæ. When the old nest is found inconvenient, and they have to migrate, it is the slaves which determine the migration, and actually carry their masters in their jaws. So utterly helpless are the masters, that when Huber shut up thirty of them without a slave, but with plenty of the food which they like best, and with their larvæ and pupæ to stimulate them to work, they did nothing; they could not even feed themselves, and many perished of hunger. Huber then introduced a single slave (F. fusca), and she instantly set to work, fed and saved the survivors; made some cells and tended the larvæ, and put all to rights. What can be more extraordinary than these well-ascertained facts? If we had not known of any other slave-making ant, it would have been hopeless to have speculated how so wonderful an instinct could have been perfected.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: It is worth noting that the species and forms found in the southern regions of the southern hemisphere, as well as on the mountain ranges of intertropical areas, do not originate from arctic environments; rather, they belong to the northern temperate zones. Furthermore, as Mr. H. C. Watson has recently observed, in moving from polar to equatorial latitudes, the Alpine or mountain floras progressively become less arctic. Additionally, many of the forms inhabiting the mountains of warmer regions in the southern hemisphere are of uncertain classification, with some naturalists categorizing them as specifically distinct while others consider them varieties. Nevertheless, certain forms are undoubtedly identical, and many, despite their close relation to northern forms, must be classified as distinct species.
output: It should be observed that the northern species and forms found in the southern parts of the southern hemisphere, and on the mountain-ranges of the intertropical regions, are not arctic, but belong to the northern temperate zones. As Mr. H. C. Watson has recently remarked, “In receding from polar towards equatorial latitudes, the Alpine or mountain floras really become less and less arctic.” Many of the forms living on the mountains of the warmer regions of the earth and in the southern hemisphere are of doubtful value, being ranked by some naturalists as specifically distinct, by others as varieties; but some are certainly identical, and many, though closely related to northern forms, must be ranked as distinct species.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: The statement that the fauna of each period is generally intermediate in character between the preceding and succeeding faunas is not fundamentally undermined by certain exceptions among genera. For example, Dr. Falconer categorized mastodons and elephants into two series, first by their mutual affinities and then by their periods of existence, revealing inconsistencies in arrangement. The species that are most extreme in character are neither the oldest nor the most recent. Furthermore, those with intermediate characteristics are not necessarily of intermediate age. If we assume, for a moment, that the record of the first appearance and disappearance of species is flawless, we still have no basis to conclude that forms produced successively must exist for equivalent durations. An ancient form might persist for a significantly longer time than a form that appeared later, especially in cases where terrestrial species inhabit isolated areas. To illustrate this concept, if the principal living and extinct races of the domestic pigeon were arranged by their serial affinities, the resulting order would not closely reflect the timeline of their emergence, nor would it accurately represent their extinction. The parent rock-pigeon is still extant, while various varieties that fall between the rock-pigeon and the carrier have become extinct. Notably, carriers, which are characterized by a long beak, originated before the short-beaked tumblers, which belong to the opposite end of the character spectrum.
output: It is no real objection to the truth of the statement, that the fauna of each period as a whole is nearly intermediate in character between the preceding and succeeding faunas, that certain genera offer exceptions to the rule. For instance, mastodons and elephants, when arranged by Dr. Falconer in two series, first according to their mutual affinities and then according to their periods of existence, do not accord in arrangement. The species extreme in character are not the oldest, or the most recent; nor are those which are intermediate in character, intermediate in age. But supposing for an instant, in this and other such cases, that the record of the first appearance and disappearance of the species was perfect, we have no reason to believe that forms successively produced necessarily endure for corresponding lengths of time: a very ancient form might occasionally last much longer than a form elsewhere subsequently produced, especially in the case of terrestrial productions inhabiting separated districts. To compare small things with great: if the principal living and extinct races of the domestic pigeon were arranged as well as they could be in serial affinity, this arrangement would not closely accord with the order in time of their production, and still less with the order of their disappearance; for the parent rock-pigeon now lives; and many varieties between the rock-pigeon and the carrier have become extinct; and carriers which are extreme in the important character of length of beak originated earlier than short-beaked tumblers, which are at the opposite end of the series in this same respect.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: At first, it seems to make the question of how the cells are built even more difficult that a great many bees work together, with one bee moving to another cell after working briefly at the first. As Huber has noted, as many as twenty individuals may work even at the beginning of the first cell. I was able to demonstrate this fact in practice by covering the edges of the hexagonal walls of a single cell, or the outer margin of the circumferential rim of a growing comb, with an extremely thin layer of melted vermilion wax. I consistently found that the color was spread very delicately by the bees—as delicately as a painter could have done with a brush—as atoms of the colored wax were taken from the spot where it had been placed and worked into the growing edges of the cells all around. The work of construction appears to be a kind of balance struck among many bees, all instinctively standing at the same relative distance from one another, all trying to sweep equal spheres, and then building up, or leaving ungnawed, the planes of intersection between these spheres. This highlights how often, in cases of difficulty, such as when two pieces of comb met at an angle, the bees would entirely pull down and rebuild the same cell in different ways, sometimes returning to a shape they had initially rejected.
output: It seems at first to add to the difficulty of understanding how the cells are made, that a multitude of bees all work together; one bee after working a short time at one cell going to another, so that, as Huber has stated, a score of individuals work even at the commencement of the first cell. I was able practically to show this fact, by covering the edges of the hexagonal walls of a single cell, or the extreme margin of the circumferential rim of a growing comb, with an extremely thin layer of melted vermilion wax; and I invariably found that the colour was most delicately diffused by the bees - as delicately as a painter could have done with his brush - by atoms of the coloured wax having been taken from the spot on which it had been placed, and worked into the growing edges of the cells all round. The work of construction seems to be a sort of balance struck between many bees, all instinctively standing at the same relative distance from each other, all trying to sweep equal spheres, and then building up, or leaving ungnawed, the planes of intersection between these spheres. It was really curious to note in cases of difficulty, as when two pieces of comb met at an angle, how often the bees would entirely pull down and rebuild in different ways the same cell, sometimes recurring to a shape which they had at first rejected.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: It is worth noting that the Galeopithecus, or flying lemur, was formerly and erroneously classified among the bats. It possesses an exceptionally broad flank membrane that extends from the corners of the jaw to the tail and encompasses the limbs as well as the elongated fingers; furthermore, this membrane is provided with an extensor muscle. Although no intermediate structural forms adapted for gliding through the air presently connect the Galeopithecus with the other Lemuridae, it is nevertheless possible to conceive that such forms formerly existed and that each had been produced by the same gradual steps as in the case of the less perfectly gliding squirrels, and that each successive grade of structure had been advantageous to its possessor. Moreover, there appears to be no insurmountable difficulty in further supposing that the membrane-connected fingers and forearm of the Galeopithecus might have been considerably elongated through natural selection, which, insofar as the organs of flight are concerned, would have transformed it into a bat. In essence, among bats whose wing membrane extends from the top of the shoulder to the tail and includes the hind legs, one may perhaps discern traces of an apparatus originally constructed for gliding through the air rather than for true flight.
output: Now look at the Galeopithecus or flying lemur, which formerly was falsely ranked amongst bats. It has an extremely wide flank-membrane, stretching from the corners of the jaw to the tail, and including the limbs and the elongated fingers: the flank membrane is, also, furnished with an extensor muscle. Although no graduated links of structure, fitted for gliding through the air, now connect the Galeopithecus with the other Lemuridæ, yet I can see no difficulty in supposing that such links formerly existed, and that each had been formed by the same steps as in the case of the less perfectly gliding squirrels; and that each grade of structure had been useful to its possessor. Nor can I see any insuperable difficulty in further believing it possible that the membrane-connected fingers and fore-arm of the Galeopithecus might be greatly lengthened by natural selection; and this, as far as the organs of flight are concerned, would convert it into a bat. In bats which have the wing-membrane extended from the top of the shoulder to the tail, including the hind-legs, we perhaps see traces of an apparatus originally constructed for gliding through the air rather than for flight.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: Among birds, contests tend to be less aggressive. Experts believe that a significant rivalry exists among male birds of many species, who seek to attract females through their songs. For example, the rock-thrush of Guiana, birds of Paradise, and others gather together, with successive males showcasing their vibrant plumage and engaging in unusual behaviors to captivate the females, who observe before ultimately choosing the most appealing partner. Observations of birds in captivity reveal that they often exhibit distinct preferences and aversions. Sir R. Heron, for instance, noted that one pied peacock was especially attractive to all his hen birds. While it might seem simplistic to credit such seemingly minor factors with influence, I cannot delve into the supporting details here. However, if humans can quickly enhance the appearance and demeanor of bantams according to their beauty standards, it seems reasonable to consider that female birds, by consistently selecting the most melodious or beautiful males over countless generations, may similarly have a significant impact on characteristics. I suspect that some established principles regarding the plumage of male and female birds, in relation to that of younger birds, can be explained by the idea that sexual selection primarily modifies plumage when birds reach breeding age or during the breeding season. The changes that result may be inherited at these corresponding stages, either by males only or by both sexes. However, I cannot elaborate further on this topic in this context.
output: Amongst birds, the contest is often of a more peaceful character. All those who have attended to the subject, believe that there is the severest rivalry between the males of many species to attract by singing the females. The rock-thrush of Guiana, birds of Paradise, and some others, congregate; and successive males display their gorgeous plumage and perform strange antics before the females, which standing by as spectators, at last choose the most attractive partner. Those who have closely attended to birds in confinement well know that they often take individual preferences and dislikes: thus Sir R. Heron has described how one pied peacock was eminently attractive to all his hen birds. It may appear childish to attribute any effect to such apparently weak means: I cannot here enter on the details necessary to support this view; but if man can in a short time give elegant carriage and beauty to his bantams, according to his standard of beauty, I can see no good reason to doubt that female birds, by selecting, during thousands of generations, the most melodious or beautiful males, according to their standard of beauty, might produce a marked effect. I strongly suspect that some well-known laws with respect to the plumage of male and female birds, in comparison with the plumage of the young, can be explained on the view of plumage having been chiefly modified by sexual selection, acting when the birds have come to the breeding age or during the breeding season; the modifications thus produced being inherited at corresponding ages or seasons, either by the males alone, or by the males and females; but I have not space here to enter on this subject.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input:
In conclusion, after reviewing all the established facts regarding the interbreeding of plants and animals, one may deduce that a certain degree of sterility, both in initial crosses and in hybrids, is an exceedingly common outcome; however, it cannot, based on our current understanding, be deemed entirely universal. 

Furthermore, we shall now examine in greater detail the circumstances and principles that govern the sterility of first crosses and hybrids. Our primary objective will be to determine whether these principles suggest that species have been specifically endowed with this characteristic to inhibit their interbreeding and prevent chaotic blending. The subsequent rules and conclusions are primarily derived from Gärtner's exemplary research on the hybridization of plants. I have made considerable efforts to ascertain the extent to which these rules are applicable to animals, and given the limited knowledge we possess concerning hybrid animals, I have been notably surprised to discover that many of the same rules are broadly relevant across both kingdoms.
output:
Finally, looking to all the ascertained facts on the intercrossing of plants and animals, it may be concluded that some degree of sterility, both in first crosses and in hybrids,is an extremely general result; but that it cannot, under our present state of knowledge, be considered as absolutely universal.

Laws governing the Sterility of first Crosses and of Hybrids. - We will now consider a little more in detail the circumstances and rules governing the sterility of first crosses and of hybrids. Our chief object will be to see whether or not the rules indicate that species have specially been endowed with this quality, in order to prevent their crossing and blending together in utter confusion. The following rules and conclusions are chiefly drawn up from Gärtner’s admirable work on the hybridisation of plants. I have taken much pains to ascertain how far the rules apply to animals, and considering how scanty our knowledge is in regard to hybrid animals, I have been surprised to find how generally the same rules apply to both kingdoms.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: The theory of descent underscores the significance of fossil remains found in closely spaced geological formations, which, despite being classified as distinct species, exhibit close relationships. It is important to note that the accumulation of each formation can often be disrupted, leading to considerable gaps between successive formations. Therefore, it is unrealistic to anticipate that any single formation will contain all the intermediate varieties between the species that emerge at the beginning and end of these periods. Instead, after these long intervals—while they may seem extensive in terms of years but are relatively brief in geological terms—we should expect to discover closely related forms, sometimes referred to as representative species. This expectation aligns with the evidence we observe, which supports the notion of gradual and subtle changes in specific forms over time.
output: On the theory of descent, the full meaning of the fact of fossil remains from closely consecutive formations, though ranked as distinct species, being closely related, is obvious. As the accumulation of each formation has often been interrupted, and as long blank intervals have intervened between successive formations, we ought not to expect to find, as I attempted to show in the last chapter, in any one or two formations all the intermediate varieties between the species which appeared at the commencement and close of these periods; but we ought to find after intervals, very long as measured by years, but only moderately long as measured geologically, closely allied forms, or, as they have been called by some authors, representative species; and these we assuredly do find. We find, in short, such evidence of the slow and scarcely sensible mutation of specific forms, as we have a just right to expect to find.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: As temperatures rise, arctic species will move northward, followed closely by those from more temperate areas. As the snow melts from the mountain bases, arctic species will occupy the newly thawed ground, gradually ascending to higher elevations as the climate continues to warm, while other species move further north. Consequently, when the warming period is complete, the same arctic species that once inhabited the lowlands of both the Old and New Worlds will find themselves isolated on remote mountain peaks, having been eliminated from lower elevations and remaining only in the arctic regions of both hemispheres. This highlights the impact of climate change on species distribution and survival.
output: As the warmth returned, the arctic forms would retreat northward, closely followed up in their retreat by the productions of the more temperate regions. And as the snow melted from the bases of the mountains, the arctic forms would seize on the cleared and thawed ground, always ascending higher and higher, as the warmth increased, whilst their brethren were pursuing their northern journey. Hence, when the warmth had fully returned, the same arctic species, which had lately lived in a body together on the lowlands of the Old and New Worlds, would be left isolated on distant mountain-summits (having been exterminated on all lesser heights) and in the arctic regions of both hemispheres.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: The family of squirrels demonstrates a range of adaptations, from those with only slightly flattened tails to the so-called flying squirrels, which have a broad expanse of skin connecting their limbs and the base of their tails. This structure functions like a parachute, enabling them to glide between trees over considerable distances. Each adaptation serves a purpose for the respective squirrel species in its environment, assisting in evasion from predators or facilitating food collection, and potentially reducing the risk of injury from falls. However, this does not imply that each squirrel's structure represents the optimal design for all natural conditions. Changes in climate, vegetation, or the introduction of new competitive rodents and predators could lead to declines in certain squirrel populations unless they adapt and evolve. This suggests that, especially in the face of changing life conditions, there could be a continuous preservation and enhancement of individuals with larger flank membranes, with each beneficial modification being passed down through generations. Ultimately, this process of natural selection could result in the evolution of an ideal flying squirrel.
output: Look at the family of squirrels; here we have the finest gradation from animals with their tails only slightly flattened, and from others, as Sir J. Richardson has remarked, with the posterior part of their bodies rather wide and with the skin on their flanks rather full, to the so-called flying squirrels; and flying squirrels have their limbs and even the base of the tail united by a broad expanse of skin, which serves as a parachute and allows them to glide through the air to an astonishing distance from tree to tree. We cannot doubt that each structure is of use to each kind of squirrel in its own country, by enabling it to escape birds or beasts of prey, or to collect food more quickly, or, as there is reason to believe, by lessening the danger from occasional falls. But it does not follow from this fact that the structure of each squirrel is the best that it is possible to conceive under all natural conditions. Let the climate and vegetation change, let other competing rodents or new beasts of prey immigrate, or old ones become modified, and all analogy would lead us to believe that some at least of the squirrels would decrease in numbers or become exterminated, unless they also became modified and improved in structure in a corresponding manner. Therefore, I can see no difficulty, more especially under changing conditions of life, in the continued preservation of individuals with fuller and fuller flank-membranes, each modification being useful, each being propagated, until by the accumulated effects of this process of natural selection, a perfect so-called flying squirrel was produced.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: When examining plants, one can observe the cumulative effects of selection by comparing the diversity of flowers among different varieties of the same species in a flower garden. This comparison can be extended to the diversity of leaves, pods, or tubers in a kitchen garden, as well as the diversity of fruit in an orchard, all while relating these traits to the flowers of the same varieties. For instance, the leaves of cabbage exhibit significant differences, while their flowers are quite similar. In contrast, the flowers of heartsease display considerable variation, whereas the leaves are more uniform. The fruit of various gooseberry types also shows notable differences in size, color, shape, and hairiness, while their flowers are relatively alike. This observation suggests that although some varieties may differ significantly in one characteristic, they typically exhibit variations in other traits as well. The laws of growth correlation, which should not be overlooked, play a crucial role in ensuring certain differences. Ultimately, it can be concluded that the ongoing selection of minor variations in leaves, flowers, or fruit will likely lead to distinct races primarily characterized by these features.
output: In regard to plants, there is another means of observing the accumulated effects of selection - namely, by comparing the diversity of flowers in the different varieties of the same species in the flower-garden; the diversity of leaves, pods, or tubers, or whatever part is valued, in the kitchen-garden, in comparison with the flowers of the same varieties; and the diversity of fruit of the same species in the orchard, in comparison with the leaves and flowers of the same set of varieties. See how different the leaves of the cabbage are, and how extremely alike the flowers; how unlike the flowers of the heartsease are, and how alike the leaves; how much the fruit of the different kinds of gooseberries differ in size, colour, shape, and hairiness, and yet the flowers present very slight differences. It is not that the varieties which differ largely in some one point do not differ at all in other points; this is hardly ever, perhaps never, the case. The laws of correlation of growth, the importance of which should never be overlooked, will ensure some differences; but, as a general rule, I cannot doubt that the continued selection of slight variations, either in the leaves, the flowers, or the fruit, will produce races differing from each other chiefly in these characters.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: It may be worth considering how varieties, which I have referred to as incipient species, can eventually transform into fully distinct species that often exhibit more noticeable differences than varieties within the same species. Additionally, one might wonder how distinct groups of species, or genera, emerge, differing from each other more significantly than the species within a single genus. These outcomes, as will be explored more thoroughly in the upcoming chapter, can often be attributed to the struggle for life. Due to this struggle, any variation, no matter how minor and regardless of its origin, may be beneficial for an individual of any species. This benefit, in the context of complex interactions with other living organisms and the environment, can lead to the preservation of that individual and is likely to be passed down to its offspring. Consequently, the offspring may have a greater chance of survival, since only a small fraction of individuals born in any species tends to survive. I refer to this principle, whereby useful variations are preserved, as Natural Selection to highlight its connection to human selection processes. We have observed that humans can achieve significant outcomes through selection, adapting living beings to their needs by accumulating slight but beneficial variations provided by nature. However, Natural Selection, as will be discussed later, operates continuously and is significantly more powerful than human efforts, much like the difference between the works of nature and those of human artistry. In summary, the process of Natural Selection plays a crucial role in the development of distinct species through their adaptations in response to environmental challenges.
output: Again, it may be asked, how is it that varieties, which I have called incipient species, become ultimately converted into good and distinct species, which in most cases obviously differ from each other far more than do the varieties of the same species? How do those groups of species, which constitute what are called distinct genera, and which differ from each other more than do the species of the same genus, arise? All these results, as we shall more fully see in the next chapter, follow inevitably from the struggle for life. Owing to this struggle for life, any variation, however slight and from whatever cause proceeding, if it be in any degree profitable to an individual of any species, in its infinitely complex relations to other organic beings and to external nature, will tend to the preservation of that individual, and will generally be inherited by its offspring. The offspring, also, will thus have a better chance of surviving, for, of the many individuals of any species which are periodically born, but a small number can survive. I have called this principle, by which each slight variation, if useful, is preserved, by the term of Natural Selection, in order to mark its relation to man’s power of selection. We have seen that man by selection can certainly produce great results, and can adapt organic beings to his own uses, through the accumulation of slight but useful variations, given to him by the hand of Nature. But Natural Selection, as we shall hereafter see, is a power incessantly ready for action, and is as immeasurably superior to man’s feeble efforts, as the works of Nature are to those of Art.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: It is worth noting that, in my view, when the males and females of any species exhibit similar general life habits while differing in structure, coloration, or ornamentation, such variations are primarily the result of sexual selection. This phenomenon suggests that individual males have, across successive generations, possessed slight advantages over their counterparts in terms of their weapons, means of defense, or attractive features, and have subsequently transmitted these advantages to their male offspring. However, I would not wish to attribute all sexual dimorphisms to this mechanism. For instance, we observe peculiar characteristics that emerge and become associated with the male sex in domesticated animals—such as the wattle found in male carrier pigeons and the horn-like protrusions observed in certain male fowl—that we cannot reasonably assume are beneficial for the males in combat or appealing to females. Furthermore, similar instances occur in nature, as exemplified by the tuft of feathers on the breast of the male turkey, which is unlikely to serve any functional or aesthetic purpose for this bird. Indeed, had this tuft developed through domestication, it would likely have been regarded as a deformity.
output: Thus it is, as I believe, that when the males and females of any animal have the same general habits of life, but differ in structure, colour, or ornament, such differences have been mainly caused by sexual selection; that is, individual males have had, in successive generations, some slight advantage over other males, in their weapons, means of defence, or charms; and have transmitted these advantages to their male offspring. Yet, I would not wish to attribute all such sexual differences to this agency: for we see peculiarities arising and becoming attached to the male sex in our domestic animals (as the wattle in male carriers, horn-like protuberances in the cocks of certain fowls, etc.), which we cannot believe to be either useful to the males in battle, or attractive to the females. We see analogous cases under nature, for instance, the tuft of hair on the breast of the turkey-cock, which can hardly be either useful or ornamental to this bird; - indeed, had the tuft appeared under domestication, it would have been called a monstrosity.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: The validity of the principle asserting that the maximum amount of life can be sustained through considerable diversification of structure is observable in numerous natural contexts. In a relatively small area, particularly one that is open to immigration and where competition among individuals is intense, one consistently encounters significant diversity among its inhabitants. For example, I discovered that a patch of turf measuring three feet by four, which had been subjected to identical conditions for many years, supported twenty species of plants, which belonged to eighteen genera and eight orders, thereby illustrating the extent of variability among these plants. This pattern is similarly evident among the plants and insects inhabiting small, uniform islets and in small freshwater ponds. Moreover, farmers have observed that the most effective food production arises from a rotation of crops that belong to various orders; nature, in turn, seems to implement what may be termed a simultaneous rotation. Most animals and plants residing in close proximity to any small area could potentially thrive there, assuming the area's conditions are not inherently unique, and they can be said to be exerting maximal efforts to survive in that locale. However, it becomes apparent that in instances of intense competition, the advantages arising from structural diversification, along with the associated differences in habits and constitution, dictate that the closely interacting inhabitants typically belong to what we refer to as different genera and orders.
output: The truth of the principle, that the greatest amount of life can be supported by great diversification of structure, is seen under many natural circumstances. In an extremely small area, especially if freely open to immigration, and where the contest between individual and individual must be severe, we always find great diversity in its inhabitants. For instance, I found that a piece of turf, three feet by four in size, which had been exposed for many years to exactly the same conditions, supported twenty species of plants, and these belonged to eighteen genera and to eight orders, which shows how much these plants differed from each other. So it is with the plants and insects on small and uniform islets; and so in small ponds of fresh water. Farmers find that they can raise most food by a rotation of plants belonging to the most different orders: nature follows what may be called a simultaneous rotation. Most of the animals and plants which live close round any small piece of ground, could live on it (supposing it not to be in any way peculiar in its nature), and may be said to be striving to the utmost to live there; but, it is seen, that where they come into the closest competition with each other, the advantages of diversification of structure, with the accompanying differences of habit and constitution, determine that the inhabitants, which thus jostle each other most closely, shall, as a general rule, belong to what we call different genera and orders.
title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin

input: It can be observed that the geological formations of each region tend to be intermittent, rather than following each other in close sequence. One notable aspect that struck me during my examination of the South American coasts, which have been uplifted by several hundred feet in recent times, is the lack of extensive recent deposits that can persist for even a relatively short geological period. Along the western coast, which is home to a unique marine fauna, tertiary beds are not well developed, and it is possible that the record of successive marine faunas may not be preserved for a distant age. Upon consideration, it becomes clear that the rising coast of western South America is unlikely to have extensive formations with recent or tertiary remains, despite the significant supply of sediment from the degradation of coast-rocks and muddy streams entering the sea. This may be due to the fact that littoral and sub-littoral deposits are continually worn away as the land slowly rises, and are subjected to the erosive action of coast-waves. In summary, the geological formations of regions like South America's western coast can often appear intermittent due to the continuous wear and tear of coastal deposits.
output: But we can, I think, see why the geological formations of each region are almost invariably intermittent; that is, have not followed each other in close sequence. Scarcely any fact struck me more when examining many hundred miles of the South American coasts, which have been upraised several hundred feet within the recent period, than the absence of any recent deposits sufficiently extensive to last for even a short geological period. Along the whole west coast, which is inhabited by a peculiar marine fauna, tertiary beds are so scantily developed, that no record of several successive and peculiar marine faunas will probably be preserved to a distant age. A little reflection will explain why along the rising coast of the western side of South America, no extensive formations with recent or tertiary remains can anywhere be found, though the supply of sediment must for ages have been great, from the enormous degradation of the coast-rocks and from muddy streams entering the sea. The explanation, no doubt, is, that the littoral and sub-littoral deposits are continually worn away, as soon as they are brought up by the slow and gradual rising of the land within the grinding action of the coast-waves.

input: The observation that all living and extinct organisms form a comprehensive natural system, organized into groups that often include both contemporary and extinct categories, aligns with the theory of natural selection. This theory accounts for extinction and the divergence of traits. This suggests that the complex relationships among species and genera within each class can be understood through these principles. It explains why certain traits are more useful for classification than others; for instance, while adaptive traits are crucial for survival, they hold little significance for classification purposes. Conversely, traits arising from rudimentary structures, despite their lack of utility for the organism, can be highly valuable for classification. Furthermore, embryological traits are considered the most significant for this purpose. Ultimately, the true connections among all living beings stem from shared ancestry or descent, indicating that the natural system is essentially genealogical. It requires us to identify ancestral lines based on the most enduring characteristics, regardless of their immediate relevance to the organism's survival.
output: The fact, as we have seen, that all past and present organic beings constitute one grand natural system, with group subordinate to group, and with extinct groups often falling in between recent groups, is intelligible on the theory of natural selection with its contingencies of extinction and divergence of character. On these same principles we see how it is, that the mutual affinities of the species and genera within each class are so complex and circuitous. We see why certain characters are far more serviceable than others for classification; - why adaptive characters, though of paramount importance to the being, are of hardly any importance in classification; why characters derived from rudimentary parts, though of no service to the being, are often of high classificatory value; and why embryological characters are the most valuable of all. The real affinities of all organic beings are due to inheritance or community of descent. The natural system is a genealogical arrangement, in which we have to discover the lines of descent by the most permanent characters, however slight their vital importance may be.

input: Additionally, a conclusion of great significance can be drawn from the preceding observations: the structure of every organic entity is fundamentally interconnected, albeit often in subtle ways, with that of all other organic entities with which it competes for resources such as food or habitat, or from which it must evade, or upon which it preys. This interrelationship is readily apparent in the dental and claw structures of the tiger, as well as in the legs and claws of the parasite that clings to the tiger’s fur. However, in the elegantly designed seed of the dandelion and in the flattened and fringed legs of the water-beetle, the connection initially appears to be limited to the elements of air and water. Nevertheless, the advantage offered by plumed seeds is undoubtedly closely tied to the fact that land is already densely populated with other vegetation, thereby facilitating the widespread dispersal of seeds to fall upon unoccupied soil. Furthermore, the configuration of the water-beetle's legs, which are expertly adapted for diving, enables it to compete effectively with other aquatic insects, hunt for nourishment, and evade becoming prey to additional predators.
output: A corollary of the highest importance may be deduced from the foregoing remarks, namely, that the structure of every organic being is related, in the most essential yet often hidden manner, to that of all other organic beings, with which it comes into competition for food or residence, or from which it has to escape, or on which it preys. This is obvious in the structure of the teeth and talons of the tiger; and in that of the legs and claws of the parasite which clings to the hair on the tiger’s body. But in the beautifully plumed seed of the dandelion, and in the flattened and fringed legs of the water-beetle, the relation seems at first confined to the elements of air and water. Yet the advantage of plumed seeds no doubt stands in the closest relation to the land being already thickly clothed by other plants; so that the seeds may be widely distributed and fall on unoccupied ground. In the water-beetle, the structure of its legs, so well adapted for diving, allows it to compete with other aquatic insects, to hunt for its own prey, and to escape serving as prey to other animals.

input: It is worth noting that man does not actually produce variability; moreover, he only unintentionally exposes organic beings to new conditions of life, and subsequently nature acts upon the organisation and causes variability. Furthermore, man can and does select the variations that are given to him by nature, and in this manner he accumulates them in any desired manner. In essence, he thereby adapts animals and plants for his own benefit or pleasure. Additionally, he may accomplish this in a methodical manner, or he may do so unconsciously by preserving the individuals most useful to him at the time, without any consideration of altering the breed. It is certain that he can largely influence the character of a breed by selecting, in each successive generation, individual differences so slight as to be quite inappreciable by an uneducated eye. Moreover, this process of selection has been the great agency in the production of the most distinct and useful domestic breeds. It is worth noting that many of the breeds produced by man possess to a large extent the character of natural species, as is shown by the inextricable doubts whether very many of them are varieties or aboriginal species.
output: Man does not actually produce variability; he only unintentionally exposes organic beings to new conditions of life, and then nature acts on the organisation, and causes variability. But man can and does select the variations given to him by nature, and thus accumulate them in any desired manner. He thus adapts animals and plants for his own benefit or pleasure. output: It must have struck most naturalists as a strange anomaly that, in the case of both animals and plants, species of the same family and even of the same genus, though agreeing closely with each other in almost their whole organisation, yet are not rarely, some of them hermaphrodites, and some of them unisexual. Furthermore, when considering fresh-water ecosystems, they represent a smaller area compared to the sea or land. Therefore, the competition among fresh-water species tends to be less fierce, leading to a slower emergence of new forms and reduced extinction rates of older forms. This is reflected in the presence of seven genera of Ganoid fishes, which are remnants of a once dominant order, as well as some unusual species like the Ornithorhynchus and Lepidosiren. These species, which exhibit features connecting distantly related orders, can be regarded as living fossils, having survived due to their existence in confined environments with lower competition.
output: We can, perhaps, on these views, understand some facts which will be again alluded to in our chapter on geographical distribution; for instance, that the productions of the smaller continent of Australia have formerly yielded, and apparently are now yielding, before those of the larger Europæo-Asiatic area. Thus, also, it is that continental productions have everywhere become so largely naturalised on islands. On a small island, the race for life will have been less severe, and there will have been less modification and less extermination. Hence, perhaps, it comes that the flora of Madeira, according to Oswald Heer, resembles the extinct tertiary flora of Europe. All fresh-water basins, taken together, make a small area compared with that of the sea or of the land; and, consequently, the competition between fresh-water productions will have been less severe than elsewhere; new forms will have been more slowly formed, and old forms more slowly exterminated. And it is in fresh water that we find seven genera of Ganoid fishes, remnants of a once preponderant order: and in fresh water we find some of the most anomalous forms now known in the world, as the Ornithorhynchus and Lepidosiren, which, like fossils, connect to a certain extent orders now widely separated in the natural scale. These anomalous forms may almost be called living fossils; they have endured to the present day, from having inhabited a confined area, and from having thus been exposed to less severe competition.

input: In comparing mongrels and hybrids, Gärtner notes that mongrels are more likely to revert to either parent form, although this difference is likely a matter of degree. This highlights the complexity of the relationship between these two groups. Gärtner also observes that when two closely related species are crossed with a third species, the resulting hybrids exhibit significant differences from one another. In contrast, when two distinct varieties of a single species are crossed with another species, the hybrids show relatively little difference. This suggests that the outcome of such crossings may be influenced by the specific characteristics of the species involved. Ultimately, however, Gärtner's conclusion is based on a limited number of experiments, and it appears to contradict the findings of Kölreuter's experiments, which raises questions about the generality of this phenomenon.
output: But to return to our comparison of mongrels and hybrids: Gärtner states that mongrels are more liable than hybrids to revert to either parent-form; but this, if it be true, is certainly only a difference in degree. Gärtner further insists that when any two species, although most closely allied to each other, are crossed with a third species, the hybrids are widely different from each other; whereas if two very distinct varieties of one species are crossed with another species, the hybrids do not differ much. But this conclusion, as far as I can make out, is founded on a single experiment; and seems directly opposed to the results of several experiments made by Kölreuter.

input: Additionally, a vast and largely unexplored area of investigation will be revealed, encompassing the causes and principles of variation, the correlation of growth, the effects of utilization and disutilization, and the direct impact of external factors. Furthermore, the examination of domesticated organisms will significantly increase in importance. In essence, a new variety developed through human intervention will become a substantially more significant and intriguing subject for analysis than the discovery of an additional species to the vast array of already documented species. Moreover, our systems of classification will ultimately become, to the extent that this is feasible, genealogical in nature; and will thereby provide a genuine representation of the underlying plan of creation. It is worth noting that the principles governing classification will likely become more straightforward once a clear objective has been established. Moreover, in the absence of explicit records of ancestry or lineage, we must endeavour to identify and trace the numerous diverging lines of descent in our natural genealogies, utilizing characteristics of any kind that have been inherited over an extended period. Additionally, rudimentary organs will provide unequivocal evidence regarding the nature of structures that have been lost over time. In addition, species and groups of species that are considered aberrant, and which may be figuratively referred to as living relics of the past, will assist us in forming a conception of the ancient forms of life. Furthermore, the study of embryology will reveal to us the structure, to some extent obscured, of the prototypical forms of each major class.
output: A grand and almost untrodden field of inquiry will be opened, on the causes and laws of variation, on correlation of growth, on the effects of use and disuse, on the direct action of external conditions, and so forth. The study of domestic productions will rise immensely in value. A new variety raised by man will be a far more important and interesting subject for study than one more species added to the infinitude of already recorded species. Our classifications will come to be, as far as they can be so made, genealogies; and will then truly give what may be called the plan of creation. The rules for classifying will no doubt become simpler when we have a definite object in view. We possess no pedigrees or armorial bearings; and we have to discover and trace the many diverging lines of descent in our natural genealogies, by characters of any kind which have long been inherited. Rudimentary organs will speak infallibly with respect to the nature of long-lost structures. Species and groups of species, which are called aberrant, and which may fancifully be called living fossils, will aid us in forming a picture of the ancient forms of life. Embryology will reveal to us the structure, in some degree obscured, of the prototypes of each great class.
