The significance of minor characteristics in classification largely stems from their correlation with other characters of varying importance. This highlights the value of considering an aggregate of characteristics in natural history. A species can differ from its allies in several key characteristics, yet its classification remains clear. This suggests that classification based on a single characteristic, regardless of its importance, is inherently flawed, as no aspect of an organism's structure is universally constant. The importance of aggregate characteristics, even when individually insignificant, explains the observation made by Linnæus that the genus determines the characters, rather than the characters defining the genus. This implies an appreciation for numerous subtle similarities that are difficult to define. 

Certain plants within the Malpighiaceæ family exhibit both perfect and degraded flowers, with the latter lacking many characteristic features of the species, genus, family, and class. However, when Aspicarpa, a genus within this family, produced only degraded flowers in France over several years, displaying significant deviations from the typical structure of the order, M. Richard nonetheless recognized that it should still be classified amongst the Malpighiaceæ. This case illustrates the nuanced approach sometimes necessary in classification. Ultimately, it demonstrates the need to consider the aggregate of characteristics rather than relying on individual traits, which can be misleading or inconsistent.
output: The importance, for classification, of trifling characters, mainly depends on their being correlated with several other characters of more or less importance. The value indeed of an aggregate of characters is very evident in natural history. Hence, as has often been remarked, a species may depart from its allies in several characters, both of high physiological importance and of almost universal prevalence, and yet leave us in no doubt where it should be ranked. Hence, also, it has been found, that a classification founded on any single character, however important that may be, has always failed; for no part of the organisation is universally constant. The importance of an aggregate of characters, even when none are important, alone explains, I think, that saying of Linnæus, that the characters do not give the genus, but the genus gives the characters; for this saying seems founded on an appreciation of many trifling points of resemblance, too slight to be defined. Certain plants, belonging to the Malpighiaceæ, bear perfect and degraded flowers; in the latter, as A. de Jussieu has remarked, “the greater number of the characters proper to the species, to the genus, to the family, to the class, disappear, and thus laugh at our classification.” But when Aspicarpa produced in France, during several years, only degraded flowers, departing so wonderfully in a number of the most important points of structure from the proper type of the order, yet M. Richard sagaciously saw, as Jussieu observes, that this genus should still be retained amongst the Malpighiaceæ. This case seems to me well to illustrate the spirit with which our classifications are sometimes necessarily founded.

input: Furthermore, if the geological record is as incomplete as I contend, and it can at least be asserted that the record cannot be demonstrated to be significantly more complete, the primary objections to the theory of natural selection are substantially reduced or may even vanish. Additionally, all the fundamental principles of paleontology evidently indicate, in my view, that species have emerged through ordinary processes of generation; older forms have been replaced by newer and more advanced forms of life, which have arisen from the ongoing laws of variation that are still in effect around us and are maintained through natural selection.
output: If then the geological record be as imperfect as I believe it to be, and it may at least be asserted that the record cannot be proved to be much more perfect, the main objections to the theory of natural selection are greatly diminished or disappear. On the other hand, all the chief laws of palæontology plainly proclaim, as it seems to me, that species have been produced by ordinary generation: old forms having been supplanted by new and improved forms of life, produced by the laws of variation still acting round us, and preserved by Natural Selection.

On the Affinities of Extinct Species to Each Other and to Living Forms

Let us now consider the mutual affinities of extinct and living species. They all fall into one grand natural system, and this fact is at once explained on the principle of descent. As a general rule, the more ancient a form is, the more it differs from living forms. However, as Buckland long ago remarked, all fossils can be classed either within still existing groups or between them. It cannot be disputed that extinct forms of life help to fill up the wide intervals between existing genera, families, and orders. This highlights that if we confine our attention either to the living or to the extinct alone, the series is far less perfect than if we combine both into one general system. With respect to the Vertebrata, whole pages could be filled with striking illustrations from our great palaeontologist, Owen, showing how extinct animals fall in between existing groups. Cuvier ranked the Ruminants and Pachyderms as the two most distinct orders of mammals, but Owen has discovered so many fossil links that he has had to alter the whole classification of these two orders, and has placed certain pachyderms in the same sub-order with ruminants; for example, he dissolves by fine gradations the apparently wide difference between the pig and the camel. In regard to the Invertebrata, Barrande, and a higher authority could not be named, asserts that he is every day taught that palaeozoic animals, though belonging to the same orders, families, or genera as those living at the present day, were not at this early epoch limited in such distinct groups as they now are. This suggests that the affinities between extinct and living species are best understood when both are considered together within a single natural system.
output: On the Affinities of extinct Species to each other, and to living forms. - Let us now look to the mutual affinities of extinct and living species. Domestic instincts are often regarded as actions that have become inherited solely due to long-continued and compulsory habit. However, this explanation is not entirely accurate. The ability of the tumbler-pigeon to tumble, for instance, is not a trait that can be taught. In fact, young birds that have never seen a pigeon tumble are still able to perform this action. Therefore, it is likely that some pigeons initially exhibited a slight tendency to tumble, and subsequent generations of selective breeding resulted in the development of this trait.

Additionally, the process of selection has played a crucial role in the development of certain traits in other animals. For example, dogs that point may have originated from individuals that naturally exhibited this tendency. Once this tendency was observed, breeders could selectively breed for this trait, resulting in the development of dogs that are skilled at pointing. Similarly, unconscious selection is still occurring, as breeders seek to acquire dogs that are well-suited for hunting and standing. 

In some cases, however, habit alone has been sufficient to bring about significant changes in animals. The domestic rabbit, for instance, is a prime example of an animal that has undergone a substantial transformation from being extremely wild to extremely tame. Nevertheless, it is unlikely that domestic rabbits were selectively bred for tameness. Instead, it is probable that the inherited change in temperament can be attributed to habit and long-continued close confinement.
output: Domestic instincts are sometimes spoken of as actions which have become inherited solely from long-continued and compulsory habit, but this, I think, is not true. No one would ever have thought of teaching, or probably could have taught, the tumbler-pigeon to tumble, - an action which, as I have witnessed, is performed by young birds, that have never seen a pigeon tumble. We may believe that some one pigeon showed a slight tendency to this strange habit, and that the long-continued selection of the best individuals in successive generations made tumblers what they now are; and near Glasgow there are house-tumblers, as I hear from Mr. Brent, which cannot fly eighteen inches high without going head over heels. It may be doubted whether any one would have thought of training a dog to point, had not some one dog naturally shown a tendency in this line; and this is known occasionally to happen, as I once saw in a pure terrier. When the first tendency was once displayed, methodical selection and the inherited effects of compulsory training in each successive generation would soon complete the work; and unconscious selection is still at work, as each man tries to procure, without intending to improve the breed, dogs which will stand and hunt best. On the other hand, habit alone in some cases has sufficed; no animal is more difficult to tame than the young of the wild rabbit; scarcely any animal is tamer than the young of the tame rabbit; but I do not suppose that domestic rabbits have ever been selected for tameness; and I presume that we must attribute the whole of the inherited change from extreme wildness to extreme tameness, simply to habit and long-continued close confinement.

The observation that forms of life change simultaneously in different parts of the world has had a significant impact on notable observers such as MM. de Verneuil and d'Archiac. They have noted the parallelism of palaeozoic forms of life in various European regions. Additionally, they have observed that similar phenomena occur in North America, leading them to conclude that modifications of species, extinctions, and introductions of new species cannot be attributed to local or temporary factors such as changes in marine currents. 

Furthermore, these events must be governed by general laws that apply to the entire animal kingdom. Similarly, M. Barrande has made similar comments, emphasizing the same point. It is clear that changes in currents, climate, or other physical conditions cannot be the primary cause of these significant changes in forms of life worldwide, regardless of the climate. As Barrande has noted, it is necessary to consider a special law that governs these phenomena. Moreover, this will become more apparent when we examine the current distribution of organic beings and observe the limited relationship between the physical conditions of various countries and the nature of their inhabitants.
output: The fact of the forms of life changing simultaneously, in the above large sense, at distant parts of the world, has greatly struck those admirable observers, MM. de Verneuil and d’Archiac. After referring to the parallelism of the palæozoic forms of life in various parts of Europe, they add, “If struck by this strange sequence, we turn our attention to North America, and there discover a series of analogous phenomena, it will appear certain that all these modifications of species, their extinction, and the introduction of new ones, cannot be owing to mere changes in marine currents or other causes more or less local and temporary, but depend on general laws which govern the whole animal kingdom.” M. Barrande has made forcible remarks to precisely the same effect. It is, indeed, quite futile to look to changes of currents, climate, or other physical conditions, as the cause of these great mutations in the forms of life throughout the world, under the most different climates. We must, as Barrande has remarked, look to some special law. We shall see this more clearly when we treat of the present distribution of organic beings, and find how slight is the relation between the physical conditions of various countries, and the nature of their inhabitants.

input: As I approached, both ladies stood to greet me, addressing me as "Miss Eyre." Eliza's welcome was somewhat curt and devoid of warmth, and she soon returned to her seat, staring into the fire as if she had forgotten my presence. Georgiana, on the other hand, offered a somewhat more engaging "How do you do?" but accompanied it with a few typical remarks about my travel and the weather, delivered in a rather drawn-out manner. Her gaze traveled over me from head to toe, taking in the drab fabric of my coat and lingering on the simple trim of my bonnet. It seems that young women often have a subtle way of indicating their disapproval without directly stating it. Their slightly condescending expressions, cool demeanor, and casual tone can convey their thoughts clearly, all while remaining polite in their words and actions. Overall, it appears that social dynamics can reveal much without explicit commentary.
output: Both ladies, as I advanced, rose to welcome me, and both addressed me by the name of “Miss Eyre.” Eliza’s greeting was delivered in a short, abrupt voice, without a smile; and then she sat down again, fixed her eyes on the fire, and seemed to forget me. Georgiana added to her “How d’ye do?” several commonplaces about my journey, the weather, and so on, uttered in rather a drawling tone: and accompanied by sundry side-glances that measured me from head to foot - now traversing the folds of my drab merino pelisse, and now lingering on the plain trimming of my cottage bonnet. Young ladies have a remarkable way of letting you know that they think you a “quiz” without actually saying the words. A certain superciliousness of look, coolness of manner, nonchalance of tone, express fully their sentiments on the point, without committing them by any positive rudeness in word or deed.
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input: Two young women came into view; one was quite tall, nearly as tall as Miss Ingram, and she appeared very thin as well, with a pale complexion and a serious expression. There was something austere about her appearance, which was heightened by the simple design of her black dress, a stiff linen collar, hair pulled back away from her face, and the understated accessories of a string of black beads and a crucifix. I suspected this was Eliza, although I could see little connection to her previous self in that elongated and colorless face. Overall, her appearance suggested a significant transformation.
output: Two young ladies appeared before me; one very tall, almost as tall as Miss Ingram - very thin too, with a sallow face and severe mien. There was something ascetic in her look, which was augmented by the extreme plainness of a straight-skirted, black, stuff dress, a starched linen collar, hair combed away from the temples, and the nun-like ornament of a string of ebony beads and a crucifix. This I felt sure was Eliza, though I could trace little resemblance to her former self in that elongated and colourless visage.

input: Blanche and Mary were both tall and straight, similar in height. Mary appeared somewhat slender for her height, while Blanche had a figure that could be compared to that of a graceful woman. I found myself particularly interested in Blanche for several reasons. First, I wanted to see if her appearance matched Mrs. Fairfax’s description. Second, I was curious to see how closely she resembled the small portrait I had painted of her. Lastly, I wondered if she would be the type of person that might appeal to Mr. Rochester’s tastes. Overall, my observations were driven by a mix of curiosity and personal interest.
output: Blanche and Mary were of equal stature, - straight and tall as poplars. Mary was too slim for her height, but Blanche was moulded like a Dian. I regarded her, of course, with special interest. First, I wished to see whether her appearance accorded with Mrs. Fairfax’s description; secondly, whether it at all resembled the fancy miniature I had painted of her; and thirdly - it will out! - whether it were such as I should fancy likely to suit Mr. Rochester’s taste.

author: Charlotte Bronte

input: The phrase I heard yesterday seemed to suggest that she was simply going to be taken back to Northumberland, her home. I may not have initially thought it indicated her impending death; however, in that moment, it became clear to me that Helen Burns was likely nearing the end of her life. I realized that she was about to transition to an unknown realm, if such a place exists. This understanding brought about a wave of horror, followed by a deep sense of sorrow, and a pressing need to see her. I inquired about which room she was in.
output: This phrase, uttered in my hearing yesterday, would have only conveyed the notion that she was about to be removed to Northumberland, to her own home. I should not have suspected that it meant she was dying; but I knew instantly now! It opened clear on my comprehension that Helen Burns was numbering her last days in this world, and that she was going to be taken to the region of spirits, if such region there were. I experienced a shock of horror, then a strong thrill of grief, then a desire - a necessity to see her; and I asked in what room she lay.

input: In such conversation, an hour quickly passed. Bessie returned my bonnet and other belongings, and with her, I left the lodge for the hall. Nearly nine years earlier, it was also with her that I had walked down the same path I was now ascending. On a dark, misty morning in January, I had departed from a hostile home, filled with a desperate and embittered heart—a sense of being an outlaw and feeling almost condemned—as I sought the distant and uncertain refuge of Lowood. Now, that same unfriendly home rose before me once more. My future remained uncertain, and I still carried an aching heart. I felt like a wanderer in the world, yet I had developed a stronger sense of trust in myself and my abilities, along with a diminished fear of oppression. The deep wounds of my past had healed, and the flames of resentment had been extinguished.
output: In such conversation an hour was soon gone: Bessie restored to me my bonnet, &c., and, accompanied by her, I quitted the lodge for the hall. It was also accompanied by her that I had, nearly nine years ago, walked down the path I was now ascending. On a dark, misty, raw morning in January, I had left a hostile roof with a desperate and embittered heart - a sense of outlawry and almost of reprobation - to seek the chilly harbourage of Lowood: that bourne so far away and unexplored. The same hostile roof now again rose before me: my prospects were doubtful yet; and I had yet an aching heart. I still felt as a wanderer on the face of the earth; but I experienced firmer trust in myself and my own powers, and less withering dread of oppression. The gaping wound of my wrongs, too, was now quite healed; and the flame of resentment extinguished.

input: The absence of his lively influence seemed especially noticeable one day when he had been called to Millcote on business and was not expected back until late. The afternoon was rainy, so a walk the group had planned to see a gypsy camp recently set up on a common beyond Hay was postponed. Some of the gentlemen had gone to the stables, while the younger men and younger ladies were playing billiards in the billiard room. The dowagers Ingram and Lynn found comfort in a quiet game of cards. Blanche Ingram, after discouraging Mrs. Dent and Mrs. Eshton’s attempts to draw her into conversation with haughty silence, first murmured over some sentimental tunes and airs on the piano, then fetched a novel from the library and threw herself onto a sofa in proud indifference, preparing to pass the tedious hours of his absence under the spell of fiction. The room and the house were quiet; only now and then the merriment of the billiard players could be heard from above.
output: The want of his animating influence appeared to be peculiarly felt one day that he had been summoned to Millcote on business, and was not likely to return till late. The afternoon was wet: a walk the party had proposed to take to see a gipsy camp, lately pitched on a common beyond Hay, was consequently deferred. Some of the gentlemen were gone to the stables: the younger ones, together with the younger ladies, were playing billiards in the billiard-room. The dowagers Ingram and Lynn sought solace in a quiet game at cards. Blanche Ingram, after having repelled, by supercilious taciturnity, some efforts of Mrs. Dent and Mrs. Eshton to draw her into conversation, had first murmured over some sentimental tunes and airs on the piano, and then, having fetched a novel from the library, had flung herself in haughty listlessness on a sofa, and prepared to beguile, by the spell of fiction, the tedious hours of absence. The room and the house were silent: only now and then the merriment of the billiard-players was heard from above.

input: It may be worth considering his perspective on this matter. He has repeatedly indicated that it is not himself, but rather his role, that he is interested in uniting with. He has mentioned to me that I am suited for work, rather than for romantic relationships, which may have some validity. However, I believe that if I am not suited for love, it follows that I might also not be suited for marriage. It could seem peculiar, Die, to be bound for life to someone who views me solely as a practical instrument. Ultimately, this raises important questions about the nature of partnership and connection.
output: “You should hear himself on the subject. He has again and again explained that it is not himself, but his office he wishes to mate. He has told me I am formed for labour - not for love: which is true, no doubt. But, in my opinion, if I am not formed for love, it follows that I am not formed for marriage. Would it not be strange, Die, to be chained for life to a man who regarded one but as a useful tool?”

input: Before I allowed myself to ask for an explanation, I tied the string of Adèle’s pinafore, which happened to be loose. After also helping her to another bun and refilling her mug with milk, I said, casually, “Indeed he is—in three days, he says; that will be next Thursday. And he will not be alone either. I do not know how many of the fine people from the Leas are coming with him. He has sent directions for all the best bedrooms to be prepared, and the library and drawing-rooms are to be cleaned out. I am to get more kitchen hands from the George Inn at Millcote and from wherever else I can. The ladies will bring their maids and the gentlemen their valets, so we shall have a full house of it.” This highlights how quickly the household must prepare for a large arrival. Mrs. Fairfax swallowed her breakfast and hastened away to begin the necessary work.

input: Fortunately, there existed an alternative entrance to the drawing-room apart from the one leading through the saloon where everyone was seated at dinner. Upon entering the apartment, we discovered it to be unoccupied; a large fire burned quietly upon the marble hearth, and wax candles illuminated the space in brilliant solitude, surrounded by the exquisite flowers that adorned the tables. The crimson curtain draped before the arch created a subtle barrier; although the separation was slight, the individuals conversing in the adjoining saloon spoke in such hushed tones that their words were indistinguishable, reduced to a gentle murmur.
output: Fortunately there was another entrance to the drawing-room than that through the saloon where they were all seated at dinner. We found the apartment vacant; a large fire burning silently on the marble hearth, and wax candles shining in bright solitude, amid the exquisite flowers with which the tables were adorned. The crimson curtain hung before the arch: slight as was the separation this drapery formed from the party in the adjoining saloon, they spoke in so low a key that nothing of their conversation could be distinguished beyond a soothing murmur.

author: Charlotte Bronte

input:
You possess a curious and scheming mind, Mr. Rochester. I worry that your principles on certain matters are unconventional.

My principles were never properly developed, Jane. They may have become somewhat flawed due to a lack of attention.

Once more, I ask seriously: may I embrace the great blessing that has been granted to me without fearing that someone else is enduring the bitter pain I felt earlier?

You may, my good little girl. There is no other person in the world who holds the same pure love for me as you do, for I take comfort in believing in your affection, Jane.
output:
“You have a curious, designing mind, Mr. Rochester. I am afraid your principles on some points are eccentric.”

“My principles were never trained, Jane: they may have grown a little awry for want of attention.”

“Once again, seriously; may I enjoy the great good that has been vouchsafed to me, without fearing that any one else is suffering the bitter pain I myself felt a while ago?”

“That you may, my good little girl: there is not another being in the world has the same pure love for me as yourself - for I lay that pleasant unction to my soul, Jane, a belief in your affection.”
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input: Eliza, John, and Georgiana were now gathered around their mother in the drawing-room. She lay reclining on a sofa by the fireside, and with her dear children beside her—for the moment neither quarreling nor crying—she looked perfectly happy. As for me, she had excused me from joining the group, saying that she regretted being obliged to keep me at a distance, but that until she heard from Bessie and could observe for herself that I was genuinely trying to develop a more sociable and childlike disposition—a more attractive and lively manner, something lighter, franker, and more natural, so to speak—she really had to exclude me from privileges meant only for contented, happy little children. This highlights how deliberately she separated me from the family circle, and ultimately suggests that my acceptance depended on meeting her expectations.
output: The said Eliza, John, and Georgiana were now clustered round their mama in the drawing-room: she lay reclined on a sofa by the fireside, and with her darlings about her (for the time neither quarrelling nor crying) looked perfectly happy. Me, she had dispensed from joining the group; saying, “She regretted to be under the necessity of keeping me at a distance; but that until she heard from Bessie, and could discover by her own observation, that I was endeavouring in good earnest to acquire a more sociable and childlike disposition, a more attractive and sprightly manner - something lighter, franker, more natural, as it were - she really must exclude me from privileges intended only for contented, happy, little children.”
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input: Meanwhile, while I focused exclusively on my master and his future bride, perceiving only them and attending only to their conversations and movements, the rest of the group engaged in their own interests and pleasures. Ladies Lynn and Ingram participated in serious discussions, nodding their turbans at one another and using their hands to express surprise, mystery, or horror, depending on the topic of their gossip, resembling exaggerated puppets. Mild Mrs. Dent conversed with kind-hearted Mrs. Eshton, and they occasionally offered me a polite word or smile. Sir George Lynn, Colonel Dent, and Mr. Eshton deliberated on politics, local matters, or legal issues. Lord Ingram flirted with Amy Eshton, while Louisa played and sang to one of the Messrs. Lynn, and Mary Ingram listened with a sense of disinterest to the charming remarks of the other. At times, everyone would momentarily cease their activities to observe and listen to the main figures, as Mr. Rochester and, by extension, Miss Ingram were the center of attention. If he left the room for an hour, a noticeable dullness would settle over the atmosphere, and his return always reinvigorated the conversation.
output: Meantime, while I thought only of my master and his future bride - saw only them, heard only their discourse, and considered only their movements of importance - the rest of the party were occupied with their own separate interests and pleasures. The Ladies Lynn and Ingram continued to consort in solemn conferences, where they nodded their two turbans at each other, and held up their four hands in confronting gestures of surprise, or mystery, or horror, according to the theme on which their gossip ran, like a pair of magnified puppets. Mild Mrs. Dent talked with good-natured Mrs. Eshton; and the two sometimes bestowed a courteous word or smile on me. Sir George Lynn, Colonel Dent, and Mr. Eshton discussed politics, or county affairs, or justice business. Lord Ingram flirted with Amy Eshton; Louisa played and sang to and with one of the Messrs. Lynn; and Mary Ingram listened languidly to the gallant speeches of the other. Sometimes all, as with one consent, suspended their by-play to observe and listen to the principal actors: for, after all, Mr. Rochester and - because closely connected with him - Miss Ingram were the life and soul of the party. If he was absent from the room an hour, a perceptible dulness seemed to steal over the spirits of his guests; and his re-entrance was sure to give a fresh impulse to the vivacity of conversation.

author: Charlotte Bronte

Additionally, the distance was not considerable, merely three miles. He had been summoned away by the unexpected demise of his father, and was currently residing at Marsh End, where he would likely remain for a fortnight. 

Furthermore, there was no one present aside from the housekeeper, and it was she alone who was available to provide assistance. In essence, I was unable to bring myself to request relief from her, owing to my reluctance to beg, and thus I departed once more. 

Moreover, I removed my handkerchief, and my thoughts turned to the loaves of bread that were available for purchase at the local shop. It is worth noting that I was overcome with a desire for even the smallest morsel, a single crust, to alleviate the pangs of hunger that I was experiencing. Instinctively, I directed my course towards the village, and upon locating the shop, I entered and, despite the presence of others, I mustered the courage to pose a request to the woman: would she be willing to provide me with a roll in exchange for my handkerchief?
output:
“Not so far - happen three mile. He had been called away by the sudden death of his father: he was at Marsh End now, and would very likely stay there a fortnight longer.”

“Nay, there was naught but her, and she was housekeeper;” and of her, reader, I could not bear to ask the relief for want of which I was sinking; I could not yet beg; and again I crawled away.

Once more I took off my handkerchief - once more I thought of the cakes of bread in the little shop. Oh, for but a crust! for but one mouthful to allay the pang of famine! Instinctively I turned my face again to the village; I found the shop again, and I went in; and though others were there besides the woman I ventured the request - “Would she give me a roll for this handkerchief?”

author: Charlotte Bronte

input: Eliza spoke very little, as she appeared to have no time for conversation. This highlights the busy nature of her daily routine. Despite her constant activity, it was not immediately clear what she accomplished or what the end result of her efforts was. She woke up early to an alarm and allocated her time into specific tasks after breakfast. Each hour had a designated activity, which she followed diligently. This suggests that she valued structure and organization in her daily life. Three times a day, she would study a Common Prayer Book, which she found particularly interesting due to the Rubric. She also spent three hours stitching a square crimson cloth with gold thread, which was intended to be an altar covering for a newly built church near Gateshead. Additionally, she devoted time to writing in her diary, working in the kitchen-garden, and managing her accounts. Ultimately, Eliza seemed content with her solitary and routine-driven lifestyle, preferring not to have her schedule disrupted by unexpected events or social interactions. This routine appeared to bring her happiness, and she was most annoyed when anything forced her to deviate from it.
output: Eliza still spoke little: she had evidently no time to talk. I never saw a busier person than she seemed to be; yet it was difficult to say what she did: or rather, to discover any result of her diligence. She had an alarm to call her up early. I know not how she occupied herself before breakfast, but after that meal she divided her time into regular portions, and each hour had its allotted task. Three times a day she studied a little book, which I found, on inspection, was a Common Prayer Book. I asked her once what was the great attraction of that volume, and she said, “the Rubric.” Three hours she gave to stitching, with gold thread, the border of a square crimson cloth, almost large enough for a carpet. In answer to my inquiries after the use of this article, she informed me it was a covering for the altar of a new church lately erected near Gateshead. Two hours she devoted to her diary; two to working by herself in the kitchen-garden; and one to the regulation of her accounts. She seemed to want no company; no conversation. I believe she was happy in her way: this routine sufficed for her; and nothing annoyed her so much as the occurrence of any incident which forced her to vary its clockwork regularity.
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input: I approached John's chair, as was my usual practice of obedience. He spent about three minutes extending his tongue toward me, seemingly testing his limits. I anticipated that he would soon strike me, and I found myself contemplating his unpleasant appearance. It is uncertain whether he sensed my thoughts, but suddenly and without warning, he struck me with considerable force. I staggered backward and, after regaining my balance, stepped back a few paces from his chair.
output: Habitually obedient to John, I came up to his chair: he spent some three minutes in thrusting out his tongue at me as far as he could without damaging the roots: I knew he would soon strike, and while dreading the blow, I mused on the disgusting and ugly appearance of him who would presently deal it. I wonder if he read that notion in my face; for, all at once, without speaking, he struck suddenly and strongly. I tottered, and on regaining my equilibrium retired back a step or two from his chair.
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input: My personal belongings were arranged on a chair by the bedside, clean and dry. My black silk frock had been hung against the wall, with the traces of the bog removed and the creases smoothed out, making it decent once again. Even my shoes and stockings had been cleaned and made presentable. The room was equipped with washing facilities, as well as a comb and brush to tidy my hair. After a lengthy and tiring process, during which I had to rest frequently, I managed to dress myself. Due to my weakened state, my clothes hung loosely on my frame, but I used a shawl to conceal this. This highlights the importance of maintaining a sense of dignity and respectability, even in difficult circumstances. Ultimately, I was able to present myself in a clean and respectable manner, with no remaining signs of the dirt and disorder that I found so degrading. With the aid of the banisters, I made my way down a stone staircase to a narrow, low passage, and from there, I found my way to the kitchen. This suggests that I was determined to regain a sense of normalcy and routine, despite my physical condition.
output: On a chair by the bedside were all my own things, clean and dry. My black silk frock hung against the wall. The traces of the bog were removed from it; the creases left by the wet smoothed out: it was quite decent. My very shoes and stockings were purified and rendered presentable. There were the means of washing in the room, and a comb and brush to smooth my hair. After a weary process, and resting every five minutes, I succeeded in dressing myself. My clothes hung loose on me; for I was much wasted, but I covered deficiencies with a shawl, and once more, clean and respectable looking - no speck of the dirt, no trace of the disorder I so hated, and which seemed so to degrade me, left - I crept down a stone staircase with the aid of the banisters, to a narrow low passage, and found my way presently to the kitchen.

author: Charlotte Bronte

input:
The other members of the household—namely, John and his wife, Leah the housemaid, and Sophie the French nurse—were decent people, though not particularly remarkable in any way. With Sophie, I used to talk in French, and sometimes I would ask her questions about her native country. However, she was not really inclined toward description or storytelling, and she generally gave answers that were so vague and confused that they tended to discourage rather than encourage further inquiry.

October, November, and December passed by. One afternoon in January, Mrs. Fairfax had asked for a holiday for Adèle because she had a cold. Since Adèle supported the request with an enthusiasm that reminded me how precious occasional holidays had been to me in my own childhood, I agreed to it, thinking that I was doing the right thing by showing some flexibility on the matter. It was a fine, calm day, though quite cold. I was tired of sitting still in the library for a whole long morning. Mrs. Fairfax had just written a letter that was waiting to be posted, so I put on my bonnet and cloak and offered to carry it to Hay. The distance, two miles, would make a pleasant winter afternoon walk. After seeing Adèle comfortably seated in her little chair by the fire in Mrs. Fairfax’s parlour, and after giving her her best wax doll—which I usually kept wrapped in silver paper in a drawer—to play with, along with a storybook for a change of amusement, and after replying to her “Revenez bientôt, ma bonne amie, ma chère Mdlle. Jeannette” with a kiss, I set out.
output:

A pause followed, filled by the process of producing and lighting a cigar. After placing it to his lips and exhaling a trail of Havana incense into the cold, sunless air, he continued.

"I enjoyed bonbons in those days, Miss Eyre, and I savored chocolate confections. Alternating between smoking and watching the carriages roll along the fashionable streets toward the nearby opera house, I spotted an elegant closed carriage drawn by a stunning pair of English horses. In the bright city night, I recognized the vehicle I had given to Céline. She was returning, and my heart raced with impatience against the iron rails I leaned upon. As expected, the carriage stopped at the hotel door. My infatuation, the very term for an opera lover, stepped out. Although wrapped in a cloak—a needless burden on such a warm June evening—I recognized her by the small foot that peeked out from the hem of her dress as she hopped from the carriage step. Leaning over the balcony, I was about to whisper 'Mon ange' in a tone intended for her ears alone when a figure jumped from the carriage after her. This person was also cloaked, but a spurred heel struck the pavement, and a hatted head passed under the arched porte cochère of the hotel.
output:
Here ensued a pause, filled up by the producing and lighting of a cigar; having placed it to his lips and breathed a trail of Havannah incense on the freezing and sunless air, he went on -

“I liked bonbons too in those days, Miss Eyre, and I was croquant - (overlook the barbarism) - croquant chocolate comfits, and smoking alternately, watching meantime the equipages that rolled along the fashionable streets towards the neighbouring opera-house, when in an elegant close carriage drawn by a beautiful pair of English horses, and distinctly seen in the brilliant city-night, I recognised the ‘voiture’ I had given Céline. She was returning: of course my heart thumped with impatience against the iron rails I leant upon. The carriage stopped, as I had expected, at the hotel door; my flame (that is the very word for an opera inamorata) alighted: though muffed in a cloak - an unnecessary encumbrance, by-the-bye, on so warm a June evening - I knew her instantly by her little foot, seen peeping from the skirt of her dress, as she skipped from the carriage-step. Bending over the balcony, I was about to murmur ‘Mon ange’ - in a tone, of course, which should be audible to the ear of love alone - when a figure jumped from the carriage after her; cloaked also; but that was a spurred heel which had rung on the pavement, and that was a hatted head which now passed under the arched porte cochère of the hotel.
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input:
As the half-hour drew to a close, the five o'clock bell struck, signaling the end of the school day. Consequently, the students proceeded to the refectory for tea, and the room was soon empty. At this point, I decided to go downstairs, and as I did, I noticed that it was already quite dark. I then sat down on the floor in a corner, seeking some solitude. Meanwhile, the emotional strength that had sustained me thus far began to wane, and a strong sense of grief took its place. Additionally, this feeling became so intense that I eventually lay down on the ground, overcome with emotion. Now, I gave in to my tears, and I wept openly, as there was no one present to offer me comfort or support, particularly Helen Burns, whose presence I misses deeply.

Previously, I had envisioned a successful and happy experience at Lowood, where I would make many friends and earn the respect and affection of my peers. Furthermore, I had made significant progress towards achieving these goals, as evidenced by my promotion to the head of my class that very morning. Moreover, I had received praise from Miss Miller and approval from Miss Temple, who had also offered to teach me drawing and French if I continued to perform well for the next two months. Nevertheless, despite these accomplishments, I was now lying on the ground, feeling defeated and wondering if I would ever be able to regain my composure and rise above my current difficulties.
output: Ere the half-hour ended, five o’clock struck; school was dismissed, and all were gone into the refectory to tea. I now ventured to descend: it was deep dusk; I retired into a corner and sat down on the floor. The spell by which I had been so far supported began to dissolve; reaction took place, and soon, so overwhelming was the grief that seized me, I sank prostrate with my face to the ground. Now I wept: Helen Burns was not here; nothing sustained me; left to myself I abandoned myself, and my tears watered the boards. I had meant to be so good, and to do so much at Lowood: to make so many friends, to earn respect and win affection. Already I had made visible progress: that very morning I had reached the head of my class; Miss Miller had praised me warmly; Miss Temple had smiled approbation; she had promised to teach me drawing, and to let me learn French, if I continued to make similar improvement two months longer: and then I was well received by my fellow-pupils; treated as an equal by those of my own age, and not molested by any; now, here I lay again crushed and trodden on; and could I ever rise more?
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

"I should indeed like to go to school," I concluded aloud, bringing my thoughts to an end.

At that moment, Bessie returned, and the carriage was heard coming up the gravel walk.

Bessie invited him into the breakfast room and led the way. From what happened afterward, I assume that during his meeting with Mrs. Reed, the apothecary suggested that I be sent to school, and this recommendation was likely accepted without much hesitation. This is supported by what Abbot said one night while sewing with Bessie in the nursery, after I had gone to bed and they believed I was asleep: she remarked that Mrs. Reed was probably glad to be rid of such a troublesome and difficult child, who always seemed to be watching everyone and secretly plotting something. I think Abbot regarded me as a kind of child-sized Guy Fawkes.
output:
“I should indeed like to go to school,” was the audible conclusion of my musings.

Bessie now returned; at the same moment the carriage was heard rolling up the gravel-walk.

Bessie invited him to walk into the breakfast-room, and led the way out. In the interview which followed between him and Mrs. Reed, I presume, from after-occurrences, that the apothecary ventured to recommend my being sent to school; and the recommendation was no doubt readily enough adopted; for as Abbot said, in discussing the subject with Bessie when both sat sewing in the nursery one night, after I was in bed, and, as they thought, asleep, “Missis was, she dared say, glad enough to get rid of such a tiresome, ill-conditioned child, who always looked as if she were watching everybody, and scheming plots underhand.” Abbot, I think, gave me credit for being a sort of infantine Guy Fawkes.
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input:
He has certainly consumed too much wine, I thought, and I was unsure how to respond to his strange question. How could I determine if he was capable of being re-transformed? 

"You appeared quite confused, Miss Eyre," he remarked. "While you are not beautiful, any more than I am handsome, your puzzled expression suits you. Furthermore, it is advantageous, as it distracts your probing gaze from my face and redirects it to the floral patterns of the rug. So, continue to puzzle. Young lady, I feel inclined to be sociable and talkative tonight."
output:
“Decidedly he has had too much wine,” I thought; and I did not know what answer to make to his queer question: how could I tell whether he was capable of being re-transformed?

“You looked very much puzzled, Miss Eyre; and though you are not pretty any more than I am handsome, yet a puzzled air becomes you; besides, it is convenient, for it keeps those searching eyes of yours away from my physiognomy, and busies them with the worsted flowers of the rug; so puzzle on. Young lady, I am disposed to be gregarious and communicative to-night.”
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input: Because I disliked you too consistently and completely to ever help you achieve prosperity. I could not forget your behavior toward me, Jane, including the fury with which you once turned on me and the tone in which you declared that you hated me more than anyone in the world. I also could not forget the unchildlike look and voice with which you insisted that the very thought of me made you ill and claimed that I had treated you with miserable cruelty. Moreover, I could not forget my own feelings when you rose up and poured out the venom of your mind in that way. I felt afraid, as if an animal that I had struck or pushed had looked up at me with human eyes and cursed me in a man’s voice. Bring me some water. Oh, make haste.
output: “Because I disliked you too fixedly and thoroughly ever to lend a hand in lifting you to prosperity. I could not forget your conduct to me, Jane - the fury with which you once turned on me; the tone in which you declared you abhorred me the worst of anybody in the world; the unchildlike look and voice with which you affirmed that the very thought of me made you sick, and asserted that I had treated you with miserable cruelty. I could not forget my own sensations when you thus started up and poured out the venom of your mind: I felt fear as if an animal that I had struck or pushed had looked up at me with human eyes and cursed me in a man’s voice. - Bring me some water! Oh, make haste!”
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

I was well contented to stand there, for I derived a child's pleasure from the contemplation of her face, her dress, her one or two ornaments, her white forehead, her clustered and shining curls, and her beaming dark eyes. input:
It's possible that I may have taken a wrong turn and become disoriented. As the natural daylight began to fade, the surroundings grew darker, and the trees seemed to close in around me. I looked around for an alternative path, but it appeared that there was no other way forward, as the dense foliage and tree trunks seemed to be intertwined with no visible opening. 

I decided to continue on, and eventually, the trees started to thin out slightly, allowing me to see a railing and then a house, although it was somewhat difficult to distinguish from the surrounding trees due to the dim light. The house's walls appeared to be in a state of disrepair, with dampness and greenery covering them. Upon entering through an unlatched portal, I found myself in a enclosed area, with the wood sweeping away in a semicircle. The space was relatively bare, with no flowers or garden beds, just a gravel walk surrounding a grassy area, set within the forest. The house had a distinctive frontage, with two pointed gables, latticed windows, and a narrow front door, which was accessible by a single step. Overall, the location tended to seem quite isolated, much like the host of the Rochester Arms had described, and the only sound that could be heard was the gentle patter of rain on the forest leaves, creating an atmosphere that was similarly quiet to a church on a weekday. In summary, the house and its surroundings appeared to be a somewhat neglected and serene spot, surrounded by the dense forest.
output:
I thought I had taken a wrong direction and lost my way. The darkness of natural as well as of sylvan dusk gathered over me. I looked round in search of another road. There was none: all was interwoven stem, columnar trunk, dense summer foliage - no opening anywhere.

I proceeded: at last my way opened, the trees thinned a little; presently I beheld a railing, then the house - scarce, by this dim light, distinguishable from the trees; so dank and green were its decaying walls. Entering a portal, fastened only by a latch, I stood amidst a space of enclosed ground, from which the wood swept away in a semicircle. There were no flowers, no garden-beds; only a broad gravel-walk girdling a grass-plat, and this set in the heavy frame of the forest. The house presented two pointed gables in its front; the windows were latticed and narrow: the front door was narrow too, one step led up to it. The whole looked, as the host of the Rochester Arms had said, “quite a desolate spot.” It was as still as a church on a week-day: the pattering rain on the forest leaves was the only sound audible in its vicinage.
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input: Mr. Rivers," I said, turning to him and looking at him, as he looked at me, openly and without diffidence, "you and your sisters have done me a great service—the greatest that a man can do for his fellow being. You have rescued me, by your noble hospitality, from death. This benefit conferred gives you an unlimited claim on my gratitude and a claim, to a certain extent, on my confidence. I will tell you as much of the history of the wanderer you have harboured as I can tell without compromising my own peace of mind—my own security, moral and physical, and that of others.

input:
I believe I can clarify the situation, sir. Last Thursday, Agnes and Catherine Johnstone were invited to have tea with friends in Lowton, and I allowed them to wear clean tuckers for the event."

"Well, this time it may be acceptable; however, please ensure this does not happen frequently. Additionally, I was surprised to discover that a lunch, consisting of bread and cheese, has been served to the girls twice in the past two weeks. How did this come about? I reviewed the regulations, and there is no mention of lunch as a designated meal. Who authorized this change?
output:
“I think I can explain that circumstance, sir. Agnes and Catherine Johnstone were invited to take tea with some friends at Lowton last Thursday, and I gave them leave to put on clean tuckers for the occasion.”

“Well, for once it may pass; but please not to let the circumstance occur too often. And there is another thing which surprised me; I find, in settling accounts with the housekeeper, that a lunch, consisting of bread and cheese, has twice been served out to the girls during the past fortnight. How is this? I looked over the regulations, and I find no such meal as lunch mentioned. Who introduced this innovation? and by what authority?”
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input:
She looked at me again, and this time there was an awareness in her gaze. It seemed she was assessing me cautiously before she spoke. 

"The servants are quite far away and probably wouldn’t hear anything," she explained. "Mrs. Fairfax’s room and yours are the closest to the master’s, but Mrs. Fairfax mentioned she heard nothing. Elderly people often sleep deeply." After a moment, she continued, attempting to sound indifferent, yet her tone was still notable. "However, you are young, Miss, and likely a light sleeper. Perhaps you heard a noise?"
output:
She again raised her eyes to me, and this time there was something of consciousness in their expression. She seemed to examine me warily; then she answered -

“The servants sleep so far off, you know, Miss, they would not be likely to hear. Mrs. Fairfax’s room and yours are the nearest to master’s; but Mrs. Fairfax said she heard nothing: when people get elderly, they often sleep heavy.” She paused, and then added, with a sort of assumed indifference, but still in a marked and significant tone - “But you are young, Miss; and I should say a light sleeper: perhaps you may have heard a noise?”
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input: I believe I can. It seems that I have always cared for my sisters deeply, and my feelings for them are based on my respect for their value and admiration for their abilities. You also possess strong principles and intellect; your preferences and behaviors are often similar to those of Diana and Mary. I find your company to be pleasant, and our conversations have provided me with comfort for quite some time. I feel that it is both easy and natural for me to welcome you into my heart as my third and youngest sister. In summary, I believe our connection can grow warmly and positively.
output: “I think I can. I know I have always loved my own sisters; and I know on what my affection for them is grounded, - respect for their worth and admiration of their talents. You too have principle and mind: your tastes and habits resemble Diana’s and Mary’s; your presence is always agreeable to me; in your conversation I have already for some time found a salutary solace. I feel I can easily and naturally make room in my heart for you, as my third and youngest sister.”
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input: The hour I spent at Millcote was somewhat trying for me. Mr. Rochester insisted that I go to a certain silk warehouse, where I was asked to choose half a dozen dresses. I disliked the task and begged to put it off, but he would not hear of it; it had to be done now. By pleading in urgent whispers, I managed to reduce the half-dozen to two, though he declared he would choose them himself. I watched with some unease as his eye wandered over the bright displays, and he settled on a rich silk in a vivid amethyst shade and a splendid pink satin. I whispered again that he might as well buy me a gold gown and a silver bonnet at once, since I could never bring myself to wear his choices. Since he could be quite stubborn, it took a great deal of effort to persuade him to exchange them for a sober black satin and a pearl-grey silk. He remarked that it might do for now, but that he would still see me glittering like a flower bed someday.
output: The hour spent at Millcote was a somewhat harassing one to me. Mr. Rochester obliged me to go to a certain silk warehouse: there I was ordered to choose half-a-dozen dresses. I hated the business, I begged leave to defer it: no - it should be gone through with now. By dint of entreaties expressed in energetic whispers, I reduced the half-dozen to two: these however, he vowed he would select himself. With anxiety I watched his eye rove over the gay stores: he fixed on a rich silk of the most brilliant amethyst dye, and a superb pink satin. I told him in a new series of whispers, that he might as well buy me a gold gown and a silver bonnet at once: I should certainly never venture to wear his choice. With infinite difficulty, for he was stubborn as a stone, I persuaded him to make an exchange in favour of a sober black satin and pearl-grey silk. “It might pass for the present,” he said; “but he would yet see me glittering like a parterre.”
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input: In examining the ruined walls and the devastated interior, I gathered evidence that the calamity had not occurred recently. Additionally, I considered that winter snows had drifted through that empty arch, and winter rains had beaten in at those hollow casements, for amidst the drenched piles of debris, spring had nurtured vegetation. Furthermore, grass and weeds grew here and there between the stones and fallen rafters. Moreover, where, in the meantime, was the unfortunate owner of this wreckage? In what land? Under what auspices? In essence, my eye involuntarily wandered to the grey church tower near the gates, and I inquired, “Is he with Damer de Rochester, sharing the shelter of his narrow marble house?”
output: In wandering round the shattered walls and through the devastated interior, I gathered evidence that the calamity was not of late occurrence. Winter snows, I thought, had drifted through that void arch, winter rains beaten in at those hollow casements; for, amidst the drenched piles of rubbish, spring had cherished vegetation: grass and weed grew here and there between the stones and fallen rafters. And oh! where meantime was the hapless owner of this wreck? In what land? Under what auspices? My eye involuntarily wandered to the grey church tower near the gates, and I asked, “Is he with Damer de Rochester, sharing the shelter of his narrow marble house?”
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input:
As evening approaches, I think I may soon see Mr. Rochester, since I have not heard his voice or step in the house today. Earlier I was somewhat afraid of meeting him, but now I would welcome it, as my long wait has made me rather impatient.

When dusk finally fell and Adèle went to play in the nursery with Sophie, I wanted to see him even more. I listened for the bell downstairs and for Leah bringing a message. Sometimes I thought I heard Mr. Rochester’s step and turned toward the door, expecting him to enter, but the door stayed shut and only darkness came through the window. It was still early, since he often sent for me at seven or eight, and it was only six. I felt I should not be entirely disappointed tonight, as I had many things to say to him. I wanted to bring up Grace Poole again and hear his answer, and to ask him directly whether he truly believed she had made the dreadful attempt the night before, and if so, why he kept her wrongdoing secret. It mattered little whether my curiosity annoyed him, since I knew the pleasure of irritating and calming him in turn and took special delight in it. A sure instinct usually kept me from going too far; I never ventured beyond the verge of provocation but liked to test my skill at the very brink. While keeping every small form of respect and propriety of my station, I could still argue with him without fear or uneasy restraint, which suited us both.
output:
“Evening approaches,” said I, as I looked towards the window. “I have never heard Mr. Rochester’s voice or step in the house to-day; but surely I shall see him before night: I feared the meeting in the morning; now I desire it, because expectation has been so long baffled that it is grown impatient.”

When dusk actually closed, and when Adèle left me to go and play in the nursery with Sophie, I did most keenly desire it. I listened for the bell to ring below; I listened for Leah coming up with a message; I fancied sometimes I heard Mr. Rochester’s own tread, and I turned to the door, expecting it to open and admit him. The door remained shut; darkness only came in through the window. Still it was not late; he often sent for me at seven and eight o’clock, and it was yet but six. Surely I should not be wholly disappointed to-night, when I had so many things to say to him! I wanted again to introduce the subject of Grace Poole, and to hear what he would answer; I wanted to ask him plainly if he really believed it was she who had made last night’s hideous attempt; and if so, why he kept her wickedness a secret. It little mattered whether my curiosity irritated him; I knew the pleasure of vexing and soothing him by turns; it was one I chiefly delighted in, and a sure instinct always prevented me from going too far; beyond the verge of provocation I never ventured; on the extreme brink I liked well to try my skill. Retaining every minute form of respect, every propriety of my station, I could still meet him in argument without fear or uneasy restraint; this suited both him and me.
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input:
Furthermore, I could not forget his expression and his pallor when he whispered, "Jane, I have received a blow—I have received a blow, Jane." Additionally, I could not forget how the arm that he rested upon my shoulder had trembled; moreover, it was no insignificant matter that could thus subdue the resolute spirit and agitate the vigorous frame of Fairfax Rochester.

"When will he come? When will he come?" I cried inwardly, as the night persisted and persisted—as my bleeding patient declined, moaned, and grew ill; and neither day nor assistance arrived. It is worth noting that I had, repeatedly, held the water to Mason's pale lips; repeatedly, I had offered him the stimulating salts: my efforts appeared ineffectual; whether bodily or mental suffering, or loss of blood, or all three combined, were rapidly overwhelming his strength. In essence, he moaned so, and appeared so weak, wild, and lost, that I feared he was dying; and I might not even speak to him.
output:
Oh! I could not forget his look and his paleness when he whispered: “Jane, I have got a blow - I have got a blow, Jane.” I could not forget how the arm had trembled which he rested on my shoulder: and it was no light matter which could thus bow the resolute spirit and thrill the vigorous frame of Fairfax Rochester.

“When will he come? When will he come?” I cried inwardly, as the night lingered and lingered - as my bleeding patient drooped, moaned, sickened: and neither day nor aid arrived. I had, again and again, held the water to Mason’s white lips; again and again offered him the stimulating salts: my efforts seemed ineffectual: either bodily or mental suffering, or loss of blood, or all three combined, were fast prostrating his strength. He moaned so, and looked so weak, wild, and lost, I feared he was dying; and I might not even speak to him.

author: Charlotte Bronte

input: And, Miss Eyre, I was so flattered by this preference of the French sylph for her British gnome that I set her up in a hotel and gave her a complete household of servants, a carriage, cashmere shawls, diamonds, lace, and so on. In short, I began to ruin myself in the accepted style, like any other sentimental fool. It seems I did not have the originality to mark out a new road to shame and destruction, but instead trod the old track with a stupid exactness, never deviating an inch from the beaten centre. I had, as I deserved to have, the fate of all other such fools. Happening to call one evening when Céline did not expect me, I found her out; but it was a warm night, and I was tired from strolling through Paris, so I sat down in her boudoir, happy to breathe the air she had so lately occupied. No—I exaggerate; I never thought there was any sacred quality about her. It was rather a sort of pastille perfume she had left, a scent of musk and amber, than an odour of sanctity. I was just beginning to stifle in the fumes of hothouse flowers and sprinkled essences when I thought to open the window and step out onto the balcony. It was moonlight and gaslight besides, and very still and serene. The balcony had a chair or two; I sat down and took out a cigar—I will take one now, if you will excuse me.
output: “And, Miss Eyre, so much was I flattered by this preference of the Gallic sylph for her British gnome, that I installed her in an hotel; gave her a complete establishment of servants, a carriage, cashmeres, diamonds, dentelles, &c. In short, I began the process of ruining myself in the received style, like any other spoony. I had not, it seems, the originality to chalk out a new road to shame and destruction, but trode the old track with stupid exactness not to deviate an inch from the beaten centre. I had - as I deserved to have - the fate of all other spoonies. Happening to call one evening when Céline did not expect me, I found her out; but it was a warm night, and I was tired with strolling through Paris, so I sat down in her boudoir; happy to breathe the air consecrated so lately by her presence. No, - I exaggerate; I never thought there was any consecrating virtue about her: it was rather a sort of pastille perfume she had left; a scent of musk and amber, than an odour of sanctity. I was just beginning to stifle with the fumes of conservatory flowers and sprinkled essences, when I bethought myself to open the window and step out on to the balcony. It was moonlight and gaslight besides, and very still and serene. The balcony was furnished with a chair or two; I sat down, and took out a cigar, - I will take one now, if you will excuse me.”
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input:
A gentle sound of rising became discernible; the curtain was drawn back from the archway, revealing the dining room, where a radiant light illuminated the silver and glass of an exquisite dessert service adorning a long table. A group of ladies stood at the entrance; they proceeded to enter, and the curtain fell behind them.

Although there were only eight, their collective presence created an illusion of a significantly larger assembly. Some were notably tall, many wore white garments, and all possessed a flowing elegance in their attire that seemed to enhance their figures, much like a mist amplifies the appearance of the moon. I rose and performed a courteous curtsey to them; one or two inclined their heads in acknowledgment, while the others regarded me with mere curiosity.
output:
A soft sound of rising now became audible; the curtain was swept back from the arch; through it appeared the dining-room, with its lit lustre pouring down light on the silver and glass of a magnificent dessert-service covering a long table; a band of ladies stood in the opening; they entered, and the curtain fell behind them.

There were but eight; yet, somehow, as they flocked in, they gave the impression of a much larger number. Some of them were very tall; many were dressed in white; and all had a sweeping amplitude of array that seemed to magnify their persons as a mist magnifies the moon. I rose and curtseyed to them: one or two bent their heads in return, the others only stared at me.
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input:
It is unpleasant and yet, I find myself drawn to you once more. I believe I will continue to feel this way, and I will compel you to admit that my feelings extend beyond mere liking; I truly love you with sincerity, intensity, and unwavering devotion.

I become quite discontented with women who only appeal to me based on their appearances. When I discover they lack depth, emotional richness, and intellect, I see only a landscape of dullness, superficiality, and perhaps ignorance, rudeness, and a lack of kindness. In contrast, I am always nurturing and loyal to those with clarity of thought and the ability to communicate well. I admire a soul that is passionate and a character that is both flexible and resilient—one that is adaptable yet steadfast, compliant yet reliable.
output:
“Distasteful! and like you again! I think I shall like you again, and yet again: and I will make you confess I do not only like, but love you - with truth, fervour, constancy.”

“To women who please me only by their faces, I am the very devil when I find out they have neither souls nor hearts - when they open to me a perspective of flatness, triviality, and perhaps imbecility, coarseness, and ill-temper: but to the clear eye and eloquent tongue, to the soul made of fire, and the character that bends but does not break - at once supple and stable, tractable and consistent - I am ever tender and true.”
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input: Additionally, it is essential to address the central issue regarding your departure from England and your collaboration with me in my future endeavors. It is clear that you harbor no objections, as you have essentially committed yourself to this course of action; your consistency precludes any withdrawal at this juncture. You must maintain a singular focus on how best to accomplish the work you have undertaken. It is advisable to simplify your complex array of interests, emotions, thoughts, desires, and objectives, consolidating all considerations into one overarching aim: to effectively and powerfully fulfill the mission of your esteemed Master. To accomplish this, it is imperative that you have a partner—not merely a brother, as that relationship is too tenuous—but rather a husband. Furthermore, I too do not seek a sister, as such a bond could be severed at any moment. I desire a wife, the sole companion whom I can influence effectively throughout my life and retain unconditionally until death.
output: “Well - well. To the main point - the departure with me from England, the co-operation with me in my future labours - you do not object. You have already as good as put your hand to the plough: you are too consistent to withdraw it. You have but one end to keep in view - how the work you have undertaken can best be done. Simplify your complicated interests, feelings, thoughts, wishes, aims; merge all considerations in one purpose: that of fulfilling with effect - with power - the mission of your great Master. To do so, you must have a coadjutor: not a brother - that is a loose tie - but a husband. I, too, do not want a sister: a sister might any day be taken from me. I want a wife: the sole helpmeet I can influence efficiently in life, and retain absolutely till death.”
title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Bronte

input:
She expressed her surprise at having forgotten, shaking her head as if in disbelief. She acknowledged her own thoughtlessness and asked for forgiveness, noting that he had valid reasons for not engaging in conversation. She mentioned that Diana and Mary had left, that Moor House was closed, and that he must be feeling quite lonely. She offered her sympathy and invited him to visit her father. 

Mr. St. John responded in a manner that seemed robotic, revealing the internal struggle he faced in declining her invitation.
output:
“I forgot!” she exclaimed, shaking her beautiful curled head, as if shocked at herself. “I am so giddy and thoughtless! Do excuse me. It had slipped my memory that you have good reasons to be indisposed for joining in my chatter. Diana and Mary have left you, and Moor House is shut up, and you are so lonely. I am sure I pity you. Do come and see papa.”

Mr. St. John spoke almost like an automaton: himself only knew the effort it cost him thus to refuse.
title: Jane Eyre

Yet despite all this, I remember feeling convinced that I had been greatly mistaken in him, and that he was a sensible, practical, and good-hearted prime fellow.
output:
At about this time, I began to observe that he was getting flushed in the face; as to myself, I felt all face, steeped in wine and smarting.

I mentioned to Mr. Pumblechook that I wished to have my new clothes sent to his house, and he was ecstatic on my so distinguishing him. I mentioned my reason for desiring to avoid observation in the village, and he lauded it to the skies. There was nobody but himself, he intimated, worthy of my confidence, and - in short, might he? Then he asked me tenderly if I remembered our boyish games at sums, and how we had gone together to have me bound apprentice, and, in effect, how he had ever been my favourite fancy and my chosen friend? If I had taken ten times as many glasses of wine as I had, I should have known that he never had stood in that relation towards me, and should in my heart of hearts have repudiated the idea. Yet for all that, I remember feeling convinced that I had been much mistaken in him, and that he was a sensible, practical, good-hearted prime fellow.

input:
Herbert greeted me warmly, making me acutely aware of the joy of friendship. After he offered some comforting words of sympathy and encouragement, we sat down to discuss the pressing question of what to do next.

Provis’s chair remained in the same spot he had left it, as he had a tendency to linger in one place, moving through his routine with his pipe, his figurine, his jackknife, and his deck of cards, as if everything was predetermined. Herbert, without realizing it, took the chair, but quickly stood up, pushed it away, and chose a different one. There was no need for either of us to express our mutual dislike for my patron; we shared that understanding without needing to say a word.
output:
Herbert received me with open arms, and I had never felt before so blessedly what it is to have a friend. When he had spoken some sound words of sympathy and encouragement, we sat down to consider the question, What was to be done?

The chair that Provis had occupied still remaining where it had stood, - for he had a barrack way with him of hanging about one spot, in one unsettled manner, and going through one round of observances with his pipe and his negro-head and his jackknife and his pack of cards, and what not, as if it were all put down for him on a slate, - I say his chair remaining where it had stood, Herbert unconsciously took it, but next moment started out of it, pushed it away, and took another. He had no occasion to say after that that he had conceived an aversion for my patron, neither had I occasion to confess my own. We interchanged that confidence without shaping a syllable.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input:
I do not think I was mistaken in feeling that there was a quiet dignity about him. The style of his clothes could no more lessen the effect of his words than it could in Heaven. He touched me gently on the forehead and went out. As soon as I had recovered enough, I hurried after him and looked for him in the nearby streets, but he was gone.

It seemed clear that I must go back to our town the next day, and in my first rush of regret I felt just as sure that I must stay at Joe’s. But after I had reserved my seat in tomorrow’s coach and had gone down to Mr. Pocket’s and back, I was not at all sure about that last point, and I began to invent reasons and make excuses for staying at the Blue Boar instead. I might be an inconvenience at Joe’s; I was not expected, and my bed might not be ready; I would be too far from Miss Havisham’s, and she could be demanding and might not like it. All the other cheats in the world are nothing compared with people who cheat themselves, and it was with such excuses that I deceived myself. It is certainly a strange thing. If I innocently accepted a bad half-crown made by someone else, that would be understandable enough; but it is another matter that I could knowingly treat the false coin of my own making as good money. A helpful stranger might pretend to fold up my bank-notes for safety and then take the notes and give me nutshells; but his trick is nothing compared with mine, when I fold up my own nutshells and pass them off to myself as notes.
output:
I had not been mistaken in my fancy that there was a simple dignity in him. The fashion of his dress could no more come in its way when he spoke these words than it could come in its way in Heaven. He touched me gently on the forehead, and went out. As soon as I could recover myself sufficiently, I hurried out after him and looked for him in the neighbouring streets; but he was gone.

It was clear that I must repair to our town next day, and in the first flow of my repentance, it was equally clear that I must stay at Joe’s. But, when I had secured my box-place by to-morrow’s coach, and had been down to Mr. Pocket’s and back, I was not by any means convinced on the last point, and began to invent reasons and make excuses for putting up at the Blue Boar. I should be an inconvenience at Joe’s; I was not expected, and my bed would not be ready; I should be too far from Miss Havisham’s, and she was exacting and mightn’t like it. All other swindlers upon earth are nothing to the self-swindlers, and with such pretences did I cheat myself. Surely a curious thing. That I should innocently take a bad half-crown of somebody else’s manufacture is reasonable enough; but that I should knowingly reckon the spurious coin of my own make as good money! An obliging stranger, under pretence of compactly folding up my bank-notes for security’s sake, abstracts the notes and gives me nutshells; but what is his sleight of hand to mine, when I fold up my own nutshells and pass them on myself as notes!

input: I lived what was, in many ways, an unhappy life, and one dominant anxiety tended to overshadow all my other worries, much like a high mountain rising above a range of mountains, and it rarely left my thoughts. Still, no new reason for fear seemed to arise. I might start up from my bed with the fresh terror that he had been discovered; I might sit listening with dread for Herbert's returning step at night, in case it should be quicker than usual and seem to bring bad news—yet despite all that, and much more of the same kind, the ordinary course of things tended to go on. Condemned to inaction and to a state of constant restlessness and suspense, I would row about in my boat and wait, and wait, and wait, as best I could. Overall, my life at that time was marked by persistent anxiety and a wearying, uncertain waiting.
output: It was an unhappy life that I lived; and its one dominant anxiety, towering over all its other anxieties, like a high mountain above a range of mountains, never disappeared from my view. Still, no new cause for fear arose. Let me start from my bed as I would, with the terror fresh upon me that he was discovered; let me sit listening, as I would with dread, for Herbert’s returning step at night, lest it should be fleeter than ordinary, and winged with evil news, - for all that, and much more to like purpose, the round of things went on. Condemned to inaction and a state of constant restlessness and suspense, I rowed about in my boat, and waited, waited, waited, as I best could.
