input: I stopped by the office to ask whether Mr. Jaggers had arrived yet, and when I found he had not, I wandered out again. This time, I walked the length of Little Britain and turned into Bartholomew Close, where I noticed that other people were waiting for Mr. Jaggers as well. Two men of secretive appearance were lounging in the close, thoughtfully fitting their feet into the cracks of the pavement as they talked; one of them remarked to the other, as they first passed me, that "Jaggers would do it if it was to be done." A group of three men and two women stood at a corner, and one of the women was weeping into her dirty shawl, while the other comforted her, pulling her own shawl over her shoulders and saying, "Jaggers is for him, 'Melia, and what more could you have?" A red-eyed little Jewish man entered the close while I lingered there, accompanied by a second Jewish man whom he sent on an errand; while the messenger was away, I observed this man, who was of a highly excitable temperament, performing a jig of anxiety beneath a lamp-post and accompanying himself in a kind of frenzy with the words, "O Jaggerth, Jaggerth, Jaggerth! all otherth ith Cag-Maggerth, give me Jaggerth!" These demonstrations of my guardian's popularity made a deep impression on me, and I admired and wondered more than ever.
output: I dropped into the office to ask if Mr. Jaggers had come in yet, and I found he had not, and I strolled out again. This time, I made the tour of Little Britain, and turned into Bartholomew Close; and now I became aware that other people were waiting about for Mr. Jaggers, as well as I. There were two men of secret appearance lounging in Bartholomew Close, and thoughtfully fitting their feet into the cracks of the pavement as they talked together, one of whom said to the other when they first passed me, that “Jaggers would do it if it was to be done.” There was a knot of three men and two women standing at a corner, and one of the women was crying on her dirty shawl, and the other comforted her by saying, as she pulled her own shawl over her shoulders, “Jaggers is for him, ’Melia, and what more could you have?” There was a red-eyed little Jew who came into the Close while I was loitering there, in company with a second little Jew whom he sent upon an errand; and while the messenger was gone, I remarked this Jew, who was of a highly excitable temperament, performing a jig of anxiety under a lamp-post and accompanying himself, in a kind of frenzy, with the words, “O Jaggerth, Jaggerth, Jaggerth! all otherth ith Cag-Maggerth, give me Jaggerth!” These testimonies to the popularity of my guardian made a deep impression on me, and I admired and wondered more than ever.

I mentioned that we played with flags. It is noteworthy that I recall the falsehoods I told on this occasion with a sense of astonishment. Furthermore, I continued to elaborate on the details of the event. Estella waved a blue flag, while I waved a red one, and Miss Havisham waved a flag covered in small gold stars from the coach window. Additionally, we all waved our swords and cheered.

Mr. Pumblechook nodded gravely and acknowledged that my account was accurate, stating that he had witnessed this himself. Consequently, both he and my mother stared at me intently. Meanwhile, I maintained a facade of innocence and stared back at them. Moreover, I busied myself by braiding the right leg of my trousers with my right hand, attempting to appear nonchalant.
output:
“We played with flags,” I said. (I beg to observe that I think of myself with amazement, when I recall the lies I told on this occasion.)

“Yes,” said I. “Estella waved a blue flag, and I waved a red one, and Miss Havisham waved one sprinkled all over with little gold stars, out at the coach-window. And then we all waved our swords and hurrahed.”

“That’s true, Mum,” said Mr. Pumblechook, with a grave nod. “That’s the state of the case, for that much I’ve seen myself.” And then they both stared at me, and I, with an obtrusive show of artlessness on my countenance, stared at them, and plaited the right leg of my trousers with my right hand.

input:
I approached the forge with a hint of apprehension, unsure of the reason, and eventually caught sight of it, only to find it closed. There was no flicker of fire, no bright sparks flying, and no sound of bellows; everything was quiet and still.

However, the house was not unoccupied, as the best parlor appeared to be in use. I noticed white curtains gently moving in the open window, which was adorned with cheerful flowers. As I quietly approached, intending to peek over the flowers, I found Joe and Biddy standing together, arm in arm, greeting me.
output:
Almost fearing, without knowing why, to come in view of the forge, I saw it at last, and saw that it was closed. No gleam of fire, no glittering shower of sparks, no roar of bellows; all shut up, and still.

But the house was not deserted, and the best parlour seemed to be in use, for there were white curtains fluttering in its window, and the window was open and gay with flowers. I went softly towards it, meaning to peep over the flowers, when Joe and Biddy stood before me, arm in arm.

author: Charles Dickens

input: The young conductress secured the gate, and we proceeded across the courtyard. The courtyard was clean and paved, yet grass was growing in every crevice. There was a narrow lane connecting the brewery buildings, and the wooden gates of this lane were open, revealing the empty and unused brewery extending up to the high enclosing wall. The cold wind felt even colder in this area compared to outside the gate, producing a shrill sound as it whistled through the open sides of the brewery, reminiscent of wind in the rigging of a ship at sea. This suggests an atmosphere of desolation and abandonment in the surroundings.
output: My young conductress locked the gate, and we went across the courtyard. It was paved and clean, but grass was growing in every crevice. The brewery buildings had a little lane of communication with it, and the wooden gates of that lane stood open, and all the brewery beyond stood open, away to the high enclosing wall; and all was empty and disused. The cold wind seemed to blow colder there than outside the gate; and it made a shrill noise in howling in and out at the open sides of the brewery, like the noise of wind in the rigging of a ship at sea.

author: Charles Dickens

I aimed to share what I learned with Joe. This reflects my intention to help him become less ignorant and more sophisticated, thereby making him more suitable for my company and less susceptible to Estella's criticism. 

Our learning took place at the old Battery on the marshes, where our tools consisted of a broken slate and a small piece of slate-pencil, complemented by Joe’s customary pipe of tobacco. Despite my efforts, Joe did not seem to retain any knowledge from one Sunday to the next, nor did he gain any significant information under my guidance. However, he would smoke his pipe at the Battery with a demeanor that suggested he felt more knowledgeable there than in any other setting, almost as if he believed he was making considerable progress. Ultimately, I hope that he felt he was.
output:
Whatever I acquired, I tried to impart to Joe. This statement sounds so well, that I cannot in my conscience let it pass unexplained. I wanted to make Joe less ignorant and common, that he might be worthier of my society and less open to Estella’s reproach.

The old Battery out on the marshes was our place of study, and a broken slate and a short piece of slate-pencil were our educational implements: to which Joe always added a pipe of tobacco. I never knew Joe to remember anything from one Sunday to another, or to acquire, under my tuition, any piece of information whatever. Yet he would smoke his pipe at the Battery with a far more sagacious air than anywhere else, - even with a learned air, - as if he considered himself to be advancing immensely. Dear fellow, I hope he did.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that approximately a month subsequent to my sister's reappearance in the kitchen, Biddy arrived at our residence with a small, speckled box containing all of her personal belongings, and her presence proved to be a significant benefit to the household. Furthermore, she was particularly advantageous to Joe, as the poor man had been deeply distressed by the constant contemplation of his wife's deteriorated condition, and had developed a habit of occasionally turning to me in the evening, while attending to her, and remarking, with his eyes moistened, that she had once been a woman of considerable physical attractiveness. Moreover, Biddy immediately assumed a highly competent and nurturing role in relation to her, as if she had been familiar with her needs since childhood; consequently, Joe was able to appreciate the greater tranquility that characterized his life, and to periodically visit the Jolly Bargemen, which provided him with a beneficial change of environment. In essence, it is notable that the individuals associated with the police had, to some extent, harbored suspicions regarding Joe's character, albeit without his knowledge, and had unanimously regarded him as a person of remarkable intelligence and depth.
output: It may have been about a month after my sister’s reappearance in the kitchen, when Biddy came to us with a small speckled box containing the whole of her worldly effects, and became a blessing to the household. Above all, she was a blessing to Joe, for the dear old fellow was sadly cut up by the constant contemplation of the wreck of his wife, and had been accustomed, while attending on her of an evening, to turn to me every now and then and say, with his blue eyes moistened, “Such a fine figure of a woman as she once were, Pip!” Biddy instantly taking the cleverest charge of her as though she had studied her from infancy; Joe became able in some sort to appreciate the greater quiet of his life, and to get down to the Jolly Bargemen now and then for a change that did him good. It was characteristic of the police people that they had all more or less suspected poor Joe (though he never knew it), and that they had to a man concurred in regarding him as one of the deepest spirits they had ever encountered.

“Well,” Joe said thoughtfully, not that it was really necessary to think about it, but because it was customary at the Jolly Bargemen to appear as though one was deeply considering every topic discussed over drinks, “well - no. No, he isn’t.” 

“What on earth is he?” the stranger asked, which seemed to me to be an unnecessarily forceful question.

Mr. Wopsle then chimed in, as someone who often discussed relationships and was mindful of which female relatives a man could not marry. He elaborated on the connections between Joe and me. After sharing his insights, Mr. Wopsle concluded with a rather dramatic quote from Richard the Third, appearing to believe that this was sufficient explanation when he added, “- as the poet says.” 

In summary, the conversation involved some thoughtful considerations and a touch of theatrical flair from Mr. Wopsle.
output:
“Well,” said Joe, meditatively, not, of course, that it could be in anywise necessary to consider about it, but because it was the way at the Jolly Bargemen to seem to consider deeply about everything that was discussed over pipes, - “well - no. No, he ain’t.”

“What the Blue Blazes is he?” asked the stranger. Which appeared to me to be an inquiry of unnecessary strength.

Mr. Wopsle struck in upon that; as one who knew all about relationships, having professional occasion to bear in mind what female relations a man might not marry; and expounded the ties between me and Joe. Having his hand in, Mr. Wopsle finished off with a most terrifically snarling passage from Richard the Third, and seemed to think he had done quite enough to account for it when he added, “ - as the poet says.”
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input: At the far end of the brewery, there was a neglected garden enclosed by an old wall. It was not too high, allowing me to climb up and catch a glimpse of the garden, which was filled with overgrown weeds. However, there was a visible path winding through the greenery, suggesting that someone had walked there recently. I noticed Estella walking away from me at that moment. Her presence felt pervasive. When I succumbed to the temptation to walk along the casks, I saw her again at the end of the yard, facing away from me. She held her brown hair in both hands and did not turn around before disappearing from my sight. Inside the brewery, a large, high-paved area where beer was once made, I initially felt overwhelmed by its somber atmosphere as I stood near the entrance. I then saw her moving among the extinguished fires and ascending a set of light iron stairs, exiting through a gallery above, which gave the impression she was stepping into the sky.
output: Behind the furthest end of the brewery, was a rank garden with an old wall; not so high but that I could struggle up and hold on long enough to look over it, and see that the rank garden was the garden of the house, and that it was overgrown with tangled weeds, but that there was a track upon the green and yellow paths, as if some one sometimes walked there, and that Estella was walking away from me even then. But she seemed to be everywhere. For when I yielded to the temptation presented by the casks, and began to walk on them, I saw her walking on them at the end of the yard of casks. She had her back towards me, and held her pretty brown hair spread out in her two hands, and never looked round, and passed out of my view directly. So, in the brewery itself, - by which I mean the large paved lofty place in which they used to make the beer, and where the brewing utensils still were. When I first went into it, and, rather oppressed by its gloom, stood near the door looking about me, I saw her pass among the extinguished fires, and ascend some light iron stairs, and go out by a gallery high overhead, as if she were going out into the sky.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input: Miss Havisham interjected, directing Jaggers to leave me alone and accompany him to dinner, which he agreed to do. As we made our way down the dimly lit stairs together, he inquired about how often I had witnessed Miss Havisham eating and drinking, offering a wide range of possibilities from many times to just once. He then replied, with a slight frown, that she would never permit anyone to see her engage in either activity since she began her current way of living. This suggests that she prefers to roam at night and discreetly take whatever food she needs.
output:
“Jaggers,” interposed Miss Havisham, much to my relief, “leave my Pip alone, and go with him to your dinner.”

He complied, and we groped our way down the dark stairs together. While we were still on our way to those detached apartments across the paved yard at the back, he asked me how often I had seen Miss Havisham eat and drink; offering me a breadth of choice, as usual, between a hundred times and once.

“And never will, Pip,” he retorted, with a frowning smile. “She has never allowed herself to be seen doing either, since she lived this present life of hers. She wanders about in the night, and then lays hands on such food as she takes.”
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input:
Additionally, it is worth noting that I was never permitted to have a candle to illuminate my path to bed, and as I ascended the stairs in darkness, with my head still reeling from the effects of Mrs. Joe's thimble being used to strike me, thereby accompanying her parting words, I was intensely aware of the considerable convenience that the prison ships posed for me. Moreover, it seemed evident that I was destined for such a fate. I had initiated a sequence of events by posing questions, and subsequently, I was progressing towards committing a serious transgression against Mrs. Joe.

Furthermore, since that period, which is now sufficiently distant, I have frequently reflected on the fact that few individuals are aware of the secrecy that exists among the young when they are subjected to intense fear. In essence, the reasonableness of the fear is of little consequence, as long as the fear itself is present. I was consumed by an overwhelming sense of dread in relation to the young man who had expressed a desire for my vital organs; I was also filled with mortal terror in response to my interlocutor with the iron leg; moreover, I was afraid of my own self, from whom a solemn promise had been extracted. It is worth noting that I had no expectation of rescue or deliverance through the agency of my sister, who consistently rejected me. Additionally, I am reluctant to contemplate the potential actions I might have taken, had I been required to do so, given the secrecy and intensity of my fear.
output:
I was never allowed a candle to light me to bed, and, as I went upstairs in the dark, with my head tingling, - from Mrs. Joe’s thimble having played the tambourine upon it, to accompany her last words, - I felt fearfully sensible of the great convenience that the hulks were handy for me. I was clearly on my way there. I had begun by asking questions, and I was going to rob Mrs. Joe.

Since that time, which is far enough away now, I have often thought that few people know what secrecy there is in the young under terror. No matter how unreasonable the terror, so that it be terror. I was in mortal terror of the young man who wanted my heart and liver; I was in mortal terror of my interlocutor with the iron leg; I was in mortal terror of myself, from whom an awful promise had been extracted; I had no hope of deliverance through my all-powerful sister, who repulsed me at every turn; I am afraid to think of what I might have done on requirement, in the secrecy of my terror.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input: During this period, I was unable to reflect on my own circumstances, and this remained the case. I lacked the capacity to focus on my situation. Furthermore, I was experiencing significant emotional distress, although it was a vague and general feeling. Additionally, I was not capable of developing a plan for the future, as it was completely beyond my abilities at that time. As I opened the shutters and observed the damp and gloomy morning, which appeared dull and gray, I felt a sense of misery. Moreover, as I walked through the rooms or sat shivering by the fire, waiting for my laundress to arrive, I couldn't help but think about my unhappy state. Nevertheless, I had difficulty understanding the reasons for my misery, or even recalling the duration of my distress, the current day of the week, or my own identity at that moment.
output: All this time I had never been able to consider my own situation, nor could I do so yet. I had not the power to attend to it. I was greatly dejected and distressed, but in an incoherent wholesale sort of way. As to forming any plan for the future, I could as soon have formed an elephant. When I opened the shutters and looked out at the wet wild morning, all of a leaden hue; when I walked from room to room; when I sat down again shivering, before the fire, waiting for my laundress to appear; I thought how miserable I was, but hardly knew why, or how long I had been so, or on what day of the week I made the reflection, or even who I was that made it.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input: They maintained a state of silence around me throughout the day, consistently ensuring that my arm remained properly dressed while providing me with cooling beverages. Each time I dozed off, I would awaken with the impression that a considerable amount of time had passed and that the chance to rescue him had slipped away. Around midnight, I rose from my bed and approached Herbert, firmly believing that I had been asleep for a full twenty-four hours and that Wednesday had already concluded. This represented the final exertion of my unease, for thereafter I fell into a deep and uninterrupted sleep.
output: They kept me very quiet all day, and kept my arm constantly dressed, and gave me cooling drinks. Whenever I fell asleep, I awoke with the notion I had had in the sluice-house, that a long time had elapsed and the opportunity to save him was gone. About midnight I got out of bed and went to Herbert, with the conviction that I had been asleep for four-and-twenty hours, and that Wednesday was past. It was the last self-exhausting effort of my fretfulness, for after that I slept soundly.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input:
It started as soon as we sat down for dinner. Mr. Wopsle delivered grace with dramatic flair, resembling a blend of a ghost from Hamlet and Richard III. He concluded with a commendable wish for genuine gratitude. At that moment, my sister turned her gaze toward me and remarked in a soft, reproachful tone, "Do you hear that? Be grateful."

Mrs. Hubble shook her head and regarded me with a somber sense of foreboding about my future. She inquired, "Why is it that the young are never grateful?" This philosophical question seemed to baffle the others until Mr. Hubble succinctly provided an answer: "Naturally vicious." Everyone responded with murmurs of "True!" and directed uncomfortable and personal looks at me.
output:
It began the moment we sat down to dinner. Mr. Wopsle said grace with theatrical declamation, - as it now appears to me, something like a religious cross of the Ghost in Hamlet with Richard the Third, - and ended with the very proper aspiration that we might be truly grateful. Upon which my sister fixed me with her eye, and said, in a low reproachful voice, “Do you hear that? Be grateful.”

Mrs. Hubble shook her head, and contemplating me with a mournful presentiment that I should come to no good, asked, “Why is it that the young are never grateful?” This moral mystery seemed too much for the company until Mr. Hubble tersely solved it by saying, “Naterally wicious.” Everybody then murmured “True!” and looked at me in a particularly unpleasant and personal manner.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input:
Biddy made considerable efforts to communicate to my sister some understanding of the situation. To the best of my knowledge, these attempts did not succeed. She laughed and nodded her head several times and even echoed Biddy's words, "Pip" and "Property." However, I wonder if these expressions carried any real meaning beyond mere sound, and I cannot help but think that her state of mind may have been quite perplexing. 

I would not have believed it if I had not experienced it myself, but as Joe and Biddy grew more relaxed and cheerful, I found myself becoming rather gloomy. While I certainly could not be dissatisfied with my circumstances, it is possible that I may have felt some discontent with myself, perhaps without fully realizing it. In summary, the contrasting emotions within me highlighted a complex inner struggle.
output:
Infinite pains were then taken by Biddy to convey to my sister some idea of what had happened. To the best of my belief, those efforts entirely failed. She laughed and nodded her head a great many times, and even repeated after Biddy, the words “Pip” and “Property.” But I doubt if they had more meaning in them than an election cry, and I cannot suggest a darker picture of her state of mind.

I never could have believed it without experience, but as Joe and Biddy became more at their cheerful ease again, I became quite gloomy. Dissatisfied with my fortune, of course I could not be; but it is possible that I may have been, without quite knowing it, dissatisfied with myself.
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

input: After we had talked for a short time, Herbert showed me the basket with a compassionate and gentle smile. He explained that it contained poor Clara's supper, which was served out every night. It included her allowance of bread, her slice of cheese, and her rum, which he drank himself. He then pointed out that the basket also held Mr. Barley's breakfast for the following day, served out to be cooked. This consisted of two mutton chops, three potatoes, some split peas, a small amount of flour, two ounces of butter, a pinch of salt, and a generous amount of black pepper. Herbert noted that all of these ingredients were stewed together and taken hot, and he remarked that it seemed like a fine dish for the gout.
output: “Look here,” said Herbert, showing me the basket, with a compassionate and tender smile, after we had talked a little; “here’s poor Clara’s supper, served out every night. Here’s her allowance of bread, and here’s her slice of cheese, and here’s her rum, - which I drink. This is Mr. Barley’s breakfast for to-morrow, served out to be cooked. Two mutton-chops, three potatoes, some split peas, a little flour, two ounces of butter, a pinch of salt, and all this black pepper. It’s stewed up together, and taken hot, and it’s a nice thing for the gout, I should think!”
title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens

Additionally, Miss Havisham had become aware of his presence at the same moment as I, and she, like everyone else, exhibited a certain degree of trepidation in his presence. Furthermore, she made a concerted effort to regain her composure, and stuttered that he was as punctual as he had always been.

Moreover, I informed him of my arrival time, and explained that Miss Havisham had expressed a desire for me to visit and meet Estella. In essence, his response was one of acknowledgement, as he remarked that Estella was a very fine young lady. This language acknowledges the power of the Legislature in this context. In contrast, New York does not include any bills of rights and does not address this issue in its constitution. It has been indicated to me that one or two states may possess bills of rights not included in this collection, but these also generally affirm the legislative authority in this area. In summary, while there are various approaches to the issue of standing armies across states, the legislative authority is often recognized in the context of potential threats to liberty.
output: 1 This statement of the matter is taken from the printed collection of State constitutions. Pennsylvania and North Carolina are the two which contain the interdiction in these words: "As standing armies in time of peace are dangerous to liberty, THEY OUGHT NOT to be kept up." This is, in truth, rather a CAUTION than a PROHIBITION. New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Delaware, and Maryland have, in each of their bills of rights, a clause to this effect: "Standing armies are dangerous to liberty, and ought not to be raised or kept up WITHOUT THE CONSENT OF THE LEGISLATURE"; which is a formal admission of the authority of the Legislature. New York has no bills of rights, and her constitution says not a word about the matter. No bills of rights appear annexed to the constitutions of the other States, except the foregoing, and their constitutions are equally silent. I am told, however that one or two States have bills of rights which do not appear in this collection; but that those also recognize the right of the legislative authority in this respect.

input: It is notable that not only the first Congress but every subsequent Congress, as well as the recent convention, has consistently agreed with the people that America's prosperity depended on its Union. Preserving and perpetuating that Union was the people's great purpose in forming the convention, and it is likewise the great purpose of the plan the convention has recommended they adopt. This highlights the question of why, at this particular time, some men are attempting to diminish the importance of the Union, or why it is suggested that three or four confederacies would be preferable to one. I am convinced that the people have always judged rightly on this matter, and that their universal and consistent attachment to the cause of the Union rests on great and weighty reasons, which I will endeavor to explain in the papers that follow. Those who promote the idea of replacing the convention's plan with a number of separate confederacies appear to recognize clearly that rejecting it would place the Union's continuation in the utmost jeopardy. That would certainly be the case, and I sincerely wish that every good citizen might foresee just as clearly that, whenever the dissolution of the Union comes, America will have reason to exclaim, in the poet's words: "FAREWELL! A LONG FAREWELL TO ALL MY GREATNESS."
output: It is worthy of remark that not only the first, but every succeeding Congress, as well as the late convention, have invariably joined with the people in thinking that the prosperity of America depended on its Union. To preserve and perpetuate it was the great object of the people in forming that convention, and it is also the great object of the plan which the convention has advised them to adopt. With what propriety, therefore, or for what good purposes, are attempts at this particular period made by some men to depreciate the importance of the Union? Or why is it suggested that three or four confederacies would be better than one? I am persuaded in my own mind that the people have always thought right on this subject, and that their universal and uniform attachment to the cause of the Union rests on great and weighty reasons, which I shall endeavor to develop and explain in some ensuing papers. They who promote the idea of substituting a number of distinct confederacies in the room of the plan of the convention, seem clearly to foresee that the rejection of it would put the continuance of the Union in the utmost jeopardy. That certainly would be the case, and I sincerely wish that it may be as clearly foreseen by every good citizen, that whenever the dissolution of the Union arrives, America will have reason to exclaim, in the words of the poet: "FAREWELL! A LONG FAREWELL TO ALL MY GREATNESS."

input: If he were to conduct a careful and critical examination of the Articles of Confederation, his astonishment would not only grow but also include a sense of indignation. He would realize that these articles, while they had cautiously limited the authority of state legislatures, did not impose any restrictions on the federal government. If he were a person of strong emotions, he would likely begin to view the resulting outcry as the deceptive tactics of an unprincipled opposition to a plan that deserved a fair and honest assessment from all true patriots. He might question how the authors of such criticisms could be so quick to condemn a proposal that aligns with the general consensus of American governance and even introduces a powerful safeguard that was absent in previous frameworks. Conversely, if he were more composed and rational, he might simply express disappointment in human nature and lament that a matter of great significance to the happiness of millions should be clouded by tactics that hinder objective judgment. Even a person of calm disposition would likely observe that such behavior seems aimed at misleading the public by stirring their emotions instead of persuading them with reasoned arguments.
output: If he should now apply himself to a careful and critical survey of the articles of Confederation, his astonishment would not only be increased, but would acquire a mixture of indignation, at the unexpected discovery, that these articles, instead of containing the prohibition he looked for, and though they had, with jealous circumspection, restricted the authority of the State legislatures in this particular, had not imposed a single restraint on that of the United States. If he happened to be a man of quick sensibility, or ardent temper, he could now no longer refrain from regarding these clamors as the dishonest artifices of a sinister and unprincipled opposition to a plan which ought at least to receive a fair and candid examination from all sincere lovers of their country! How else, he would say, could the authors of them have been tempted to vent such loud censures upon that plan, about a point in which it seems to have conformed itself to the general sense of America as declared in its different forms of government, and in which it has even superadded a new and powerful guard unknown to any of them? If, on the contrary, he happened to be a man of calm and dispassionate feelings, he would indulge a sigh for the frailty of human nature, and would lament, that in a matter so interesting to the happiness of millions, the true merits of the question should be perplexed and entangled by expedients so unfriendly to an impartial and right determination. Even such a man could hardly forbear remarking, that a conduct of this kind has too much the appearance of an intention to mislead the people by alarming their passions, rather than to convince them by arguments addressed to their understandings.

input: In the observations I have shared so far, my fellow citizens, I have tried to help you guard against any attempts, from whatever source, to influence your decision on a matter of great importance to your welfare through impressions other than those that may arise from the evidence of truth. You will no doubt also have gathered from the general direction of these remarks that they come from a source that is not unfriendly to the new Constitution. Yes, my countrymen, I admit to you that, after giving it careful consideration, I am clearly of the view that it is in your interest to adopt it. I am convinced that this is the safest course for your liberty, your dignity, and your happiness. I do not pretend to have reservations I do not feel. I will not entertain you with an appearance of deliberation when I have already decided. I openly acknowledge my convictions to you, and I will freely lay before you the reasons on which they are based. A awareness of good intentions tends to reject ambiguity. I will not, however, multiply assurances on this point. My motives must remain within my own heart. My arguments will be open to everyone and can be judged by everyone. They will at least be offered in a spirit that will not disgrace the cause of truth, and I hope they may help you weigh this important question with the seriousness it deserves.
output: In the course of the preceding observations, I have had an eye, my fellow-citizens, to putting you upon your guard against all attempts, from whatever quarter, to influence your decision in a matter of the utmost moment to your welfare, by any impressions other than those which may result from the evidence of truth. input: This situation is particularly important in a governmental structure where the laws of the entire system can be undermined by the laws of its individual parts. When local tribunals are granted ultimate jurisdiction, there is the potential for contradictions stemming from differing opinions, as well as concerns arising from local biases and regulations. Each time local regulations come into play, there is a risk that the specific laws may take precedence over the general laws. This highlights the tendency for officials to show a distinct preference for the authority that grants them their power.
output: This is the more necessary where the frame of the government is so compounded that the laws of the whole are in danger of being contravened by the laws of the parts. In this case, if the particular tribunals are invested with a right of ultimate jurisdiction, besides the contradictions to be expected from difference of opinion, there will be much to fear from the bias of local views and prejudices, and from the interference of local regulations. As often as such an interference was to happen, there would be reason to apprehend that the provisions of the particular laws might be preferred to those of the general laws; for nothing is more natural to men in office than to look with peculiar deference towards that authority to which they owe their official existence.

input: The experiment has revealed that the initial expectations were misguided. The observations made indicate that there is a critical need for a fundamental change in the underlying principles of the system. If there is a genuine intention to ensure the Union's effectiveness and longevity, it is necessary to move away from the ineffective approach of legislating for the States as a whole. Instead, the laws of the federal government should be applied directly to individual citizens. The existing plan of quotas and requisitions should be seen as impractical and unfair. Consequently, it is essential for the Union to be granted the full authority to raise military forces, construct and equip naval fleets, and generate the revenue needed to establish and maintain an army and navy, following the standard practices employed by other governments.
output: The experiment has, however, demonstrated that this expectation was ill-founded and illusory; and the observations, made under the last head, will, I imagine, have sufficed to convince the impartial and discerning, that there is an absolute necessity for an entire change in the first principles of the system; that if we are in earnest about giving the Union energy and duration, we must abandon the vain project of legislating upon the States in their collective capacities; we must extend the laws of the federal government to the individual citizens of America; we must discard the fallacious scheme of quotas and requisitions, as equally impracticable and unjust. The result from all this is that the Union ought to be invested with full power to levy troops; to build and equip fleets; and to raise the revenues which will be required for the formation and support of an army and navy, in the customary and ordinary modes practiced in other governments.

input: One concern that may arise is that the outcomes of such appeals might not effectively serve to uphold the constitutional balance of the government. It tends to be observed that republican governments often lean towards an expansion of the legislative branch, sometimes at the expense of the other branches. Consequently, appeals to the populace may typically originate from the executive and judicial branches. However, it is worth considering whether both sides would have equal opportunities during the trial. If we examine their respective situations, we notice that the members of the executive and judiciary are relatively few in number and may only be recognized by a limited segment of the population. Their positions, shaped by how they are appointed and the nature of their roles, can create a distance from the people, which may impact their popularity. In contrast, the legislative members tend to be more numerous and are more integrated into the community. Their connections, whether through family, friendship, or acquaintanceship, often encompass a significant portion of the influential members of society. The nature of their public responsibilities suggests that they hold a more immediate and personal connection with the rights and liberties of the people. Given these circumstances, it seems unlikely that the opposing party would have an equal opportunity for a favorable outcome. Overall, these factors may influence the dynamics of such appeals.
output: But the greatest objection of all is, that the decisions which would probably result from such appeals would not answer the purpose of maintaining the constitutional equilibrium of the government. We have seen that the tendency of republican governments is to an aggrandizement of the legislative at the expense of the other departments. The appeals to the people, therefore, would usually be made by the executive and judiciary departments. But whether made by one side or the other, would each side enjoy equal advantages on the trial? Let us view their different situations. The members of the executive and judiciary departments are few in number, and can be personally known to a small part only of the people. The latter, by the mode of their appointment, as well as by the nature and permanency of it, are too far removed from the people to share much in their prepossessions. The former are generally the objects of jealousy, and their administration is always liable to be discolored and rendered unpopular. The members of the legislative department, on the other hand, are numerous. They are distributed and dwell among the people at large. Their connections of blood, of friendship, and of acquaintance embrace a great proportion of the most influential part of the society. The nature of their public trust implies a personal influence among the people, and that they are more immediately the confidential guardians of the rights and liberties of the people. With these advantages, it can hardly be supposed that the adverse party would have an equal chance for a favorable issue.

input: Before any significant change can occur, it is important to note that the Senate must first compromise its integrity. output: Before such a revolution can be effected, the Senate, it is to be observed, must in the first place corrupt itself; must next corrupt the State legislatures; must then corrupt the House of Representatives; and must finally corrupt the people at large. It is evident that the Senate must be first corrupted before it can attempt an establishment of tyranny. Without corrupting the State legislatures, it cannot prosecute the attempt, because the periodical change of members would otherwise regenerate the whole body. Without exerting the means of corruption with equal success on the House of Representatives, the opposition of that coequal branch of the government would inevitably defeat the attempt; and without corrupting the people themselves, a succession of new representatives would speedily restore all things to their pristine order. Is there any man who can seriously persuade himself that the proposed Senate can, by any possible means within the compass of human address, arrive at the object of a lawless ambition, through all these obstructions?

input: In the Ottoman Empire, the sovereign holds significant authority over the lives and welfare of his subjects but does not possess the power to impose new taxes directly. As a result, he allows provincial governors, known as bashaws, to exploit the populace, extracting funds that the sovereign then uses to address his own needs and those of the state. This situation parallels the decline of the central government in America, which has been eroding towards a state of near collapse. This suggests that the well-being of the citizens in both nations could be significantly enhanced if capable authorities were entrusted with the responsibility of generating the revenue necessary to meet public demands.
output: In the Ottoman or Turkish empire, the sovereign, though in other respects absolute master of the lives and fortunes of his subjects, has no right to impose a new tax. The consequence is that he permits the bashaws or governors of provinces to pillage the people without mercy; and, in turn, squeezes out of them the sums of which he stands in need, to satisfy his own exigencies and those of the state. In America, from a like cause, the government of the Union has gradually dwindled into a state of decay, approaching nearly to annihilation. Who can doubt, that the happiness of the people in both countries would be promoted by competent authorities in the proper hands, to provide the revenues which the necessities of the public might require?

input: It has been noted by various speakers and writers in support of the Constitution that if the federal government's power to tax internally were to prove cumbersome in practice, it may choose to refrain from using it and instead rely on requisitions. In response to this point, some have asked why the government cannot simply omit this power from the outset and rely on requisitions from the start. There are a couple of possible responses to this question. One is that, if it can be done efficiently, exercising the power of internal taxation may often be preferable because it tends to be more effective, and it is difficult to determine beforehand, without actual experience, whether this power cannot be used to good effect - in fact, it seems likely that it can. Another response is that having this power in the Constitution can often lend greater weight to requisitions, as states may be more motivated to take action when they know the Union has the ability to act independently. Overall, the inclusion of internal taxation power in the Constitution may have a number of potential benefits, and its presence can help to make requisitions more effective.
output: It has been very properly observed by different speakers and writers on the side of the Constitution, that if the exercise of the power of internal taxation by the Union should be discovered on experiment to be really inconvenient, the federal government may then forbear the use of it, and have recourse to requisitions in its stead. By way of answer to this, it has been triumphantly asked, Why not in the first instance omit that ambiguous power, and rely upon the latter resource? Two solid answers may be given. The first is, that the exercise of that power, if convenient, will be preferable, because it will be more effectual; and it is impossible to prove in theory, or otherwise than by the experiment, that it cannot be advantageously exercised. The contrary, indeed, appears most probable. The second answer is, that the existence of such a power in the Constitution will have a strong influence in giving efficacy to requisitions. When the States know that the Union can apply itself without their agency, it will be a powerful motive for exertion on their part.

output: The process of election affords a moral certainty, that the office of President will never fall to the lot of any man who is not in an eminent degree endowed with the requisite qualifications. Talents for low intrigue, and the little arts of popularity, may alone suffice to elevate a man to the first honors in a single State; but it will require other talents, and a different kind of merit, to establish him in the esteem and confidence of the whole Union, or of so considerable a portion of it as would be necessary to make him a successful candidate for the distinguished office of President of the United States. input: Additionally, the conclusion that can be deduced from these observations is that a simple declaration of the constitutional boundaries of the various departments on a formal document is not a sufficient safeguard against the encroachments that lead to a tyrannical concentration of all governmental powers in the same hands. Furthermore, it is worth noting that the establishment of a system to prevent the overreach of any one department of government is crucial, and one possible method involves appealing to the people through a convention. In essence, the author of the "Notes on the State of Virginia" has provided a valuable contribution to this discussion, having appended to that work a draft of a constitution that was intended to be presented to a convention, anticipated to be convened in 1783 by the legislature, for the purpose of establishing a constitution for that commonwealth. Moreover, the plan in question exhibits a distinctive and innovative approach to thinking, characterized by its comprehensive and precise nature, and is particularly noteworthy due to its demonstration of a strong commitment to republican governance and a perceptive understanding of the potential dangers against which it should be protected. It is worth noting that one of the precautionary measures proposed by the author, which appears to be a novel concept, is especially relevant to the subject of our current investigation, and therefore should not be disregarded, as it relates to the means of safeguarding the weaker departments of power against the encroachments of the stronger.
output:
The conclusion which I am warranted in drawing from these observations is, that a mere demarcation on parchment of the constitutional limits of the several departments, is not a sufficient guard against those encroachments which lead to a tyrannical concentration of all the powers of government in the same hands.

Method of Guarding Against the Encroachments of Any One Department of Government by Appealing to the People Through a Convention.

THE author of the "Notes on the State of Virginia," quoted in the last paper, has subjoined to that valuable work the draught of a constitution, which had been prepared in order to be laid before a convention, expected to be called in 1783, by the legislature, for the establishment of a constitution for that commonwealth. The plan, like every thing from the same pen, marks a turn of thinking, original, comprehensive, and accurate; and is the more worthy of attention as it equally displays a fervent attachment to republican government and an enlightened view of the dangerous propensities against which it ought to be guarded. One of the precautions which he proposes, and on which he appears ultimately to rely as a palladium to the weaker departments of power against the invasions of the stronger, is perhaps altogether his own, and as it immediately relates to the subject of our present inquiry, ought not to be overlooked.

input: The British system serves as a significant example regarding the nature of political assemblies. In the UK, the Senate, which is hereditary, consists of wealthy nobles and is not elected for a fixed term, unlike the six-year terms seen in other systems. The House of Representatives, on the other hand, has a longer term of seven years but is elected by a relatively small segment of the population, rather than the entire populace, as is common in other democracies. This situation illustrates the potential for aristocratic dominance and tyranny, which some argue could emerge in the United States over time. However, British history suggests that this hereditary assembly was unable to protect its interests against the growing influence of the House of Representatives. Once it lost the backing of the monarch, it was ultimately overwhelmed by the strength of the popular branch.
output: But if anything could silence the jealousies on this subject, it ought to be the British example. The Senate there instead of being elected for a term of six years, and of being unconfined to particular families or fortunes, is an hereditary assembly of opulent nobles. The House of Representatives, instead of being elected for two years, and by the whole body of the people, is elected for seven years, and, in very great proportion, by a very small proportion of the people. Here, unquestionably, ought to be seen in full display the aristocratic usurpations and tyranny which are at some future period to be exemplified in the United States. Unfortunately, however, for the anti-federal argument, the British history informs us that this hereditary assembly has not been able to defend itself against the continual encroachments of the House of Representatives; and that it no sooner lost the support of the monarch, than it was actually crushed by the weight of the popular branch.

The President has the authority to nominate individuals for various positions. These positions include ambassadors, public ministers, consuls, judges of the Supreme Court, and other officers of the United States. The advice and consent of the Senate is required for these appointments, unless otherwise specified in the Constitution. 

Meanwhile, Congress has the option to establish laws that grant the President sole authority to appoint certain inferior officers. Alternatively, Congress may choose to vest this authority in the courts of law or the heads of departments, depending on what they deem appropriate. 

The President also has the power to fill vacancies that arise during the Senate's recess. In such cases, the President can grant commissions that will remain in effect until the end of the Senate's next session. This provision ensures that the government can continue to function smoothly, even when the Senate is not in session.
output: THE President is "to nominate, and, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, judges of the Supreme Court, and all other officers of the United States whose appointments are not otherwise provided for in the Constitution. But the Congress may by law vest the appointment of such inferior officers as they think proper, in the President alone, or in the courts of law, or in the heads of departments. The President shall have power to fill up all vacancies which may happen during the recess of the Senate, by granting commissions which shall expire at the end of their next session."

input: The additional protections that may be offered to republican governance, individual freedoms, and property through the adoption of the proposed plan primarily include the limitations that the preservation of the Union can place on local factions and uprisings, as well as on the ambitions of influential individuals within individual states. These individuals may sometimes gain enough support from leaders and favored groups to potentially dominate the populace. The prevention of large military establishments, which can often arise from conflicts between states in a fragmented scenario, is another consideration. The plan also provides a firm assurance of a republican form of government for each state, completely rules out titles of nobility, and includes measures designed to prevent state governments from engaging in practices that could undermine property rights and public trust. These factors have contributed to a general decline in moral standards among citizens. In summary, the proposed plan offers several potential safeguards to promote stability and uphold democratic principles.
output: The additional securities to republican government, to liberty and to property, to be derived from the adoption of the plan under consideration, consist chiefly in the restraints which the preservation of the Union will impose on local factions and insurrections, and on the ambition of powerful individuals in single States, who may acquire credit and influence enough, from leaders and favorites, to become the despots of the people; in the diminution of the opportunities to foreign intrigue, which the dissolution of the Confederacy would invite and facilitate; in the prevention of extensive military establishments, which could not fail to grow out of wars between the States in a disunited situation; in the express guaranty of a republican form of government to each; in the absolute and universal exclusion of titles of nobility; and in the precautions against the repetition of those practices on the part of the State governments which have undermined the foundations of property and credit, have planted mutual distrust in the breasts of all classes of citizens, and have occasioned an almost universal prostration of morals.

input: It may be somewhat unexpected that during a popular revolution, individuals would find a balanced position that effectively delineates the distinction between power and privilege, thereby harmonizing the authority of governance with the protection of individual rights. A failure to achieve this crucial balance can often lead to various challenges and discomforts that we face. If we are not careful to avoid repeating this mistake in our future efforts to improve our systems, we may find ourselves shifting from one unrealistic idea to another, implementing change after change without making any significant progress toward improvement. In summary, maintaining this balance is essential for meaningful advancement.
output: IT WAS a thing hardly to be expected that in a popular revolution the minds of men should stop at that happy mean which marks the salutary boundary between POWER and PRIVILEGE, and combines the energy of government with the security of private rights. A failure in this delicate and important point is the great source of the inconveniences we experience, and if we are not cautious to avoid a repetition of the error, in our future attempts to rectify and ameliorate our system, we may travel from one chimerical project to another; we may try change after change; but we shall never be likely to make any material change for the better.

output:
Favorable as this view of the subject may be, some observations remain which will place it in a light still more satisfactory.

In the first place it is to be remembered that the general government is not to be charged with the whole power of making and administering laws. Its jurisdiction is limited to certain enumerated objects, which concern all the members of the republic, but which are not to be attained by the separate provisions of any. The subordinate governments, which can extend their care to all those other subjects which can be separately provided for, will retain their due authority and activity. Were it proposed by the plan of the convention to abolish the governments of the particular States, its adversaries would have some ground for their objection; though it would not be difficult to show that if they were abolished the general government would be compelled, by the principle of self-preservation, to reinstate them in their proper jurisdiction.

THE remaining charge against the House of Representatives, which I am to examine, is grounded on a supposition that the number of members will not be augmented from time to time, as the progress of population may demand.

In addition to these difficulties, one must consider the conflicting claims of larger and smaller States. It is reasonable to assume that larger States would seek a level of government participation commensurate with their greater wealth and significance. Conversely, smaller States would be equally protective of the equality they currently enjoy. It is unlikely that either side would fully concede to the other, indicating that any resolution would necessitate compromise. Furthermore, it is highly probable that once the ratio of representation was established, this compromise would lead to renewed conflict between the parties regarding the organization of the government and the allocation of its powers. This struggle would aim to enhance the significance of the branches where each party had gained the most influence. The Constitution contains elements that support these assumptions, suggesting that the convention was forced to prioritize practical considerations over theoretical ideals.
output:
Here, then, are three sources of vague and incorrect definitions: indistinctness of the object, imperfection of the organ of conception, inadequateness of the vehicle of ideas. Any one of these must produce a certain degree of obscurity. The convention, in delineating the boundary between the federal and State jurisdictions, must have experienced the full effect of them all.

To the difficulties already mentioned may be added the interfering pretensions of the larger and smaller States. We cannot err in supposing that the former would contend for a participation in the government, fully proportioned to their superior wealth and importance; and that the latter would not be less tenacious of the equality at present enjoyed by them. We may well suppose that neither side would entirely yield to the other, and consequently that the struggle could be terminated only by compromise. It is extremely probable, also, that after the ratio of representation had been adjusted, this very compromise must have produced a fresh struggle between the same parties, to give such a turn to the organization of the government, and to the distribution of its powers, as would increase the importance of the branches, in forming which they had respectively obtained the greatest share of influence. There are features in the Constitution which warrant each of these suppositions; and as far as either of them is well founded, it shows that the convention must have been compelled to sacrifice theoretical propriety to the force of extraneous considerations.

input: Let us consider the possibility that the definitions outlining the authority of the convention may have been fundamentally at odds with one another. It seems plausible that the convention believed that a national and effective government could not be meaningfully influenced by changes and provisions in the Articles of Confederation. In this context, one might contemplate which aspects of this definition should have been accepted and which should have been dismissed. It raises questions about what holds greater significance and what holds lesser significance. Which serves as the ultimate goal, and which serves merely as a method? Those who meticulously analyze delegated powers and those who consistently oppose the exercises made by the convention may find it helpful to address these inquiries. They might consider whether it was more crucial for the well-being of the American people to disregard the Articles of Confederation in favor of establishing a sufficient government and maintaining the Union, or whether it was more important to retain the Articles and forgo the formation of an adequate government. Additionally, they may reflect on whether the preservation of these articles was intended as the ultimate goal, with the reform of the government being a means to achieve it, or if the establishment of a government that adequately supports national happiness was indeed the intended goal of the articles, which may have warranted their replacement as insufficient tools. In summary, these questions invite thoughtful contemplation of the balance between governance and foundational documents.
output: Suppose, then, that the expressions defining the authority of the convention were irreconcilably at variance with each other; that a NATIONAL and ADEQUATE GOVERNMENT could not possibly, in the judgment of the convention, be affected by ALTERATIONS and PROVISIONS in the ARTICLES OF CONFEDERATION; which part of the definition ought to have been embraced, and which rejected? Which was the more important, which the less important part? Which the end; which the means? Let the most scrupulous expositors of delegated powers; let the most inveterate objectors against those exercised by the convention, answer these questions. Let them declare, whether it was of most importance to the happiness of the people of America, that the articles of Confederation should be disregarded, and an adequate government be provided, and the Union preserved; or that an adequate government should be omitted, and the articles of Confederation preserved. Let them declare, whether the preservation of these articles was the end, for securing which a reform of the government was to be introduced as the means; or whether the establishment of a government, adequate to the national happiness, was the end at which these articles themselves originally aimed, and to which they ought, as insufficient means, to have been sacrificed.

THAT there may happen cases in which the national government may be necessitated to resort to force, cannot be denied. Our own experience has corroborated the lessons taught by the examples of other nations; that emergencies of this sort will sometimes arise in all societies, however constituted; that seditions and insurrections are, unhappily, maladies as inseparable from the body politic as tumors and eruptions from the natural body; that the idea of governing at all times by the simple force of law (which we have been told is the only admissible principle of republican government), has no place but in the reveries of those political doctors whose sagacity disdains the admonitions of experimental instruction.

input: The task of enumerating the specific powers or means that are not necessary or proper for carrying out the general powers would have been highly impractical. Additionally, this approach would have been subject to a significant objection, namely that any omission in the enumeration would have been equivalent to a direct grant of authority. In order to avoid this consequence, an alternative approach could have been to attempt a partial enumeration of the exceptions, describing the remaining powers in general terms, such as those that are not necessary or proper. However, this method would have likely resulted in an enumeration that only includes a limited number of the excepted powers. Furthermore, the powers that would have been included in the enumeration would have been those that are least likely to be assumed or tolerated, as they would have been deemed the least necessary or proper. Meanwhile, the unnecessary and improper powers that are part of the remaining powers would have been less explicitly excluded than if no partial enumeration had been made.
output: Had they attempted to enumerate the particular powers or means not necessary or proper for carrying the general powers into execution, the task would have been no less chimerical; and would have been liable to this further objection, that every defect in the enumeration would have been equivalent to a positive grant of authority. If, to avoid this consequence, they had attempted a partial enumeration of the exceptions, and described the residue by the general terms, NOT NECESSARY OR PROPER, it must have happened that the enumeration would comprehend a few of the excepted powers only; that these would be such as would be least likely to be assumed or tolerated, because the enumeration would of course select such as would be least necessary or proper; and that the unnecessary and improper powers included in the residuum, would be less forcibly excepted, than if no partial enumeration had been made.

Moreover, many individuals were indeed deceived and misled, but the majority of the people reasoned and decided prudently; and they are fortunate in reflecting on the fact that they did so.
output: Admit, for so is the fact, that this plan is only RECOMMENDED, not imposed, yet let it be remembered that it is neither recommended to BLIND approbation, nor to BLIND reprobation; but to that sedate and candid consideration which the magnitude and importance of the subject demand, and which it certainly ought to receive. But this (as was remarked in the foregoing number of this paper) is more to be wished than expected, that it may be so considered and examined. Experience on a former occasion teaches us not to be too sanguine in such hopes. It is not yet forgotten that well-grounded apprehensions of imminent danger induced the people of America to form the memorable Congress of 1774. That body recommended certain measures to their constituents, and the event proved their wisdom; yet it is fresh in our memories how soon the press began to teem with pamphlets and weekly papers against those very measures. Not only many of the officers of government, who obeyed the dictates of personal interest, but others, from a mistaken estimate of consequences, or the undue influence of former attachments, or whose ambition aimed at objects which did not correspond with the public good, were indefatigable in their efforts to persuade the people to reject the advice of that patriotic Congress. Many, indeed, were deceived and deluded, but the great majority of the people reasoned and decided judiciously; and happy they are in reflecting that they did so.

input: From another perspective, an unstable government causes significant harm. A lack of confidence in public councils discourages every useful undertaking whose success and profit may depend on the continuation of existing arrangements. What prudent merchant would risk his fortune in a new branch of commerce when he cannot be sure that his plans will not be made unlawful before they can be carried out? What farmer or manufacturer would invest in the encouragement given to a particular cultivation or establishment when he has no assurance that his preparatory labors and advances will not make him a victim of an inconstant government? Ultimately, no great improvement or worthy enterprise can proceed that requires the support of a steady system of national policy.
output: In another point of view, great injury results from an unstable government. The want of confidence in the public councils damps every useful undertaking, the success and profit of which may depend on a continuance of existing arrangements. What prudent merchant will hazard his fortunes in any new branch of commerce when he knows not but that his plans may be rendered unlawful before they can be executed? What farmer or manufacturer will lay himself out for the encouragement given to any particular cultivation or establishment, when he can have no assurance that his preparatory labors and advances will not render him a victim to an inconstant government? In a word, no great improvement or laudable enterprise can go forward which requires the auspices of a steady system of national policy.

input: The second category of powers, held by the federal government, includes those that govern relations with foreign nations. These powers are to make treaties, to send and receive ambassadors, public ministers, and consuls, and to define and punish acts of piracy and felonies occurring on the high seas, as well as offenses against international law. Additionally, this category encompasses the regulation of foreign commerce, which includes the authority to prohibit the importation of slaves after the year 1808 and to impose an intermediate duty of ten dollars per person to discourage such importations.
output: THE SECOND class of powers, lodged in the general government, consists of those which regulate the intercourse with foreign nations, to wit: to make treaties; to send and receive ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls; to define and punish piracies and felonies committed on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations; to regulate foreign commerce, including a power to prohibit, after the year 1808, the importation of slaves, and to lay an intermediate duty of ten dollars per head, as a discouragement to such importations.

input: Some may argue that the limitation on funding for army support to a two-year period might not be effective, as the Executive could potentially leverage a sufficiently large military force to compel compliance from the populace, thus finding means to sustain operations without legislative approval. However, this raises the question of how it would be possible for the Executive to acquire such a formidable force during peacetime. If we consider that a significant military presence might arise from a domestic uprising or an external conflict, it would then be a situation not addressed by the original concern, which specifically pertains to maintaining troops during peacetime. It is unlikely that many would seriously argue against the necessity of having military forces to suppress a rebellion or defend against an invasion. If, under these circumstances, the defense of the community requires a considerable army that could threaten liberty, this represents a complex situation that cannot be entirely prevented by any form of government. Such a situation could even emerge from a mutual defense agreement, should the need arise for allies to raise a joint force for protection. Overall, the challenges of maintaining liberty in the face of external or internal threats can be quite intricate and often beyond the scope of simple preventative measures.
output: It has been said that the provision which limits the appropriation of money for the support of an army to the period of two years would be unavailing, because the Executive, when once possessed of a force large enough to awe the people into submission, would find resources in that very force sufficient to enable him to dispense with supplies from the acts of the legislature. But the question again recurs, upon what pretense could he be put in possession of a force of that magnitude in time of peace? If we suppose it to have been created in consequence of some domestic insurrection or foreign war, then it becomes a case not within the principles of the objection; for this is levelled against the power of keeping up troops in time of peace. Few persons will be so visionary as seriously to contend that military forces ought not to be raised to quell a rebellion or resist an invasion; and if the defense of the community under such circumstances should make it necessary to have an army so numerous as to hazard its liberty, this is one of those calamities for which there is neither preventative nor cure. It cannot be provided against by any possible form of government; it might even result from a simple league offensive and defensive, if it should ever be necessary for the confederates or allies to form an army for common defense.

input: In the course of the preceding papers, I have endeavored, my fellow citizens, to present to you, in a clear and persuasive manner, the significance of Union for your political safety and well-being. Additionally, I have revealed to you a complex array of dangers to which you would be subjected if you allow the sacred bond that unites the people of America to be severed or dissolved by ambition, avarice, jealousy, or misrepresentation. Furthermore, throughout the inquiry I intend to undertake with you, the truths I aim to convey will receive further validation from facts and arguments that have previously gone unnoticed. Moreover, if the path you must continue to traverse appears to you to be cumbersome or burdensome at times, I encourage you to remember that you seek knowledge on a matter that is of utmost importance to a free people. It is worth noting that the terrain you navigate is inherently vast and that the challenges of this journey have been needlessly complicated by the convolutions created by sophistry. It will be my objective to clear the impediments to your advancement in as concise a manner as possible, without sacrificing substance for expediency.
output: IN THE course of the preceding papers, I have endeavored, my fellow citizens, to place before you, in a clear and convincing light, the importance of Union to your political safety and happiness. I have unfolded to you a complication of dangers to which you would be exposed, should you permit that sacred knot which binds the people of America together be severed or dissolved by ambition or by avarice, by jealousy or by misrepresentation. In the sequel of the inquiry through which I propose to accompany you, the truths intended to be inculcated will receive further confirmation from facts and arguments hitherto unnoticed. If the road over which you will still have to pass should in some places appear to you tedious or irksome, you will recollect that you are in quest of information on a subject the most momentous which can engage the attention of a free people, that the field through which you have to travel is in itself spacious, and that the difficulties of the journey have been unnecessarily increased by the mazes with which sophistry has beset the way. It will be my aim to remove the obstacles from your progress in as compendious a manner as it can be done, without sacrificing utility to despatch.

The convention, it appears, regarded the Senate as the most suitable repository of this significant trust. Individuals who are adept at recognizing the inherent complexities of the matter will exhibit less haste in condemning that perspective and will demonstrate a greater propensity to consider the arguments that may reasonably be assumed to have informed it.

Additionally, one may inquire into the true essence of the institution itself. Is it not intended as a mechanism for a national investigation into the conduct of public officials? If this is indeed the purpose, who better to serve as the inquisitors for the nation than its own representatives? It is not contested that the authority to initiate the inquiry, or in other terms, to propose the impeachment, should reside within one branch of the legislative body. Furthermore, will not the rationale supporting the appropriateness of this arrangement compellingly advocate for the inclusion of the other branch of that body in the inquiry? The model from which the concept of this institution has been derived clearly guided the convention in this direction. In Great Britain, it is the responsibility of the House of Commons to initiate impeachment proceedings, while the House of Lords is tasked with adjudicating those proceedings. Several state constitutions have emulated this practice. Both branches appear to have viewed the impeachment process as a check that the legislative body holds over the executive officials of the government. Is this not the appropriate perspective from which it should be understood?
output:
The convention, it appears, thought the Senate the most fit depositary of this important trust. Those who can best discern the intrinsic difficulty of the thing, will be least hasty in condemning that opinion, and will be most inclined to allow due weight to the arguments which may be supposed to have produced it.

What, it may be asked, is the true spirit of the institution itself? Is it not designed as a method of NATIONAL INQUEST into the conduct of public men? If this be the design of it, who can so properly be the inquisitors for the nation as the representatives of the nation themselves? It is not disputed that the power of originating the inquiry, or, in other words, of preferring the impeachment, ought to be lodged in the hands of one branch of the legislative body. Will not the reasons which indicate the propriety of this arrangement strongly plead for an admission of the other branch of that body to a share of the inquiry? The model from which the idea of this institution has been borrowed, pointed out that course to the convention. In Great Britain it is the province of the House of Commons to prefer the impeachment, and of the House of Lords to decide upon it. Several of the State constitutions have followed the example. As well the latter, as the former, seem to have regarded the practice of impeachments as a bridle in the hands of the legislative body upon the executive servants of the government. Is not this the true light in which it ought to be regarded?
