author: Thomas Paine

input:
It hardly needs to be said that the crown is the dominant element in the English constitution, and it is self-evident that its entire importance comes simply from its role as the source of offices and pensions. This highlights that while we have been wise enough to shut and lock a door against absolute monarchy, we have at the same time been foolish enough to put the crown in possession of the key.

The prejudice of Englishmen in favor of their own system of government by king, lords, and commons arises as much or more from national pride as from reason. Individuals are undoubtedly safer in England than in some other countries, but the will of the king is as much the law of the land in Britain as in France, with this difference: instead of coming directly from his mouth, it is delivered to the people in the more imposing form of an act of parliament. Ultimately, the fate of Charles the First has only made kings more subtle, not more just.
output:
That the crown is this overbearing part in the English constitution needs not be mentioned, and that it derives its whole consequence merely from being the giver of places and pensions is self-evident, wherefore, though we have been wise enough to shut and lock a door against absolute monarchy, we at the same time have been foolish enough to put the crown in possession of the key.

The prejudice of Englishmen, in favour of their own government by king, lords and commons, arises as much or more from national pride than reason. Individuals are undoubtedly safer in England than in some other countries, but the will of the king is as much the law of the land in Britain as in France, with this difference, that instead of proceeding directly from his mouth, it is handed to the people under the more formidable shape of an act of parliament. For the fate of Charles the first, hath only made kings more subtle - not more just.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: The authority of Great Britain over this continent is a form of government that will inevitably come to an end. This highlights the impermanence of the current system, making it difficult for individuals with a serious mindset to find pleasure in contemplating the future. The knowledge that the present constitution is temporary can be a source of concern, particularly for parents who want to ensure a stable future for their children. This suggests that the current government may not be able to provide long-term security for the legacy they wish to leave behind. Ultimately, the fact that the next generation will be burdened with debt raises questions about the responsibility of the current generation to take action. By considering the potential consequences of their decisions, individuals can better understand their duty and make more informed choices. This can be achieved by taking a long-term perspective, looking ahead a few years and considering the potential impact of their actions on future generations.
output: The authority of Great-Britain over this continent, is a form of government, which sooner or later must have an end: And a serious mind can draw no true pleasure by looking forward, under the painful and positive conviction, that what he calls "the present constitution" is merely temporary. As parents, we can have no joy, knowing that this government is not sufficiently lasting to ensure any thing which we may bequeath to posterity: And by a plain method of argument, as we are running the next generation into debt, we ought to do the work of it, otherwise we use them meanly and pitifully. In order to discover the line of our duty rightly, we should take our children in our hand, and fix our station a few years farther into life; that eminence will present a prospect, which a few present fears and prejudices conceal from our sight.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: Almost three thousand years elapsed from the Mosaic account of creation until the Jews, influenced by a national delusion, requested a king. During this time, their government operated as a type of republic, administered by a judge and the elders of the tribes, except in extraordinary circumstances when the Almighty intervened. They had no kings, and it was considered sinful to recognize any being by that title except the Lord of Hosts. When one reflects on the idolatrous reverence given to kings, it becomes understandable that the Almighty, who is protective of His honor, would disapprove of a form of government that so audaciously encroaches upon the prerogatives of heaven.
output: Near three thousand years passed away from the Mosaic account of the creation, till the Jews under a national delusion requested a king. Till then their form of government (except in extraordinary cases, where the Almighty interposed) was a kind of republic administred by a judge and the elders of the tribes. Kings they had none, and it was held sinful to acknowledge any being under that title but the Lord of Hosts. And when a man seriously reflects on the idolatrous homage which is paid to the persons of Kings, he need not wonder, that the Almighty ever jealous of his honor, should disapprove of a form of government which so impiously invades the prerogative of heaven.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: In nearly every aspect of defense, we are well supplied. Hemp grows so abundantly that we have no shortage of cordage. Our iron is superior to that of other countries, and our small arms are equal to any in the world. We can cast cannon whenever we wish, and we produce saltpetre and gunpowder daily. Our knowledge improves by the hour. Resolution is inherent to our character, and courage has never abandoned us. This suggests that we lack nothing essential. Why, then, do we hesitate? From Britain we can expect nothing but ruin. If Britain is once again permitted to govern America, this continent will no longer be worth living in. Jealousies will continually arise, insurrections will constantly occur, and who will step forward to suppress them? Who will risk his life to force his own countrymen into obedience to a foreign power? The dispute between Pennsylvania and Connecticut over certain unlocated lands highlights the weakness of British authority and proves that only Continental authority can regulate Continental matters.
output: In almost every article of defense we abound. Hemp flourishes even to rankness, so that we need not want cordage. Our iron is superior to that of other countries. Our small arms equal to any in the world. Cannon we can cast at pleasure. Saltpetre and gunpowder we are every day producing. Our knowledge is hourly improving. Resolution is our inherent character, and courage hath never yet forsaken us. Wherefore, what is it that we want? Why is it that we hesitate? From Britain we can expect nothing but ruin. If she is once admitted to the government of America again, this Continent will not be worth living in. Jealousies will be always arising; insurrections will be constantly happening; and who will go forth to quell them? Who will venture his life to reduce his own countrymen to a foreign obedience? The difference between Pennsylvania and Connecticut, respecting some unlocated lands, shews the insignificance of a British government, and fully proves, that nothing but Continental authority can regulate Continental matters.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: The king has the authority to veto legislation in England, as any law requires his approval. This raises questions about the appropriateness of a young individual, often just twenty-one years old, having the power to reject laws proposed by millions who are older and more experienced. This situation highlights a certain absurdity in governance. However, it is important to recognize that the context differs significantly between England and America. The king's veto is considerably more perilous in America, where he is less likely to approve legislation aimed at strengthening defense, compared to his approach in England, where he generally supports such measures. Ultimately, the implications of the king's veto in America are much more severe than in England.
output: But the king you will say has a negative in England; the people there can make no laws without his consent. In point of right and good order, there is something very ridiculous, that a youth of twenty-one (which hath often happened) shall say to several millions of people, older and wiser than himself, I forbid this or that act of yours to be law. But in this place I decline this sort of reply, though I will never cease to expose the absurdity of it, and only answer, that England being the King's residence, and America not so, makes quite another case. The king's negative here is ten times more dangerous and fatal than it can be in England, for there he will scarcely refuse his consent to a bill for putting England into as strong a state of defence as possible, and in America he would never suffer such a bill to be passed.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
The king retains significant governing powers, which grants him a negative influence over the legislation of the entire continent. Given his history as a staunch opponent of liberty and his evident desire for arbitrary authority, one must question whether he is a suitable individual to dictate, "You shall make no laws without my approval." It is common knowledge among the inhabitants of America that, under the current constitution, this continent can only enact laws with the king's consent. Furthermore, it is evident that, based on past events, he will permit only those laws that serve his interests. 

The absence of laws in America can enslave us just as effectively as if we were subjected to laws imposed from England. Once matters are settled, it is clear that the full power of the crown will be applied to keep this continent subdued and compliant. Instead of advancing, we risk regressing or becoming embroiled in constant disputes and futile petitions. We are already more empowered than the king desires, and it is likely he will strive to diminish our status in the future. 

To distill the issue to its essence, can a power that is envious of our success be deemed appropriate for governance? Anyone who responds negatively to this question embodies the spirit of independence, which fundamentally revolves around whether we will have the authority to create our own laws or whether the king, our foremost adversary, will dictate, "There will be no laws except those I approve."
output: First. The powers of governing still remaining in the hands of the king, he will have a negative over the whole legislation of this continent. And as he hath shewn himself such an inveterate enemy to liberty, and discovered such a thirst for arbitrary power; is he, or is he not, a proper man to say to these colonies, "You shall make no laws but what I please." And is there any inhabitant in America so ignorant, as not to know, that according to what is called the present constitution, that this continent can make no laws but what the king gives leave to; and is there any man so unwise, as not to see, that (considering what has happened) he will suffer no law to be made here, but such as suit his purpose. We may be as effectually enslaved by the want of laws in America, as by submitting to laws made for us in England. After matters are made up (as it is called) can there be any doubt, but the whole power of the crown will be exerted, to keep this continent as low and humble as possible? Instead of going forward we shall go backward, or be perpetually quarrelling or ridiculously petitioning. - We are already greater than the king wishes us to be, and will he not hereafter endeavour to make us less? To bring the matter to one point. Is the power who is jealous of our prosperity, a proper power to govern us? Whoever says No to this question is an independant, for independancy means no more, than, whether we shall make our own laws, or whether the king, the greatest enemy this continent hath, or can have, shall tell us "there shall be no laws but such as I like."
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: The cause at hand is of significant importance, as it affects a substantial portion of the world. This highlights the fact that the issue is not limited to a single city, country, province, or kingdom, but rather encompasses an entire continent, which is roughly one eighth of the habitable globe. The implications of this cause extend far beyond the present moment, as the outcome will have a lasting impact on future generations. Ultimately, the decisions made now will influence the course of history, affecting people to some degree until the end of time. This period can be seen as a critical time for forming a unified continent, built on principles of faith and honor. The significance of this moment is such that even a small mistake or setback now could have far-reaching consequences, much like a small mark on a young tree that will grow and become more pronounced over time, leaving a lasting impression for posterity to observe.
output: The sun never shined on a cause of greater worth. 'Tis not the affair of a city, a country, a province, or a kingdom, but of a continent - of at least one eighth part of the habitable globe. 'Tis not the concern of a day, a year, or an age; posterity are virtually involved in the contest, and will be more or less affected, even to the end of time, by the proceedings now. Now is the seed time of continental union, faith and honor. The least fracture now will be like a name engraved with the point of a pin on the tender rind of a young oak; the wound will enlarge with the tree, and posterity read it in full grown characters.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
Britain is often referred to as the parent country, a notion that warrants closer examination. However, if this assertion is true, it doesn't reflect positively on Britain's conduct. Generally, even the most primitive creatures do not harm their own offspring, and similarly, savage societies do not wage war on their family members. Therefore, the claim, if accurate, would be a source of shame for Britain. Nevertheless, this statement is not entirely true, and the term "parent country" has been used in a misleading manner by the king and his supporters, who have a hidden agenda to influence the vulnerable minds of the people.

In reality, Europe, rather than England, is the parent country of America. Historically, this new world has served as a refuge for individuals who have been persecuted for their beliefs in civil and religious liberty, originating from various parts of Europe. These people have fled to America, not because they were escaping the nurturing care of a mother country, but rather because they were seeking to escape the oppressive treatment of a tyrannical power. Furthermore, it is worth noting that the same tyrannical forces that drove the initial emigrants away from their homes continue to pursue their descendants to this day, which is particularly relevant in the case of England.
output: But Britain is the parent country, say some. Then the more shame upon her conduct. Even brutes do not devour their young, nor savages make war upon their families; wherefore the assertion, if true, turns to her reproach; but it happens not to be true, or only partly so, and the phrase parent or mother country hath been jesuitically adopted by the king and his parasites, with a low papistical design of gaining an unfair bias on the credulous weakness of our minds. Europe, and not England, is the parent country of America. This new world hath been the asylum for the persecuted lovers of civil and religious liberty from every part of Europe. Hither have they fled, not from the tender embraces of the mother, but from the cruelty of the monster; and it is so far true of England, that the same tyranny which drove the first emigrants from home, pursues their descendants still.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
The colonies have demonstrated a notable spirit of order and obedience to continental government, which is sufficient to alleviate concerns and promote a sense of stability. This highlights the lack of justification for fears regarding the relationship between colonies, except for those based on unfounded and unrealistic assumptions, such as the notion that one colony will strive for superiority over another.

This suggests that the absence of distinctions between colonies eliminates the potential for superiority, as perfect equality removes any incentive for competition. The republics of Europe, for example, are generally at peace, with countries like Holland and Switzerland experiencing minimal foreign or domestic conflict. In contrast, monarchical governments are often plagued by instability, as the presence of a crown can attract power-hungry individuals and foster an atmosphere of pride and insolence that can lead to conflicts with foreign powers. Ultimately, this contrast underscores the potential benefits of republican governments, which are founded on more natural principles and may be better equipped to negotiate disputes and maintain peace.
output:
The colonies have manifested such a spirit of good order and obedience to continental government, as is sufficient to make every reasonable person easy and happy on that head. No man can assign the least pretence for his fears, on any other grounds, than such as are truly childish and ridiculous, viz. that one colony will be striving for superiority over another.

Where there are no distinctions there can be no superiority, perfect equality affords no temptation. The republics of Europe are all (and we may say always) in peace. Holland and Swisserland are without wars, foreign or domestic: Monarchical governments, it is true, are never long at rest; the crown itself is a temptation to enterprizing ruffians at home; and that degree of pride and insolence ever attendant on regal authority, swells into a rupture with foreign powers, in instances, where a republican government, by being formed on more natural principles, would negociate the mistake.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input: Moreover, the European continent is characterized by a high density of kingdoms, which renders it inherently prone to conflict, and consequently, whenever a state of war emerges between England and any foreign power, the commercial activities of America are severely disrupted owing to its historical connection with Britain. Furthermore, it is worth noting that the outcome of future conflicts may differ significantly from those of the past, and should this be the case, the proponents of reconciliation will likely advocate for separation in the future, as neutrality would provide a more secure means of protection than military intervention. In essence, all that is just and natural suggests that separation is the most desirable course of action. Additionally, the sacrifices made by those who have lost their lives, as well as the inherent voice of nature, collectively urge that the time for separation hasn has arrived. It is worth noting that the geographical distance between England and America, as ordained by the Almighty, serves as a compelling and natural indication that the authority of one over the other was never intended by divine design. Moreover, the historical context in which the continent was discovered lends considerable weight to this argument, and the manner in which it was populated further reinforces its validity. Additionally, the discovery of America preceded the reformation, suggesting that the Almighty intended to provide a sanctuary for those who would be persecuted in subsequent years, when their homeland would no longer offer them friendship or safety.
output: Europe is too thickly planted with kingdoms to be long at peace, and whenever a war breaks out between England and any foreign power, the trade of America goes to ruin, because of her connection with Britain. The next war may not turn out like the last, and should it not, the advocates for reconciliation now will be wishing for separation then, because, neutrality in that case, would be a safer convoy than a man of war. Every thing that is right or natural pleads for separation. The blood of the slain, the weeping voice of nature cries, 'Tis time to part. Even the distance at which the Almighty hath placed England and America, is a strong and natural proof, that the authority of the one, over the other, was never the design of Heaven. The time likewise at which the continent was discovered, adds weight to the argument, and the manner in which it was peopled encreases the force of it. The reformation was preceded by the discovery of America, as if the Almighty graciously meant to open a sanctuary to the persecuted in future years, when home should afford neither friendship nor safety.
title: Common Sense
author: Thomas Paine

input:
In essence, as all individuals acknowledge the measure and differ only in their perspectives regarding the timing, let us conduct a comprehensive examination of the circumstances in order to eliminate misunderstandings and, if feasible, ascertain the precise moment. However, we need not delve deeply, for our inquiry halts immediately; the time has indeed revealed itself to us. The widespread agreement and the remarkable unity of all phenomena substantiate this assertion.

Moreover, our significant strength resides not in mere numbers but in our unity; nevertheless, our current numbers are adequate to withstand the forces of the entire world. At present, the continent boasts the largest assembly of armed and disciplined personnel of any power on Earth. We have reached a level of strength where no single colony can sustain itself independently, and when united, we possess the capacity to achieve our objectives. Any lesser or greater outcome could have dire consequences. Our land forces are already sufficient, and regarding naval matters, we cannot ignore the fact that Britain would never permit an American warship to be constructed as long as the continent remained under her control. Therefore, we would not be further advanced in that domain a century from now than we are today; in truth, we would likely be at a disadvantage, as the timber resources of the country continue to deplete, and what remains will ultimately be distant and challenging to obtain.
output:
As all men allow the measure, and vary only in their opinion of the time, let us, in order to remove mistakes, take a general survey of things, and endeavour, if possible, to find out the very time. But we need not go far, the inquiry ceases at once, for, the time hath found us. The general concurrence, the glorious union of all things prove the fact.

It is not in numbers, but in unity, that our great strength lies; yet our present numbers are sufficient to repel the force of all the world. The Continent hath, at this time, the largest body of armed and disciplined men of any power under Heaven; and is just arrived at that pitch of strength, in which no single colony is able to support itself, and the whole, when united, can accomplish the matter, and either more, or, less than this, might be fatal in its effects. Our land force is already sufficient, and as to naval affairs, we cannot be insensible, that Britain would never suffer an American man of war to be built, while the continent remained in her hands. Wherefore, we should be no forwarder an hundred years hence in that branch, than we are now; but the truth is, we should be less so, because the timber of the country is every day diminishing, and that, which will remain at last, will be far off and difficult to procure.
title: Common Sense

Suddenly, Hook came face to face with Peter. The other onlookers stepped back, creating a circle around them. 

For some time, the two adversaries studied each other. Hook displayed a slight shudder, while Peter wore an enigmatic smile. 

Without further conversation, they engaged in combat. Initially, neither fighter gained the upper hand. Peter demonstrated exceptional skill as a swordsman, parrying rapidly and countering with feints that occasionally slipped past Hook's defenses. However, Peter's shorter reach hindered him from delivering a decisive blow. Hook, while not lacking in skill, was somewhat less agile with his wrist movements. He advanced with force, hoping to end the duel with a signature thrust he had learned from Barbecue in Rio. To his surprise, this thrust was repeatedly deflected. Frustrated, Hook attempted to close the distance and strike with his iron hook, which had been swinging through the air. Peter evaded the hook and lunged aggressively, piercing Hook in the ribs. Upon seeing his own blood, which he found distasteful, Hook dropped his sword and realized that he was at Peter's mercy.
output:
Thus suddenly Hook found himself face to face with Peter. The others drew back and formed a ring around them.

For long the two enemies looked at one another, Hook shuddering slightly, and Peter with the strange smile upon his face.

Without more words they fell to, and for a space there was no advantage to either blade. Peter was a superb swordsman, and parried with dazzling rapidity; ever and anon he followed up a feint with a lunge that got past his foe’s defence, but his shorter reach stood him in ill stead, and he could not drive the steel home. Hook, scarcely his inferior in brilliancy, but not quite so nimble in wrist play, forced him back by the weight of his onset, hoping suddenly to end all with a favourite thrust, taught him long ago by Barbecue at Rio; but to his astonishment he found this thrust turned aside again and again. Then he sought to close and give the quietus with his iron hook, which all this time had been pawing the air; but Peter doubled under it and, lunging fiercely, pierced him in the ribs. At the sight of his own blood, whose peculiar colour, you remember, was offensive to him, the sword fell from Hook’s hand, and he was at Peter’s mercy.

His demeanor was notably sophisticated, which left her too captivated to protest, despite being just a young girl.

This suggests that Hook had a momentary influence over her, which is significant because her reaction had unexpected consequences. If she had chosen to reject his arm, she would likely have been thrown through the air like the others. In that case, Hook might not have been present when the children were tied up, and without that presence, he would not have uncovered Slightly’s secret. Ultimately, without knowledge of the secret, he would not have been able to attempt to harm Peter.
output:
A different treatment was accorded to Wendy, who came last. With ironical politeness Hook raised his hat to her, and, offering her his arm, escorted her to the spot where the others were being gagged. He did it with such an air, he was so frightfully distingué, that she was too fascinated to cry out. She was only a little girl.

Perhaps it is tell-tale to divulge that for a moment Hook entranced her, and we tell on her only because her slip led to strange results. Had she haughtily unhanded him (and we should have loved to write it of her), she would have been hurled through the air like the others, and then Hook would probably not have been present at the tying of the children; and had he not been at the tying he would not have discovered Slightly’s secret, and without the secret he could not presently have made his foul attempt on Peter’s life.

input: Peter emerged from the powder magazine with the shell in his hands and calmly threw it overboard. This highlights the contrast between his composure and the chaos around him. As for Hook, misguided as he was, we may take some comfort, without sympathizing with him, that he ultimately remained true to the traditions of his background. The other boys were now flying around him, mocking and scornful, while he staggered across the deck, striking up at them uselessly. His mind was no longer with them; it was drifting back to the playing fields of long ago, or to being sent up for good, or to watching the wall-game from a famous wall. His shoes were right, his waistcoat was right, his tie was right, and his socks were right.
output:
But Peter issued from the powder magazine with the shell in his hands, and calmly flung it overboard.

What sort of form was Hook himself showing? Misguided man though he was, we may be glad, without sympathising with him, that in the end he was true to the traditions of his race. The other boys were flying around him now, flouting, scornful; and he staggered about the deck striking up at them impotently, his mind was no longer with them; it was slouching in the playing fields of long ago, or being sent up for good, or watching the wall-game from a famous wall. And his shoes were right, and his waistcoat was right, and his tie was right, and his socks were right.

input: The structure was rough and simple, resembling what young bears might have built as an underground house under similar conditions. Nevertheless, one recess in the wall, no larger than a bird-cage, served as the private apartment of Tinker Bell. A tiny curtain could shut it off from the rest of the house, and Tink, who was most fastidious, always kept this curtain drawn when dressing or undressing. No woman, however large, could have possessed a more exquisite boudoir and bed-chamber combined. The couch, as she always called it, was a genuine Queen Mab with club legs, and she varied the bedspreads according to which fruit-blossom was in season. Her mirror was a Puss-in-Boots, of which only three unchipped examples are now known to fairy dealers. The washstand was a Pie-crust and reversible, the chest of drawers an authentic Charming the Sixth, and the carpet and rugs belonged to the best early period of Margery and Robin. A chandelier from Tiddlywinks was present for appearances, but she naturally lit the residence herself. Tink was very contemptuous of the rest of the house, as was perhaps inevitable, and her chamber, though beautiful, appeared rather conceited, giving the impression of a nose permanently turned up.

input: A dozen of her strongest warriors stood around the brave Tiger Lily, and they suddenly saw the treacherous pirates approaching. The illusion through which they had viewed victory fell from their eyes. They would no longer be tortured at the stake. The happy hunting grounds were now their destination. They knew this, but as their fathers' sons they conducted themselves honorably. Even then they had time to form a phalanx that would have been difficult to break if they had risen quickly, but the traditions of their race forbade this. It is written that the noble savage must never show surprise in the presence of the white man. Therefore, although the sudden appearance of the pirates must have been terrible to them, they remained motionless for a moment, without a muscle moving, as if the enemy had come by invitation. Then, indeed, with tradition gallantly upheld, they seized their weapons, and the air was torn with the war cry. However, it was now too late.
output: Around the brave Tiger Lily were a dozen of her stoutest warriors, and they suddenly saw the perfidious pirates bearing down upon them. Fell from their eyes then the film through which they had looked at victory. No more would they torture at the stake. For them the happy hunting-grounds was now. They knew it; but as their father’s sons they acquitted themselves. input: The following day, Peter took the initiative to measure Wendy, John, and Michael for hollow trees. This highlights the importance of a proper fit, as Hook's earlier scorn for the boys' desire for individual trees was misguided. The fact is, unless a tree is tailored to a person's size, navigating its interior can be challenging. This is because the boys' varying sizes required unique measurements. To successfully move up and down a hollow tree, one must Draw in their breath at the top and release it at the right moment to descend, while ascending requires alternating draws and releases, accompanied by a wriggling motion. Ultimately, once this technique is mastered, the process becomes effortless and graceful, allowing individuals to perform these actions without conscious thought.
output: One of the first things Peter did next day was to measure Wendy and John and Michael for hollow trees. Hook, you remember, had sneered at the boys for thinking they needed a tree apiece, but this was ignorance, for unless your tree fitted you it was difficult to go up and down, and no two of the boys were quite the same size. Once you fitted, you drew in your breath at the top, and down you went at exactly the right speed, while to ascend you drew in and let out alternately, and so wriggled up. Of course, when you have mastered the action you are able to do these things without thinking of them, and nothing can be more graceful.

input:
She was aware that night had not actually fallen, but a darkness similar to night had descended. In fact, the situation was even more ominous. It was not yet present, but its impending arrival was signaled by a shiver that ran through the sea. The question was, what exactly was approaching?

This prompted her to recall all the stories she had heard about Marooners' Rock, a place notorious for being used by ruthless captains to abandon sailors, leaving them to perish. This highlights the tragic fate that awaited those stranded on the rock, as they would inevitably drown when the tide rose and the rock became submerged.
output:
It was not, she knew, that night had come, but something as dark as night had come. No, worse than that. It had not come, but it had sent that shiver through the sea to say that it was coming. What was it?

There crowded upon her all the stories she had been told of Marooners’ Rock, so called because evil captains put sailors on it and leave them there to drown. They drown when the tide rises, for then it is submerged.

input: Peter was about to boast, but his expression changed to one of surprise instead. He swam toward the boat, and as his crew illuminated the way with a light, he quickly reached them. In the glow of the lantern, Wendy observed his hook grasping the side of the boat. She noticed his dark, sinister face as he emerged from the water, and she felt a tremor of fear. She had a strong desire to swim away, but Peter remained firmly in place. He was filled with energy and burdened by his own arrogance. “Am I not a wonder? Oh, I am a wonder!” he whispered to her. Although she agreed with him, she felt relieved that his claim went unheard by anyone other than herself.
output:
Peter may have been about to crow, but his face puckered in a whistle of surprise instead.

He was swimming to the boat, and as his men showed a light to guide him he had soon reached them. In the light of the lantern Wendy saw his hook grip the boat’s side; she saw his evil swarthy face as he rose dripping from the water, and, quaking, she would have liked to swim away, but Peter would not budge. He was tingling with life and also top-heavy with conceit. “Am I not a wonder, oh, I am a wonder!” he whispered to her, and though she thought so also, she was really glad for the sake of his reputation that no one heard him except herself.

input: Mrs. Darling first learned of Peter while she was tidying up her children's minds. This nightly habit is common to every good mother: after her children are asleep, she goes through their minds and sets things in order for the next morning, returning the many items that have shifted during the day to their proper places. If you could stay awake (though of course you cannot), you would see your own mother doing this, and you would find it very interesting to watch. It is much like tidying up drawers. You would likely see her on her knees, lingering with amusement over some of your contents, wondering where on earth you had picked this thing up, making discoveries both sweet and not so sweet, pressing one thing to her cheek as if it were as nice as a kitten, and hurriedly putting another out of sight. When you wake in the morning, the naughtiness and bad tempers with which you went to bed have been folded up small and placed at the bottom of your mind, and on top, beautifully aired, are your prettier thoughts, ready for you to put on.

He successfully replicated the sound, but this action had an unexpected consequence. The creature itself heard the noise and began to follow Peter, although its motivations are unclear. It is possible that the creature was attempting to reclaim what it had lost, or it may have simply been following out of friendship, believing that it was hearing its own sound. Regardless, the creature's actions were driven by a fixed idea, and it was not an intelligent animal.
output: Without giving a thought to what might be the feelings of a fellow-creature thus abruptly deprived of its closest companion, Peter began to consider how he could turn the catastrophe to his own use; and he decided to tick, so that wild beasts should believe he was the crocodile and let him pass unmolested. He ticked superbly, but with one unforeseen result. The crocodile was among those who heard the sound, and it followed him, though whether with the purpose of regaining what it had lost, or merely as a friend under the belief that it was again ticking itself, will never be certainly known, for, like slaves to a fixed idea, it was a stupid beast.

For the last time his dogs admired Hook, and devotedly they did his bidding. The boys, pretending to struggle, were pushed into the cabin and the door was closed on them.

“Now, listen!” cried Hook, and all listened. But not one dared to face the door. Yes, one, Wendy, who all this time had been bound to the mast. It was for neither a scream nor a crow that she was watching, it was for the reappearance of Peter.

If the gatherer gathers too much, nature takes out of the man what she puts into his chest, swells the estate, but kills the owner. Nature hates monopolies and exceptions. The waves of the sea do not more speedily seek a level from their loftiest tossing, than the varieties of condition tend to equalize themselves. There is always some leveling circumstance that puts down the overbearing, the strong, the rich, the fortunate, substantially on the same ground with all others. Is a man too strong and fierce for society, and by temper and position a bad citizen, - a morose ruffian, with a dash of the pirate in him; - nature sends him a troop of pretty sons and daughters, who are getting along in the dame's classes at the village school, and love and fear for them smooths his grim scowl to courtesy. From a young age, I have been interested in writing about the concept of compensation. It seemed to me that life was more advanced than theology in this area, and that ordinary people had a deeper understanding of the subject than religious leaders. Additionally, the various documents that relate to this doctrine have always fascinated me, due to their diverse nature and widespread presence in everyday life. These documents are essentially the everyday objects and interactions that surround us, including the tools we use, the food we eat, and the transactions we engage in.

Furthermore, the doctrine of compensation appears to offer a unique perspective on the human experience, one that reveals a sense of divinity and the underlying spirit of the world. This perspective is unencumbered by traditional beliefs and instead focuses on the eternal and universal aspects of human existence. Moreover, the doctrine has the potential to inspire and guide individuals during difficult times, providing a sense of direction and purpose. If this concept could be expressed in a way that captures its essential truth and beauty, it would likely serve as a source of comfort and illumination in times of uncertainty.
output: Ever since I was a boy, I have wished to write a discourse on Compensation: for it seemed to me when very young, that on this subject life was ahead of theology, and the people knew more than the preachers taught. The documents, too, from which the doctrine is to be drawn, charmed my fancy by their endless variety, and lay always before me, even in sleep; for they are the tools in our hands, the bread in our basket, the transactions of the street, the farm, and the dwelling-house, greetings, relations, debts and credits, the influence of character, the nature and endowment of all men. It seemed to me, also, that in it might be shown men a ray of divinity, the present action of the soul of this world, clean from all vestige of tradition, and so the heart of man might be bathed by an inundation of eternal love, conversing with that which he knows was always and always must be, because it really is now. It appeared, moreover, that if this doctrine could be stated in terms with any resemblance to those bright intuitions in which this truth is sometimes revealed to us, it would be a star in many dark hours and crooked passages in our journey that would not suffer us to lose our way.

Matthew Arnold, in a speech about Emerson given in Boston, provided a thoughtful assessment of Emerson's position in the literary hierarchy. While some may perceive Arnold's perspective as lacking appreciation, more objective readers are likely to find merit in his evaluation of the prominent American figure.

After analyzing Emerson's poetry, Arnold concludes that he does not consider Emerson to be among the great poets or the great writers of literature. He identifies great writers as individuals such as Cicero, Plato, Bacon, Pascal, Swift, and Voltaire—those who possess a natural genius for style. Arnold notes that the presence of impressive passages in someone's work does not necessarily indicate that they are a great writer. Although Emerson includes passages of noble and moving eloquence, sharp wit, and keen observations of nature, Arnold maintains that he does not classify Emerson as a great writer. This perspective aligns with Carlyle's critique of Emerson's literary and poetic works, which he describes as too ethereal, speculative, and theoretical, suggesting a preference for more concrete and tangible expressions in writing.
output:
Matthew Arnold, in an address on Emerson delivered in Boston, gave an excellent estimate of the rank we should accord to him in the great hierarchy of letters. Some, perhaps, will think that Arnold was unappreciative and cold, but dispassionate readers will be inclined to agree with his judgment of our great American.

After a review of the poetical works of Emerson the English critic draws his conclusions as follows:

"I do not then place Emerson among the great poets. But I go farther, and say that I do not place him among the great writers, the great men of letters. Who are the great men of letters? They are men like Cicero, Plato, Bacon, Pascal, Swift, Voltaire - writers with, in the first place, a genius and instinct for style.... Brilliant and powerful passages in a man's writings do not prove his possession of it. Emerson has passages of noble and pathetic eloquence; he has passages of shrewd and felicitous wit; he has crisp epigram; he has passages of exquisitely touched observation of nature. Yet he is not a great writer.... Carlyle formulates perfectly the defects of his friend's poetic and literary productions when he says: 'For me it is too ethereal, speculative, theoretic; I will have all things condense themselves, take shape and body, if they are to have my sympathy.'...

Furthermore, the meticulous care and fostering of the physique, inspired by this national ethos, represent one of the most notable characteristics of Greek culture, a quality that could be judiciously emulated in contemporary society.

input: These fleeting pleasures and subtle pains exist for curiosity, not for actual living. They should not be indulged. Engaging in such pursuits is akin to weaving cobwebs instead of fabric. Our friendships often reach shallow and unsatisfactory conclusions because we have infused them with ephemeral qualities, rather than the resilience of genuine human connection. The principles of friendship are profound, serious, and timeless, intertwined with the laws of nature and morality. However, we have focused on immediate gratification, seeking quick satisfaction. We grasp at the slowest fruits in the expansive garden of existence, fruits that require many seasons to ripen. We pursue our friends not with reverence but with a possessive desire that seeks to claim them as our own. This effort is in vain. We are equipped with subtle oppositions that emerge upon meeting, transforming all lyrical beauty into mundane reality. Most individuals lower themselves to meet one another. All interactions necessitate compromise, and, alarmingly, the unique essence of each beautiful nature fades as they draw closer. Actual society, even among the virtuous and talented, becomes a constant source of disappointment. After careful planning for encounters, we find ourselves plagued by frustrating misunderstandings, unexpected indifference, and sudden outbursts of wit and vitality during moments that should celebrate friendship and intellectual exchange. Our abilities do not function as they should, leading both individuals to find solace in solitude.
output: 8. Yet these uneasy pleasures and fine pains are for curiosity, and not for life. They are not to be indulged. This is to weave cobweb, and not cloth. Our friendships hurry to short and poor conclusions, because we have made them a texture of wine and dreams, instead of the tough fiber of the human heart. The laws of friendship are great, austere, and eternal, of one web with the laws of nature and of morals. But we have aimed at a swift and petty benefit, to suck a sudden sweetness. We snatch at the slowest fruit in the whole garden of God, which many summers and many winters must ripen. We seek our friend not sacredly but with an adulterate passion which would appropriate him to ourselves. In vain. We are armed all over with subtle antagonisms, which, as soon as we meet, begin to play, and translate all poetry into stale prose. Almost all people descend to meet. All association must be a compromise, and, what is worst, the very flower and aroma of the flower of each of the beautiful natures disappears as they approach each other. What a perpetual disappointment is actual society, even of the virtuous and gifted! After interviews have been compassed with long foresight, we must be tormented presently by baffled blows, by sudden, unseasonable apathies, by epilepsies of wit and of animal spirits, in the heyday of friendship and thought. Our faculties do not play us true, and both parties are relieved by solitude.

Additionally, the discourses entitled Nature and The American Scholar embody the fundamental principles of Emerson's philosophical, poetic, and moral instruction. In essence, it is worth noting that Emerson, like all great educators, possessed a relatively limited number of core principles and theories that formed the basis of his teachings. Furthermore, these essential principles of existence can be succinctly articulated in a brief phrase, encompassing concepts such as self-reliance, cultural refinement, intellectual and moral autonomy, the divine nature of humanity and the natural world, the importance of labor, and the pursuit of lofty ideals.

Moreover, Emerson devoted the latter portion of his life to lecturing and literary pursuits. It is worth noting that his son, Dr. Edward Emerson, provided a fascinating account of the process by which his father's lectures were constructed. Moreover, throughout his life, Emerson maintained a journal, which he referred to as his intellectual repository. The ideas and thoughts recorded in this journal were meticulously indexed, and a significant number of them ultimately appeared in his published works, having been carefully selected, expanded, and refined over time. Additionally, these thoughts were initially recorded in a chronological manner, without regard to order or organization, but were later categorized, elaborated upon, and illustrated, ultimately being incorporated into lectures or discourses, and subjected to repeated scrutiny and revision before being finally refined and published in essay form.
output:
These two discourses, Nature and The American Scholar, strike the keynote of Emerson's philosophical, poetical, and moral teachings. In fact he had, as every great teacher has, only a limited number of principles and theories to teach. These principles of life can all be enumerated in twenty words - self-reliance, culture, intellectual and moral independence, the divinity of nature and man, the necessity of labor, and high ideals.

Emerson spent the latter part of his life in lecturing and in literary work. His son, Dr. Edward Emerson, gave an interesting account of how these lectures were constructed. "All through his life he kept a journal. This book, he said, was his 'Savings Bank.' The thoughts thus received and garnered in his journals were indexed, and a great many of them appeared in his published works. They were religiously set down just as they came, in no order except chronological, but later they were grouped, enlarged or pruned, illustrated, worked into a lecture or discourse, and, after having in this capacity undergone repeated testing and rearranging, were finally carefully sifted and more rigidly pruned, and were printed as essays."

input: This law often shapes the regulations of cities and nations. It may be futile to build or conspire against it, as mismanagement tends not to persist for long. While it may seem that no checks exist against a new wrongdoing, these checks likely exist and will eventually surface. In the case of a harsh government, the safety of the leader may be compromised. Similarly, excessive taxation can lead to minimal revenue. If the criminal justice system is excessively harsh, juries may be less likely to convict. Conversely, if the laws are too lenient, individuals may seek private retribution. In a highly energized democracy, citizens may react with intensified vigor, making life feel more vibrant. Ultimately, the true essence and contentment of human life often appear to transcend the extremes of circumstance, adapting relatively well across various conditions. The impact of individual character tends to remain consistent across different forms of governance, whether in Turkey or New England. Historically, even under the ancient despots of Egypt, it seems that individuals were as free as cultural conditions would permit.
output: This law writes the laws of cities and nations. It is in vain to build or plot or combine against it. Things refuse to be mismanaged long. Res nolunt diu male administrari. Though no checks to a new evil appear, the checks exist, and will appear. If the government is cruel, the governor's life is not safe. If you tax too high, the revenue will yield nothing. If you make the criminal code sanguinary, juries will not convict. If the law is too mild, private vengeance comes in. If the government is a terrific democracy, the pressure is resisted by an overcharge of energy in the citizen, and life glows with a fiercer flame. The true life and satisfactions of man seem to elude the utmost rigors or felicities of condition, and to establish themselves with great indifferency under all varieties of circumstances. Under all governments the influence of character remains the same, - in Turkey and in New England about alike. Under the primeval despots of Egypt, history honestly confesses that man must have been as free as culture could make him.

input: The world can often be seen encapsulated in a drop of dew. The essence of the universe seems to manifest within each specific point. Where there is goodness, one may also find evil; where there is attraction, there can also be aversion; and where there is strength, there may exist limitations. Overall, this perspective highlights the interconnected nature of existence.
output: The world globes itself in a drop of dew. The microscope cannot find the animalcule which is less perfect for being little. Eyes, ears, taste, smell, motion, resistance, appetite, and organs of reproduction that take hold on eternity, - all find room to consist in the small creature. So do we put our life into every act. The true doctrine of omnipresence is, that God reappears with all his parts in every moss and cobweb. The value of the universe contrives to throw itself into every point. If the good is there, so is the evil; if the affinity, so the repulsion; if the force, so the limitation.

input: Virtues are generally seen as the exception rather than the rule. There is the man and his virtues. Men perform what is called a good action, such as an act of courage or charity, much as they would pay a fine to make up for their daily absence from parade. Their works are done as an apology or excuse for their living in the world, as invalids and the insane pay a high board. Their virtues are penances. I do not wish to atone, but to live. My life is for itself and not for a spectacle. I much prefer that it should be of a lower strain, so long as it is genuine and consistent, than that it should be glittering and unsteady. I wish it to be sound and sweet, and not to need diet and bleeding. I ask primary evidence that you are a man, and refuse this appeal from the man to his actions. I know that for myself it makes no difference whether I do or refrain from those actions which are considered excellent. I cannot consent to pay for a privilege where I have an intrinsic right. Few and mean as my gifts may be, I actually am, and do not need for my own assurance or the assurance of my fellows any secondary testimony. This highlights a preference for authentic existence over performed virtue. Ultimately, the passage suggests that being genuinely oneself requires no external validation.

This address was given at Cambridge in 1837, before the Harvard Chapter of the Phi Beta Kappa Society, a college fraternity whose members are typically drawn from the top twenty-five students in each graduating class. The society holds annual meetings, which have often served as occasions for addresses by some of the most distinguished scholars and thinkers of the day.

I greet you at the beginning of our literary year. Our anniversary is one of hope, and perhaps not enough of labor. We do not meet for games of strength or skill, for the recitation of histories, tragedies, and odes, like the ancient Greeks; for parliaments of love and poetry, like the Troubadours; nor for the advancement of science, like our contemporaries in the British and European capitals. So far, our holiday has tended to be simply a friendly sign of the survival of the love of letters among a people too busy to give letters much more. As such, it can be precious as the sign of an enduring instinct. Perhaps the time has already come when it may ought to be, and will be, something else; when the sluggish intellect of this continent will look out from under its iron lids and fill the postponed expectation of the world with something better than the exertions of mechanical skill. Our day of dependence, our long apprenticeship to the learning of other lands, is drawing to a close. The millions around us who are rushing into life cannot always be fed on the dry remains of foreign harvests. Events and actions arise that must be sung, and that will sing themselves. Who can doubt that poetry may revive and lead in a new age, as the star in the constellation Harp, which now flames in our zenith, astronomers say, shall one day be the pole-star for a thousand years? In short, this occasion suggests both a continuing love of letters and the possibility of a new and more independent cultural voice.

input: The actions and events of our childhood and youth now exist as subjects of tranquil observation. They remain suspended like vivid images in the atmosphere. Conversely, our recent actions and the matters currently at hand elude our capacity for speculation. Our emotions still flow through these experiences. We are as unaware of them as we are of our feet, hands, or brains. The new deed remains an integral part of life, temporarily immersed within our unconscious existence. During a moment of contemplation, it detaches itself from life much like a ripe fruit, transforming into a thought within the mind. Instantly, it is elevated and transfigured; the perishable has assumed an incorruptible state. Henceforth, it becomes an object of beauty, regardless of its humble origin and surroundings. Furthermore, it is important to note the impossibility of anticipating this act. In its immature form, it is incapable of flight, radiance, or vibrancy; it exists merely as a dull grub. However, without any prior notice, the same entity unfurls magnificent wings and emerges as an angel of wisdom. Thus, there exists no fact or event in our personal history that will not, in due time, shed its adhesive and inert quality, astounding us by ascending from our being into the celestial realm. The cradle and infancy, school and playground, the fears associated with boys, dogs, and reprimands, the affection for young girls and berries, along with many other experiences that once dominated our perception, have already faded. Friends and family, profession and political affiliations, town and countryside, nation and world must also rise and resonate in harmony.
output: The actions and events of our childhood and youth are now matters of calmest observation. They lie like fair pictures in the air. Not so with our recent actions, - with the business which we now have in hand. On this we are quite unable to speculate. Our affections as yet circulate through it. We no more feel or know it than we feel the feet, or the hand, or the brain of our body. The new deed is yet a part of life, - remains for a time immersed in our unconscious life. In some contemplative hour it detaches itself from the life like a ripe fruit, to become a thought of the mind. Instantly it is raised, transfigured; the corruptible has put on incorruption. Henceforth it is an object of beauty, however base its origin and neighborhood. Observe, too, the impossibility of antedating this act. In its grub state it cannot fly, it cannot shine, it is a dull grub. But suddenly, without observation, the selfsame thing unfurls beautiful wings, and is an angel of wisdom. So is there no fact, no event, in our private history, which shall not, sooner or later, lose its adhesive, inert form, and astonish us by soaring from our body into the empyrean. Cradle and infancy, school and playground, the fear of boys, and dogs, and ferules, the love of little maids and berries, and many another fact that once filled the whole sky, are gone already; friend and relative, profession and party, town and country, nation and world, must also soar and sing.

input: It is foolish to fear that our ties may become too spiritual, as though in that way we might lose some genuine affection. Whatever correction of our common views we make from insight, nature will surely confirm us in, and though it may appear to deprive us of some pleasure, it will repay us with a greater one. Let us feel, if we choose, the absolute isolation of the individual. We are certain that we possess everything within ourselves. We travel to Europe, or we pursue particular persons, or we read books, in the instinctive belief that these will draw it forth and reveal us to ourselves. We are all beggars. The persons are such as we are; Europe is an old, faded garment of the dead; the books are their ghosts. Let us abandon this idolatry. Let us renounce this mendicancy. Let us even bid our dearest friends farewell and defy them, saying, "Who are you? Release me. I will be dependent no longer." Ah! Do you not see, my brother, that in this way we part only to meet again on a higher plane, and to belong to one another only the more because we belong more to ourselves? A friend is two-faced: he looks to the past and the future. He is the child of all my preceding hours, the prophet of those to come, and the herald of a greater friend.
output: 22. It is foolish to be afraid of making our ties too spiritual, as if so we could lose any genuine love. Whatever correction of our popular views we make from insight, nature will be sure to bear us out in, and though it seem to rob us of some joy, will repay us with a greater. Let us feel, if we will, the absolute insulation of man. We are sure that we have all in us. We go to Europe, or we pursue persons, or we read books, in the instinctive faith that these will call it out and reveal us to ourselves. Beggars all. The persons are such as we; the Europe, an old faded garment of dead persons; the books, their ghosts. Let us drop this idolatry. Let us give over this mendicancy. Let us even bid our dearest friends farewell, and defy them, saying, "Who are you? Unhand me. I will be dependent no more." Ah! seest thou not, O brother, that thus we part only to meet again on a higher platform, and only be more each other's, because we are more our own? A friend is Janus-faced: he looks to the past and the future. He is the child of all my foregoing hours, the prophet of those to come, and the harbinger of a greater friend.

input: It is worth noting that we now find ourselves as a collective, lacking individuality. Humanity does not hold reverence for one another, nor is the brilliance of intellect encouraged to remain introspective in order to connect with the vast internal depths of thought; rather, it seeks external validation, soliciting a mere cup of water from the vessels of others. Additionally, it is essential for each individual to embark on their journey alone. I find greater solace in the quietude of a church before the commencement of the service than in any delivered sermon. The individuals present appear distant, cool, and pure, each encircled by their own sacred space or sanctuary. Therefore, let us always choose to remain seated in contemplation. Why should we bear the shortcomings of our friends, spouses, parents, or children simply because they occupy our shared space or share our lineage? I recognize that every individual shares the essence of my being, and I, in turn, share the essence of all humanity. However, I shall not adopt their irritability or folly, nor shall I feel shame on their behalf. Furthermore, the nature of one's solitude must transcend mere physical separation; it should be spiritual and uplifting. At times, it may seem as if the entire world conspires to inundate you with trivial demands. Friends, clients, children, illness, fear, want, and charity all simultaneously knock at your door and implore, "Join us." However, it is vital to maintain your dignity; do not descend into their chaos. The annoyance that others may inflict upon me is a consequence of my own weak curiosity. No individual can approach me without my consent. In essence, "What we cherish, we possess, yet through desire, we deprive ourselves of that very affection."
output: But now we are a mob. Man does not stand in awe of man, nor is his genius admonished to stay at home to put itself in communication with the internal ocean, but it goes abroad to beg a cup of water of the urns of other men. We must go alone. I like the silent church before the service begins, better than any preaching. How far off, how cool, how chaste the persons look, begirt each one with a precinct or sanctuary! So let us always sit. Why should we assume the faults of our friend, or wife, or father, or child, because they sit around our hearth, or are said to have the same blood? All men have my blood, and I have all men's. Not for that will I adopt their petulance or folly, even to the extent of being ashamed of it. But your isolation must not be mechanical, but spiritual, that is, must be elevation. At times the whole world seems to be in conspiracy to importune you with emphatic trifles. Friend, client, child, sickness, fear, want, charity, all knock at once at thy closet door, and say, "Come out unto us." But keep thy state; come not into their confusion. The power men possess to annoy men, I give them by a weak curiosity. No man can come near me but through my act. "What we love that we have, but by desire we bereave ourselves of the love."

In the works of earlier English dramatists, particularly in the plays of Beaumont and Fletcher, there is a consistent acknowledgment of gentility. Noble behavior appears easily identifiable within the society of their time, much like distinguishing colors in the American populace today. When a character such as Rodrigo, Pedro, or Valerio makes an entrance, even if he is unfamiliar, the duke or governor immediately recognizes him as a gentleman and extends endless civilities. In contrast, all others are regarded as lesser individuals.

This appreciation for personal qualities is mirrored in their works, which often feature heroic characters and dialogues. In plays like Bonduca, Sophocles, the Mad Lover, and the Double Marriage, the speakers exhibit earnestness and sincerity, allowing the dialogue to elevate into poetry with minimal plot developments. For instance, in a notable scene, the Roman Martius has triumphed over Athens, except for the indomitable spirits of Sophocles, the duke of Athens, and his wife, Dorigen. Martius becomes infatuated with Dorigen’s beauty and attempts to spare her husband’s life. However, Sophocles refuses to plead for his own life, despite knowing that a simple request could secure it, leading to the impending execution of both men.
output: 1. In the elder English dramatists, and mainly in the plays of Beaumont and Fletcher, there is a constant recognition of gentility, as if a noble behavior were as easily marked in the society of their age, as color is in our American population. When any Rodrigo, Pedro, or Valerio enters, though he be a stranger, the duke or governor exclaims, This is a gentleman, - and proffers civilities without end; but all the rest are slag and refuse. In harmony with this delight in personal advantages, there is in their plays a certain heroic cast of character and dialogue, - as in Bonduca, Sophocles, the Mad Lover, the Double Marriage, - wherein the speaker is so earnest and cordial, and on such deep grounds of character, that the dialogue, on the slightest additional incident in the plot, rises naturally into poetry. Among many texts, take the following. The Roman Martius has conquered Athens - all but the invincible spirits of Sophocles, the duke of Athens, and Dorigen, his wife. The beauty of the latter inflames Martius, and he seeks to save her husband; but Sophocles will not ask his life, although assured, that a word will save him, and the execution of both proceeds.

input:
It can be argued that virtues such as truth, frankness, courage, love, humility, and prudence may often be interconnected, as they tend to contribute to a person's overall well-being. While it is uncertain whether all matter will ultimately be found to be composed of a single element, such as oxygen or hydrogen, it is possible that the world of human behavior and actions may be viewed as being made up of a unified whole, with many principles and values being intertwined. As we explore the world around us, we may find that many of our actions and decisions can be related to a set of fundamental principles, which can be thought of as a kind of moral framework.

The eye and its field of vision can be seen as a representation of this idea, with the horizon forming a kind of boundary or limit. This pattern of a central point surrounded by a circumference is repeated throughout nature, and may be considered a symbol of great significance. The concept of a circle with its center everywhere and its circumference nowhere, as described by St. Augustine, can be seen as a powerful metaphor for the nature of the world and our place in it. Throughout our lives, we may be constantly learning and interpreting the meaning of this and other forms, and one possible lesson is that every action has consequences and may be part of a larger cycle of cause and effect. Additionally, it may be possible to draw a larger circle around any given action or event, suggesting that there is always more to learn and discover, and that every ending can also be a new beginning. In summary, the world and our experiences in it may be characterized by a series of interconnected patterns and cycles, with every event and action being part of a larger whole.
output:
Thus truth, frankness, courage, love, humility, and all the virtues range themselves on the side of prudence, or the art of securing a present well-being. I do not know if all matter will be found to be made of one element, as oxygen or hydrogen, at last, but the world of manners and actions is wrought of one stuff, and begin where we will we are pretty sure in a short space to be mumbling our ten commandments.

The eye is the first circle; the horizon which it forms is the second; and throughout nature this primary picture is repeated without end. It is the highest emblem in the cipher of the world. St. Augustine described the nature of God as a circle whose centre was everywhere and its circumference nowhere. We are all our lifetime reading the copious sense of this first of forms. One moral we have already deduced in considering the circular or compensatory character of every human action. Another analogy we shall now trace, that every action admits of being outdone. Our life is an apprenticeship to the truth that around every circle another can be drawn; that there is no end in nature, but every end is a beginning; that there is always another dawn risen on mid-noon, and under every deep a lower deep opens.

We are too old to care about fashion, and too old to expect the support of anyone greater or more powerful. This suggests that we should take pleasure in the affections and habits that grow near us. He believed that without her art, she was nothing, and that he could have helped her achieve greatness, making her famous and revered by the world. In his view, she had wasted her potential and was now merely a mediocre actress with a pretty face.
output:
He flung himself down on the sofa and turned away his face. “You have killed my love,” he muttered.

She looked at him in wonder and laughed. He made no answer. She came across to him, and with her little fingers stroked his hair. She knelt down and pressed his hands to her lips. He drew them away, and a shudder ran through him.

Then he leaped up and went to the door. “Yes,” he cried, “you have killed my love. You used to stir my imagination. Now you don’t even stir my curiosity. You simply produce no effect. I loved you because you were marvellous, because you had genius and intellect, because you realized the dreams of great poets and gave shape and substance to the shadows of art. You have thrown it all away. You are shallow and stupid. My God! how mad I was to love you! What a fool I have been! You are nothing to me now. I will never see you again. I will never think of you. I will never mention your name. You don’t know what you were to me, once. Why, once... Oh, I can’t bear to think of it! I wish I had never laid eyes upon you! You have spoiled the romance of my life. How little you can know of love, if you say it mars your art! Without your art, you are nothing. I would have made you famous, splendid, magnificent. The world would have worshipped you, and you would have borne my name. What are you now? A third-rate actress with a pretty face.”

input: Additionally, it is evident that the portrait in question reflects an excessive degree of self-absorption. Furthermore, I must confess that I was not aware of the extent of your vanity, Basil. In essence, I fail to perceive any discernible resemblance between your rugged and strong facial features, accompanied by your dark hair, and the youthful subject of the portrait, who appears to embody a delicate and refined beauty, reminiscent of a figure crafted from ivory and rose petals. Moreover, it is worth noting that the young man in question bears a striking similarity to Narcissus, whereas you, Basil, possess an intellectual countenance, which, by its very nature, detracts from the overall aesthetic appeal of your features. It is a general principle that genuine beauty is compromised by the presence of an intellectual expression, as the latter tends to introduce a mode of exaggeration that disrupts the harmony of the face. Moreover, when an individual engages in intense mental activity, their physical appearance often becomes distorted, with one feature becoming disproportionately prominent. For instance, a review of successful individuals in various learned professions reveals that they frequently possess unattractive physical characteristics. However, this tendency is not observed in the Church, where the clergy tend to maintain a more youthful and pleasant appearance, largely due to the fact that they are not required to engage in original thought. Instead, they often repeat the ideas and phrases that were imparted to them at a young age, which enables them to preserve a more agreeable and unblemished countenance. In the case of your enigmatic young friend, whose name you have not seen fit to disclose, but whose portrait has nonetheless captivated my attention, it appears that he is not prone to intellectual pursuits. I am reasonably certain that he is a being of considerable physical beauty, unencumbered by the burdens of mental exertion, and one who would be a welcome presence during the winter months, when natural beauty is scarce, as well as during the summer, when a respite from intellectual stimulation is desirable. In conclusion, Basil, it is unlikely that you bear a strong resemblance to this individual.
output: “Too much of yourself in it! Upon my word, Basil, I didn’t know you were so vain; and I really can’t see any resemblance between you, with your rugged strong face and your coal-black hair, and this young Adonis, who looks as if he was made out of ivory and rose-leaves. Why, my dear Basil, he is a Narcissus, and you - well, of course you have an intellectual expression and all that. But beauty, real beauty, ends where an intellectual expression begins. Intellect is in itself a mode of exaggeration, and destroys the harmony of any face. The moment one sits down to think, one becomes all nose, or all forehead, or something horrid. Look at the successful men in any of the learned professions. How perfectly hideous they are! Except, of course, in the Church. But then in the Church they don’t think. A bishop keeps on saying at the age of eighty what he was told to say when he was a boy of eighteen, and as a natural consequence he always looks absolutely delightful. Your mysterious young friend, whose name you have never told me, but whose picture really fascinates me, never thinks. I feel quite sure of that. He is some brainless beautiful creature who should be always here in winter when we have no flowers to look at, and always here in summer when we want something to chill our intelligence. Don’t flatter yourself, Basil: you are not in the least like him.”

input: The novel can be described as lacking a conventional plot and featuring only one character. It serves as a psychological exploration of a young Parisian who seems to spend his life attempting to embody the passions and ideas of various eras, rather than his own in the nineteenth century. In a way, he appears to synthesize the diverse moods that humanity has experienced over time, appreciating both the artificial renunciations that some might call virtue and the more instinctive rebellions that others may refer to as sin. The writing style is notable for its intricate quality, combining vividness and obscurity, and it is rich with slang, older expressions, technical terminology, and elaborate rephrasings. This style is characteristic of some of the most esteemed figures within the French Symbolist movement. The metaphors presented could be seen as both extravagant and delicately nuanced. The sensory experiences depicted often draw from mystical philosophy, making it difficult at times to discern whether the reader is engaging with the spiritual revelations of a medieval saint or the troubling admissions of a contemporary sinner. The book may be perceived as unsettling, with a lingering scent of incense that seems to permeate its pages and affect the mind. The rhythmic flow of the sentences, marked by intricate refrains and carefully repeated phrases, can induce a state of reverie in the reader, leading them to lose track of the waning day and the encroaching shadows. In summary, this novel offers a complex and immersive reading experience that can provoke deep reflection.
output: It was a novel without a plot and with only one character, being, indeed, simply a psychological study of a certain young Parisian who spent his life trying to realize in the nineteenth century all the passions and modes of thought that belonged to every century except his own, and to sum up, as it were, in himself the various moods through which the world-spirit had ever passed, loving for their mere artificiality those renunciations that men have unwisely called virtue, as much as those natural rebellions that wise men still call sin. The style in which it was written was that curious jewelled style, vivid and obscure at once, full of argot and of archaisms, of technical expressions and of elaborate paraphrases, that characterizes the work of some of the finest artists of the French school of Symbolistes. There were in it metaphors as monstrous as orchids and as subtle in colour. The life of the senses was described in the terms of mystical philosophy. One hardly knew at times whether one was reading the spiritual ecstasies of some mediæval saint or the morbid confessions of a modern sinner. It was a poisonous book. The heavy odour of incense seemed to cling about its pages and to trouble the brain. The mere cadence of the sentences, the subtle monotony of their music, so full as it was of complex refrains and movements elaborately repeated, produced in the mind of the lad, as he passed from chapter to chapter, a form of reverie, a malady of dreaming, that made him unconscious of the falling day and creeping shadows.
