input: Sibyl's story had certainly been quite a romantic tale. She had often portrayed death in her performances, but now it seemed that death had reached out to her and taken her away. It is unclear how she might have acted in that final, sorrowful scene. Perhaps, in her moment of passing, she did not express anger but instead surrendered to love, which may now hold a sacred place in his memory. It is possible that her sacrifice, giving up her life for love, could overshadow any pain he experienced on that terrible night at the theater. When he remembers her, it may be as a remarkable tragic figure whose existence highlights the profound nature of love. Reflecting on her innocence, her charming imagination, and her gentle grace brought tears to his eyes, which he quickly wiped away as he turned back to the image before him. In essence, Sibyl's memory may linger as a poignant reminder of both love and loss.
output: Poor Sibyl! What a romance it had all been! She had often mimicked death on the stage. Then Death himself had touched her and taken her with him. How had she played that dreadful last scene? Had she cursed him, as she died? No; she had died for love of him, and love would always be a sacrament to him now. She had atoned for everything by the sacrifice she had made of her life. He would not think any more of what she had made him go through, on that horrible night at the theatre. When he thought of her, it would be as a wonderful tragic figure sent on to the world’s stage to show the supreme reality of love. A wonderful tragic figure? Tears came to his eyes as he remembered her childlike look, and winsome fanciful ways, and shy tremulous grace. He brushed them away hastily and looked again at the picture.

output:
He thought for a moment. “Can you remember any great error that you committed in your early days, Duchess?” he asked, looking at her across the table.

“A dangerous theory!” came from Sir Thomas’s tight lips. Lady Agatha shook her head, but could not help being amused. Mr. Erskine listened.

“Yes,” he continued, “that is one of the great secrets of life. Nowadays most people die of a sort of creeping common sense, and discover when it is too late that the only things one never regrets are one’s mistakes.”

input: You are unchanged. I wonder what your future will hold. Do not jeopardize it with renunciations. At this moment, you embody perfection. Do not render yourself incomplete. You are entirely flawless now. You need not deny this; you are aware of it. Moreover, Dorian, do not mislead yourself. Life is not controlled by will or intention. Instead, it is a matter of nerves, fibers, and the slowly developed cells where thought resides and passion dreams. You may believe yourself to be safe and strong. However, it only takes a particular hue in a room, a morning sky, a cherished perfume that evokes subtle memories, a line from a long-forgotten poem, or a melody from a piece of music you no longer play—these are the elements that shape our lives. Browning has addressed this in his writing; yet, our senses evoke these experiences for us. There are times when the scent of lilacs suddenly envelops me, compelling me to relive the most peculiar month of my life. I wish I could swap places with you, Dorian. The world has judged us both, but it has always revered you. This admiration will endure. You represent what the age seeks and fears it has discovered. I am grateful that you have never created anything tangible—no sculptures, no paintings, no external expressions. Life itself has been your art. You have composed your existence into music. Your days are your sonnets.
output: “Yes, you are the same. I wonder what the rest of your life will be. Don’t spoil it by renunciations. At present you are a perfect type. Don’t make yourself incomplete. You are quite flawless now. You need not shake your head: you know you are. Besides, Dorian, don’t deceive yourself. Life is not governed by will or intention. Life is a question of nerves, and fibres, and slowly built-up cells in which thought hides itself and passion has its dreams. You may fancy yourself safe and think yourself strong. But a chance tone of colour in a room or a morning sky, a particular perfume that you had once loved and that brings subtle memories with it, a line from a forgotten poem that you had come across again, a cadence from a piece of music that you had ceased to play - I tell you, Dorian, that it is on things like these that our lives depend. Browning writes about that somewhere; but our own senses will imagine them for us. There are moments when the odour of lilas blanc passes suddenly across me, and I have to live the strangest month of my life over again. I wish I could change places with you, Dorian. The world has cried out against us both, but it has always worshipped you. It always will worship you. You are the type of what the age is searching for, and what it is afraid it has found. I am so glad that you have never done anything, never carved a statue, or painted a picture, or produced anything outside of yourself! Life has been your art. You have set yourself to music. Your days are your sonnets.”

There is one marked peculiarity about this paper, a thing nobody seems to notice but myself, and that is that it changes as the light changes.

The wallpaper is dull enough to confuse the eye as it tries to follow the pattern, and pronounced enough to be constantly irritating and to invite close study. When one traces the lame, uncertain curves for even a short distance, they suddenly seem to destroy themselves, plunging off at outrageous angles and dissolving into unheard-of contradictions.
output:
It is a big, airy room, the whole floor nearly, with windows that look all ways, and air and sunshine galore. It was nursery first and then playground and gymnasium, I should judge; for the windows are barred for little children, and there are rings and things in the walls.

It is dull enough to confuse the eye in following, pronounced enough to constantly irritate, and provoke study, and when you follow the lame, uncertain curves for a little distance they suddenly commit suicide - plunge off at outrageous angles, destroy themselves in unheard-of contradictions.

I am sitting by the window now, up in this atrocious nursery, and there is nothing to hinder my writing as much as I please, save lack of strength.

By daylight she is subdued, quiet. I fancy it is the pattern that keeps her so still. It is so puzzling. It keeps me quiet by the hour.

output:

But there is something else about that paper - the smell! I noticed it the moment we came into the room, but with so much air and sun it was not bad. Now we have had a week of fog and rain, and whether the windows are open or not, the smell is here.

Then in the very bright spots she keeps still, and in the very shady spots she just takes hold of the bars and shakes them hard.

output:

I get positively angry with the impertinence of it and the everlastingness. Up and down and sideways they crawl, and those absurd, unblinking eyes are everywhere. There is one place where two breadths didn’t match, and the eyes go all up and down the line, one a little higher than the other.

I never saw so much expression in an inanimate thing before, and we all know how much expression they have! I used to lie awake as a child and get more entertainment and terror out of blank walls and plain furniture than most children could find in a toy-store.

output:

output:
John says I mustn’t lose my strength, and has me take cod-liver oil and lots of tonics and things, to say nothing of ale and wine and rare meat.

Dear John! He loves me very dearly, and hates to have me sick. I tried to have a real earnest reasonable talk with him the other day, and tell him how I wish he would let me go and make a visit to Cousin Henry and Julia.

But he said I wasn’t able to go, nor able to stand it after I got there; and I did not make out a very good case for myself, for I was crying before I had finished.

“My dear,” he said, “I kindly ask you, for my sake, for our child's well-being, and for your own, to refrain from entertaining that thought! It can often be quite dangerous and alluring for someone with your temperament. It tends to be a misleading and unwise notion. Would you consider trusting me as your physician when I share this with you?”

Naturally, I chose to remain silent on that topic, and we soon drifted off to sleep. He believed I had fallen asleep first, though I was still awake, spending hours trying to determine if the front pattern and the back pattern actually moved in unison or independently.
output:
“My darling,” said he, “I beg of you, for my sake and for our child’s sake, as well as for your own, that you will never for one instant let that idea enter your mind! There is nothing so dangerous, so fascinating, to a temperament like yours. It is a false and foolish fancy. Can you not trust me as a physician when I tell you so?”

So of course I said no more on that score, and we went to sleep before long. He thought I was asleep first, but I wasn’t, - I lay there for hours trying to decide whether that front pattern and the back pattern really did move together or separately.

output:

input: It's worth noting that the donations to this building came from individuals of various sects, so caution was exercised when selecting trustees to oversee the property, in order to prevent any one sect from gaining too much influence, which may have led to the building being used primarily for that sect's purposes, potentially contradicting the original intention. To achieve a balance, a trustee from each major sect was appointed, including a representative from the Church of England, a Presbyterian, a Baptist, and a Moravian, among others. In the event of a vacancy due to death, the remaining trustees would elect a new member from among the contributors. However, the Moravian trustee tended to have a difficult relationship with his colleagues, and after his passing, they decided not to appoint another trustee from the same sect. This decision created a new challenge, as the trustees had to find a way to avoid inadvertently giving too much representation to another sect through their new selection, and overall, the goal was to maintain a fair and balanced approach to managing the building.
output: It is to be noted that the contributions to this building being made by people of different sects, care was taken in the nomination of trustees, in whom the building and ground was to be vested, that a predominancy should not be given to any sect, lest in time that predominancy might be a means of appropriating the whole to the use of such sect, contrary to the original intention. It was therefore that one of each sect was appointed, viz., one Church-of-England man, one Presbyterian, one Baptist, one Moravian, etc., those, in case of vacancy by death, were to fill it by election from among the contributors. The Moravian happen'd not to please his colleagues, and on his death they resolved to have no other of that sect. The difficulty then was, how to avoid having two of some other sect, by means of the new choice.

input:
A well-known Greek philosopher lived around 582-500 B.C. The Golden Verses attributed to him likely originated later. He suggests that individuals should reflect on their actions around evening or bedtime. This practice allows one to conclude the day with a judgment of conscience, transforming the review of daily conduct into a form of evening prayer.

I decided to dedicate one week to focusing strictly on each virtue in succession. During the first week, I aimed to avoid even the slightest offense against Temperance, while allowing the other virtues to be assessed as usual. Each evening, I noted the faults I had committed during the day. If I could keep my designated line, marked T, free of blemishes during this week, I believed that the habit of Temperance would strengthen, while its opposite would diminish. This progress would encourage me to extend my focus to include the next virtue, enabling me to maintain both lines without imperfections the following week. By continuing in this manner, I anticipated completing a full cycle in thirteen weeks, allowing for four cycles each year. Similar to someone tending a garden who does not attempt to remove all the weeds at once, which would be overwhelming, I focused on one section at a time. Once I successfully tended to the first area, I could move on to the next. I hoped to find motivation in observing my progress in virtue, as I cleared my lines of imperfections. Ultimately, after thirteen weeks of daily reflection, I wished to admire a clean record of my efforts.
output:
A famous Greek philosopher, who lived about 582-500 B. C. The Golden Verses here ascribed to him are probably of later origin. "The time which he recommends for this work is about even or bed-time, that we may conclude the action of the day with the judgment of conscience, making the examination of our conversation an evening song to God."

I determined to give a week's strict attention to each of the virtues successively. Thus, in the first week, my great guard was to avoid every the least offense against Temperance, leaving the other virtues to their ordinary chance, only marking every evening the faults of the day. Thus, if in the first week I could keep my first line, marked T, clear of spots, I suppos'd the habit of that virtue so much strengthen'd, and its opposite weaken'd, that I might venture extending my attention to include the next, and for the following week keep both lines clear of spots. Proceeding thus to the last, I could go thro' a course compleat in thirteen weeks, and four courses in a year. And like him who, having a garden to weed, does not attempt to eradicate all the bad herbs at once, which would exceed his reach and his strength, but works on one of the beds at a time, and, having accomplish'd the first, proceeds to a second, so I should have, I hoped, the encouraging pleasure of seeing on my pages the progress I made in virtue, by clearing successively my lines of their spots, till in the end, by a number of courses, I should be happy in viewing a clean book, after a thirteen weeks' daily examination.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: Our debates thoroughly immersed me in the subject, and subsequently, I wrote and published an anonymous pamphlet titled "The Nature and Necessity of a Paper Currency." This pamphlet was generally well received by the common people, however, it was not as well received by the wealthy individuals. The wealthy individuals disliked it because it increased and strengthened the demand for more money. Moreover, they lacked writers who were able to effectively respond to it, and as a result, their opposition gradually weakened. Consequently, the point was ultimately carried by a majority in the House. Furthermore, my friends in the House, who believed I had provided some benefit, decided to reward me by giving me the task of printing the money, which proved to be a very profitable endeavor and a significant help to me. Additionally, this opportunity wasnear another advantage that I gained as a result of my ability to write.
output: Our debates possess'd me so fully of the subject, that I wrote and printed an anonymous pamphlet on it, entitled "The Nature and Necessity of a Paper Currency." It was well receiv'd by the common people in general; but the rich men dislik'd it, for it increas'd and strengthen'd the clamor for more money, and they happening to have no writers among them that were able to answer it, their opposition slacken'd, and the point was carried by a majority in the House. My friends there, who conceiv'd I had been of some service, thought fit to reward me by employing me in printing the money; a very profitable jobb and a great help to me. This was another advantage gain'd by my being able to write.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: Keimer's printing shop was equipped with an old, damaged press and a small, worn font of English type. He was currently using this type to compose an elegy for Aquilla Rose, a young man known for his intelligence, good character, and reputation in the town as a respected clerk of the Assembly and a budding poet. While Keimer also attempted to write poetry, his efforts were not very successful. He approached writing by composing directly in type from memory, which meant he had no written copy to refer to. This lack of multiple type cases and the demands of the elegy meant that no one could assist him in this task. I took it upon myself to organize his press, which he had not yet used and did not fully understand, and I promised to return to print the elegy once he had it ready. In the meantime, I completed a small job for Bradford, where I was staying and eating. A few days later, Keimer called for me to print the elegy. At that point, he had acquired another set of type cases and a pamphlet to reprint, which I began working on.
output: Keimer's printing-house, I found, consisted of an old shatter'd press, and one small, worn-out font of English, which he was then using himself, composing an Elegy on Aquilla Rose, before mentioned, an ingenious young man, of excellent character, much respected in the town, clerk of the Assembly, and a pretty poet. Keimer made verses too, but very indifferently. He could not be said to write them, for his manner was to compose them in the types directly out of his head. So there being no copy, but one pair of cases, and the Elegy likely to require all the letter, no one could help him. I endeavour'd to put his press (which he had not yet us'd, and of which he understood nothing) into order fit to be work'd with; and, promising to come and print off his Elegy as soon as he should have got it ready, I return'd to Bradford's, who gave me a little job to do for the present, and there I lodged and dieted. A few days after, Keimer sent for me to print off the Elegy. And now he had got another pair of cases, and a pamphlet to reprint, on which he set me to work.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input:
As I walked up the street, I glanced around until I reached the area near the market house, where I encountered a boy carrying bread. Since I had often eaten bread as a meal, I asked the boy where he had obtained it, and then I proceeded to the baker's shop he had recommended, which was located on Second Street. I requested a type of biscuit similar to what we had in Boston, but it appeared that such biscuits were not made in Philadelphia. Consequently, I asked for a three-penny loaf, and the baker informed me that they did not have any available.

Therefore, I was not aware of the difference in currency or the varying prices of the bread, and I did not know the names of the different types of bread, so I asked the baker to give me three-penny worth of any kind. The baker gave me three large, puffy rolls, and I was surprised by the quantity, but I accepted them and, having no space in my pockets, I walked away with a roll under each arm and ate the third one. Meanwhile, I continued up Market Street as far as Fourth Street, passing by the residence of Mr. Read, who was the father of my future wife. She was standing at the door and saw me, and she likely thought I appeared awkward and ridiculous, as I certainly did.

Subsequently, I turned and walked down Chestnut Street and part of Walnut Street, eating my roll along the way, and I eventually found myself back at the Market Street wharf, near the boat I had arrived on. I went to the boat to get a drink of river water, and, after finishing one of my rolls, I gave the other two to a woman and her child who had traveled with us on the boat and were waiting to continue their journey.
output: Then I walked up the street, gazing about till near the market-house I met a boy with bread. I had made many a meal on bread, and, inquiring where he got it, I went immediately to the baker's he directed me to, in Second-street, and ask'd for bisket, intending such as we had in Boston; but they, it seems, were not made in Philadelphia. Then I asked for a three-penny loaf, and was told they had none such. So not considering or knowing the difference of money, and the greater cheapness nor the names of his bread, I bade him give me three-penny worth of any sort. He gave me, accordingly, three great puffy rolls. I was surpris'd at the quantity, but took it, and, having no room in my pockets, walk'd off with a roll under each arm, and eating the other. Thus I went up Market-street as far as Fourth-street, passing by the door of Mr. Read, my future wife's father; when she, standing at the door, saw me, and thought I made, as I certainly did, a most awkward, ridiculous appearance. Then I turned and went down Chestnut-street and part of Walnut-street, eating my roll all the way, and, coming round, found myself again at Market-street wharf, near the boat I came in, to which I went for a draught of the river water; and, being filled with one of my rolls, gave the other two to a woman and her child that came down the river in the boat with us, and were waiting to go farther.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input:
One day is worth two tomorrows. Furthermore, if you have tasks to accomplish tomorrow, it is advisable to complete them today. 

If you were in the position of a servant, would you not feel a sense of shame if your esteemed master were to find you lacking in diligence? Thus, if you are your own master, it is imperative that you feel a sense of shame upon discovering yourself in idleness. 

Moreover, if you remain steadfast in your efforts, you will witness significant results. It is worth noting that consistent effort can erode even the hardest stones, and through diligence and patience, the mouse was capable of gnawing through a cable. Similarly, small, persistent actions can topple even the mightiest oaks.
output:
One To-day is worth two To-morrows, and farther, Have you somewhat to do To-morrow, do it To-day.

If you were a Servant, would you not be ashamed that a good Master should catch you idle? Are you then your own Master, be ashamed to catch yourself idle.

Stick to it steadily; and you will see great Effects, for Constant Dropping wears away Stones, and by Diligence and Patience the Mouse ate in two the Cable; and Little Strokes fell great Oaks.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: Upon completing my tasks and ensuring my fort was well-stocked with provisions, I received a letter from the governor informing me that he had convened the Assembly and requested my attendance, provided that the situation on the frontiers no longer required my presence. This highlights the governor's consideration of my role in the region. My friends in the Assembly also urged me to attend the meeting through their letters, and with my three planned forts now completed and the local inhabitants feeling secure enough to remain on their farms, I decided to return. This suggests that the security situation had improved significantly. The presence of Colonel Clapham, a New England officer experienced in Indian warfare, who was visiting our establishment, further facilitated my decision, as he agreed to take command. I formally appointed him by issuing a commission, which was read aloud to the garrison, and introduced him as a more suitable commander due to his military expertise. After offering some words of encouragement, I bid them farewell. Ultimately, I was escorted to Bethlehem, where I rested for a few days to recover from my fatigue. The comforts of a good bed were a notable change from my previous accommodations, where I had been sleeping on the floor of our hut at Gnadenhut with only a few blankets.
output: I had hardly finish'd this business, and got my fort well stor'd with provisions, when I receiv'd a letter from the governor, acquainting me that he had call'd the Assembly, and wished my attendance there, if the posture of affairs on the frontiers was such that my remaining there was no longer necessary. My friends, too, of the Assembly, pressing me by their letters to be, if possible, at the meeting, and my three intended forts being now compleated, and the inhabitants contented to remain on their farms under that protection, I resolved to return; the more willingly, as a New England officer, Colonel Clapham, experienced in Indian war, being on a visit to our establishment, consented to accept the command. I gave him a commission, and, parading the garrison, had it read before them, and introduc'd him to them as an officer who, from his skill in military affairs, was much more fit to command them than myself; and, giving them a little exhortation, took my leave. I was escorted as far as Bethlehem, where I rested a few days to recover from the fatigue I had undergone. The first night, being in a good bed, I could hardly sleep, it was so different from my hard lodging on the floor of our hut at Gnaden wrapt only in a blanket or two.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input:
The objective was to develop the habit of various virtues. It was determined that focusing on one virtue at a time would be more effective than attempting to address all of them simultaneously. Once a virtue was mastered, attention would shift to the next, continuing this way through all thirteen virtues. This approach also considered that mastering some virtues could facilitate the acquisition of others, leading to a specific arrangement. 

Temperance was prioritized first because it promotes a calm and clear mindset, essential for maintaining vigilance against longstanding habits and ongoing temptations. Once temperance was established, the practice of Silence became more manageable. The intention was to gain knowledge while improving in virtue, recognizing that valuable insights are often obtained through listening rather than speaking. This decision aimed to counteract a tendency towards excessive talking and joking, which attracted shallow social interactions.

Following Silence, Order was deemed important as it would provide more time for focusing on personal projects and studies. Once Resolution became habitual, it would strengthen the commitment to achieving the subsequent virtues. The virtues of Frugality and Industry were expected to aid in alleviating remaining debts and fostering financial independence, thus facilitating the practice of Sincerity and Justice, among others. In line with the advice from Pythagoras’s Golden Verses, it was concluded that a daily examination of progress would be necessary, leading to the development of a structured method for this self-assessment.
output: My intention being to acquire the habitude of all these virtues, I judg'd it would be well not to distract my attention by attempting the whole at once, but to fix it on one of them at a time; and, when I should be master of that, then to proceed to another, and so on, till I should have gone thro' the thirteen; and, as the previous acquisition of some might facilitate the acquisition of certain others, I arrang'd them with that view, as they stand above. Temperance first, as it tends to procure that coolness and clearness of head, which is so necessary where constant vigilance was to be kept up, and guard maintained against the unremitting attraction of ancient habits, and the force of perpetual temptations. This being acquir'd and establish'd, Silence would be more easy; and my desire being to gain knowledge at the same time that I improv'd in virtue, and considering that in conversation it was obtain'd rather by the use of the ears than of the tongue, and therefore wishing to break a habit I was getting into of prattling, punning, and joking, which only made me acceptable to trifling company, I gave Silence the second place. This and the next, Order, I expected would allow me more time for attending to my project and my studies. Resolution, once become habitual, would keep me firm in my endeavours to obtain all the subsequent virtues; Frugality and Industry freeing me from my remaining debt, and producing affluence and independence, would make more easy the practice of Sincerity and Justice, etc., etc. Conceiving then, that, agreeably to the advice of Pythagoras in his Golden Verses, daily examination would be necessary, I contrived the following method for conducting that examination.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: I have provided a detailed account of my journey, and I shall also elaborate on my initial arrival in that city, so that you may, in your mind, juxtapose such improbable beginnings with the reputation I have subsequently established there. On that occasion, I was attired in my working attire, as my finest garments were yet to arrive by sea. I was unkempt from my travels; my pockets were filled with shirts and stockings, and I was unfamiliar with anyone nor did I know where to seek accommodation. I was exhausted from the rigors of travel, rowing, and lack of rest, and I experienced considerable hunger. Furthermore, my entire financial reserve consisted of a Dutch dollar and approximately a shilling in copper coins. I tendered the latter to the boatmen for my passage, who initially refused it due to my rowing efforts; however, I insisted that they accept it. It is worth noting that an individual may sometimes exhibit greater generosity when possessing only a small amount of money than when in possession of considerable wealth, perhaps out of a concern for being perceived as having insufficient funds.
output: I have been the more particular in this description of my journey, and shall be so of my first entry into that city, that you may in your mind compare such unlikely beginnings with the figure I have since made there. I was in my working dress, my best clothes being to come round by sea. I was dirty from my journey; my pockets were stuff'd out with shirts and stockings, and I knew no soul nor where to look for lodging. I was fatigued with traveling, rowing, and want of rest, I was very hungry; and my whole stock of cash consisted of a Dutch dollar, and about a shilling in copper. The latter I gave the people of the boat for my passage, who at first refus'd it, on account of my rowing; but I insisted on their taking it. A man being sometimes more generous when he has but a little money than when he has plenty, perhaps thro' fear of being thought to have but little.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: An ironmonger in London, however, adopted a substantial portion of my pamphlet and developed it into his own work. He made minor changes to the machine, which somewhat impaired its operation, and obtained a patent for it there. As I was told, he made a small fortune from it. This is not the only instance of patents being taken out for my inventions by others, although not always with the same success. I never contested these patents, as I had no desire to profit from patents myself and disliked disputes. The use of these fireplaces in very many houses, both in this colony and in neighboring ones, has been and continues to be a great saving of wood for the inhabitants.
output: An ironmonger in London however, assuming a good deal of my pamphlet, and working it up into his own, and making some small changes in the machine, which rather hurt its operation, got a patent for it there, and made, as I was told, a little fortune by it. And this is not the only instance of patents taken out for my inventions by others, tho' not always with the same success, which I never contested, as having no desire of profiting by patents myself, and hating disputes. The use of these fireplaces in very many houses, both of this and the neighbouring colonies, has been, and is, a great saving of wood to the inhabitants.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: During our discussion, a waiter approached to inform me that two gentlemen downstairs wished to speak with me. I proceeded to meet them and discovered they were two members of our Quaker community. They explained that eight of them were gathered at a nearby tavern. They indicated that they were willing to vote with us if necessary, although they hoped it would not come to that. They requested that we refrain from seeking their support if we could manage without it, as their participation in that vote might create tensions with their elders and friends. Feeling confident in our majority, I returned upstairs and, after a moment of apparent hesitation, agreed to postpone for one more hour. Mr. Morris considered this request to be very reasonable. Surprisingly, none of his opposing colleagues showed up, which he found quite surprising. When the hour concluded, we passed the resolution with a vote of eight to one. Since eight of the twenty-two Quakers were prepared to support us, and thirteen were absent, suggesting they did not wish to challenge the proposal, I later estimated the ratio of Quakers who were genuinely against defense to be one in twenty-one. These individuals were all recognized members of their society and were in good standing, having received proper notice of the matters discussed at that meeting. Overall, this outcome indicated a strong inclination toward support among the Quakers present.
output: While we were disputing this, a waiter came to tell me two gentlemen below desir'd to speak with me. I went down, and found they were two of our Quaker members. They told me there were eight of them assembled at a tavern just by; that they were determin'd to come and vote with us if there should be occasion, which they hop'd would not be the case, and desir'd we would not call for their assistance if we could do without it, as their voting for such a measure might embroil them with their elders and friends. Being thus secure of a majority, I went up, and after a little seeming hesitation, agreed to a delay of another hour. This Mr. Morris allow'd to be extreamly fair. Not one of his opposing friends appear'd, at which he express'd great surprize; and, at the expiration of the hour, we carri'd the resolution eight to one; and as, of the twenty-two Quakers, eight were ready to vote with us, and thirteen, by their absence, manifested that they were not inclin'd to oppose the measure, I afterward estimated the proportion of Quakers sincerely against defense as one to twenty-one only; for these were all regular members of that society, and in good reputation among them, and had due notice of what was propos'd at that meeting.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: Moreover, it was my intention in this work to elucidate and reinforce the doctrine that actions deemed vicious are not detrimental solely because they are proscribed, but rather they are proscribed because they are inherently detrimental, taking into account solely the nature of humanity. Additionally, it is worth noting that, as a consequence, it is in the interest of every individual who aspires to be happy, even within the present world, to cultivate virtue. Furthermore, in light of the fact that there exists a numerous class of affluent merchants, nobility, states, and princes who require trustworthy agents to manage their affairs, and given the relative scarcity of such individuals, I would have endeavoured to persuade young people that the qualities of probity and integrity are among the most likely to secure a fortunate outcome for those of limited means.
output: In this piece it was my design to explain and enforce this doctrine, that vicious actions are not hurtful because they are forbidden, but forbidden because they are hurtful, the nature of man alone considered; that it was, therefore, everyone's interest to be virtuous who wish'd to be happy even in this world; and I should, from this circumstance (there being always in the world a number of rich merchants, nobility, states, and princes, who have need of honest instruments for the management of their affairs, and such being so rare), have endeavoured to convince young persons that no qualities were so likely to make a poor man's fortune as those of probity and integrity.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: The subscriptions that followed may have been more generous, but they tended to slow down, and it became clear that they might not be enough without some support from the Assembly. As a result, it was proposed that a petition be submitted to request this assistance, which was subsequently done. Initially, the country members may not have been entirely enthusiastic about the project, as they were concerned that it would primarily benefit the city, and therefore believed that the citizens should bear the costs alone. They also questioned whether the citizens as a whole were in favor of the project. In response to my argument that the project had received sufficient approval to suggest that it would be possible to raise around two thousand pounds through voluntary donations, the country members were skeptical, and it can often be said that they considered this estimate to be somewhat unrealistic. In summary, the project's funding faced potential challenges and disagreements among the members regarding its benefits and feasibility.
output: The subscriptions afterwards were more free and generous; but, beginning to flag, I saw they would be insufficient without some assistance from the Assembly, and therefore propos'd to petition for it, which was done. The country members did not at first relish the project; they objected that it could only be serviceable to the city, and therefore the citizens alone should be at the expense of it; and they doubted whether the citizens themselves generally approv'd of it. My allegation on the contrary, that it met with such approbation as to leave no doubt of our being able to raise two thousand pounds by voluntary donations, they considered as a most extravagant supposition, and utterly impossible.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin

input: It appears that my plan to write and publish this comment was not ultimately carried out. input: If the demand did not originate from the crown, the phrase was deemed inappropriate, necessitating the creation of an alternative. For example, when there was a shortage of gunpowder—specific to the garrison at Louisburg—the New England government requested a grant of some from Pennsylvania. This request was strongly advocated by Governor Thomas. However, the Pennsylvania House could not allocate funds for purchasing gunpowder, as it was considered a wartime necessity. Instead, they approved a grant of three thousand pounds to be given to the governor, designating it for the purchase of bread, flour, wheat, or other grains. Some council members, wishing to complicate matters for the House, advised the governor to reject the provisions, arguing that they did not align with his original request. The governor responded, stating, "I shall accept the money, for I fully understand their intent; other grain is gunpowder." He proceeded to buy gunpowder with the funds, and there was no subsequent objection.
output: But, if the demand was not directly from the crown, that phrase was found not so proper, and some other was to be invented. As, when powder was wanting (I think it was for the garrison at Louisburg), and the government of New England solicited a grant of some from Pennsylvania, which was much urg'd on the House by Governor Thomas, they could not grant money to buy powder, because that was an ingredient of war; but they voted an aid to New England of three thousand pounds, to be put into the hands of the governor, and appropriated it for the purchasing of bread, flour, wheat or other grain. Some of the council, desirous of giving the House still further embarrassment, advis'd the governor not to accept provision, as not being the thing he had demanded; but he repli'd, "I shall take the money, for I understand very well their meaning; other grain is gunpowder," which he accordingly bought, and they never objected to it.

The service may be manageable and straightforward, as the army tends to march only about twelve miles each day. The wagons and baggage horses, which carry essential supplies for the army's well-being, are required to travel at the same pace as the troops and cannot move faster. For the sake of security, these resources are often positioned in ways that ensure their safety, whether during marches or while encamped.

If you are indeed, as I believe you are, loyal and devoted subjects to the king, you may find an opportunity to provide valuable assistance while also making it easier for yourselves. Individuals who cannot spare a wagon, four horses, and a driver from their plantation operations may consider collaborating. For example, one person could supply the wagon, another could provide one or two horses, and yet another could handle driving, allowing you to share the payment among yourselves. However, if you choose not to offer this support voluntarily when reasonable compensation is available, it may lead to questions about your loyalty. The king's affairs must proceed, and it would be disheartening for the many brave soldiers who have come so far to protect you to be left idle due to a reluctance to meet reasonable expectations. Wagons and horses are necessary, and if no one steps forward, there may be coercive measures taken, leaving you to seek compensation elsewhere, which may not be met with much sympathy or regard. In summary, it may be prudent to consider how you can contribute positively while ensuring your own interests are also protected.
output:
"The service will be light and easy, for the army will scarce march above twelve miles per day, and the waggons and baggage-horses, as they carry those things that are absolutely necessary to the welfare of the army, must march with the army, and no faster; and are, for the army's sake, always placed where they can be most secure, whether in a march or in a camp.

"If you are really, as I believe you are, good and loyal subjects to his majesty, you may now do a most acceptable service, and make it easy to yourselves; for three or four of such as cannot separately spare from the business of their plantations a waggon and four horses and a driver, may do it together, one furnishing the waggon, another one or two horses, and another the driver, and divide the pay proportionately between you; but if you do not this service to your king and country voluntarily, when such good pay and reasonable terms are offered to you, your loyalty will be strongly suspected. The king's business must be done; so many brave troops, come so far for your defense, must not stand idle through your backwardness to do what may be reasonably expected from you; waggons and horses must be had; violent measures will probably be used, and you will be left to seek for a recompense where you can find it, and your case, perhaps, be little pitied or regarded.

input: I had some reason to think that the defense of the country was generally acceptable to them, as long as they were not expected to participate directly. I noticed that a larger number of them than I had anticipated, although opposed to engaging in offensive warfare, were supportive of defense efforts. Numerous pamphlets were published both in favor of and against the issue, including some authored by reputable Quakers advocating for defense, which I believe influenced many of their younger members. Overall, it seems that the conversation around defense may have shifted some opinions within the community.
output: Indeed I had some cause to believe that the defense of the country was not disagreeable to any of them, provided they were not requir'd to assist in it. And I found that a much greater number of them than I could have imagined, tho' against offensive war, were clearly for the defensive. Many pamphlets pro and con were publish'd on the subject, and some by good Quakers, in favour of defense, which I believe convinc'd most of their younger people.

input: The incident involving Vernon's money may be considered one of the earlier significant mistakes of my life, and it can often be seen as a situation that tended to support my father's assessment that I was not yet ready to handle important business matters. However, Sir William, after reading the letter, seemed to think that my father was being overly cautious. It is worth noting that people can vary greatly in terms of their abilities and characteristics, and discretion does not necessarily come with age, nor is it always absent in younger individuals. Sir William then offered to assist me, saying that since my father would not provide support, he would do so himself, and he asked me to provide a list of necessary items to be obtained from England, which he would then procure, with the understanding that I would repay him when I was able to do so. He appeared to be genuinely committed to having a skilled printer in the area and seemed confident that I would succeed. At the time, I had not shared my plans to set up a business with anyone in Philadelphia, and I chose to keep this information private. In hindsight, it is possible that if others had known about my reliance on the governor, they may have advised me to be cautious, given his reputation for making promises that he did not intend to keep. Nevertheless, since he had made these offers without being solicited, it was difficult for me to doubt his sincerity, and I tended to view him as one of the most trustworthy individuals. Overall, this experience may have highlighted the importance of carefully evaluating the people one relies on for support and guidance.
output: The breaking into this money of Vernon's was one of the first great errata of my life; and this affair show'd that my father was not much out in his judgment when he suppos'd me too young to manage business of importance. But Sir William, on reading his letter, said he was too prudent. There was great difference in persons; and discretion did not always accompany years, nor was youth always without it. "And since he will not set you up," says he, "I will do it myself. Give me an inventory of the things necessary to be had from England, and I will send for them. You shall repay me when you are able; I am resolv'd to have a good printer here, and I am sure you must succeed." This was spoken with such an appearance of cordiality, that I had not the least doubt of his meaning what he said. I had hitherto kept the proposition of my setting up, a secret in Philadelphia, and I still kept it. Had it been known that I depended on the governor, probably some friend, that knew him better, would have advis'd me not to rely on him, as I afterwards heard it as his known character to be liberal of promises which he never meant to keep. Yet, unsolicited as he was by me, how could I think his generous offers insincere? I believ'd him one of the best men in the world.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: To proceed with the march, I gathered the companies at Bethlehem, which is the main settlement of that community. I was surprised to observe that it was well-prepared for defense, likely due to the fear instigated by the destruction of Gnadenhut. The primary structures were protected by a stockade, and they had acquired a significant amount of arms and ammunition from New York. Additionally, they placed small paving stones between the windows of their tall stone houses to be used by the women against any Indigenous individuals attempting to break in. The armed members of the community were also vigilant, maintaining a watch as systematically as in any military garrison. In a discussion with Bishop Spangenberg, I expressed my astonishment, as I had understood that they received an act of Parliament that exempted them from military service in the colonies. This led me to believe they held a principled opposition to bearing arms. He clarified that this was not a long-standing principle for them, but at the time they received that act, it was perceived as a belief by many in their community. However, they found that only a few actually adhered to it. This suggests that they may have either misunderstood their own convictions or misled Parliament. Ultimately, it appears that practical considerations, particularly the immediate threat, can often override abstract principles.
output: In order to march thither, I assembled the companies at Bethlehem, the chief establishment of those people. I was surprised to find it in so good a posture of defense; the destruction of Gnadenhut had made them apprehend danger. The principal buildings were defended by a stockade; they had purchased a quantity of arms and ammunition from New York, and had even plac'd quantities of small paving stones between the windows of their high stone houses, for their women to throw down upon the heads of any Indians that should attempt to force into them. The armed brethren, too, kept watch, and reliev'd as methodically as in any garrison town. In conversation with the bishop, Spangenberg, I mention'd this my surprise; for, knowing they had obtained an act of Parliament exempting them from military duties in the colonies, I had suppos'd they were conscientiously scrupulous of bearing arms. He answer'd me that it was not one of their established principles, but that, at the time of their obtaining that act, it was thought to be a principle with many of their people. On this occasion, however, they, to their surprise, found it adopted by but a few. It seems they were either deceiv'd in themselves, or deceiv'd the Parliament; but common sense, aided by present danger, will sometimes be too strong for whimsical opinions.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: Moreover, it is worth noting that the motivations behind this apparent shift in sentiment are unclear, and it is uncertain whether it was a genuine change of heart or merely a strategic maneuver. Additionally, it is possible that they presumed we were too deeply invested in our emotional involvement to withdraw, and therefore sought to facilitate a clandestine marriage, thereby retaining the freedom to bestow or withhold their favor as they saw fit. In essence, I harbored suspicions regarding the sincerity of their intentions, and as a result, I chose to terminate my interactions with them. Furthermore, Mrs. Godfrey subsequently presented me with more favorable reports regarding their disposition, and attempted to persuade me to reestablish contact; however, I unequivocally affirmed my decision to sever all ties with that family. It is worth noting that the Godfreys took umbrage with my stance, and as a consequence, we found ourselves at odds, leading to their eventual departure, wherein they vacated the premises, leaving me in sole occupancy of the house, and I resolved henceforth to decline any further applications for residency.
output: Whether this was a real change of sentiment or only artifice, on a supposition of our being too far engaged in affection to retract, and therefore that we should steal a marriage, which would leave them at liberty to give or withhold what they pleas'd, I know not; but I suspected the latter, resented it, and went no more. Mrs. Godfrey brought me afterward some more favorable accounts of their disposition, and would have drawn me on again; but I declared absolutely my resolution to have nothing more to do with that family. This was resented by the Godfreys; we differed, and they removed, leaving me the whole house, and I resolved to take no more inmates.

input: It's worth noting that, in the autumn of the previous year, I had helped to establish a group of acquaintances who shared my interest in self-improvement, which we referred to as the Junto. We would typically meet on Friday evenings, and I had developed a set of rules to guide our discussions. These rules suggested that each member, on a rotating basis, should pose questions or topics related to morals, politics, or natural philosophy for the group to consider. Additionally, every three months, each member was expected to write and present an essay on a subject of their choice. Our discussions were led by a president and were intended to be conducted in a spirit of genuine inquiry, with the goal of seeking truth rather than simply winning an argument. To promote a respectful and constructive atmosphere, we tended to discourage absolute statements and direct contradictions, and, after a time, we even implemented small fines to discourage such behavior. In summary, the Junto was a club focused on mutual improvement, where members engaged in respectful discussions and debates on a variety of topics.
output: I should have mentioned before, that, in the autumn of the preceding year, I had form'd most of my ingenious acquaintance into a club of mutual improvement, which was called the Junto; we met on Friday evenings. The rules that I drew up required that every member, in his turn, should produce one or more queries on any point of Morals, Politics, or Natural Philosophy, to be discuss'd by the company; and once in three months produce and read an essay of his own writing, on any subject he pleased. Our debates were to be under the direction of a president, and to be conducted in the sincere spirit of inquiry after truth, without fondness for dispute, or desire of victory; and, to prevent warmth, all expressions of positiveness in opinions, or direct contradiction, were after some time made contraband, and prohibited under small pecuniary penalties.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: From childhood, I had always found joy in this practice. I studied and practiced all of Thevenot's motions and positions while also incorporating some of my own ideas, focusing on creating a style that was both graceful and practical. I took this opportunity to showcase my skills to the company, and I was pleased to receive their admiration. Eventually, he suggested that we travel throughout Europe together, supporting ourselves by working in our craft. Initially, I was open to this idea; however, after discussing it with my good friend Mr. Denham, who I often visited during my free time, he advised against it. He encouraged me to concentrate on returning to Pennsylvania, as he was planning to do.
output: I had from a child been ever delighted with this exercise, had studied and practis'd all Thevenot's motions and positions, added some of my own, aiming at the graceful and easy as well as the useful. All these I took this occasion of exhibiting to the company, and was much flatter'd by their admiration; and Wygate, who was desirous of becoming a master, grew more and more attach'd to me on that account, as well as from the similarity of our studies. He at length proposed to me traveling all over Europe together, supporting ourselves everywhere by working at our business. I was once inclined to it; but, mentioning it to my good friend Mr. Denham, with whom I often spent an hour when I had leisure, he dissuaded me from it, advising me to think only of returning to Pennsylvania, which he was now about to do.

input:
Upon my return to Philadelphia, I observed that the association was thriving. The non-Quaker residents largely embraced it, forming companies and electing their captains, lieutenants, and ensigns in accordance with the new law. Dr. B. came to visit me and detailed the efforts he had made to cultivate a favorable opinion of the law, attributing much of its acceptance to these endeavors. I had previously taken pride in believing that my Dialogue was the primary influence; however, I remained open to the possibility that he was correct, so I allowed him to maintain his view, which I believe is often the best approach in such situations. 

During a meeting, the officers selected me to serve as colonel of the regiment, a position I accepted this time. I do not recall the exact number of companies we had, but we mustered around twelve hundred well-prepared men, along with an artillery unit equipped with six brass field-pieces. They had become so skilled that they could fire twelve times per minute. On the occasion of my first review of the regiment, they accompanied me to my residence and honored me with a salute, firing several rounds before my door, which caused some of my electrical apparatus to shake and break. Unfortunately, my new title proved equally fragile, as all our commissions were soon rendered void by a repeal of the law in England.
output: Being returned to Philadelphia, I found the association went on swimmingly, the inhabitants that were not Quakers having pretty generally come into it, formed themselves into companies, and chose their captains, lieutenants, and ensigns, according to the new law. Dr. B. visited me, and gave me an account of the pains he had taken to spread a general good liking to the law, and ascribed much to those endeavours. I had had the vanity to ascribe all to my Dialogue; however, not knowing but that he might be in the right, I let him enjoy his opinion, which I take to be generally the best way in such cases. The officers, meeting, chose me to be colonel of the regiment, which I this time accepted. I forget how many companies we had, but we paraded about twelve hundred well-looking men, with a company of artillery, who had been furnished with six brass field-pieces, which they had become so expert in the use of as to fire twelve times in a minute. The first time I reviewed my regiment they accompanied me to my house, and would salute me with some rounds fired before my door, which shook down and broke several glasses of my electrical apparatus. And my new honour proved not much less brittle; for all our commissions were soon after broken by a repeal of the law in England.

author: Benjamin Franklin

input: I had previously been living with Godfrey, who occupied part of my house along with his wife and children. He used one side of the shop for his glazier's business, although he spent little time working there as he was often engrossed in mathematics. Mrs. Godfrey sought to arrange a match for me with her relative's daughter, frequently creating opportunities for us to meet. This effort led to a serious courtship on my part, as the young woman possessed many admirable qualities. The older generation supported my intentions by inviting me to supper repeatedly and allowing us time together. Eventually, it became necessary to discuss the situation. Mrs. Godfrey facilitated our negotiations. I informed her that I expected a sum of money with their daughter sufficient to settle my remaining debt for the printing house, which I estimated to be around one hundred pounds. She later informed me that they could not provide that amount. I suggested they could mortgage their home at the loan office. After several days, I received their response, which was that they disapproved of the match. They had inquired about my business and learned from Bradford that the printing industry was not very profitable. They expressed concerns that my types would soon wear out and that additional investment would be needed. They mentioned that S. Keimer and D. Harry had both failed, and they believed I would likely face a similar fate. As a result, I was forbidden from visiting their home, and their daughter was kept away from me.
output: I had hitherto continu'd to board with Godfrey, who lived in part of my house with his wife and children, and had one side of the shop for his glazier's business, tho' he worked little, being always absorbed in his mathematics. Mrs. Godfrey projected a match for me with a relation's daughter, took opportunities of bringing us often together, till a serious courtship on my part ensu'd, the girl being in herself very deserving. The old folks encourag'd me by continual invitations to supper, and by leaving us together, till at length it was time to explain. Mrs. Godfrey manag'd our little treaty. I let her know that I expected as much money with their daughter as would pay off my remaining debt for the printing-house, which I believe was not then above a hundred pounds. She brought me word they had no such sum to spare; I said they might mortgage their house in the loan-office. The answer to this, after some days, was, that they did not approve the match; that, on inquiry of Bradford, they had been informed the printing business was not a profitable one; the types would soon be worn out, and more wanted; that S. Keimer and D. Harry had failed one after the other, and I should probably soon follow them; and, therefore, I was forbidden the house, and the daughter shut up.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: Captain Orme, who served as one of the general's aides-de-camp, was severely injured and accompanied the general until his passing, which occurred a few days later. According to Captain Orme, the general may have been in shock, as he remained largely silent on the first day, uttering only a brief phrase at night, "Who would have thought it?" The general can often be characterized as being quiet, and this trend tends to continue the following day, with him speaking only briefly towards the end, saying "We shall better know how to deal with them another time". He passed away just a few minutes after making this statement, and it can be said that the general's final days were marked by a sense of quiet reflection.
output: Captain Orme, who was one of the general's aids-de-camp, and, being grievously wounded, was brought off with him, and continu'd with him to his death, which happen'd in a few days, told me that he was totally silent all the first day, and at night only said, "Who would have thought it?" That he was silent again the following day, saying only at last, "We shall better know how to deal with them another time"; and dy'd in a few minutes after.

input: At the beginning of January, the effort to construct forts commenced. A detachment was dispatched to the Minisink area with orders to build a fort for the protection of that region. Another group was sent to the lower part of the area with similar instructions. The decision was made to accompany the remaining forces to Gnadenhut, where a fort was deemed particularly essential. The Moravians provided five wagons to transport tools, supplies, and baggage.
output: It was the beginning of January when we set out upon this business of building forts. I sent one detachment toward the Minisink, with instructions to erect one for the security of that upper part of the country, and another to the lower part, with similar instructions; and I concluded to go myself with the rest of my force to Gnadenhut, where a fort was tho't more immediately necessary. The Moravians procur'd me five waggons for our tools, stores, baggage, etc.

input: A question once arose between Collins and me regarding the propriety of educating the female sex in learning and their abilities for study. He held the opinion that it was improper and that women were naturally unequal to it. I took the contrary side, perhaps partly for the sake of dispute. He was naturally more eloquent and had a ready abundance of words, and sometimes, as I thought, he overwhelmed me more by his fluency than by the strength of his reasons. Since we parted without settling the point and were not to see one another again for some time, I sat down to put my arguments in writing, which I copied fairly and sent to him. He answered, and I replied. Three or four letters had passed on each side when my father happened to find my papers and read them. Without entering into the discussion, he took the occasion to speak with me about the manner of my writing. He observed that, although I had the advantage of my opponent in correct spelling and punctuation, which I owed to the printing house, I fell far short in elegance of expression, in method, and in perspicuity, of which he convinced me by several instances. I saw the justice of his remarks, and from that point I grew more attentive to the manner of writing and determined to endeavor at improvement.
output: A question was once, somehow or other, started between Collins and me, of the propriety of educating the female sex in learning, and their abilities for study. He was of opinion that it was improper, and that they were naturally unequal to it. I took the contrary side, perhaps a little for dispute's sake. He was naturally more eloquent, had a ready plenty of words, and sometimes, as I thought, bore me down more by his fluency than by the strength of his reasons. As we parted without settling the point, and were not to see one another again for some time, I sat down to put my arguments in writing, which I copied fair and sent to him. He answered, and I replied. Three or four letters of a side had passed, when my father happened to find my papers and read them. Without entering into the discussion, he took occasion to talk to me about the manner of my writing; observed that, though I had the advantage of my antagonist in correct spelling and pointing (which I ow'd to the printing-house), I fell far short in elegance of expression, in method and in perspicuity, of which he convinced me by several instances. I saw the justice of his remarks, and thence grew more attentive to the manner in writing, and determined to endeavor at improvement.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input:
In conclusion, it may be observed that experience maintains a costly institution of learning, yet those lacking wisdom will acquire instruction through no other means, and scarcely even through that; for it is indeed true that advice may be offered, but conduct cannot be imparted, as Poor Richard remarks. Furthermore, it should be remembered that those who refuse counsel cannot be assisted, as Poor Richard states; and moreover, that if reason is not heeded, she will assuredly administer correction.

I am greatly pleased by your description of Paradise and by your design for residing there; and I largely approve of your conclusion that, in the interim, we ought to derive whatever benefit we can from this world. Moreover, in my view, we might all derive greater benefit from it than we presently do, and endure less hardship, if we would take care not to pay too much for whistles. For it appears to me that most of the unhappy individuals we encounter have become so through neglect of that very precaution.
output:
And now to conclude, Experience keeps a dear School, but Fools will learn in no other, and scarce in that; for it is true, we may give Advice, but we cannot give Conduct, as Poor Richard says: However, remember this, They that won't be counseled, can't be helped, as Poor Richard says: and farther, That if you will not hear Reason, she'll surely rap your Knuckles.

I am charmed with your description of Paradise, and with your plan of living there; and I approve much of your conclusion, that, in the meantime, we should draw all the good we can from this world. In my opinion, we might all draw more good from it than we do, and suffer less evil, if we would take care not to give too much for whistles. For to me it seems, that most of the unhappy people we meet with, are become so by neglect of that caution.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: Before we received news of the defeat, the two Doctors Bond approached me with a subscription paper to raise funds for a grand firework display. This event was planned to celebrate our anticipated capture of Fort Duquesne. I responded with a serious expression, indicating that it would be prudent to wait until we had confirmation of a victory before preparing for celebrations. They appeared surprised by my reluctance to support their proposal. One of them exclaimed, "Surely you do not think the fort will not be taken?" I replied that while I could not definitively say it would not, I understood that the outcomes of war are highly unpredictable. I shared my reasons for my skepticism; as a result, the subscription effort was abandoned. This decision spared the projectors from the disappointment they would have faced had the fireworks been prepared. Later, Dr. Bond expressed his disapproval of my cautious outlook.
output: Before we had the news of this defeat, the two Doctors Bond came to me with a subscription paper for raising money to defray the expense of a grand firework, which it was intended to exhibit at a rejoicing on receipt of the news of our taking Fort Duquesne. I looked grave, and said it would, I thought, be time enough to prepare for the rejoicing when we knew we should have occasion to rejoice. They seem'd surpris'd that I did not immediately comply with their proposal. "Why the d - - l!" says one of them, "you surely don't suppose that the fort will not be taken?" "I don't know that it will not be taken, but I know that the events of war are subject to great uncertainty." I gave them the reasons of my doubting; the subscription was dropt, and the projectors thereby missed the mortification they would have undergone if the firework had been prepared. Dr. Bond, on some other occasion afterward, said that he did not like Franklin's forebodings.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input:
Among my friends in the House, Mr. Hamilton is notable. He had recently returned from England and held a seat in the House. He actively supported my interests during that time and continued to do so until his passing. 

Around this period, Mr. Vernon reminded me of the debt I owed him, though he did not apply any pressure. I wrote him a sincere letter acknowledging the debt and requested a bit more time to repay it, which he kindly granted. Once I was able, I repaid the principal amount along with interest and expressed my gratitude, thereby addressing the oversight to some extent.
output:
Among my friends in the House I must not forget Mr. Hamilton, before mentioned, who was then returned from England, and had a seat in it. He interested himself for me strongly in that instance, as he did in many others afterward, continuing his patronage till his death.

Mr. Vernon, about this time, put me in mind of the debt I ow'd him, but did not press me. I wrote him an ingenuous letter of acknowledgment, crav'd his forbearance a little longer, which he allow'd me, and as soon as I was able, I paid the principal with interest, and many thanks; so that erratum was in some degree corrected.
title: Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
author: Benjamin Franklin

input: Some of my friends expressed concerns that my involvement in these matters might lead to discontent among that group, potentially jeopardizing my standing in the Assembly of the province, where they held a significant majority. A young man, who also had connections within the House and aspired to take over my role as clerk, informed me that it was likely I would be replaced in the upcoming election. With good intentions, he suggested that I consider resigning, as it might be more honorable than being removed. In response, I mentioned having heard of a public figure who adhered to a principle of neither seeking nor declining an office when offered. He then desir'd I would at least give him my advice. He laugh'd and thank'd me, and said he would take my advice.
