The buck-eye does not grow in New England, and the mocking-bird is rarely heard here. The wild-goose is more of a cosmopolite than we; he breaks his fast in Canada, takes a luncheon in the Ohio, and plumes himself for the night in a southern bayou. Even the bison, to some extent, keeps pace with the seasons, cropping the pastures of the Colorado only till a greener and sweeter grass awaits him by the Yellowstone. Yet we think that if rail-fences are pulled down, and stone-walls piled up on our farms, bounds are henceforth set to our lives and our fates decided. If you are chosen town-clerk, forsooth, you cannot go to Tierra del Fuego this summer: but you may go to the land of infernal fire nevertheless. The universe is wider than our views of it.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: Eventually, the jays arrive, and their distinctive calls can often be heard from quite a distance as they cautiously approach, moving stealthily from tree to tree. They gather the kernels that the squirrels have dropped. Perched on a pitch-pine branch, they sometimes attempt to swallow a kernel that is too large, which may lead to them choking. After much effort, they manage to regurgitate it and spend a considerable amount of time trying to crack it open by striking it with their beaks. While they may appear to be stealing, I found it hard to hold them in high regard. In contrast, the squirrels, although initially a bit hesitant, go about their business as if reclaiming what belongs to them. This scene highlights the differing behaviors of these two species in their interactions with their environment.
output: At length the jays arrive, whose discordant screams were heard long before, as they were warily making their approach an eighth of a mile off, and in a stealthy and sneaking manner they flit from tree to tree, nearer and nearer, and pick up the kernels which the squirrels have dropped. Then, sitting on a pitch-pine bough, they attempt to swallow in their haste a kernel which is too big for their throats and chokes them; and after great labor they disgorge it, and spend an hour in the endeavor to crack it by repeated blows with their bills. They were manifestly thieves, and I had not much respect for them; but the squirrels, though at first shy, went to work as if they were taking what was their own.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input:
I am, perhaps, too high-born to be owned as property, to be a secondary figure in control, or to serve as a useful servant and instrument to any sovereign state throughout the world.

Someone who gives himself entirely to his fellow-men may often appear to them useless and selfish, while someone who gives himself only partially to them tends to be called a benefactor and philanthropist.

How, then, might a man properly behave toward the American government today? I would answer that he cannot, without disgrace, be associated with it. I cannot for an instant recognize as my government that political organization which is also the slave's government.
output:
“I am too high-born to be propertied, To be a secondary at control, Or useful serving-man and instrument To any sovereign state throughout the world.”

He who gives himself entirely to his fellow-men appears to them useless and selfish; but he who gives himself partially to them is pronounced a benefactor and philanthropist.

How does it become a man to behave toward the American government today? I answer that he cannot without disgrace be associated with it. I cannot for an instant recognize that political organization as my government which is the slave’s government also.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: No way of presenting a matter tends to serve us so well in the end as the truth. This alone tends to wear well. For the most part, we may not really be where we are, but in a false position. Through a weakness in our natures, we suppose a case and put ourselves into it, and hence we can be in two cases at the same time, which can make it doubly difficult to get out. In sane moments, we regard only the facts, the case that is. Say what you have to say, not what you ought to say. Any truth is generally better than make-believe. Tom Hyde, the tinker, standing on the gallows, was asked if he had anything to say. "Tell the tailors," he said, "to remember to make a knot in their thread before they take the first stitch." His companion's prayer is forgotten. In the end, a simple truth often stays with us longer than anything else.
output: No face which we can give to a matter will stead us so well at last as the truth. This alone wears well. For the most part, we are not where we are, but in a false position. Through an infirmity of our natures, we suppose a case, and put ourselves into it, and hence are in two cases at the same time, and it is doubly difficult to get out. In sane moments we regard only the facts, the case that is. Say what you have to say, not what you ought. Any truth is better than make-believe. Tom Hyde, the tinker, standing on the gallows, was asked if he had anything to say. “Tell the tailors,” said he, “to remember to make a knot in their thread before they take the first stitch.” His companion’s prayer is forgotten.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: When the ground was not yet fully covered, and again near the end of winter when the snow had melted on my south hillside and around my wood-pile, the partridges came out of the woods in the morning and evening to feed there. Whichever side you walk in the woods, the partridge bursts away on whirring wings, jarring snow from the dry leaves and twigs above, which sifts down in the sunbeams like golden dust. This brave bird is not easily frightened by winter. It is frequently covered by drifts, and it is said that it sometimes plunges from wing into the soft snow, where it remains concealed for a day or two. I used to start them in the open land as well, where they had come out of the woods at sunset to bud the wild apple trees. They will come regularly every evening to particular trees, where the cunning sportsman lies in wait for them, and the distant orchards next to the woods suffer considerably for this reason. I am glad that the partridge gets fed, at any rate. It is Nature's own bird, which lives on buds and diet-drink.
output: When the ground was not yet quite covered, and again near the end of winter, when the snow was melted on my south hill-side and about my wood-pile, the partridges came out of the woods morning and evening to feed there. Whichever side you walk in the woods the partridge bursts away on whirring wings, jarring the snow from the dry leaves and twigs on high, which comes sifting down in the sun-beams like golden dust; for this brave bird is not to be scared by winter. It is frequently covered up by drifts, and, it is said, “sometimes plunges from on wing into the soft snow, where it remains concealed for a day or two.” I used to start them in the open land also, where they had come out of the woods at sunset to “bud” the wild apple-trees. They will come regularly every evening to particular trees, where the cunning sportsman lies in wait for them, and the distant orchards next the woods suffer thus not a little. I am glad that the partridge gets fed, at any rate. It is Nature’s own bird which lives on buds and diet-drink.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that there exists another pond of similar characteristics, namely White Pond, located in Nine Acre Corner, approximately two and a half miles to the west. Furthermore, despite being familiar with the majority of ponds within a dozen miles of this central location, it is evident that few possess the same level of purity and serenity as this particular body of water. In essence, successive generations have likely utilized, admired, and studied this pond, only to eventually pass on, leaving its water to remain remarkably green and transparent. Moreover, it is notable that this pond does not appear to be fed by an intermittent spring. It is possible that on the morning when Adam and Eve were expelled from Eden, Walden Pond was already in existence, experiencing the gentle rains and mist of spring, accompanied by a southerly wind, and teeming with numerous ducks and geese that were unaware of the fall of man, at a time when such unspoiled lakes were sufficient for their needs. Moreover, even at that early stage, the pond had commenced its cyclical pattern of rising and falling, clarifying its waters, and acquiring the distinctive hue that it presently exhibits, thereby obtaining a divine mandate to be the unique Walden Pond, distinguished as a distiller of celestial dews. It is worth noting that this pond may have been revered as the Castalian Fountain in the literary traditions of numerous forgotten nations, and it is conceivable that nymphs presided over it during the Golden Age. In addition, this pond is a treasure of exceptional quality, which the town of Concord wears as a jewel in its crown.
output: We have one other pond just like this, White Pond, in Nine Acre Corner, about two and a half miles westerly; but, though I am acquainted with most of the ponds within a dozen miles of this centre I do not know a third of this pure and well-like character. Successive nations perchance have drank at, admired, and fathomed it, and passed away, and still its water is green and pellucid as ever. Not an intermitting spring! Perhaps on that spring morning when Adam and Eve were driven out of Eden Walden Pond was already in existence, and even then breaking up in a gentle spring rain accompanied with mist and a southerly wind, and covered with myriads of ducks and geese, which had not heard of the fall, when still such pure lakes sufficed them. Even then it had commenced to rise and fall, and had clarified its waters and colored them of the hue they now wear, and obtained a patent of heaven to be the only Walden Pond in the world and distiller of celestial dews. Who knows in how many unremembered nations’ literatures this has been the Castalian Fountain? or what nymphs presided over it in the Golden Age? It is a gem of the first water which Concord wears in her coronet.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: It is worth noting that the state does not intentionally confront an individual's intellectual or moral sense; rather, it focuses solely on the physical body and the senses of the individual. The state operates not with superior intellect or integrity, but with the advantage of greater physical strength. I was not born to be coerced; I will breathe in my own manner. Let us examine who possesses greater strength. What power does a multitude truly have? Only those who adhere to a higher law than I can compel me. They seek to force me to conform to their own likeness. I do not hear of individuals being compelled to live in a certain manner by the masses. What kind of existence would that entail? When I encounter a government that demands, "Your money or your life," I question why I should feel urgency in relinquishing my money. The government may be in a dire situation and uncertain of its next steps; however, that is not my concern. It must find its own solutions, just as I do. It is not worthwhile to lament the situation. I am not accountable for the effective operation of societal machinery; I am not the offspring of the engineer. I observe that when an acorn and a chestnut fall next to one another, neither remains inert to accommodate the other; instead, both follow their own inherent laws, growing and thriving to the best of their abilities until one, perhaps, overshadows and ultimately destroys the other. If a plant cannot thrive according to its nature, it will perish; the same holds true for a human being.
output: Thus the state never intentionally confronts a man’s sense, intellectual or moral, but only his body, his senses. It is not armed with superior wit or honesty, but with superior physical strength. I was not born to be forced. I will breathe after my own fashion. Let us see who is the strongest. What force has a multitude? They only can force me who obey a higher law than I. They force me to become like themselves. I do not hear of men being forced to live this way or that by masses of men. What sort of life were that to live? When I meet a government which says to me, “Your money or your life,” why should I be in haste to give it my money? It may be in a great strait, and not know what to do: I cannot help that. It must help itself; do as I do. It is not worth the while to snivel about it. I am not responsible for the successful working of the machinery of society. I am not the son of the engineer. I perceive that, when an acorn and a chestnut fall side by side, the one does not remain inert to make way for the other, but both obey their own laws, and spring and grow and flourish as best they can, till one, perchance, overshadows and destroys the other. If a plant cannot live according to its nature, it dies; and so a man.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: As I traversed the lengthy causeway constructed for the railroad that extends through the meadows, I encountered numerous gusts of wind that were both blustery and biting, for there exists no location where the wind is permitted such unfettered movement. When the frost had nipped at my cheek, despite my unrefined nature, I turned to present the other cheek as well. Furthermore, the conditions were not significantly improved along the carriage road from Brister’s Hill. I arrived in town reminiscent of a welcoming Indian, as the elements from the expansive open fields were heaped between the confines of the Walden road, and a mere thirty minutes sufficed to erase any evidence of the last traveler. Upon my return, I discovered that fresh drifts had formed, through which I struggled to navigate, where the industrious north-west wind had deposited the fine, powdery snow around a sharp bend in the road, and not a single rabbit's track, nor even the delicate imprint of a meadow mouse, was discernible. Nevertheless, it is worth noting that I seldom failed to discover, even in the depths of winter, a warm and vibrant swamp where the grass and skunk cabbage continued to thrive with enduring greenery, and where a hardier bird occasionally awaited the arrival of spring.
output: As I walked over the long causeway made for the railroad through the meadows, I encountered many a blustering and nipping wind, for nowhere has it freer play; and when the frost had smitten me on one cheek, heathen as I was, I turned to it the other also. Nor was it much better by the carriage road from Brister’s Hill. For I came to town still, like a friendly Indian, when the contents of the broad open fields were all piled up between the walls of the Walden road, and half an hour sufficed to obliterate the tracks of the last traveller. And when I returned new drifts would have formed, through which I floundered, where the busy north-west wind had been depositing the powdery snow round a sharp angle in the road, and not a rabbit’s track, nor even the fine print, the small type, of a meadow mouse was to be seen. Yet I rarely failed to find, even in mid-winter, some warm and springly swamp where the grass and the skunk-cabbage still put forth with perennial verdure, and some hardier bird occasionally awaited the return of spring.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: I was also treated to the sound of a hooting owl. At close range, the sound can be perceived as melancholy, as if it is meant to evoke the final cries of a human being. This sound is characterized by a unique blend of mournful and musical qualities, which can be somewhat unsettling. Additionally, the sound is reminiscent of certain eerie and disturbing images. However, when the owl's call is answered from a distant location, the sound becomes more melodious. The distant call is typically a series of haunting yet musical notes, such as a repetitive hooting sound. Nevertheless, the overall effect of the owl's call is generally pleasing, regardless of the time of day or season in which it is heard. Furthermore, the sound of the owl can be enjoyed in various contexts, whether it is summer or winter, and doesn't necessarily evoke negative associations.
output: I was also serenaded by a hooting owl. Near at hand you could fancy it the most melancholy sound in Nature, as if she meant by this to stereotype and make permanent in her choir the dying moans of a human being, - some poor weak relic of mortality who has left hope behind, and howls like an animal, yet with human sobs, on entering the dark valley, made more awful by a certain gurgling melodiousness, - I find myself beginning with the letters gl when I try to imitate it, - expressive of a mind which has reached the gelatinous mildewy stage in the mortification of all healthy and courageous thought. It reminded me of ghouls and idiots and insane howlings. But now one answers from far woods in a strain made really melodious by distance, - Hoo hoo hoo, hoorer hoo; and indeed for the most part it suggested only pleasing associations, whether heard by day or night, summer or winter.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: He interested me because he tended to be so quiet and solitary, and yet he seemed so happy; he had a well of good humor and contentment that often overflowed in his eyes. His mirth generally seemed without alloy. Sometimes I would see him at his work in the woods, felling trees, and he would often greet me with a laugh of inexpressible satisfaction, along with a salutation in Canadian French, though he spoke English as well. When I approached him, he would usually suspend his work, and with half-suppressed mirth lie along the trunk of a pine he had felled, and, peeling off the inner bark, roll it up into a ball and chew it while he laughed and talked. Such an exuberance of animal spirits did he have that he sometimes tumbled down and rolled on the ground with laughter at anything that made him think and tickled him. Looking round upon the trees, he would exclaim, “By George! I can enjoy myself well enough here chopping; I want no better sport.” Sometimes, when at leisure, he amused himself all day in the woods with a pocket pistol, firing salutes to himself at regular intervals as he walked. In the winter he had a fire by which at noon he warmed his coffee in a kettle; and as he sat on a log to eat his dinner, the chickadees would sometimes come round and alight on his arm and peck at the potato in his fingers; and he said that he “liked to have the little fellers about him.” Overall, he seemed to find genuine contentment in simple pleasures and quiet companionship.
output: He interested me because he was so quiet and solitary and so happy withal; a well of good humor and contentment which overflowed at his eyes. His mirth was without alloy. Sometimes I saw him at his work in the woods, felling trees, and he would greet me with a laugh of inexpressible satisfaction, and a salutation in Canadian French, though he spoke English as well. When I approached him he would suspend his work, and with half-suppressed mirth lie along the trunk of a pine which he had felled, and, peeling off the inner bark, roll it up into a ball and chew it while he laughed and talked. Such an exuberance of animal spirits had he that he sometimes tumbled down and rolled on the ground with laughter at any thing which made him think and tickled him. Looking round upon the trees he would exclaim, - “By George! I can enjoy myself well enough here chopping; I want no better sport.” Sometimes, when at leisure, he amused himself all day in the woods with a pocket pistol, firing salutes to himself at regular intervals as he walked. In the winter he had a fire by which at noon he warmed his coffee in a kettle; and as he sat on a log to eat his dinner the chickadees would sometimes come round and alight on his arm and peck at the potato in his fingers; and he said that he “liked to have the little fellers about him.”

author: Henry David Thoreau

input: I begin my morning tasks by taking an axe and a pail to search for water, which may sometimes feel elusive. After a cold and snowy night, finding it can require a bit of luck. Each winter, the liquid surface of the pond, which tends to respond to every breath of wind and reflects various lights and shadows, freezes to a depth of approximately one to one and a half feet. This thickness may support even heavy teams, and if snow covers it equally, it can be difficult to tell apart from a flat field. Much like the marmots in the surrounding hills, the pond seems to close its eyelids and becomes dormant for three months or more. As I stand on the snow-covered landscape, resembling a pasture set amid the hills, I first cut through a foot of snow and then break through a foot of ice to create an opening beneath me. Kneeling to drink, I gaze down into the serene world of the fish, illuminated by a soft light akin to that through a frosted window, revealing a bright sandy floor reminiscent of summertime. In this tranquil underwater realm, a gentle calm prevails, mirroring the cool demeanor of its inhabitants. It appears that heaven can be found both beneath our feet and above our heads.
output: Then to my morning work. First I take an axe and pail and go in search of water, if that be not a dream. After a cold and snowy night it needed a divining rod to find it. Every winter the liquid and trembling surface of the pond, which was so sensitive to every breath, and reflected every light and shadow, becomes solid to the depth of a foot or a foot and a half, so that it will support the heaviest teams, and perchance the snow covers it to an equal depth, and it is not to be distinguished from any level field. Like the marmots in the surrounding hills, it closes its eye-lids and becomes dormant for three months or more. Standing on the snow-covered plain, as if in a pasture amid the hills, I cut my way first through a foot of snow, and then a foot of ice, and open a window under my feet, where, kneeling to drink, I look down into the quiet parlor of the fishes, pervaded by a softened light as through a window of ground glass, with its bright sanded floor the same as in summer; there a perennial waveless serenity reigns as in the amber twilight sky, corresponding to the cool and even temperament of the inhabitants. Heaven is under our feet as well as over our heads.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input:
Life within us resembles the water in a river. It has the potential to rise this year higher than ever before, flooding the dry uplands. This may very well be the significant year that wipes out all our muskrats. The land where we reside has not always been dry. I envision the distant banks that the stream once washed long ago, before scientific records began to document its floods. 

Everyone has heard the tale that has circulated throughout New England about a strong and beautiful bug that emerged from the dry leaf of an old apple-tree table. This table, which stood in a farmer's kitchen for sixty years, was first located in Connecticut and later in Massachusetts. The bug hatched from an egg laid in the living tree many years before, as evidenced by counting the annual rings of wood. It was heard gnawing its way out for several weeks, likely warmed by the heat of a nearby urn. 

Who does not find their belief in resurrection and immortality bolstered by this story? Who can say what beautiful and winged life, whose egg has lain buried for ages beneath many layers of wood in the lifeless remnants of society, was initially placed in the living tree? This egg has gradually transformed into a semblance of its well-aged tomb. Perhaps it has been gnawing its way out for years, while the astonished family of man gathered around the festive table. Eventually, this life may unexpectedly emerge from society's most mundane and everyday furniture, finally able to enjoy its summer existence.
output: The life in us is like the water in the river. It may rise this year higher than man has ever known it, and flood the parched uplands; even this may be the eventful year, which will drown out all our muskrats. It was not always dry land where we dwell. I see far inland the banks which the stream anciently washed, before science began to record its freshets. Every one has heard the story which has gone the rounds of New England, of a strong and beautiful bug which came out of the dry leaf of an old table of apple-tree wood, which had stood in a farmer’s kitchen for sixty years, first in Connecticut, and afterward in Massachusetts, - from an egg deposited in the living tree many years earlier still, as appeared by counting the annual layers beyond it; which was heard gnawing out for several weeks, hatched perchance by the heat of an urn. Who does not feel his faith in a resurrection and immortality strengthened by hearing of this? Who knows what beautiful and winged life, whose egg has been buried for ages under many concentric layers of woodenness in the dead dry life of society, deposited at first in the alburnum of the green and living tree, which has been gradually converted into the semblance of its well-seasoned tomb, - heard perchance gnawing out now for years by the astonished family of man, as they sat round the festive board, - may unexpectedly come forth from amidst society’s most trivial and handselled furniture, to enjoy its perfect summer life at last!
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: Before I reached the pond, some fresh impulse had compelled John Field to emerge with a changed perspective, abandoning "bogging" before this sunset. However, the unfortunate man only disturbed a couple of fish while I successfully caught a respectable string, attributing his misfortune to luck. When we switched positions in the boat, the luck seemed to alter as well. It is worth noting that I hope John Field does not encounter this account unless it serves to encourage his improvement, as he attempts to sustain himself by means of some derivative, traditional approach in this primitive new land, relying on shiners to catch perch. Admittedly, shiners can serve as effective bait at times. Despite possessing a worldview entirely his own, John remains a poor man, destined to endure poverty, burdened by his inherited Irish legacy and his ancestral ties to hardship, and thereby unlikely to ascend in this world—neither he nor his descendants—until their bog-trotting feet are equipped with wings.
output: Before I had reached the pond some fresh impulse had brought out John Field, with altered mind, letting go “bogging” ere this sunset. But he, poor man, disturbed only a couple of fins while I was catching a fair string, and he said it was his luck; but when we changed seats in the boat luck changed seats too. Poor John Field! - I trust he does not read this, unless he will improve by it, - thinking to live by some derivative old country mode in this primitive new country, - to catch perch with shiners. It is good bait sometimes, I allow. With his horizon all his own, yet he a poor man, born to be poor, with his inherited Irish poverty or poor life, his Adam’s grandmother and boggy ways, not to rise in this world, he nor his posterity, till their wading webbed bog-trotting feet get talaria to their heels.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: I have taken responsibility for the wild stock of the town, which presents considerable challenges for a diligent herdsman due to their propensity to leap over fences. Additionally, I have monitored the less frequented recesses and corners of the farm; however, I did not consistently ascertain whether Jonas or Solomon was working in a specific field on any given day, as that matter did not pertain to my responsibilities. Furthermore, I have irrigated the red huckleberry, the sand cherry, and the nettle tree, in addition to the red pine and the black ash, as well as the white grape and the yellow violet, which otherwise might have perished during arid seasons.
output: I have looked after the wild stock of the town, which give a faithful herdsman a good deal of trouble by leaping fences; and I have had an eye to the unfrequented nooks and corners of the farm; though I did not always know whether Jonas or Solomon worked in a particular field to-day; that was none of my business. I have watered the red huckleberry, the sand cherry and the nettle tree, the red pine and the black ash, the white grape and the yellow violet, which might have withered else in dry seasons.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: Some years ago, the State approached me on behalf of the church and commanded me to pay a certain sum toward the support of a clergyman whose preaching my father attended but I never did. It said, "Pay it, or be locked up in the jail." I declined to pay. Unfortunately, another man saw fit to pay it. I did not see why the schoolmaster should be taxed to support the priest, and not the priest the schoolmaster, for I was not the State's schoolmaster but supported myself by voluntary subscription. I did not see why the lyceum should not present its tax bill and have the State back its demand as well as the church. However, at the request of the selectmen, I condescended to make some such statement as this in writing: "Know all men by these presents, that I, Henry Thoreau, do not wish to be regarded as a member of any incorporated society which I have not joined." I gave this to the town clerk, and he has it. The State, having thus learned that I did not wish to be regarded as a member of that church, has never made a like demand on me since, though it said that it must adhere to its original presumption that time. If I had known how to name them, I should then have signed off in detail from all the societies which I never signed on to, but I did not know where to find such a complete list.
output: Some years ago, the State met me in behalf of the church, and commanded me to pay a certain sum toward the support of a clergyman whose preaching my father attended, but never I myself. “Pay it,” it said, “or be locked up in the jail.” I declined to pay. But, unfortunately, another man saw fit to pay it. I did not see why the schoolmaster should be taxed to support the priest, and not the priest the schoolmaster; for I was not the State’s schoolmaster, but I supported myself by voluntary subscription. I did not see why the lyceum should not present its tax-bill, and have the State to back its demand, as well as the church. However, at the request of the selectmen, I condescended to make some such statement as this in writing: - “Know all men by these presents, that I, Henry Thoreau, do not wish to be regarded as a member of any incorporated society which I have not joined.” This I gave to the town-clerk; and he has it. The State, having thus learned that I did not wish to be regarded as a member of that church, has never made a like demand on me since; though it said that it must adhere to its original presumption that time. If I had known how to name them, I should then have signed off in detail from all the societies which I never signed on to; but I did not know where to find such a complete list.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: Gilpin, in his examination of the forest borderers of England, asserts that "the encroachments of trespassers, and the houses and fences thus raised on the borders of the forest," were "considered as great nuisances by the old forest law, and were severely punished under the name of purprestures, as tending ad terrorem ferarum - ad nocumentum forestæ, &c.," due to their alarming effect on the game and their detrimental impact on the forest. However, I found myself more concerned with the preservation of the venison and the vert than with the interests of hunters or woodchoppers, and I felt this concern as intensely as if I had been the Lord Warden himself. Furthermore, should any part of the forest be burned, even if I were to cause it accidentally, I experienced a sorrow that was deeper and more enduring than that felt by the proprietors; indeed, I mourned even when it was the proprietors who cut it down. It is my hope that our farmers, when they engage in the act of cutting down a forest, might feel a modicum of the reverence that the ancient Romans exhibited when they approached the thinning of, or allowing light into, a consecrated grove (lucum conlucare). In essence, I wish they would recognize it as sacred to some deity. The Romans, in such instances, would offer an expiatory sacrifice and pray, "Whatever god or goddess thou art to whom this grove is sacred, be propitious to me, my family, and children, etc."
output: Gilpin, in his account of the forest borderers of England, says that “the encroachments of trespassers, and the houses and fences thus raised on the borders of the forest,” were “considered as great nuisances by the old forest law, and were severely punished under the name of purprestures, as tending ad terrorem ferarum - ad nocumentum forestæ, &c.,” to the frightening of the game and the detriment of the forest. But I was interested in the preservation of the venison and the vert more than the hunters or woodchoppers, and as much as though I had been the Lord Warden himself; and if any part was burned, though I burned it myself by accident, I grieved with a grief that lasted longer and was more inconsolable than that of the proprietors; nay, I grieved when it was cut down by the proprietors themselves. I would that our farmers when they cut down a forest felt some of that awe which the old Romans did when they came to thin, or let in the light to, a consecrated grove (lucum conlucare), that is, would believe that it is sacred to some god. The Roman made an expiatory offering, and prayed, Whatever god or goddess thou art to whom this grove is sacred, be propitious to me, my family, and children, &c.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: In the morning, our breakfasts were typically delivered through a hole in the door, served in small, specially designed tin pans that could hold about a pint of chocolate, along with some brown bread and an iron spoon. When the time came to return the vessels, I may have been a bit naive to consider giving back the leftover bread, but my companion suggested that it would be better to save it for later, possibly for lunch or dinner. It's worth noting that he was often let out to work in a nearby field, where he would help with haying, and he would usually be gone until around noon. On this particular occasion, he bid me farewell, mentioning that he was unsure if our paths would cross again, which may have been a possibility given our uncertain circumstances. Overall, this experience tends to illustrate the daily routines and uncertainties of life in this situation.
output: In the morning, our breakfasts were put through the hole in the door, in small oblong-square tin pans, made to fit, and holding a pint of chocolate, with brown bread, and an iron spoon. When they called for the vessels again, I was green enough to return what bread I had left; but my comrade seized it, and said that I should lay that up for lunch or dinner. Soon after, he was let out to work at haying in a neighboring field, whither he went every day, and would not be back till noon; so he bade me good-day, saying that he doubted if he should see me again.

input: For a week, I perceived the repetitive and searching clangor of a solitary goose during the fog-laden mornings, as it sought its companion, thereby populating the woods with the sound of a more vibrant life than the environment could support. In April, the pigeons reappeared, flying in small, organized flocks, and eventually, I heard the martins twittering above my clearing, despite my initial belief that the township did not possess a sufficient number to allow for my enjoyment of their presence. I speculated that these martins belonged to an ancient lineage that inhabited hollow trees long before the arrival of Europeans. Moreover, in nearly all climates, the tortoise and the frog serve as early indicators and heralds of this season, as birds take flight with their melodies and vibrant plumage, plants emerge and blossom, and winds circulate, all of which contribute to correcting the slight oscillation of the poles and maintaining the equilibrium of Nature.
output: For a week I heard the circling, groping clangor of some solitary goose in the foggy mornings, seeking its companion, and still peopling the woods with the sound of a larger life than they could sustain. In April the pigeons were seen again flying express in small flocks, and in due time I heard the martins twittering over my clearing, though it had not seemed that the township contained so many that it could afford me any, and I fancied that they were peculiarly of the ancient race that dwelt in hollow trees ere white men came. In almost all climes the tortoise and the frog are among the precursors and heralds of this season, and birds fly with song and glancing plumage, and plants spring and bloom, and winds blow, to correct this slight oscillation of the poles and preserve the equilibrium of Nature.

input:
It is worth noting that individuals adorn themselves with garment after garment, as if they were exogenous plants that thrive through external additions. Our outer attire, often delicate and fanciful, serves as our epidermis or a false skin, which is detached from our essence and can be removed without causing significant harm. In contrast, our more substantial garments, consistently worn, represent our cellular integument or cortex. However, our shirts signify our liber or true bark, which cannot be removed without jeopardizing the integrity of the individual. I contend that all cultures, at various times, don something that is analogous to the shirt. 

Furthermore, it is preferable for an individual to be dressed in such a manner that they can easily identify their own person in the darkness. Additionally, a life lived with compactness and preparedness allows one to exit a besieged town, akin to the ancient philosopher, without the burden of possessions and with a sense of ease. While one thick garment may serve the same purpose as multiple thinner ones, and affordable clothing is available at prices that cater to a wide range of consumers, it is notable that a durable coat can be purchased for five dollars, lasting several years. Thick trousers can be acquired for two dollars, cowhide boots for one dollar and fifty cents a pair, a summer hat for twenty-five cents, and a winter cap for sixty-two and a half cents, or one can create superior items at home for a minimal expense. In light of this, it begs the question: where is the individual so impoverished that, dressed in such a suit of their own earning, they would not attract the respect of wise men?
output: We don garment after garment, as if we grew like exogenous plants by addition without. Our outside and often thin and fanciful clothes are our epidermis, or false skin, which partakes not of our life, and may be stripped off here and there without fatal injury; our thicker garments, constantly worn, are our cellular integument, or cortex; but our shirts are our liber or true bark, which cannot be removed without girdling and so destroying the man. I believe that all races at some seasons wear something equivalent to the shirt. It is desirable that a man be clad so simply that he can lay his hands on himself in the dark, and that he live in all respects so compactly and preparedly, that, if an enemy take the town, he can, like the old philosopher, walk out the gate empty-handed without anxiety. While one thick garment is, for most purposes, as good as three thin ones, and cheap clothing can be obtained at prices really to suit customers; while a thick coat can be bought for five dollars, which will last as many years, thick pantaloons for two dollars, cowhide boots for a dollar and a half a pair, a summer hat for a quarter of a dollar, and a winter cap for sixty-two and a half cents, or a better be made at home at a nominal cost, where is he so poor that, clad in such a suit, of his own earning, there will not be found wise men to do him reverence?

input: For sixteen days, I observed from my window a group of around a hundred men engaged in work akin to farming, utilizing teams of horses and a variety of agricultural tools. This scene resembled images typically found in almanacs. Each time I looked outside, I was reminded of fables and parables related to nature and labor. However, now that the workers have departed, it is likely that in about thirty days, I will gaze from the same window at the tranquil, green waters of Walden, which will reflect the clouds and trees, creating a solitary atmosphere devoid of human presence. It is possible that I might hear a solitary loon or see a lone fisherman in a small boat, quietly observing his reflection on the water, where once many men worked diligently.
output: Thus for sixteen days I saw from my window a hundred men at work like busy husbandmen, with teams and horses and apparently all the implements of farming, such a picture as we see on the first page of the almanac; and as often as I looked out I was reminded of the fable of the lark and the reapers, or the parable of the sower, and the like; and now they are all gone, and in thirty days more, probably, I shall look from the same window on the pure sea-green Walden water there, reflecting the clouds and the trees, and sending up its evaporations in solitude, and no traces will appear that a man has ever stood there. Perhaps I shall hear a solitary loon laugh as he dives and plumes himself, or shall see a lonely fisher in his boat, like a floating leaf, beholding his form reflected in the waves, where lately a hundred men securely labored.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that I have had the experience of standing at the very foundation of a rainbow's arc, which filled the lower layer of the atmosphere, imbuing the surrounding grass and leaves with its hues, and dazzling me as if I were gazing through a prism of colored crystal. Furthermore, this phenomenon created a veritable lake of rainbow light, in which, for a brief period, I existed in a state of unbridled wonder, much like a creature inhabiting a realm of unencumbered joy. In essence, if this experience had endured for a longer duration, it may have had a profound impact on my daily pursuits and overall existence. Moreover, as I walked along the railroad causeway, I would often marvel at the halo of light that surrounded my shadow, and I would readily imagine myself to be among the select few who are endowed with a special distinction. It is worth noting that a visitor to my residence once remarked that the shadows of certain individuals who had preceded him, specifically those of Irish origin, did not exhibit this halo, suggesting that it was a phenomenon exclusive to natives of the region. Moreover, the memoirs of Benvenuto Cellini reveal that, following a particularly disturbing dream or vision that he experienced during his confinement in the castle of St. Angelo, a brilliant light appeared above the shadow of his head at dawn and dusk, regardless of whether he was in Italy or France, and this phenomenon was especially pronounced when the grass was damp with dew. This was likely the same phenomenon to which I have alluded, which is often observed in the morning, but also at other times, and even under the light of the moon. Although this phenomenon is a constant presence, it is not commonly noticed, and, in the case of an individual with a vivid imagination, such as Cellini, it could serve as a basis for superstition. Additionally, it is worth noting that Cellini mentions having shared this experience with only a select few. Nevertheless, it is worth considering that those who are aware of being regarded in any way are, in fact, distinguished individuals.
output: Once it chanced that I stood in the very abutment of a rainbow’s arch, which filled the lower stratum of the atmosphere, tinging the grass and leaves around, and dazzling me as if I looked through colored crystal. It was a lake of rainbow light, in which, for a short while, I lived like a dolphin. If it had lasted longer it might have tinged my employments and life. As I walked on the railroad causeway, I used to wonder at the halo of light around my shadow, and would fain fancy myself one of the elect. One who visited me declared that the shadows of some Irishmen before him had no halo about them, that it was only natives that were so distinguished. Benvenuto Cellini tells us in his memoirs, that, after a certain terrible dream or vision which he had during his confinement in the castle of St. Angelo, a resplendent light appeared over the shadow of his head at morning and evening, whether he was in Italy or France, and it was particularly conspicuous when the grass was moist with dew. This was probably the same phenomenon to which I have referred, which is especially observed in the morning, but also at other times, and even by moonlight. Though a constant one, it is not commonly noticed, and, in the case of an excitable imagination like Cellini’s, it would be basis enough for superstition. Beside, he tells us that he showed it to very few. But are they not indeed distinguished who are conscious that they are regarded at all?

input: With a bit more careful thought about what they choose to pursue, most people can often become, in a meaningful sense, students and observers of the world, since human nature and our shared destiny tend to be interesting to everyone alike. When we accumulate property for ourselves or for later generations, when we establish a family or a state, or even when we seek fame, we remain mortal; but when we engage with truth, we can be said to share in something lasting, and we may feel less fear of change or misfortune. The oldest Egyptian or Hindu philosopher may have lifted a corner of the veil from the statue of the divine, and that trembling robe can still remain lifted, so that I may look upon a glory as fresh as his, since it was I in him who was then so bold, and it is he in me who now reviews the vision. No dust tends to settle on that robe, and no time seems to have passed since that divinity was revealed. The time we truly make good use of, or that can be made good use of, is perhaps neither past, present, nor future.
output: With a little more deliberation in the choice of their pursuits, all men would perhaps become essentially students and observers, for certainly their nature and destiny are interesting to all alike. In accumulating property for ourselves or our posterity, in founding a family or a state, or acquiring fame even, we are mortal; but in dealing with truth we are immortal, and need fear no change nor accident. The oldest Egyptian or Hindoo philosopher raised a corner of the veil from the statue of the divinity; and still the trembling robe remains raised, and I gaze upon as fresh a glory as he did, since it was I in him that was then so bold, and it is he in me that now reviews the vision. No dust has settled on that robe; no time has elapsed since that divinity was revealed. That time which we really improve, or which is improvable, is neither past, present, nor future.

input: On this summer afternoon, hawks are seen circling above the clearing, while wild pigeons fly in pairs and threes, adding movement and sound to the environment as they perch on the white pine branches behind the house. A fishhawk dives into the pond, creating ripples on the surface as it catches a fish. Nearby, a mink emerges from the marsh and captures a frog along the shore. The sedge bends under the weight of reed-birds that move around the area. Additionally, the distant sound of railroad cars can be heard, fluctuating like the beat of a partridge, as they transport travelers from Boston to the countryside. This experience contrasts with that of a boy who was sent to live with a farmer in the eastern part of town. He eventually ran away, returning home feeling disheartened and homesick, having found the rural area to be dull and lacking in life. He noted that it seemed so isolated that he could not even hear the whistle of a train. This suggests that such a remote place may no longer exist in Massachusetts today.
output: As I sit at my window this summer afternoon, hawks are circling about my clearing; the tantivy of wild pigeons, flying by twos and threes athwart my view, or perching restless on the white-pine boughs behind my house, gives a voice to the air; a fishhawk dimples the glassy surface of the pond and brings up a fish; a mink steals out of the marsh before my door and seizes a frog by the shore; the sedge is bending under the weight of the reed-birds flitting hither and thither; and for the last half hour I have heard the rattle of railroad cars, now dying away and then reviving like the beat of a partridge, conveying travellers from Boston to the country. For I did not live so out of the world as that boy who, as I hear, was put out to a farmer in the east part of the town, but ere long ran away and came home again, quite down at the heel and homesick. He had never seen such a dull and out-of-the-way place; the folks were all gone off; why, you couldn’t even hear the whistle! I doubt if there is such a place in Massachusetts now: -

author: Henry David Thoreau

input:
The author recalls a past experience of losing a hound, a bay horse, and a turtle-dove, and continues to seek them. They have engaged with various travelers, sharing details about the animals' tracks and calls. Some individuals have expressed familiarity with the hound's bark, the horse's footsteps, and the sighting of the dove, showing a shared concern for the lost animals.

This highlights the author's dedication to observing nature, as they often rise early in the morning, long before any neighbors begin their day. This suggests a deep commitment to their pursuits, as they have encountered townsmen such as farmers and woodchoppers during these early hours. Ultimately, while the author acknowledges that their presence does not directly influence the sunrise, it underscores the significance of being present to witness the natural world unfold.
output:
I long ago lost a hound, a bay horse, and a turtle-dove, and am still on their trail. Many are the travellers I have spoken concerning them, describing their tracks and what calls they answered to. I have met one or two who had heard the hound, and the tramp of the horse, and even seen the dove disappear behind a cloud, and they seemed as anxious to recover them as if they had lost them themselves.

To anticipate, not the sunrise and the dawn merely, but, if possible, Nature herself! How many mornings, summer and winter, before yet any neighbor was stirring about his business, have I been about mine! No doubt, many of my townsmen have met me returning from this enterprise, farmers starting for Boston in the twilight, or woodchoppers going to their work. It is true, I never assisted the sun materially in his rising, but, doubt not, it was of the last importance only to be present at it.

author: Henry David Thoreau

input: I once had some visitors who are not usually counted among the town’s poor, though perhaps they should be; in any case, they may be counted among the world’s poor. These were guests who tend to appeal not to your hospitality but rather to your sense of what might be called hospital-ness; they sincerely wish to be helped, and they often begin their request by informing you that they have resolved, among other things, never to help themselves. I would ask of a visitor that he not be actually starving, though he may have the very best appetite in the world, however he came by it. People who are objects of charity are not usually guests. There were men who did not seem to know when their visit had ended, even though I had gone back to my own affairs and was answering them from farther and farther away. Men of almost every degree of cleverness called on me during the migrating season. Some had more wit than they knew what to do with; there were runaway slaves with plantation manners, who listened from time to time, like the fox in the fable, as if they heard the hounds baying on their trail, and who looked at me pleadingly, as much as to say, —. In short, these visitors were less guests in the usual sense than people whose need and manner tended to test the limits of hospitality.
output: I had some guests from those not reckoned commonly among the town’s poor, but who should be; who are among the world’s poor, at any rate; guests who appeal, not to your hospitality, but to your hospitalality; who earnestly wish to be helped, and preface their appeal with the information that they are resolved, for one thing, never to help themselves. I require of a visitor that he be not actually starving, though he may have the very best appetite in the world, however he got it. Objects of charity are not guests. Men who did not know when their visit had terminated, though I went about my business again, answering them from greater and greater remoteness. Men of almost every degree of wit called on me in the migrating season. Some who had more wits than they knew what to do with; runaway slaves with plantation manners, who listened from time to time, like the fox in the fable, as if they heard the hounds a-baying on their track, and looked at me beseechingly, as much as to say, -

input: I happened to be walking across the fields the following night, at around the same time, and I heard a low moaning sound at this location. As I approached in the darkness, I found the sole surviving member of the family, who had inherited both the virtues and vices of his ancestors. He was lying on his stomach, peering over the cellar wall at the still smoldering remains below, and muttering to himself. This highlights the strong emotional connection he had to the place. He had spent the day working in the river meadows, but had taken the first opportunity to visit the site of his family's home and his own youth. He examined the cellar from various angles, lying down to get a closer look, as if searching for something valuable among the ruins. Ultimately, he was left to survey the remnants of what once was. My presence seemed to offer him some comfort, and he showed me, as well as the darkness allowed, the location of the well, which fortunately had not been destroyed by the fire. He also searched for the well-sweep that his father had made, feeling for the iron hook that had been used to secure a heavy load. This suggests that the well-sweep held significant sentimental value for him. I was able to feel the hook for myself, and I still notice it on my daily walks, as it serves as a tangible link to the family's history.
output: It chanced that I walked that way across the fields the following night, about the same hour, and hearing a low moaning at this spot, I drew near in the dark, and discovered the only survivor of the family that I know, the heir of both its virtues and its vices, who alone was interested in this burning, lying on his stomach and looking over the cellar wall at the still smouldering cinders beneath, muttering to himself, as is his wont. He had been working far off in the river meadows all day, and had improved the first moments that he could call his own to visit the home of his fathers and his youth. He gazed into the cellar from all sides and points of view by turns, always lying down to it, as if there was some treasure, which he remembered, concealed between the stones, where there was absolutely nothing but a heap of bricks and ashes. The house being gone, he looked at what there was left. He was soothed by the sympathy which my mere presence implied, and showed me, as well as the darkness permitted, where the well was covered up; which, thank Heaven, could never be burned; and he groped long about the wall to find the well-sweep which his father had cut and mounted, feeling for the iron hook or staple by which a burden had been fastened to the heavy end, - all that he could now cling to, - to convince me that it was no common “rider.” I felt it, and still remark it almost daily in my walks, for by it hangs the history of a family.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input:
This is the house that I may have built; this is the man who lives in the house that I possibly constructed. 

These are the people who may occasionally worry the man living in the house that I built.

I didn't have much concern for the hen-harriers, as I didn't keep any chickens; however, I tended to be more apprehensive about the men-harriers. 

I often received more cheerful visitors than before. Children would come to pick berries, railroad workers might take a leisurely walk on Sunday mornings in their clean shirts, fishermen and hunters would visit, along with poets and philosophers; in essence, all sincere travelers who ventured into the woods for a sense of freedom and genuinely distanced themselves from the village. I was always prepared to greet them with a warm, “Welcome, friends!” as I had some familiarity with that community. 

In summary, the house and its occupants often attracted a diverse group of visitors seeking a connection with nature and freedom.
output:
This is the house that I built; This is the man that lives in the house that I built;

These are the folks that worry the man That lives in the house that I built.

I did not fear the hen-harriers, for I kept no chickens; but I feared the men-harriers rather.

I had more cheering visitors than the last. Children come a-berrying, railroad men taking a Sunday morning walk in clean shirts, fishermen and hunters, poets and philosophers; in short, all honest pilgrims, who came out to the woods for freedom’s sake, and really left the village behind, I was ready to greet with, - “Welcome, Englishmen! welcome, Englishmen!” for I had had communication with that race.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: Those summer days, which some of my contemporaries devoted to the fine arts in Boston or Rome, and others to contemplation in India, and still others to trade in London or New York, I devoted, along with the other farmers of New England, to husbandry. This was not because I wanted beans to eat, for I am by nature a Pythagorean where beans are concerned, whether they mean porridge or voting, and I exchanged them for rice. Perhaps it was because some must work in fields, if only for the sake of tropes and expression, in order to serve a parable-maker one day. On the whole, it was a rare amusement, which, if continued too long, might have become a dissipation. Although I gave the plants no manure and did not hoe them all at once, I hoed them unusually well as far as I went, and I was paid for it in the end. As Evelyn says, “there being in truth no compost or lætation whatsoever comparable to this continual motion, repastination, and turning of the mould with the spade.” He adds elsewhere that “the earth, especially if fresh, has a certain magnetism in it, by which it attracts the salt, power, or virtue (call it either) which gives it life, and is the logic of all the labor and stir we keep about it, to sustain us; all dungings and other sordid temperings being but the vicars succedaneous to this improvement.” Moreover, this being one of those “worn-out and exhausted lay fields which enjoy their sabbath,” it had perhaps, as Sir Kenelm Digby thinks likely, attracted “vital spirits” from the air. I harvested twelve bushels of beans.
output: Those summer days which some of my contemporaries devoted to the fine arts in Boston or Rome, and others to contemplation in India, and others to trade in London or New York, I thus, with the other farmers of New England, devoted to husbandry. Not that I wanted beans to eat, for I am by nature a Pythagorean, so far as beans are concerned, whether they mean porridge or voting, and exchanged them for rice; but, perchance, as some must work in fields if only for the sake of tropes and expression, to serve a parable-maker one day. It was on the whole a rare amusement, which, continued too long, might have become a dissipation. input: In early May, with support from a few acquaintances, I set up the frame of my house, primarily to foster a sense of community rather than out of necessity. I may have felt quite honored by the involvement of those who helped me, and I hope that they will one day assist in the construction of even larger structures. I began to move into my house on July 4th, as soon as it had been boarded and roofed, with the boards carefully aligned to ensure they were resistant to rain. I had laid the foundation for a chimney at one end prior to boarding, transporting two cartloads of stones from the pond by hand. After finishing my planting in the fall, I built the chimney before needing a fire for warmth, cooking outdoors in the meantime, which I still believe can be more convenient and enjoyable than traditional methods. During storms, when my bread wasn’t yet baked, I would place a few boards over the fire and sit beneath them to keep an eye on my loaf, finding some pleasant moments in that experience. Although my hands were often busy at that time, my reading was limited, and even the smallest scraps of paper I found on the ground became just as entertaining to me as a classic text like the Iliad. In summary, these experiences reflect a blend of practicality and enjoyment in my early days of settling into my new home.
output: At length, in the beginning of May, with the help of some of my acquaintances, rather to improve so good an occasion for neighborliness than from any necessity, I set up the frame of my house. No man was ever more honored in the character of his raisers than I. They are destined, I trust, to assist at the raising of loftier structures one day. I began to occupy my house on the 4th of July, as soon as it was boarded and roofed, for the boards were carefully feather-edged and lapped, so that it was perfectly impervious to rain; but before boarding I laid the foundation of a chimney at one end, bringing two cartloads of stones up the hill from the pond in my arms. I built the chimney after my hoeing in the fall, before a fire became necessary for warmth, doing my cooking in the mean while out of doors on the ground, early in the morning: which mode I still think is in some respects more convenient and agreeable than the usual one. When it stormed before my bread was baked, I fixed a few boards over the fire, and sat under them to watch my loaf, and passed some pleasant hours in that way. In those days, when my hands were much employed, I read but little, but the least scraps of paper which lay on the ground, my holder, or tablecloth, afforded me as much entertainment, in fact answered the same purpose as the Iliad.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input:
In retrospect, my past aspirations for how I wanted to spend my life wouldn't be immediately apparent to readers who are familiar with the actual events that have unfolded. Meanwhile, those who are not acquainted with my history would likely be astonished by my previous desires. Additionally, I will provide a brief overview of some of the endeavors that I have pursued in the past.

Generally, I have been eager to make the most of every moment, regardless of the time of day or weather conditions. Furthermore, I have sought to exist in the present, which is the point at which the past and future converge. Naturally, this has involved being mindful of the importance of living in the moment. Nevertheless, some aspects of my experiences may be difficult to understand, as my line of work inherently involves a certain level of complexity. Moreover, while I am willing to share my knowledge with others, some details may remain obscure due to the intrinsic nature of my profession. Overall, I am inclined to be forthcoming about my experiences, and I do not intend to withhold information from those who are interested.
output:
If I should attempt to tell how I have desired to spend my life in years past, it would probably surprise those of my readers who are somewhat acquainted with its actual history; it would certainly astonish those who know nothing about it. I will only hint at some of the enterprises which I have cherished.

In any weather, at any hour of the day or night, I have been anxious to improve the nick of time, and notch it on my stick too; to stand on the meeting of two eternities, the past and future, which is precisely the present moment; to toe that line. You will pardon some obscurities, for there are more secrets in my trade than in most men’s, and yet not voluntarily kept, but inseparable from its very nature. I would gladly tell all that I know about it, and never paint “No Admittance” on my gate.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: Many autumn days, and indeed winter days, were spent outside the town, trying to hear what was in the wind, to hear it and carry it express. I nearly sank all my capital into this, and lost my own breath as well, running in the face of it. This suggests how much effort was devoted to something so intangible. If it had concerned either of the political parties, depend upon it, it would have appeared in the Gazette with the earliest intelligence. At other times I watched from the observatory of some cliff or tree, to telegraph any new arrival; or waited at evening on the hill-tops for the sky to fall, so that I might catch something, though I never caught much, and that, manna-wise, would dissolve again in the sun. This highlights how elusive such pursuits ultimately proved.
output: So many autumn, ay, and winter days, spent outside the town, trying to hear what was in the wind, to hear and carry it express! I well-nigh sunk all my capital in it, and lost my own breath into the bargain, running in the face of it. If it had concerned either of the political parties, depend upon it, it would have appeared in the Gazette with the earliest intelligence. At other times watching from the observatory of some cliff or tree, to telegraph any new arrival; or waiting at evening on the hill-tops for the sky to fall, that I might catch something, though I never caught much, and that, manna-wise, would dissolve again in the sun.

input: As spring approached, the red squirrels began to take shelter beneath my house, frequently appearing in pairs directly beneath my feet while I engaged in reading or writing. They produced an array of peculiar sounds, including chuckling, chirruping, vocal pirouetting, and gurgling, which were unlike any I had ever encountered. Moreover, when I stamped my feet in an attempt to quiet them, their chirruping only intensified, as if they had completely abandoned any sense of fear or respect in their exuberant antics, openly challenging humanity to intervene. It is worth noting that they remained entirely unresponsive to my arguments, either failing to acknowledge their validity or disregarding them entirely, ultimately resorting to a form of irresistible invective.
output: At the approach of spring the red-squirrels got under my house, two at a time, directly under my feet as I sat reading or writing, and kept up the queerest chuckling and chirruping and vocal pirouetting and gurgling sounds that ever were heard; and when I stamped they only chirruped the louder, as if past all fear and respect in their mad pranks, defying humanity to stop them. No you don’t - chickaree - chickaree. They were wholly deaf to my arguments, or failed to perceive their force, and fell into a strain of invective that was irresistible.

input: The most widespread and persistent error requires the greatest impartiality to maintain. Those who are noble are most likely to incur the mild criticism that the virtue of patriotism commonly attracts. Those who, while disapproving of a government's character and policies, nonetheless give it their allegiance and support are undoubtedly its most conscientious supporters, and thus often the most serious obstacles to reform. Some are petitioning the State to dissolve the Union and to disregard the President's requisitions. Why do they not dissolve it themselves—the union between themselves and the State—and refuse to pay their quota into its treasury? Do they not stand in the same relation to the State that the State stands in to the Union? And have not the same reasons prevented the State from resisting the Union that have prevented them from resisting the State?
output: The broadest and most prevalent error requires the most disinterested virtue to sustain it. input: It is difficult to accept that our factory system represents the most effective means through which individuals may acquire clothing. Furthermore, the circumstances of the workers are increasingly resembling those of their English counterparts, a development that is hardly surprising. This trend occurs because, to the best of my knowledge and observation, the primary objective appears to be not the well-being and honest clothing of humanity, but rather the substantial profit of corporations. In essence, over time, individuals tend to achieve only those goals at which they aim. Consequently, even if they do not succeed immediately, it is preferable for them to set their sights on higher ideals.
output: I cannot believe that our factory system is the best mode by which men may get clothing. The condition of the operatives is becoming every day more like that of the English; and it cannot be wondered at, since, as far as I have heard or observed, the principal object is, not that mankind may be well and honestly clad, but, unquestionably, that corporations may be enriched. In the long run men hit only what they aim at. Therefore, though they should fail immediately, they had better aim at something high.
title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau

input: If others pay the tax that is demanded of me, out of a sympathy with the State, they are only doing what they have already done in their own case, or rather they are aiding injustice to a greater extent than the State requires. If they pay the tax out of a mistaken concern for the individual being taxed, in order to save his property or keep him out of jail, it is because they have not wisely considered how far they allow their private feelings to interfere with the public good.
output: If others pay the tax which is demanded of me, from a sympathy with the State, they do but what they have already done in their own case, or rather they abet injustice to a greater extent than the State requires. input: During the long winter evenings, when snow falls heavily and the wind blows through the woods, I receive occasional visits from an elderly settler who is said to have created Walden Pond and surrounded it with pine trees. This highlights the interesting history of the area and the people who have shaped it. He shares stories of the past and the present, and we manage to have a pleasant evening together, enjoying each other's company and discussing various topics. This suggests that even without material comforts, it is possible to have a enjoyable and meaningful social interaction. My friend is a wise and humorous person who keeps a low profile, and despite rumors of his passing, his whereabouts remain unknown. Ultimately, his secrecy has become a notable aspect of his character. In my neighborhood, there is also an elderly woman who is not often seen by others, but I occasionally visit her fragrant herb garden, where I gather plants and listen to her stories. She has a remarkable memory and a talent for storytelling, able to recall the origins of various fables and the facts behind them, which she claims to have witnessed during her youth. This suggests that she has a deep understanding of the past and its cultural significance. She is a robust and lively person who appreciates all seasons and is likely to outlive her children, giving her a unique perspective on life and its many experiences.
output: I have occasional visits in the long winter evenings, when the snow falls fast and the wind howls in the wood, from an old settler and original proprietor, who is reported to have dug Walden Pond, and stoned it, and fringed it with pine woods; who tells me stories of old time and of new eternity; and between us we manage to pass a cheerful evening with social mirth and pleasant views of things, even without apples or cider, - a most wise and humorous friend, whom I love much, who keeps himself more secret than ever did Goffe or Whalley; and though he is thought to be dead, none can show where he is buried. An elderly dame, too, dwells in my neighborhood, invisible to most persons, in whose odorous herb garden I love to stroll sometimes, gathering simples and listening to her fables; for she has a genius of unequalled fertility, and her memory runs back farther than mythology, and she can tell me the original of every fable, and on what fact every one is founded, for the incidents occurred when she was young. A ruddy and lusty old dame, who delights in all weathers and seasons, and is likely to outlive all her children yet.

input: Since I tend to prefer some things over others and especially value my freedom, and since I can often live simply and still do well, I did not particularly wish to spend my time earning rich carpets or other fine furniture, or delicate cooking, or a house in the Grecian or Gothic style just yet. If there are those for whom acquiring these things is no interruption, and who know how to use them once acquired, I can leave that pursuit to them. Some people are "industrious" and may appear to love labor for its own sake, or perhaps because it keeps them out of worse trouble; to such people I have nothing to say at present. Those who might not know what to do with more leisure than they now enjoy, I could suggest work twice as hard as they do—work until they pay for themselves and obtain their free papers. For myself, I found that the occupation of a day-laborer tended to be the most independent of any, especially since it required only thirty or forty days in a year to support oneself. The laborer's day ends with the going down of the sun, and he is then free to devote himself to his chosen pursuit, independent of his labor; but his employer, who speculates from month to month, tends to have no respite from one end of the year to the other.
output: As I preferred some things to others, and especially valued my freedom, as I could fare hard and yet succeed well, I did not wish to spend my time in earning rich carpets or other fine furniture, or delicate cookery, or a house in the Grecian or the Gothic style just yet. Those who would not know what to do with more leisure than they now enjoy, I might advise to work twice as hard as they do, - work till they pay for themselves, and get their free papers. The laborer’s day ends with the going down of the sun, and he is then free to devote himself to his chosen pursuit, independent of his labor; but his employer, who speculates from month to month, has no respite from one end of the year to the other.

input:
One evening, as I came in with a candle, I was somewhat startled to hear him say, in a slightly trembling voice, "I am lying here in the dark waiting for death." The light was only about a foot from his eyes. I made myself murmur, "Oh, nonsense!" and stood over him as if frozen in place.

I have never seen anything quite like the change that came over his features, and I hope never to see it again. I was not really moved, I must admit; I was fascinated. It was as though a veil had been torn away. On that pale, ivory face I saw an expression of dark pride, of pitiless power, of cowardly terror—of an intense and hopeless despair. Perhaps he was reliving his whole life, in every detail of desire, temptation, and surrender, during that supreme moment of complete knowledge. He cried out in a whisper at some image, at some vision—he cried out twice, a cry that was barely more than a breath.
output:
“One evening coming in with a candle I was startled to hear him say a little tremulously, ‘I am lying here in the dark waiting for death.’ The light was within a foot of his eyes. I forced myself to murmur, ‘Oh, nonsense!’ and stood over him as if transfixed.

“Anything approaching the change that came over his features I have never seen before, and hope never to see again. Oh, I wasn’t touched. I was fascinated. It was as though a veil had been rent. I saw on that ivory face the expression of sombre pride, of ruthless power, of craven terror - of an intense and hopeless despair. Did he live his life again in every detail of desire, temptation, and surrender during that supreme moment of complete knowledge? He cried in a whisper at some image, at some vision - he cried out twice, a cry that was no more than a breath:

Moreover, these particular recommendations were once again coming to light.
