I’ve seen the devil of violence, and the devil of greed, and the devil of hot desire; but, by all the stars! these were strong, lusty, red-eyed devils, that swayed and drove men - men, I tell you. But as I stood on this hillside, I foresaw that in the blinding sunshine of that land I would become acquainted with a flabby, pretending, weak-eyed devil of a rapacious and pitiless folly. How insidious he could be, too, I was only to find out several months later and a thousand miles farther. For a moment I stood appalled, as though by a warning. Finally I descended the hill, obliquely, towards the trees I had seen.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: We experienced a breakdown, as I had anticipated, and were forced to stop for repairs at the edge of an island. This setback was the first event that undermined Kurtz's confidence. One morning, he handed me a bundle of papers and a photograph, all secured with a shoelace. He instructed me to keep it safe, saying, "This noxious fool," referring to the manager, "is capable of prying into my boxes when I am not looking." In the afternoon, I found him lying on his back with his eyes closed. I quietly withdrew, but I heard him mutter, "Live rightly, die, die..." I paused to listen, but nothing more followed. Was he rehearsing a speech in his sleep, or was this merely a fragment from a newspaper article? He had been writing for the papers and intended to do so again, claiming it was "for the furthering of my ideas. It is a duty."
output: “We broke down - as I had expected - and had to lie up for repairs at the head of an island. This delay was the first thing that shook Kurtz’s confidence. One morning he gave me a packet of papers and a photograph - the lot tied together with a shoe-string. ‘Keep this for me,’ he said. ‘This noxious fool’ (meaning the manager) ‘is capable of prying into my boxes when I am not looking.’ In the afternoon I saw him. He was lying on his back with closed eyes, and I withdrew quietly, but I heard him mutter, ‘Live rightly, die, die...’ I listened. There was nothing more. Was he rehearsing some speech in his sleep, or was it a fragment of a phrase from some newspaper article? He had been writing for the papers and meant to do so again, ‘for the furthering of my ideas. It’s a duty.’
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: Upon reaching the bank, I noticed a wide trail cutting through the grass. I felt a surge of excitement as I thought to myself, "He cannot walk; he is crawling on all fours; I have him." The grass was damp with dew. I walked quickly, my fists clenched. I vaguely considered confronting him and delivering a punishment, although I cannot be certain. My mind wandered to the elderly woman with the cat, who seemed entirely inappropriate for the situation. I recalled a group of pilgrims aiming their rifles into the air, their Winchesters held at their sides. I imagined that I might never return to the steamer and envisioned a life alone in the woods, defenseless, into old age. Such trivial thoughts, indeed. I also remember confusing the sound of the drum with the rhythm of my own heartbeat, feeling reassured by its steady cadence.
output: “As soon as I got on the bank I saw a trail - a broad trail through the grass. I remember the exultation with which I said to myself, ‘He can’t walk - he is crawling on all-fours - I’ve got him.’ The grass was wet with dew. I strode rapidly with clenched fists. I fancy I had some vague notion of falling upon him and giving him a drubbing. I don’t know. I had some imbecile thoughts. The knitting old woman with the cat obtruded herself upon my memory as a most improper person to be sitting at the other end of such an affair. I saw a row of pilgrims squirting lead in the air out of Winchesters held to the hip. I thought I would never get back to the steamer, and imagined myself living alone and unarmed in the woods to an advanced age. Such silly things - you know. And I remember I confounded the beat of the drum with the beating of my heart, and was pleased at its calm regularity.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: Dusk settled over the scene. I found myself waiting in a spacious drawing room featuring three long windows that stretched from floor to ceiling, resembling luminous, draped columns. The gilt legs and backs of the furniture glimmered in soft, indistinct curves. The tall marble fireplace exuded a cold, monumental whiteness. In one corner, a grand piano stood prominently, its dark surfaces gleaming like a polished sarcophagus. Suddenly, a high door opened and then closed. I stood up.
output: “The dusk was falling. I had to wait in a lofty drawing-room with three long windows from floor to ceiling that were like three luminous and bedraped columns. The bent gilt legs and backs of the furniture shone in indistinct curves. The tall marble fireplace had a cold and monumental whiteness. A grand piano stood massively in a corner; with dark gleams on the flat surfaces like a sombre and polished sarcophagus. A high door opened - closed. I rose.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: This I did directly after the simple funeral was over. We were proceeding at half-speed, maintaining our position in the middle of the stream, and I listened to the conversation around me. They had abandoned Kurtz, they had abandoned the station; Kurtz was deceased, and the station had been consumed by fire, and so forth. The red-haired pilgrim was beside himself with the thought that at least this unfortunate Kurtz had been properly avenged. He exclaimed that they must have made a glorious slaughter of them in the bush, and asked what I thought of it. He positively danced, the bloodthirsty little ginger-haired fellow. Moreover, he had nearly fainted when he saw the wounded man. I could not help remarking that they had made a glorious lot of smoke, at any rate. I had observed, from the manner in which the tops of the bushes rustled and flew, that almost all of the shots had gone too high. One cannot hit anything unless one takes aim and fires from the shoulder, but these individuals fired from the hip with their eyes closed. The retreat, I maintained, and I was correct, was caused by the screeching of the steam whistle. Upon this they forgot Kurtz and began to howl at me with indignant protests.
output: “This I did directly the simple funeral was over. We were going half-speed, keeping right in the middle of the stream, and I listened to the talk about me. They had given up Kurtz, they had given up the station; Kurtz was dead, and the station had been burnt - and so on - and so on. The red-haired pilgrim was beside himself with the thought that at least this poor Kurtz had been properly avenged. ‘Say! We must have made a glorious slaughter of them in the bush. Eh? What do you think? Say?’ He positively danced, the bloodthirsty little gingery beggar. And he had nearly fainted when he saw the wounded man! I could not help saying, ‘You made a glorious lot of smoke, anyhow.’ I had seen, from the way the tops of the bushes rustled and flew, that almost all the shots had gone too high. You can’t hit anything unless you take aim and fire from the shoulder; but these chaps fired from the hip with their eyes shut. The retreat, I maintained - and I was right - was caused by the screeching of the steam whistle. Upon this they forgot Kurtz, and began to howl at me with indignant protests.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that I slapped him on the back and shouted, "We shall have rivets." He scrambled to his feet, exclaiming, "No, rivets," as though he could not believe his ears. Furthermore, in a low voice, he uttered, "You... eh?" It is worth noting that I do not know why we behaved like lunatics. Moreover, I put my finger to the side of my nose and nodded mysteriously, prompting him to cry, "Good for you," and snap his fingers above his head, lifting one foot. In essence, we attempted to dance, and our capering on the iron deck resulted in a frightful clatter that emanated from the hulk. This noise was subsequently echoed back by the virgin forest on the other bank of the creek, creating a thundering roll that likely disturbed some of the pilgrims in their hovels. Additionally, a dark figure momentarily obscured the lighted doorway of the manager's hut, only to vanish, and then, a second or so later, the doorway itself disappeared from view as well. We stopped, and the silence, which had been driven away by the stamping of our feet, flowed back again from the recesses of the land. Moreover, the great wall of vegetation, an exuberant and entangled mass of trunks, branches, leaves, boughs, and festoons, stood motionless in the moonlight, resembling a rioting invasion of soundless life, a rolling wave of plants piled up and crested, ready to topple over the creek and sweep every little man out of his little existence. However, it remained still. Furthermore, a deadened burst of mighty splashes and snorts reached us from afar, as though some prehistoric creature had been taking a bath of glitter in the great river. In essence, the boiler-maker remarked in a reasonable tone, "After all, why shouldn't we get the rivets?" It is worth noting that I could not think of any reason why we should not. Additionally, I replied confidently, "They will come in three weeks."
output: “I slapped him on the back and shouted, ‘We shall have rivets!’ He scrambled to his feet exclaiming, ‘No! Rivets!’ as though he couldn’t believe his ears. Then in a low voice, ‘You... eh?’ I don’t know why we behaved like lunatics. I put my finger to the side of my nose and nodded mysteriously. ‘Good for you!’ he cried, snapped his fingers above his head, lifting one foot. I tried a jig. We capered on the iron deck. A frightful clatter came out of that hulk, and the virgin forest on the other bank of the creek sent it back in a thundering roll upon the sleeping station. It must have made some of the pilgrims sit up in their hovels. A dark figure obscured the lighted doorway of the manager’s hut, vanished, then, a second or so after, the doorway itself vanished, too. We stopped, and the silence driven away by the stamping of our feet flowed back again from the recesses of the land. The great wall of vegetation, an exuberant and entangled mass of trunks, branches, leaves, boughs, festoons, motionless in the moonlight, was like a rioting invasion of soundless life, a rolling wave of plants, piled up, crested, ready to topple over the creek, to sweep every little man of us out of his little existence. And it moved not. A deadened burst of mighty splashes and snorts reached us from afar, as though an icthyosaurus had been taking a bath of glitter in the great river. ‘After all,’ said the boiler-maker in a reasonable tone, ‘why shouldn’t we get the rivets?’ Why not, indeed! I did not know of any reason why we shouldn’t. ‘They’ll come in three weeks,’ I said confidently.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: Kurtz spoke, and his voice resonated deeply until the very end. It seemed to endure even as it concealed the emptiness within his heart beneath an impressive facade of eloquence. He appeared to struggle, grappling with troubling thoughts that were now populated by vague images of wealth and recognition, circling around his undeniable talent for grand expression. Thoughts of my Intended, my position, my career, and my ideals occasionally surfaced amidst his lofty sentiments. The essence of the original Kurtz lingered near the bedside of this hollow imitation, destined soon to be laid to rest in the earth. Yet, both the dark love and the profound hatred from the mysteries he had encountered seemed to vie for control over a soul that was filled with basic emotions, yearning for deceptive fame, false status, and the mere appearance of success and power. In summary, the complexity of Kurtz's character reflects the tension between his lofty aspirations and the darker truths of his existence.
output: “Kurtz discoursed. A voice! a voice! It rang deep to the very last. It survived his strength to hide in the magnificent folds of eloquence the barren darkness of his heart. Oh, he struggled! he struggled! The wastes of his weary brain were haunted by shadowy images now - images of wealth and fame revolving obsequiously round his unextinguishable gift of noble and lofty expression. My Intended, my station, my career, my ideas - these were the subjects for the occasional utterances of elevated sentiments. The shade of the original Kurtz frequented the bedside of the hollow sham, whose fate it was to be buried presently in the mould of primeval earth. But both the diabolic love and the unearthly hate of the mysteries it had penetrated fought for the possession of that soul satiated with primitive emotions, avid of lying fame, of sham distinction, of all the appearances of success and power.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: It is worth noting that I was not surprised to observe an individual seated aft on the deck, with his legs dangling over the mud. I had developed a certain camaraderie with the few mechanics present at that station, who, for reasons related to their perceived lack of refinement, were naturally looked down upon by the other pilgrims. This particular individual was the foreman, a boiler-maker by trade, and he was known for his strong work ethic. He possessed a tall, slender frame, a yellow complexion, and large, intense eyes. His demeanor appeared troubled, and his scalp was completely bald, resembling the palm of my hand; however, the hair that had fallen seemed to have taken root on his chin, thriving in its new environment, as his beard extended down to his waist. He was a widower with six young children, whom he had entrusted to the care of a sister during his time away. His greatest passion was pigeon-flying, and he was both an enthusiast and a connoisseur in this regard. After work hours, he would occasionally visit from his hut to engage in discussions about his children and his pigeons. During work, when he had to maneuver in the mud beneath the steamboat, he would secure his beard with a white cloth he carried specifically for that purpose, which featured loops to fasten over his ears. In the evenings, he could be observed squatting by the bank, meticulously rinsing that cloth in the creek before solemnly spreading it on a bush to dry.
output: “I was not surprised to see somebody sitting aft, on the deck, with his legs dangling over the mud. You see I rather chummed with the few mechanics there were in that station, whom the other pilgrims naturally despised - on account of their imperfect manners, I suppose. This was the foreman - a boiler-maker by trade - a good worker. He was a lank, bony, yellow-faced man, with big intense eyes. His aspect was worried, and his head was as bald as the palm of my hand; but his hair in falling seemed to have stuck to his chin, and had prospered in the new locality, for his beard hung down to his waist. He was a widower with six young children (he had left them in charge of a sister of his to come out there), and the passion of his life was pigeon-flying. He was an enthusiast and a connoisseur. He would rave about pigeons. After work hours he used sometimes to come over from his hut for a talk about his children and his pigeons; at work, when he had to crawl in the mud under the bottom of the steamboat, he would tie up that beard of his in a kind of white serviette he brought for the purpose. It had loops to go over his ears. In the evening he could be seen squatted on the bank rinsing that wrapper in the creek with great care, then spreading it solemnly on a bush to dry.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: It seems that this individual may have acted without much forethought, much like Kurtz, swayed by external influences. Once I had changed into a dry pair of slippers, I took it upon myself to assist him, first removing the spear from his side, an action I must admit I approached with my eyes tightly shut. As I pulled him through the doorway, I felt his weight pressing against me, and I found myself holding him from behind in a rather desperate embrace. He was surprisingly heavy, perhaps heavier than anyone might expect. Without much hesitation, I then tipped him overboard. The current quickly swept him away, and I observed his body roll over twice before he disappeared from view entirely. Meanwhile, the other individuals present, including the manager and the pilgrims, gathered around the pilot-house, their chatter resembling excited birds, and I sensed a wave of disapproval regarding my prompt decision. It was unclear why they wished to keep the body there; perhaps they considered preserving it in some way. However, I also heard a more disquieting murmur from the deck below, indicating that my friends, the wood-cutters, were equally upset, though their reasons seemed somewhat misplaced. I had resolved that if my former helmsman were to be consumed, only the fish would have him. While he had not distinguished himself as a helmsman in life, in death he might have posed a significant temptation that could lead to unforeseen complications. Furthermore, I was eager to take over the steering, as the man in pink pajamas had proven to be rather ineffective at the task. In summary, the situation highlighted the complexities of decision-making in distressing circumstances.
output: “Poor fool! If he had only left that shutter alone. He had no restraint, no restraint - just like Kurtz - a tree swayed by the wind. As soon as I had put on a dry pair of slippers, I dragged him out, after first jerking the spear out of his side, which operation I confess I performed with my eyes shut tight. His heels leaped together over the little doorstep; his shoulders were pressed to my breast; I hugged him from behind desperately. Oh! he was heavy, heavy; heavier than any man on earth, I should imagine. Then without more ado I tipped him overboard. The current snatched him as though he had been a wisp of grass, and I saw the body roll over twice before I lost sight of it for ever. All the pilgrims and the manager were then congregated on the awning-deck about the pilot-house, chattering at each other like a flock of excited magpies, and there was a scandalized murmur at my heartless promptitude. What they wanted to keep that body hanging about for I can’t guess. Embalm it, maybe. But I had also heard another, and a very ominous, murmur on the deck below. My friends the wood-cutters were likewise scandalized, and with a better show of reason - though I admit that the reason itself was quite inadmissible. Oh, quite! I had made up my mind that if my late helmsman was to be eaten, the fishes alone should have him. He had been a very second-rate helmsman while alive, but now he was dead he might have become a first-class temptation, and possibly cause some startling trouble. Besides, I was anxious to take the wheel, the man in pink pyjamas showing himself a hopeless duffer at the business.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: They had come together unavoidably, in the manner of two vessels becalmed in proximity to one another, and ultimately lay side by side, their surfaces in contact. I suppose that Kurtz desired an audience, for on a certain occasion, while encamped in the forest, they had conversed throughout the night, or more probably Kurtz had spoken at length. "We talked of everything," he said, quite transported at the recollection. "I forgot there was such a thing as sleep. The night did not seem to last an hour. Everything! Everything!... Of love, too." "Ah, he talked to you of love!" I said, much amused. "It isn't what you think," he cried, almost passionately. "It was in general. He made me see things - things."
output: “They had come together unavoidably, like two ships becalmed near each other, and lay rubbing sides at last. I suppose Kurtz wanted an audience, because on a certain occasion, when encamped in the forest, they had talked all night, or more probably Kurtz had talked. ‘We talked of everything,’ he said, quite transported at the recollection. ‘I forgot there was such a thing as sleep. The night did not seem to last an hour. Everything! Everything!... Of love, too.’ ‘Ah, he talked to you of love!’ I said, much amused. ‘It isn’t what you think,’ he cried, almost passionately. ‘It was in general. He made me see things - things.’
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: He expressed with considerable formality that if they had not shared the same profession, he would have kept the situation to himself, regardless of the consequences. He indicated his belief that there was active hostility directed towards him from these white men. In response, I recalled a conversation I had overheard and confirmed, "The manager thinks you ought to be hanged." His reaction to this information was initially amusing to me, but then he became earnest, stating that he should leave quietly. He noted that he could do nothing more for Kurtz and that they would inevitably find some reason to target him. He pointed out that a military post was located three hundred miles away. I suggested that perhaps he should leave if he had any friends among the local tribes. He affirmed that he had plenty of friends among them, describing them as simple people who wanted nothing from him. He hesitated briefly, expressing that he did not wish any harm to come to the white men, but he was concerned about Mr. Kurtz’s reputation. He acknowledged our shared profession, and I reassured him, "Mr. Kurtz’s reputation is safe with me." At that moment, I was unaware of how genuine my words were.
output: “He stated with a good deal of formality that had we not been ‘of the same profession,’ he would have kept the matter to himself without regard to consequences. ‘He suspected there was an active ill-will towards him on the part of these white men that - ’ ‘You are right,’ I said, remembering a certain conversation I had overheard. ‘The manager thinks you ought to be hanged.’ He showed a concern at this intelligence which amused me at first. ‘I had better get out of the way quietly,’ he said earnestly. ‘I can do no more for Kurtz now, and they would soon find some excuse. What’s to stop them? There’s a military post three hundred miles from here.’ ‘Well, upon my word,’ said I, ‘perhaps you had better go if you have any friends amongst the savages near by.’ ‘Plenty,’ he said. ‘They are simple people - and I want nothing, you know.’ He stood biting his lip, then: ‘I don’t want any harm to happen to these whites here, but of course I was thinking of Mr. Kurtz’s reputation - but you are a brother seaman and - ’ ‘All right,’ said I, after a time. ‘Mr. Kurtz’s reputation is safe with me.’ I did not know how truly I spoke.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: I had really turned to the wilderness, not to Mr. Kurtz, who, I was willing to admit, was as good as buried. And for a moment it seemed to me as though I too were buried in a vast grave full of secrets that are hard to put into words. I felt an unbearable weight pressing on my chest, the smell of the damp earth, the unseen presence of a corruption that seemed to have won, the darkness of a night that could not be penetrated.... The Russian tapped me on the shoulder. I heard him mumbling and stammering something about "brother seaman - couldn't conceal - knowledge of matters that would affect Mr. Kurtz's reputation." I waited. For him, clearly, Mr. Kurtz was not in his grave; I suspect that for him Mr. Kurtz was one of the immortals. "Well!" I said at last, "speak out. As it happens, I am Mr. Kurtz's friend - in a way."
output: “I had turned to the wilderness really, not to Mr. Kurtz, who, I was ready to admit, was as good as buried. And for a moment it seemed to me as if I also were buried in a vast grave full of unspeakable secrets. I felt an intolerable weight oppressing my breast, the smell of the damp earth, the unseen presence of victorious corruption, the darkness of an impenetrable night.... The Russian tapped me on the shoulder. I heard him mumbling and stammering something about ‘brother seaman - couldn’t conceal - knowledge of matters that would affect Mr. Kurtz’s reputation.’ I waited. For him evidently Mr. Kurtz was not in his grave; I suspect that for him Mr. Kurtz was one of the immortals. ‘Well!’ said I at last, ‘speak out. As it happens, I am Mr. Kurtz’s friend - in a way.’
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: There was an agent wrapped up in a long overcoat and sleeping on a chair on deck within about three feet of me. The yells had not woken him; he was snoring very softly; I left him to his sleep and jumped ashore. I did not betray Mr. Kurtz — I had been ordered never to betray him — it seemed written that I should be loyal to the nightmare of my choice. I was anxious to deal with this shadow by myself alone, and to this day I don't really know why I was so reluctant to share with anyone the peculiar darkness of that experience.
output: “There was an agent buttoned up inside an ulster and sleeping on a chair on deck within three feet of me. The yells had not awakened him; he snored very slightly; I left him to his slumbers and leaped ashore. I did not betray Mr. Kurtz - it was ordered I should never betray him - it was written I should be loyal to the nightmare of my choice. I was anxious to deal with this shadow by myself alone - and to this day I don’t know why I was so jealous of sharing with any one the peculiar blackness of that experience.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: She walked with steady, deliberate steps, wearing striped and fringed cloths and treading the earth proudly, with a slight jingle and flash of unusual ornaments. She carried her head high, and her hair was styled in a shape that can often resemble a helmet. She wore brass leggings to the knee and brass wire gauntlets to the elbow, had a crimson spot on her tawny cheek, and wore numerous necklaces of glass beads around her neck. Strange charms and gifts from witch-men hung about her, glittering and trembling at every step. She may well have carried the value of several elephant tusks upon her. She seemed both fierce and splendid, wild-eyed and magnificent; there was something that can feel ominous and stately in her deliberate progress. In the hush that had suddenly fallen upon the whole sorrowful land, the immense wilderness, the vast body of fertile and mysterious life, seemed to look at her thoughtfully, as though it were looking at the image of its own dark and passionate soul. Overall, her presence tends to suggest a striking and uneasy grandeur.
output: “She walked with measured steps, draped in striped and fringed cloths, treading the earth proudly, with a slight jingle and flash of barbarous ornaments. She carried her head high; her hair was done in the shape of a helmet; she had brass leggings to the knee, brass wire gauntlets to the elbow, a crimson spot on her tawny cheek, innumerable necklaces of glass beads on her neck; bizarre things, charms, gifts of witch-men, that hung about her, glittered and trembled at every step. She must have had the value of several elephant tusks upon her. She was savage and superb, wild-eyed and magnificent; there was something ominous and stately in her deliberate progress. And in the hush that had fallen suddenly upon the whole sorrowful land, the immense wilderness, the colossal body of the fecund and mysterious life seemed to look at her, pensive, as though it had been looking at the image of its own tenebrous and passionate soul.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: Additionally, all the pilgrims hastened to witness the spectacle, whereas I remained behind and continued with my meal. Furthermore, it is likely that my actions were perceived as being somewhat insensitive. However, I must note that my appetite was not particularly robust at the time. Moreover, the presence of a lamp in the vicinity, which provided a source of illumination, served as a stark contrast to the intense darkness that existed outside. In essence, I avoided any further interaction with the individual who had uttered a profound pronouncement regarding the trajectory of his existence on this earth. It is worth noting that the voice had ceased to be audible. Moreover, the question of what else had been present in the area remained a mystery. Additionally, I am aware that on the following day, the pilgrims interred something in a grave situated in a muddy location.
output: “All the pilgrims rushed out to see. I remained, and went on with my dinner. I believe I was considered brutally callous. However, I did not eat much. There was a lamp in there - light, don’t you know - and outside it was so beastly, beastly dark. I went no more near the remarkable man who had pronounced a judgment upon the adventures of his soul on this earth. The voice was gone. What else had been there? But I am of course aware that next day the pilgrims buried something in a muddy hole.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: However, that was not the case. Instead of the expected rivets, there was an arrival that may have felt overwhelming, almost as if it were an unexpected event. Over the course of the next three weeks, this arrival unfolded in stages, each section led by a donkey carrying a white man dressed in new clothing and tan shoes, who would often bow from that height to the fascinated onlookers. Following closely behind was a group of weary and somewhat disgruntled individuals, who may have felt frustrated by their journey. They brought along numerous tents, camp chairs, tin boxes, white cases, and brown bales, which would be hastily deposited in the courtyard, adding to a somewhat chaotic atmosphere at the station. Five such groups arrived, creating an impression of disordered movement, as if they were bringing back the belongings from various shops and stores, perhaps for shared use in the wilderness. The scene presented itself as a confusing mix of items that, while could be considered valuable on their own, were made to seem like the result of some hasty plundering due to the circumstances surrounding their arrival. In summary, what unfolded was a complex and puzzling situation marked by both the presence of valuable goods and the chaos of human behavior.
output: “But they didn’t. Instead of rivets there came an invasion, an infliction, a visitation. It came in sections during the next three weeks, each section headed by a donkey carrying a white man in new clothes and tan shoes, bowing from that elevation right and left to the impressed pilgrims. A quarrelsome band of footsore sulky niggers trod on the heels of the donkey; a lot of tents, camp-stools, tin boxes, white cases, brown bales would be shot down in the courtyard, and the air of mystery would deepen a little over the muddle of the station. Five such instalments came, with their absurd air of disorderly flight with the loot of innumerable outfit shops and provision stores, that, one would think, they were lugging, after a raid, into the wilderness for equitable division. It was an inextricable mess of things decent in themselves but that human folly made look like the spoils of thieving.
title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that my daily compensation, as previously mentioned, amounted to one dollar and fifty cents. Furthermore, I had formally agreed to this rate of pay, and I duly earned the specified amount, which was subsequently paid to me, thereby rendering it my legitimate property. Moreover, it was my obligation, upon the conclusion of each week on Saturday night, to surrender the entirety of this sum to Master Hugh. In essence, the rationale behind this requirement was not that he had contributed to the acquisition of this money, nor that I was indebted to him, nor that he possessed any legitimate claim to it. It is worth noting that his entitlement to this money was based solely on his ability to exert control over me and compel me to relinquish it. Moreover, the prerogative of a pirate on the high seas, with its intimidating presence, is analogous to this situation, in that it too is founded on the principle of coercive power rather than legitimate authority.
output: I was now getting, as I have said, one dollar and fifty cents per day. I contracted for it; I earned it; it was paid to me; it was rightfully my own; yet, upon each returning Saturday night, I was compelled to deliver every cent of that money to Master Hugh. And why? Not because he earned it, - not because he had any hand in earning it, - not because I owed it to him, - nor because he possessed the slightest shadow of a right to it; but solely because he had the power to compel me to give it up. The right of the grim-visaged pirate upon the high seas is exactly the same.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: The situation is profoundly sorrowful. The children, who once filled her life with joy through their songs and dances, are now absent. In her age and frailty, she searches for a simple drink of water. Instead of the laughter of her children, the days are filled with the sorrowful calls of doves, and the nights are pierced by the unsettling cries of owls. The atmosphere is heavy with despair. As she faces the end of life, when the burdens of age weigh her down and the cycle of life comes into focus, she experiences a poignant mix of helplessness. At this critical moment, when the warmth of care from children is most needed, my elderly grandmother, who lovingly raised twelve children, finds herself alone in her small hut, surrounded by the fading glow of dying embers. She stands, she sits, she falters, she struggles, and ultimately she passes away, without any of her children or grandchildren by her side to comfort her or honor her memory. It raises the question of whether a just God may take note of such heartache.
output:
“Gone, gone, sold and gone To the rice swamp dank and lone, Where the slave-whip ceaseless swings, Where the noisome insect stings, Where the fever-demon strews Poison with the falling dews, Where the sickly sunbeams glare Through the hot and misty air: - Gone, gone, sold and gone To the rice swamp dank and lone, From Virginia hills and waters - Woe is me, my stolen daughters!”

The hearth is desolate. The children, the unconscious children, who once sang and danced in her presence, are gone. She gropes her way, in the darkness of age, for a drink of water. Instead of the voices of her children, she hears by day the moans of the dove, and by night the screams of the hideous owl. All is gloom. The grave is at the door. And now, when weighed down by the pains and aches of old age, when the head inclines to the feet, when the beginning and ending of human existence meet, and helpless infancy and painful old age combine together - at this time, this most needful time, the time for the exercise of that tenderness and affection which children only can exercise towards a declining parent - my poor old grandmother, the devoted mother of twelve children, is left all alone, in yonder little hut, before a few dim embers. She stands - she sits - she staggers - she falls - she groans - she dies - and there are none of her children or grandchildren present, to wipe from her wrinkled brow the cold sweat of death, or to place beneath the sod her fallen remains. Will not a righteous God visit for these things?
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Additionally, Colonel Lloyd maintained a large and meticulously cultivated garden, which provided nearly constant occupation for four individuals, in addition to the head gardener, Mr. M'Durmond. Furthermore, this garden was likely the most significant attraction of the estate. Moreover, during the summer months, visitors arrived from distant and nearby locations, including Baltimore, Easton, and Annapolis, to view the garden. It is worth noting that the garden was replete with a wide variety of fruits, ranging from the robust apple of the northern regions to the delicate orange of the southern areas. In essence, the garden was a notable source of difficulty on the plantation, as its exceptional produce presented a considerable temptation to the numerous hungry boys, as well as the older slaves, belonging to the colonel, few of whom possessed the self-control to resist it. Moreover, scarcely a day passed during the summer without some slave receiving corporal punishment for stealing fruit. The colonel was compelled to employ various tactics to prevent his slaves from entering the garden. It is worth noting that the most effective strategy was to coat the fence with tar all around, and subsequently, if a slave was found with tar on their person, it was considered sufficient evidence that they had either entered the garden or attempted to do so. In either case, the individual was severely punished by the head gardener. Additionally, this approach proved to be successful, as the slaves developed a profound fear of tar, equivalent to their fear of physical punishment, and they appeared to recognize the impossibility of coming into contact with tar without being contaminated.
output: Colonel Lloyd kept a large and finely cultivated garden, which afforded almost constant employment for four men, besides the chief gardener, (Mr. M’Durmond.) This garden was probably the greatest attraction of the place. During the summer months, people came from far and near - from Baltimore, Easton, and Annapolis - to see it. It abounded in fruits of almost every description, from the hardy apple of the north to the delicate orange of the south. This garden was not the least source of trouble on the plantation. Its excellent fruit was quite a temptation to the hungry swarms of boys, as well as the older slaves, belonging to the colonel, few of whom had the virtue or the vice to resist it. Scarcely a day passed, during the summer, but that some slave had to take the lash for stealing fruit. The colonel had to resort to all kinds of stratagems to keep his slaves out of the garden. The last and most successful one was that of tarring his fence all around; after which, if a slave was caught with any tar upon his person, it was deemed sufficient proof that he had either been into the garden, or had tried to get in. In either case, he was severely whipped by the chief gardener. This plan worked well; the slaves became as fearful of tar as of the lash. They seemed to realize the impossibility of touching tar without being defiled.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Sunday represented my sole opportunity for leisure. I engaged in a state resembling a beastly stupor, teetering between sleep and wakefulness, beneath a large tree. At intervals, I would rise, experiencing a fleeting surge of energetic freedom that briefly illuminated my soul, accompanied by a faint glimmer of hope that would flicker momentarily before dissipating. Subsequently, I would descend once more, lamenting my lamentable condition. There were moments when I contemplated taking my own life, along with that of Covey; however, I was restrained by an interplay of hope and fear. My experiences on this plantation now appear more akin to a dream than to a harsh reality.
output: Sunday was my only leisure time. I spent this in a sort of beast-like stupor, between sleep and wake, under some large tree. At times I would rise up, a flash of energetic freedom would dart through my soul, accompanied with a faint beam of hope, that flickered for a moment, and then vanished. I sank down again, mourning over my wretched condition. I was sometimes prompted to take my life, and that of Covey, but was prevented by a combination of hope and fear. My sufferings on this plantation seem now like a dream rather than a stern reality.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: While I resided with my master in St. Michael's, there was a young white man, Mr. Wilson, who proposed to establish a Sabbath school for the education of those enslaved individuals who might be inclined to learn how to read the New Testament. We convened on only three occasions, when Mr. West and Mr. Fairbanks, both class leaders, accompanied by numerous others, approached us with sticks and various projectiles, forcibly dispersing us and prohibiting any future meetings. In essence, this incident marked the conclusion of our modest Sabbath school in the devout town of St. Michael's.
output: While I lived with my master in St. Michael’s, there was a white young man, a Mr. Wilson, who proposed to keep a Sabbath school for the instruction of such slaves as might be disposed to learn to read the New Testament. We met but three times, when Mr. West and Mr. Fairbanks, both class-leaders, with many others, came upon us with sticks and other missiles, drove us off, and forbade us to meet again. Thus ended our little Sabbath school in the pious town of St. Michael’s.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input:
Come, both the righteous and the wrongdoers, listen as I share how devoted priests may discipline individuals like Jack and Nell, while some women may trade and children can sometimes be sold. They may preach about casting all wrongdoers into hell, yet simultaneously sing about a divine unity.

They may bleat and make noises like goats, consume less favored individuals, and focus on minor faults. They may dress in fine dark clothing, yet may also take hold of those less fortunate with harshness, supposedly for the sake of divine unity.

They might speak fervently of the rewards promised by Christ, while they may also bind his likeness with a cord. They could scold and wield a whip, and in a troubling manner, consider selling their fellow believers for the sake of a constrained version of unity. Overall, this reflects the complexities and contradictions in the pursuit of a higher moral standard.
output:
“Come, saints and sinners, hear me tell How pious priests whip Jack and Nell, And women buy and children sell, And preach all sinners down to hell, And sing of heavenly union.

“They’ll bleat and baa, dona like goats, Gorge down black sheep, and strain at motes, Array their backs in fine black coats, Then seize their negroes by their throats, And choke, for heavenly union.

“They’ll loudly talk of Christ’s reward, And bind his image with a cord, And scold, and swing the lash abhorred, And sell their brother in the Lord To handcuffed heavenly union.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: My master used religious teachings to justify his cruel actions. This highlights the extent to which he used faith to rationalize his behavior. For instance, on one occasion, he tied up a young woman who was lame and whipped her with a heavy cowskin on her bare shoulders, resulting in blood dripping from her wounds. In an attempt to justify this violent act, he would cite a specific biblical passage, which states that individuals who fail to fulfill their master's will will be punished with many stripes. This suggests that he believed his actions were sanctioned by a higher authority. Ultimately, this incident illustrates the ways in which my master used religious doctrine to legitimize his cruel treatment of others.
output: I have said my master found religious sanction for his cruelty. As an example, I will state one of many facts going to prove the charge. I have seen him tie up a lame young woman, and whip her with a heavy cowskin upon her naked shoulders, causing the warm red blood to drip; and, in justification of the bloody deed, he would quote this passage of Scripture - “He that knoweth his master’s will, and doeth it not, shall be beaten with many stripes.”
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: I was born in Tuckahoe, which is located near Hillsborough and approximately twelve miles from Easton, in Talbot county, Maryland. It's worth noting that I may not have a completely accurate understanding of my age, as I have never had access to any official records that confirm it. Many slaves, it tends to, are not aware of their exact ages, and some masters may prefer to keep this information from them. In my experience, it's rare for a slave to know their birthday, and they can often only estimate it based on seasonal events, such as planting-time or harvest-time. Not knowing my own age was a source of discomfort for me, even as a child, and it may have been frustrating to see the white children being able to state their ages while I could not. I was not allowed to ask my master about my age, as he may have viewed such inquiries as inappropriate and potentially indicative of a rebellious attitude. Based on a conversation I overheard my master having in 1835, in which he mentioned that I was around seventeen years old at the time, I can estimate that I am now likely between twenty-seven and twenty-eight years old. Overall, it appears that the circumstances of my birth and upbringing have made it difficult for me to determine my exact age with certainty.
output: I was born in Tuckahoe, near Hillsborough, and about twelve miles from Easton, in Talbot county, Maryland. I have no accurate knowledge of my age, never having seen any authentic record containing it. By far the larger part of the slaves know as little of their ages as horses know of theirs, and it is the wish of most masters within my knowledge to keep their slaves thus ignorant. I do not remember to have ever met a slave who could tell of his birthday. They seldom come nearer to it than planting-time, harvest-time, cherry-time, spring-time, or fall-time. A want of information concerning my own was a source of unhappiness to me even during childhood. The white children could tell their ages. I could not tell why I ought to be deprived of the same privilege. I was not allowed to make any inquiries of my master concerning it. He deemed all such inquiries on the part of a slave improper and impertinent, and evidence of a restless spirit. The nearest estimate I can give makes me now between twenty-seven and twenty-eight years of age. I come to this, from hearing my master say, some time during 1835, I was about seventeen years old.
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

input: Shortly after I went to Mr. Ruggles, he asked where I wished to go, since he considered it unsafe for me to remain in New York. I told him I was a calker and would prefer to go where I could find work. I considered going to Canada, but he advised against it and instead recommended New Bedford, believing I could find employment there in my trade. At this time, Anna, my intended wife, arrived; I had written to her immediately after reaching New York, despite my homeless and helpless condition, to inform her of my successful escape and to ask her to come at once. A few days after she arrived, Mr. Ruggles called in the Rev. J. W. C. Pennington, who, in the presence of Mr. Ruggles, Mrs. Michaels, and two or three others, performed the marriage ceremony and gave us a certificate, of which the following is an exact copy: -
