input: The development of human institutions can be seen as a process that unfolds in a particular way, only to later unravel in a corresponding manner, albeit in reverse order. This highlights the idea that the foundation of power is rooted in key elements such as wisdom, humility, and sincerity, which were exemplified by the apostles. The early Christian communities, driven by reverence rather than obligation, freely followed the teachings of the apostles, with their consciences unencumbered and their actions subject only to civil authority. As the Christian flock grew, presbyters began to assemble and discuss their teachings, effectively binding themselves to adhere to the decrees of their assemblies. This suggests that the presbyters then assumed the people were also obliged to follow their doctrine, and those who refused were excluded from their community, a practice known as excommunication, not due to infidelity, but rather disobedience. This marked the first limitation on Christian liberty. Ultimately, the increasing number of presbyters led to a hierarchy, where presbyters from major cities or provinces gained authority over local presbyters and adopted the title of bishops. This was the second constraint on Christian liberty. The bishop of Rome, leveraging the city's imperial status, the title of Pontifex Maximus, and eventually the privileges associated with St. Peter, especially when the emperors' power waned, assumed authority over all other bishops within the empire. This was the third and final restriction, culminating in the full establishment of pontifical power.
output: But as the Inventions of men are woven, so also are they ravelled out; the way is the same, but the order is inverted: The web begins at the first Elements of Power, which are Wisdom, Humility, Sincerity, and other vertues of the Apostles, whom the people converted, obeyed, out of Reverence, not by Obligation: Their Consciences were free, and their Words and Actions subject to none but the Civill Power. Afterwards the Presbyters (as the Flocks of Christ encreased) assembling to consider what they should teach, and thereby obliging themselves to teach nothing against the Decrees of their Assemblies, made it to be thought the people were thereby obliged to follow their Doctrine, and when they refused, refused to keep them company, (that was then called Excommunication,) not as being Infidels, but as being disobedient: And this was the first knot upon their Liberty. And the number of Presbyters encreasing, the Presbyters of the chief City or Province, got themselves an authority over the parochiall Presbyters, and appropriated to themselves the names of Bishops: And this was a second knot on Christian Liberty. Lastly, the Bishop of Rome, in regard of the Imperiall City, took upon him an Authority (partly by the wills of the Emperours themselves, and by the title of Pontifex Maximus, and at last when the Emperours were grown weak, by the priviledges of St. Peter) over all other Bishops of the Empire: Which was the third and last knot, and the whole Synthesis and Construction of the Pontificall Power.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: It's possible that certain forces have taken advantage of our lack of understanding and introduced spiritual errors, which can often be attributed to several key factors. One factor may be the misinterpretation or disregard of scriptural teachings, as it's likely that errors occur when we don't fully comprehend the scriptures. Another factor can be the influence of pagan ideologies, such as the mythical concepts of daemons found in ancient poetry, which tend to be based on fictional or imaginary entities, like ghosts or fairies, that may be perceived as real but are actually products of human imagination. Additionally, the blending of scriptural teachings with remnants of ancient religions and philosophical ideas, particularly those of Aristotle, may also contribute to spiritual errors. Furthermore, the inclusion of unverified traditions and questionable historical accounts can lead to further confusion. As a result, we may err by giving credence to misleading information and false ideologies, which can be presented in a way that contradicts one's own knowledge or conscience. In this chapter, the focus will be on the first of these factors, which involves the misuse of scripture to deceive people, and this topic will be explored in more detail. Overall, it's clear that spiritual errors can arise from a combination of factors, and it's helpful to examine these factors in order to better understand the sources of confusion.
output: The Enemy has been here in the Night of our naturall Ignorance, and sown the tares of Spirituall Errors; and that, First, by abusing, and putting out the light of the Scriptures: For we erre, not knowing the Scriptures. Secondly, by introducing the Daemonology of the Heathen Poets, that is to say, their fabulous Doctrine concerning Daemons, which are but Idols, or Phantasms of the braine, without any reall nature of their own, distinct from humane fancy; such as are dead mens Ghosts, and Fairies, and other matter of old Wives tales. Thirdly, by mixing with the Scripture divers reliques of the Religion, and much of the vain and erroneous Philosophy of the Greeks, especially of Aristotle. Fourthly, by mingling with both these, false, or uncertain Traditions, and fained, or uncertain History. And so we come to erre, by "giving heed to seducing Spirits," and the Daemonology of such "as speak lies in Hypocrisie," (or as it is in the Originall, 1 Tim. 4.1,2. "of those that play the part of lyars") "with a seared conscience," that is, contrary to their own knowledge. Concerning the first of these, which is the Seducing of men by abuse of Scripture, I intend to speak briefly in this Chapter.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input:
Imitation can be seen as a form of respect, indicating strong approval. However, imitating an enemy is perceived as a sign of disrespect. 

Honoring those whom someone else respects serves to honor that individual as well, reflecting a positive judgment of their choices. Conversely, showing respect to an enemy undermines that individual's standing.

Involving someone in decision-making or difficult tasks signifies respect, as it reflects a belief in their wisdom or abilities. On the other hand, denying someone the chance to contribute in such situations suggests a lack of respect.
output:
To imitate, is to Honour; for it is vehemently to approve. To imitate ones Enemy, is to Dishonour.

To honour those another honours, is to Honour him; as a signe of approbation of his judgement. To honour his Enemies, is to Dishonour him.

To employ in counsell, or in actions of difficulty, is to Honour; as a signe of opinion of his wisdome, or other power. To deny employment in the same cases, to those that seek it, is to Dishonour.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: When examining the specifics of a subject's true liberty, it's essential to consider what actions can be refused without injustice, even if commanded by a sovereign. This involves understanding what rights are relinquished when a commonwealth is formed, or, in other words, what liberties individuals deny themselves by acknowledging the actions of their chosen sovereign. The act of submission encompasses both obligation and liberty, which can be inferred through arguments based on this submission, as any obligation on an individual typically arises from their own actions. Since all people are naturally free, it's crucial to derive these arguments from either the explicit words of submission, such as "I authorise all his actions," or from the intention behind submitting to a sovereign's power, which is often understood by the purpose of the submission. The subject's obligation and liberty may then be derived from these words or the underlying purpose of establishing sovereignty, namely, to maintain peace among subjects and defend against common enemies. In summary, a subject's true liberty can be understood by carefully considering the rights relinquished upon forming a commonwealth and the intentions behind submitting to a sovereign's authority.
output: To come now to the particulars of the true Liberty of a Subject; that is to say, what are the things, which though commanded by the Soveraign, he may neverthelesse, without Injustice, refuse to do; we are to consider, what Rights we passe away, when we make a Common-wealth; or (which is all one,) what Liberty we deny our selves, by owning all the Actions (without exception) of the Man, or Assembly we make our Soveraign. For in the act of our Submission, consisteth both our Obligation, and our Liberty; which must therefore be inferred by arguments taken from thence; there being no Obligation on any man, which ariseth not from some Act of his own; for all men equally, are by Nature Free. And because such arguments, must either be drawn from the expresse words, "I Authorise all his Actions," or from the Intention of him that submitteth himselfe to his Power, (which Intention is to be understood by the End for which he so submitteth;) The Obligation, and Liberty of the Subject, is to be derived, either from those Words, (or others equivalent;) or else from the End of the Institution of Soveraignty; namely, the Peace of the Subjects within themselves, and their Defence against a common Enemy.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input:
The Natural Cause of Religion, and the Anxiety Concerning the Time to Come

Moreover, the first two factors give rise to anxiety. For once it is established that there are causes for all things that have occurred up to the present or shall occur hereafter, it is impossible for a person who continually endeavors to secure himself against the evil he fears and to obtain the good he desires not to remain in a perpetual state of solicitude regarding the time to come. Additionally, every person, especially those who are excessively prudent, exists in a condition similar to that of Prometheus. Furthermore, just as Prometheus, which interpreted means the Prudent Man, was bound to Mount Caucasus, a place of extensive prospect, where an eagle feeding upon his liver devoured during the day as much as was restored during the night, so too does that person who looks too far ahead in concern for the future have his heart gnawed throughout the day by fear of death, poverty, or other calamity. In essence, he has no repose, nor pause from his anxiety, except in sleep.
output: The Naturall Cause Of Religion, The Anxiety Of The Time To Come The two first, make Anxiety. For being assured that there be causes of all things that have arrived hitherto, or shall arrive hereafter; it is impossible for a man, who continually endeavoureth to secure himselfe against the evill he feares, and procure the good he desireth, not to be in a perpetuall solicitude of the time to come; So that every man, especially those that are over provident, are in an estate like to that of Prometheus. For as Prometheus, (which interpreted, is, The Prudent Man,) was bound to the hill Caucasus, a place of large prospect, where, an Eagle feeding on his liver, devoured in the day, as much as was repayred in the night: So that man, which looks too far before him, in the care of future time, hath his heart all the day long, gnawed on by feare of death, poverty, or other calamity; and has no repose, nor pause of his anxiety, but in sleep.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Speech plays a crucial role in helping individuals remember the relationships between causes and effects by assigning names and establishing connections between them. Names can be categorized into two types: proper names, which refer to a specific entity, such as Peter or This Tree, and common names, which apply to multiple entities, such as Man or Tree. Although common names represent a single term, they denote various particular things. This classification leads to the concept of universality, where names are seen as the only universal entities, whereas the things they refer to are always individual and singular. This suggests that the inherent uniqueness of each named entity stands in contrast to the broader, collective nature of names themselves.
output:
The manner how Speech serveth to the remembrance of the consequence of causes and effects, consisteth in the imposing of Names, and the Connexion of them.

Of Names, some are Proper, and singular to one onely thing; as Peter, John, This Man, This Tree: and some are Common to many things; as Man, Horse, Tree; every of which though but one Name, is nevertheless the name of divers particular things; in respect of all which together, it is called an Universall; there being nothing in the world Universall but Names; for the things named, are every one of them Individual and Singular.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Again, it can often be helpful for every sovereign to ensure that justice is taught. Since justice consists in not taking from anyone what is theirs, this tends to mean teaching people not to deprive their neighbor, whether by violence or fraud, of anything that the sovereign authority has assigned to them. Among the things people possess as their own, those that may be dearest to a person are their own life and limbs; next, for most people, come those tied to marital affection; and after that, wealth and the means of living. Therefore, people should be taught to refrain from violence against one another's person through private revenge, from violating marital honor, and from seizing one another's goods by force or obtaining them through fraud. For this purpose, it also seems necessary to show them the harmful consequences of false judgment, whether through the corruption of judges or witnesses, since this can remove the distinction of ownership and make justice ineffective. All of these matters are suggested in the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth commandments. In short, teaching justice means helping people respect the lives, relationships, and property of others, and upholding honest judgment that protects these things.
output: Again, every Soveraign Ought to cause Justice to be taught, which (consisting in taking from no man what is his) is as much as to say, to cause men to be taught not to deprive their Neighbour, by violence, or fraud, of any thing which by the Soveraign Authority is theirs. Of things held in propriety, those that are dearest to a man are his own life, & limbs; and in the next degree, (in most men,) those that concern conjugall affection; and after them riches and means of living. Therefore the People are to be taught, to abstain from violence to one anothers person, by private revenges; from violation of conjugall honour; and from forcibly rapine, and fraudulent surreption of one anothers goods. For which purpose also it is necessary they be shewed the evill consequences of false Judgement, by corruption either of Judges or Witnesses, whereby the distinction of propriety is taken away, and Justice becomes of no effect: all which things are intimated in the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth Commandements.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: The authors of The Religion of the Gentiles noted the second basis for religion, which is humanity's lack of understanding of causes. As a result, people tend to attribute their fortunes to causes that have no apparent connection. Consequently, these authors took the opportunity to exploit this ignorance by introducing a group of secondary and subordinate gods. Specifically, they attributed the cause of fertility to Venus, the cause of arts to Apollo, and the cause of cunning and cleverness to Mercury. Additionally, they assigned the cause of storms and tempests to Aeolus, and other effects to other gods. Therefore, there existed among the heathens a vast array of gods that was nearly equivalent to the variety of human activities.
output: The same authors of the Religion of the Gentiles, observing the second ground for Religion, which is mens Ignorance of causes; and thereby their aptnesse to attribute their fortune to causes, on which there was no dependence at all apparent, took occasion to obtrude on their ignorance, in stead of second causes, a kind of second and ministeriall Gods; ascribing the cause of Foecundity, to Venus; the cause of Arts, to Apollo; of Subtilty and Craft, to Mercury; of Tempests and stormes, to Aeolus; and of other effects, to other Gods: insomuch as there was amongst the Heathen almost as great variety of Gods, as of businesse.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input:
Additionally, a prior agreement renders a subsequent one null and void. For an individual who has relinquished their right to one person on a given day does not possess the same right to transfer it to another person on the following day; consequently, the later promise does not confer any right and is therefore invalid.

Furthermore, a covenant that precludes self-defense against force by means of force is invariably void. In essence, as has been previously demonstrated, no individual can relinquish or abandon their right to protect themselves from death, injury, and imprisonment, which are the primary motivations for surrendering any right. Therefore, the promise to refrain from resisting force in a covenant does not transfer any right and is not binding. Moreover, although an individual may enter into a covenant with the stipulation that they will suffer the consequences of death if they fail to comply with certain conditions, they cannot covenant to refrain from resisting force when their life is threatened. It is worth noting that human nature dictates the selection of the lesser evil, which in this case is the risk of death associated with resistance, rather than the greater evil of certain and imminent death resulting from a failure to resist. Additionally, this principle is universally acknowledged, as evidenced by the practice of escorting criminals to execution or prison with armed guards, despite the fact that these individuals have consented to the laws that have led to their condemnation.
output:
A former Covenant, makes voyd a later. For a man that hath passed away his Right to one man to day, hath it not to passe to morrow to another: and therefore the later promise passeth no Right, but is null.

A Covenant not to defend my selfe from force, by force, is alwayes voyd. For (as I have shewed before) no man can transferre, or lay down his Right to save himselfe from Death, Wounds, and Imprisonment, (the avoyding whereof is the onely End of laying down any Right,) and therefore the promise of not resisting force, in no Covenant transferreth any right; nor is obliging. For though a man may Covenant thus, "Unlesse I do so, or so, kill me;" he cannot Covenant thus "Unless I do so, or so, I will not resist you, when you come to kill me." For man by nature chooseth the lesser evill, which is danger of death in resisting; rather than the greater, which is certain and present death in not resisting. And this is granted to be true by all men, in that they lead Criminals to Execution, and Prison, with armed men, notwithstanding that such Criminals have consented to the Law, by which they are condemned.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

To this head, I also refer all those doctrines that serve to maintain the possession of this spiritual sovereignty once it has been acquired. First, that the Pope in his public capacity cannot err. This highlights that anyone who believes this to be true will readily obey him in whatever he commands.

Second, that all other bishops, in whatever commonwealth, do not hold their right either immediately from God or mediately from their civil sovereigns, but from the Pope. This suggests that in every Christian commonwealth there come to be many powerful men (for bishops are such) who depend on the Pope and owe obedience to him, even though he is a foreign prince. Ultimately, by this means he is able, as he has done many times, to raise a civil war against a state that does not submit to being governed according to his pleasure and interest.
output:
To this head, I referre also all those Doctrines, that serve them to keep the possession of this spirituall Soveraignty after it is gotten. As first, that the Pope In His Publique Capacity Cannot Erre. For who is there, that beleeving this to be true, will not readily obey him in whatsoever he commands?

Secondly, that all other Bishops, in what Common-wealth soever, have not their Right, neither immediately from God, nor mediately from their Civill Soveraigns, but from the Pope, is a Doctrine, by which there comes to be in every Christian Common-wealth many potent men, (for so are Bishops,) that have their dependance on the Pope, and owe obedience to him, though he be a forraign Prince; by which means he is able, (as he hath done many times) to raise a Civill War against the State that submits not it self to be governed according to his pleasure and Interest.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input:
If the metaphysics and physics discussed are not considered vain philosophy, then there has never been any philosophy that deserves that label. This suggests that St. Paul’s warning to avoid such philosophy is important. 

In terms of moral and civil philosophy, similar or even greater absurdities can be found. For instance, when a person commits an unjust action—defined as an action that goes against the law—some argue that God is the primary cause of the law and also the cause of all actions. However, they claim that God is not the cause of the injustice, which is the failure of the action to align with the law. This highlights the inconsistency in such reasoning. One might as well assert that one person creates both a straight line and a crooked line, while another person is responsible for their incongruity. This illustrates the flaw in the philosophy of those who reach conclusions without fully understanding their premises. It also reflects an attempt to grasp the incomprehensible and to redefine attributes of honor as attributes of nature. This distinction seems to be made to support the doctrine of free will, which posits that human will is not subject to the will of God.
output:
If such Metaphysiques, and Physiques as this, be not Vain Philosophy, there was never any; nor needed St. Paul to give us warning to avoid it.

And for their Morall, and Civill Philosophy, it hath the same, or greater absurdities. If a man doe an action of Injustice, that is to say, an action contrary to the Law, God they say is the prime cause of the Law, and also the prime cause of that, and all other Actions; but no cause at all of the Injustice; which is the Inconformity of the Action to the Law. This is Vain Philosophy. A man might as well say, that one man maketh both a streight line, and a crooked, and another maketh their Incongruity. And such is the Philosophy of all men that resolve of their Conclusions, before they know their Premises; pretending to comprehend, that which is Incomprehensible; and of Attributes of Honour to make Attributes of Nature; as this distinction was made to maintain the Doctrine of Free-Will, that is, of a Will of man, not subject to the Will of God.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: This highlights the idea that a king with limited power is not superior to those who have the authority to impose those limitations. Ultimately, this means that such a king is not supreme, and therefore not sovereign. This suggests that sovereignty resides with the assembly that has the right to limit the king's power. As a result, the form of government in this scenario is not a monarchy, but rather either a democracy or an aristocracy. A historical example of this can be seen in ancient Sparta, where the kings held the privilege of leading the armies, but sovereignty actually lay with the Ephors.
output: Secondly, that King whose power is limited, is not superiour to him, or them that have the power to limit it; and he that is not superiour, is not supreme; that is to say not Soveraign. The Soveraignty therefore was alwaies in that Assembly which had the Right to Limit him; and by consequence the government not Monarchy, but either Democracy, or Aristocracy; as of old time in Sparta; where the Kings had a priviledge to lead their Armies; but the Soveraignty was in the Ephori.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: The phrase "And Jesus full of the Holy Ghost" from Luke 4:1, which is expressed as "of the Holy Spirit" in Matthew 4:1 and Mark 1:12, can be understood in the context of his zeal to fulfill the work assigned to him by God the Father. However, interpreting this phrase as referring to a ghost implies that God himself, who is identified as our Savior, was filled with God, which is not a proper or meaningful interpretation. The reason behind translating "Spirits" as "Ghosts," a term that holds no significance in either the celestial or terrestrial realms and merely denotes imaginary entities in the human mind, is not the focus of this discussion. What I will assert is that the term "Spirit" in this context does not refer to such notions. It denotes either a real substance or metaphorically represents some extraordinary capacity of the mind or body.
output: Likewise these words (Luke 4.1.) "And Jesus full of the Holy Ghost" (that is, as it is exprest, Mat. 4.1. and Mar. 1.12. "of the Holy Spirit",) may be understood, for Zeal to doe the work for which hee was sent by God the Father: but to interpret it of a Ghost, is to say, that God himselfe (for so our Saviour was,) was filled with God; which is very unproper, and unsignificant. How we came to translate Spirits, by the word Ghosts, which signifieth nothing, neither in heaven, nor earth, but the Imaginary inhabitants of mans brain, I examine not: but this I say, the word Spirit in the text signifieth no such thing; but either properly a reall Substance, or Metaphorically, some extraordinary Ability of Affection of the Mind, or of the Body.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: In Bodies Politique, the authority of the Representative is generally regarded as limited, with the boundaries of this authority often defined by the Sovereign Power. Unlimited power might be viewed as absolute sovereignty. Within a Commonwealth, the Sovereign is typically seen as the ultimate Representative of all subjects, which means that no one else can claim to represent any segment of the population unless permitted by the Sovereign. Allowing a group of subjects to have a fully independent Representative could be interpreted as relinquishing control over that portion of the Commonwealth, potentially undermining its unity and security, which the Sovereign is unlikely to intend through any grant that does not explicitly relieve them of their obligations. The implications of language may not always reflect the Sovereign's true intentions, particularly when other interpretations suggest a different meaning, highlighting a common tendency for misunderstanding and miscalculation among people. In summary, the relationship between sovereignty and representation is complex and requires careful consideration.
output: In Bodies Politique, the power of the Representative is alwaies Limited: And that which prescribeth the limits thereof, is the Power Soveraign. For Power Unlimited, is absolute Soveraignty. And the Soveraign, in every Commonwealth, is the absolute Representative of all the Subjects; and therefore no other, can be Representative of any part of them, but so far forth, as he shall give leave; And to give leave to a Body Politique of Subjects, to have an absolute Representative to all intents and purposes, were to abandon the Government of so much of the Commonwealth, and to divide the Dominion, contrary to their Peace and Defence, which the Soveraign cannot be understood to doe, by any Grant, that does not plainly, and directly discharge them of their subjection. For consequences of words, are not the signes of his will, when other consequences are signes of the contrary; but rather signes of errour, and misreckoning; to which all mankind is too prone.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Once the concept of separated essences is accepted, it leads to numerous other absurdities. This highlights the challenge of assigning a place to these forms, given that they are considered real. Since they are also deemed incorporeal and lacking in dimensional quantity, and it is widely acknowledged that place is associated with dimension and can only be occupied by corporeal entities, a distinction is made to maintain credibility. This suggests that the terms used to describe the location of these forms, such as "definitive" rather than "circumscriptive", are essentially meaningless and serve only to obscure the issue. Ultimately, the concept of circumscription refers to the determination or definition of a thing's place, rendering the distinction between these terms pointless. In the case of the essence of a man, which is said to be his soul, it is claimed that the entire soul is present in every part of the body, regardless of size, without the total amount of soul increasing with the size of the body. This implies a paradoxical understanding of the soul's presence in the body. This situation arises from the notion of an incorporeal soul separated from the body, and it is necessary to accept such absurdities in order to believe in the existence of such a soul.
output: Being once fallen into this Error of Separated Essences, they are thereby necessarily involved in many other absurdities that follow it. For seeing they will have these Forms to be reall, they are obliged to assign them some place. But because they hold them Incorporeall, without all dimension of Quantity, and all men know that Place is Dimension, and not to be filled, but by that which is Corporeall; they are driven to uphold their credit with a distinction, that they are not indeed any where Circumscriptive, but Definitive: Which Terms being meer Words, and in this occasion insignificant, passe onely in Latine, that the vanity of them may bee concealed. For the Circumscription of a thing, is nothing else but the Determination, or Defining of its Place; and so both the Terms of the Distinction are the same. And in particular, of the Essence of a Man, which (they say) is his Soule, they affirm it, to be All of it in his little Finger, and All of it in every other Part (how small soever) of his Body; and yet no more Soule in the Whole Body, than in any one of those Parts. Can any man think that God is served with such absurdities? And yet all this is necessary to beleeve, to those that will beleeve the Existence of an Incorporeall Soule, Separated from the Body.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Of artificial persons, some have their words and actions owned by those whom they represent. In that case, the person is the actor, and the one who owns his words and actions may be called the author; here the actor tends to act by authority. For what, in speaking of goods and possessions, is called an owner—in Latin dominus, in Greek kurios—can, when speaking of actions, be called an author. And just as the right of possession is called dominion, so the right of doing any action can be called authority. Thus by authority is generally understood a right of doing any act, and something done by authority is done by commission or licence from the one whose right it is. In short, authority is the right to act, and acting by authority means acting with permission from the person who holds that right.
output: Of Persons Artificiall, some have their words and actions Owned by those whom they represent. And then the Person is the Actor; and he that owneth his words and actions, is the AUTHOR: In which case the Actor acteth by Authority. For that which in speaking of goods and possessions, is called an Owner, and in latine Dominus, in Greeke Kurios; speaking of Actions, is called Author. And as the Right of possession, is called Dominion; so the Right of doing any Action, is called AUTHORITY. So that by Authority, is alwayes understood a Right of doing any act: and Done By Authority, done by Commission, or Licence from him whose right it is.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Although Moses did not compile the Books in their entirety as we have them today, he did write everything attributed to him. For instance, the Volume of the Law appears to be found in Deuteronomy 11 and continues through to Chapter 27. This Law was also commanded to be inscribed on stones when the Israelites entered the land of Canaan, as noted in Deuteronomy 31:9. Moses personally wrote this Law and entrusted it to the Priests and Elders of Israel, instructing them to read it to the entire nation every seventh year during the Feast of Tabernacles. This Law was the one that God commanded the future kings to obtain a copy of from the Priests and Levites to place beside the Ark of the Covenant, as mentioned in Deuteronomy 31:26. This same Law, which had been lost for a time, was later discovered by Hilkiah and sent to King Josiah. Upon hearing it, Josiah had the Law read to the people and renewed the covenant between God and the Israelites, as detailed in 2 Kings 22:8 and 23:1-3.
output: But though Moses did not compile those Books entirely, and in the form we have them; yet he wrote all that which hee is there said to have written: as for example, the Volume of the Law, which is contained, as it seemeth in the 11 of Deuteronomie, and the following Chapters to the 27. which was also commanded to be written on stones, in their entry into the land of Canaan. (Deut. 31. 9) And this did Moses himself write, and deliver to the Priests and Elders of Israel, to be read every seventh year to all Israel, at their assembling in the feast of Tabernacles. And this is that Law which God commanded, that their Kings (when they should have established that form of Government) should take a copy of from the Priests and Levites to lay in the side of the Arke; (Deut. 31. 26) and the same which having been lost, was long time after found again by Hilkiah, and sent to King Josias, who causing it to be read to the People, renewed the Covenant between God and them. (2 King. 22. 8 & 23. 1,2,3)
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: A universal name is assigned to various entities based on shared qualities or characteristics. In contrast, a proper name refers to a specific entity only. Universal names have varying degrees of scope; some encompass larger categories, while others are more limited. This suggests that broader terms can include narrower ones. For instance, the term "Body" has a broader meaning than "Man," as it includes it, while "Man" and "Rational" are mutually inclusive, having the same scope. It is also important to recognize that a name does not solely refer to a single word. Sometimes, a name may consist of several words used together. For example, the phrase "He Who Observes the Laws of His Country" can represent the single concept of "Just."
output:
One Universall name is imposed on many things, for their similitude in some quality, or other accident: And whereas a Proper Name bringeth to mind one thing onely; Universals recall any one of those many.

And of Names Universall, some are of more, and some of lesse extent; the larger comprehending the lesse large: and some again of equall extent, comprehending each other reciprocally. As for example, the Name Body is of larger signification than the word Man, and conprehendeth it; and the names Man and Rationall, are of equall extent, comprehending mutually one another. But here wee must take notice, that by a Name is not alwayes understood, as in Grammar, one onely word; but sometimes by circumlocution many words together. For all these words, Hee That In His Actions Observeth The Lawes Of His Country, make but one Name, equivalent to this one word, Just.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Abraham is recognized as the Father of the Faithful and the first in the Kingdom of God through Covenant. The Covenant was initially established with him, in which he committed himself and his descendants to acknowledge and follow the commands of God. This obligation extended beyond the moral laws that could be discerned through the light of Nature. It also included commands that God would convey to him specifically through Dreams and Visions. Regarding the moral law, the people were already bound to it and did not require a formal contract for the promise of the Land of Canaan. There was no agreement that could enhance or reinforce the natural obligation that both they and all humanity have to obey God Almighty. Therefore, the Covenant Abraham entered into with God involved recognizing as divine commandments those messages he received in Dreams or Visions, and he was tasked with sharing those commands with his family and ensuring their adherence to them.
output: The Father of the Faithfull, and first in the Kingdome of God by Covenant, was Abraham. For with him was the Covenant first made; wherein he obliged himself, and his seed after him, to acknowledge and obey the commands of God; not onely such, as he could take notice of, (as Morall Laws,) by the light of Nature; but also such, as God should in speciall manner deliver to him by Dreams and Visions. For as to the Morall law, they were already obliged, and needed not have been contracted withall, by promise of the Land of Canaan. Nor was there any Contract, that could adde to, or strengthen the Obligation, by which both they, and all men else were bound naturally to obey God Almighty: And therefore the Covenant which Abraham made with God, was to take for the Commandement of God, that which in the name of God was commanded him, in a Dream, or Vision, and to deliver it to his family, and cause them to observe the same.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Even in the presence of a large group, if individuals base their actions solely on their own judgments and desires, they may not find the defense or protection they need, whether from a common enemy or from each other. When there is a divergence of opinions on how to best utilize their combined strength, it can often lead to complications rather than cooperation, ultimately diminishing their power through mutual opposition. This division may result in them being easily overcome by a small, unified group. Furthermore, in the absence of a common threat, they may turn against one another in pursuit of their individual interests. If we consider a scenario where a large group of people agrees to adhere to principles of justice and natural laws without a common authority to maintain order, it might be reasonable to suggest that humanity could function in this way. In such a case, there may be no need for civil government or a commonwealth, as peace could exist without the requirement for subjection.
output: And be there never so great a Multitude; yet if their actions be directed according to their particular judgements, and particular appetites, they can expect thereby no defence, nor protection, neither against a Common enemy, nor against the injuries of one another. For being distracted in opinions concerning the best use and application of their strength, they do not help, but hinder one another; and reduce their strength by mutuall opposition to nothing: whereby they are easily, not onely subdued by a very few that agree together; but also when there is no common enemy, they make warre upon each other, for their particular interests. For if we could suppose a great Multitude of men to consent in the observation of Justice, and other Lawes of Nature, without a common Power to keep them all in awe; we might as well suppose all Man-kind to do the same; and then there neither would be nor need to be any Civill Government, or Common-wealth at all; because there would be Peace without subjection.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: The institution now referred to as a university represents the merging and incorporation of various public schools under a single governance within a particular town or city. The main schools were established to focus on three professions: the Roman religion, Roman law, and medicine. The study of philosophy is considered secondary, serving primarily as a support to the Roman religion. The reliance on Aristotle's authority in this context suggests that the study is not truly philosophy, which should be independent of specific authors, but rather a form of Aristotelian thought. Geometry, until recently, was largely excluded, as it was viewed as relevant only to strict truths. Individuals who demonstrated exceptional skill in this area were often regarded with suspicion, perceived as magicians with diabolical arts.
output: That which is now called an University, is a Joyning together, and an Incorporation under one Government of many Publique Schools, in one and the same Town or City. In which, the principal Schools were ordained for the three Professions, that is to say, of the Romane Religion, of the Romane Law, and of the Art of Medicine. And for the study of Philosophy it hath no otherwise place, then as a handmaid to the Romane Religion: And since the Authority of Aristotle is onely current there, that study is not properly Philosophy, (the nature whereof dependeth not on Authors,) but Aristotelity. And for Geometry, till of very late times it had no place at all; as being subservient to nothing but rigide Truth. And if any man by the ingenuity of his owne nature, had attained to any degree of perfection therein, hee was commonly thought a Magician, and his Art Diabolicall.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Fourthly, since every subject is, by this institution, the author of all the actions and judgments of the sovereign instituted, it follows that whatever he does can be no injury to any of his subjects, nor should he be accused of injustice by any of them. For he who does something by authority from another does no injury thereby to the one by whose authority he acts. But by this institution of a commonwealth, every particular person is the author of all that the sovereign does; and consequently, anyone who complains of injury from his sovereign complains of something of which he himself is the author, and therefore ought not to accuse any man but himself—nor even himself of injury, because it is impossible to do injury to oneself. It is true that those who hold sovereign power may commit iniquity, but not injustice, or injury in the proper sense of the word. In short, because the sovereign acts with the authority of every subject, his actions cannot be counted as injustice toward them, though they may still be iniquitous.
output: Fourthly, because every Subject is by this Institution Author of all the Actions, and Judgements of the Soveraigne Instituted; it followes, that whatsoever he doth, it can be no injury to any of his Subjects; nor ought he to be by any of them accused of Injustice. For he that doth any thing by authority from another, doth therein no injury to him by whose authority he acteth: But by this Institution of a Common-wealth, every particular man is Author of all the Soveraigne doth; and consequently he that complaineth of injury from his Soveraigne, complaineth of that whereof he himselfe is Author; and therefore ought not to accuse any man but himselfe; no nor himselfe of injury; because to do injury to ones selfe, is impossible. It is true that they that have Soveraigne power, may commit Iniquity; but not Injustice, or Injury in the proper signification.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Individuals dispatched by a private party within a troubled state, despite being received, do not serve as public or private ministers of the commonwealth. This is because their actions lack the commonwealth’s authority. Similarly, an ambassador sent by a prince to extend congratulations, express condolences, or participate in a ceremony, while operating under public authority, is still considered a private individual. This distinction arises because the matter at hand pertains to the individual personally, rather than to the state. Additionally, if a person is sent to another country to secretly gather intelligence on their strategies and military capacity, the authority and purpose may be public. However, since only his own interests are acknowledged, he remains a private minister, albeit one serving the commonwealth. This role can be likened to an eye within a natural body. Moreover, those designated to receive petitions or other information from the populace function as public ministers. They serve as the public ear and represent their sovereign in this capacity.
output: But such as are sent by Authoritie only of some private partie of a troubled State, though they be received, are neither Publique, nor Private Ministers of the Common-wealth; because none of their actions have the Common-wealth for Author. Likewise, an Ambassador sent from a Prince, to congratulate, condole, or to assist at a solemnity, though Authority be Publique; yet because the businesse is Private, and belonging to him in his naturall capacity; is a Private person. Also if a man be sent into another Country, secretly to explore their counsels, and strength; though both the Authority, and the Businesse be Publique; yet because there is none to take notice of any Person in him, but his own; he is but a Private Minister; but yet a Minister of the Common-wealth; and may be compared to an Eye in the Body naturall. And those that are appointed to receive the Petitions or other informations of the People, and are as it were the publique Eare, are Publique Ministers, and represent their Soveraign in that office.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Additionally, the process of evangelization is likened by our Saviour to the act of fishing, wherein individuals are persuaded to embrace obedience, as opposed to being coerced or punished. Furthermore, it is noteworthy that he did not instruct his apostles to become hunters of men, but rather fishers of men, thereby emphasizing the role of persuasion in this endeavour. Moreover, the evangelization process is also compared to leaven, the sowing of seed, and the multiplication of a grain of mustard-seed, all of which exclude the notion of compulsion, and consequently, preclude the possibility of actual reigning during that period. In essence, the primary function of Christ's ministers is evangelization, which entails the proclamation of Christ and preparation for his second coming, analogous to the evangelization of John Baptist, which served as a preparation for his first coming.
output: And is compared by our Saviour, to Fishing; that is, to winning men to obedience, not by Coercion, and Punishing; but by Perswasion: and therefore he said not to his Apostles, hee would make them so many Nimrods, Hunters Of Men; But Fishers Of Men. It is compared also to Leaven; to Sowing of Seed, and to the Multiplication of a grain of Mustard-seed; by all which Compulsion is excluded; and consequently there can in that time be no actual Reigning. The work of Christs Ministers, is Evangelization; that is, a Proclamation of Christ, and a preparation for his second comming; as the Evangelization of John Baptist, was a preparation to his first coming.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input:
That which individuals desire is often characterized as love, while those things they dislike are described as objects of hate. Therefore, desire and love can be considered synonymous, with the distinction that desire typically indicates the absence of the object, whereas love frequently suggests its presence. Similarly, aversion denotes absence, while hate implies the presence of the object.

With regard to appetites and aversions, some are innate to humans, such as the appetite for food and the urges related to excretion and relief, which may more accurately be classified as aversions due to the sensations experienced in the body. There are also a limited number of other innate appetites. The remainder, which pertains to specific desires, arises from personal experience and the observation of their effects on oneself or others. For instances involving things that are completely unknown to us or believed not to exist, our desire is limited to the urge to taste and explore. In contrast, our aversion extends not only to things we know to be harmful but also to those we are uncertain whether they may cause harm.
output:
That which men Desire, they are also sayd to LOVE; and to HATE those things, for which they have Aversion. So that Desire, and Love, are the same thing; save that by Desire, we alwayes signifie the Absence of the object; by Love, most commonly the Presence of the same. So also by Aversion, we signifie the Absence; and by Hate, the Presence of the Object.

Of Appetites, and Aversions, some are born with men; as Appetite of food, Appetite of excretion, and exoneration, (which may also and more properly be called Aversions, from somewhat they feele in their Bodies;) and some other Appetites, not many. The rest, which are Appetites of particular things, proceed from Experience, and triall of their effects upon themselves, or other men. For of things wee know not at all, or believe not to be, we can have no further Desire, than to tast and try. But Aversion wee have for things, not onely which we know have hurt us; but also that we do not know whether they will hurt us, or not.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: The term "Body," in its most general sense, refers to that which fills or occupies a specific space or imagined area. This concept does not rely on imagination; it is a real component of what we identify as the Universe. The Universe, being the collection of all Bodies, consists entirely of real parts that are Bodies. Consequently, anything that can be described as a Body is also a part of this collective of all Bodies within the Universe. Furthermore, because Bodies are subject to change, they exhibit various appearances to the senses of living creatures. This variability is referred to as Substance, meaning it is subject to different conditions, such as being in motion or at rest. Bodies can also appear to our senses as hot or cold, and can vary in color, smell, taste, or sound. This diversity in appearance, which arises from the interaction of Bodies with our sensory organs, is attributed to changes in the Bodies themselves and is termed Accidents of those Bodies. In this context, Substance and Body convey the same meaning. Therefore, the phrase "Incorporeal Substance" is contradictory, similar to stating "an Incorporeal Body."
output: The Word Body, in the most generall acceptation, signifieth that which filleth, or occupyeth some certain room, or imagined place; and dependeth not on the imagination, but is a reall part of that we call the Universe. For the Universe, being the Aggregate of all Bodies, there is no reall part thereof that is not also Body; nor any thing properly a Body, that is not also part of (that Aggregate of all Bodies) the Universe. The same also, because Bodies are subject to change, that is to say, to variety of apparence to the sense of living creatures, is called Substance, that is to say, Subject, to various accidents, as sometimes to be Moved, sometimes to stand Still; and to seem to our senses sometimes Hot, sometimes Cold, sometimes of one Colour, Smel, Tast, or Sound, somtimes of another. And this diversity of Seeming, (produced by the diversity of the operation of bodies, on the organs of our sense) we attribute to alterations of the Bodies that operate, & call them Accidents of those Bodies. And according to this acceptation of the word, Substance and Body, signifie the same thing; and therefore Substance Incorporeall are words, which when they are joined together, destroy one another, as if a man should say, an Incorporeall Body.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: The consent of a subject to sovereign power is encompassed in the statement "I authorise, or take upon me, all his actions." This highlights the absence of any restriction on the subject's former natural liberty. By granting the sovereign the authority to take their life, the subject is not necessarily bound to take their own life when commanded to do so. This suggests a distinction between authorizing someone else to perform an action and personally committing to perform that action. Ultimately, the statement "kill me, or my fellow, if you please" implies a different level of commitment than "I will kill my self, or my fellow." It follows from this that
output: Again, the Consent of a Subject to Soveraign Power, is contained in these words, "I Authorise, or take upon me, all his actions;" in which there is no restriction at all, of his own former naturall Liberty: For by allowing him to Kill Me, I am not bound to Kill my selfe when he commands me. "’Tis one thing to say ‘Kill me, or my fellow, if you please;’ another thing to say, ‘I will kill my selfe, or my fellow.’" It followeth therefore, that
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: The sixth reference can be found in Luke 16:9, which suggests, "Make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails, they may receive you into eternal dwellings." This verse is sometimes interpreted as supporting the practice of invoking departed saints. However, a clearer understanding may be that we should cultivate relationships with the poor using our resources, which could lead to their prayers for us while they are alive. The idea that "whoever is generous to the poor lends to the Lord" further emphasizes this point. The seventh reference is found in Luke 23:42, where one of the criminals crucified alongside Jesus says, "Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom." This is sometimes taken to imply that there may be forgiveness of sins after death. However, the reasoning may not be entirely sound. Jesus forgave the criminal at that moment, and it is believed that he will be remembered and raised to eternal life upon Christ's return. Together, these passages suggest the importance of generosity and the hope of redemption.
output: The sixth place is Luke 16. 9. "Make yee friends of the unrighteous Mammon, that when yee faile, they may receive you into Everlasting Tabernacles." This he alledges to prove Invocation of Saints departed. But the sense is plain, That we should make friends with our Riches, of the Poore, and thereby obtain their Prayers whilest they live. "He that giveth to the Poore, lendeth to the Lord. "The seventh is Luke 23. 42. "Lord remember me when thou commest into thy Kingdome:" Therefore, saith hee, there is Remission of sins after this life. But the consequence is not good. Our Saviour then forgave him; and at his comming againe in Glory, will remember to raise him againe to Life Eternall.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input:
The arguments presented to demonstrate that bishops receive their jurisdiction from the pope, given that the pope himself lacks jurisdiction in the domains of other princes, may not be entirely convincing. However, as they also suggest that bishops can often receive jurisdiction from their civil sovereigns, it may be helpful to review these arguments. 

One such argument is based on Numbers 11, where Moses, unable to manage the affairs of the Israelites alone, was instructed by God to select seventy elders and impart some of his spirit to them. This can be interpreted as indicating that the elders derived their authority from Moses, rather than having their own independent spiritual power. It tends to be understood that this transfer of spirit did not diminish Moses' own authority, but rather emphasized the source of the elders' power. Given that Moses held complete sovereignty over the Jewish commonwealth, it can be inferred that the elders' authority came from the civil sovereign. This interpretation may suggest that, in Christian commonwealths, bishops may receive their authority from the civil sovereign, and that the pope's authority is generally limited to his own territories, rather than extending to the territories of other states. In summary, the argument proposes that bishops typically derive their jurisdiction from the civil sovereign in their respective commonwealths.
output:
The arguments by which he would prove, that Bishops receive their Jurisdiction from the Pope (seeing the Pope in the Dominions of other Princes hath no Jurisdiction himself,) are all in vain. Yet because they prove, on the contrary, that all Bishops receive Jurisdiction when they have it from their Civill Soveraigns, I will not omit the recitall of them.

The first, is from Numbers 11. where Moses not being able alone to undergoe the whole burthen of administring the affairs of the People of Israel, God commanded him to choose Seventy Elders, and took part of the spirit of Moses, to put it upon those Seventy Elders: by which it is understood, not that God weakened the spirit of Moses, for that had not eased him at all; but that they had all of them their authority from him; wherein he doth truly, and ingenuously interpret that place. But seeing Moses had the entire Soveraignty in the Common-wealth of the Jews, it is manifest, that it is thereby signified, that they had their Authority from the Civill Soveraign: and therefore that place proveth, that Bishops in every Christian Common-wealth have their Authority from the Civill Soveraign; and from the Pope in his own Territories only, and not in the Territories of any other State.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: When considering the thoughts of man, I will first examine them singly, and afterward in their train or dependence upon one another. Taken singly, each thought may be understood as a representation or appearance of some quality or other accident of a body outside us, which is commonly called an object. This object tends to work upon the eyes, ears, and other parts of a man's body, and through this variety of working it can often produce a variety of appearances. The original of all these thoughts is what we call sense, for there is generally no conception in a man's mind that has not at first, either wholly or in part, been begotten upon the organs of sense, and the rest are derived from that original.
output:
Concerning the Thoughts of man, I will consider them first Singly, and afterwards in Trayne, or dependance upon one another. Singly, they are every one a Representation or Apparence, of some quality, or other Accident of a body without us; which is commonly called an Object. Which Object worketh on the Eyes, Eares, and other parts of mans body; and by diversity of working, produceth diversity of Apparences.

The Originall of them all, is that which we call Sense; (For there is no conception in a mans mind, which hath not at first, totally, or by parts, been begotten upon the organs of Sense.) The rest are derived from that originall.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input:
Every crime originates from a flaw in understanding, an error in reasoning, or an overpowering passion. A flaw in understanding manifests as ignorance, while an error in reasoning results in a misguided opinion. Furthermore, ignorance comes in three forms: ignorance of the law, ignorance of authority, and ignorance of penalties. Ignorance of the law of nature does not excuse anyone. It is presumed that anyone who has reached the use of reason understands that they should not do to others what they would not want done to themselves. Therefore, wherever a person may go, any action contrary to that law is considered a crime. 

For instance, if a person arrives from the Indies and persuades others to adopt a new religion or teaches them anything that leads to disobedience of local laws, that person commits a crime, regardless of their conviction in the truth of their teachings. This is true not only because their doctrine may be false, but also because they are engaging in behavior they would not accept from others, specifically, trying to change the religion of those who live there. In contrast, ignorance of civil law may excuse a person in a foreign land until the law is explained to them, as civil law does not take effect until it is made known.
output: The source of every Crime, is some defect of the Understanding; or some errour in Reasoning, or some sudden force of the Passions. Defect in the Understanding, is Ignorance; in Reasoning, Erroneous Opinion. Again, ignorance is of three sort; of the Law, and of the Soveraign, and of the Penalty. Ignorance of the Law of Nature Excuseth no man; because every man that hath attained to the use of Reason, is supposed to know, he ought not to do to another, what he would not have done to himselfe. Therefore into what place soever a man shall come, if he do any thing contrary to that Law, it is a Crime. If a man come from the Indies hither, and perswade men here to receive a new Religion, or teach them any thing that tendeth to disobedience of the Lawes of this Country, though he be never so well perswaded of the truth of what he teacheth, he commits a Crime, and may be justly punished for the same, not onely because his doctrine is false, but also because he does that which he would not approve in another, namely, that comming from hence, he should endeavour to alter the Religion there. But ignorance of the Civill Law, shall Excuse a man in a strange Country, till it be declared to him; because, till then no Civill Law is binding.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input:
The nutrition of a commonwealth is comprised of several key elements, including the availability and distribution of essential materials that support life. Additionally, it involves the preparation and conveyance of these materials to the public through convenient channels. 

The availability of materials is naturally limited to commodities that are obtained from the land and sea, which are often referred to as the primary sources of sustenance. Generally, these commodities are either freely provided by nature or acquired through human labor. 

The materials that make up the nutrients necessary for a commonwealth consist of animals, vegetables, and minerals, which are readily available on or near the surface of the earth. Therefore, the primary requirement for obtaining these nutrients is the labor and industry required to harvest them. Moreover, the abundance of these nutrients largely depends on the labor and industry of humans, with the exception of divine favor.
output:
The NUTRITION of a Common-wealth consisteth, in the Plenty, and Distribution of Materials conducing to Life: In Concoction, or Preparation; and (when concocted) in the Conveyance of it, by convenient conduits, to the Publique use.

As for the Plenty of Matter, it is a thing limited by Nature, to those commodities, which from (the two breasts of our common Mother) Land, and Sea, God usually either freely giveth, or for labour selleth to man-kind.

For the Matter of this Nutriment, consisting in Animals, Vegetals, and Minerals, God hath freely layd them before us, in or neer to the face of the Earth; so as there needeth no more but the labour, and industry of receiving them. Insomuch as Plenty dependeth (next to Gods favour) meerly on the labour and industry of men.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input:
The ownership a subject has over their land entails the right to prevent other subjects from using it. However, this ownership does not extend to excluding the Sovereign, whether that Sovereign is an Assembly or a Monarch. The Sovereign, representing the Commonwealth, acts solely for the sake of the common peace and security. Consequently, any distribution of land must align with this purpose. Therefore, any decision made by the Sovereign that undermines this goal contradicts the interests of all subjects who have entrusted their peace and safety to the Sovereign's judgment. Such actions would be regarded as null and void by the collective will of the subjects.

It is true that a Sovereign Monarch or a majority in a Sovereign Assembly may decide to act contrary to their better judgment, driven by their own desires. This behavior constitutes a breach of trust and a violation of natural law. Nonetheless, this does not grant any subject the right to wage war against, accuse of injustice, or speak ill of their Sovereign. The subjects have endorsed the Sovereign's actions, thereby making those actions their own. The circumstances in which the commands of Sovereigns conflict with equity and natural law will be examined in further detail later.
output:
Propriety Of A Subject Excludes Not The Dominion Of The Soveraign, But Onely Of Another Subject

From whence we may collect, that the Propriety which a subject hath in his lands, consisteth in a right to exclude all other subjects from the use of them; and not to exclude their Soveraign, be it an Assembly, or a Monarch. For seeing the Soveraign, that is to say, the Common-wealth (whose Person he representeth,) is understood to do nothing but in order to the common Peace and Security, this Distribution of lands, is to be understood as done in order to the same: And consequently, whatsoever Distribution he shall make in prejudice thereof, is contrary to the will of every subject, that committed his Peace, and safety to his discretion, and conscience; and therefore by the will of every one of them, is to be reputed voyd. It is true, that a Soveraign Monarch, or the greater part of a Soveraign Assembly, may ordain the doing of many things in pursuit of their Passions, contrary to their own consciences, which is a breach of trust, and of the Law of Nature; but this is not enough to authorise any subject, either to make warre upon, or so much as to accuse of Injustice, or any way to speak evill of their Soveraign; because they have authorised all his actions, and in bestowing the Soveraign Power, made them their own. But in what cases the Commands of Soveraigns are contrary to Equity, and the Law of Nature, is to be considered hereafter in another place.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Considering the aforementioned properties of just and rational adjudication, it is worth noting the admirable structure of the Courts of Justice established for both Common Pleas and Public Pleas in England. By Common Pleas, I refer to those cases in which both the complainant and the defendant are subjects; conversely, by Public Pleas, which are also known as Pleas of the Crown, I denote instances where the complainant is the Sovereign. In this context, there existed two distinct orders of individuals: one comprised of Lords and the other of Commons. The Lords possessed the privilege of having only fellow Lords serve as judges in all capital crimes, with the number present being at their discretion. This arrangement was universally recognized as a privilege of favor, and their judges were exclusively those whom they themselves had selected. In all disputes, every subject, as well as the Lords in civil controversies, were judged by individuals from the locality where the matter in question arose. They were permitted to raise objections until a final agreement was reached among twelve men without exception, who then rendered the judgment. Thus, with the ability to choose their own judges, there could be no valid argument from the party as to why the sentence should not be considered final. Furthermore, these public individuals, who derive authority from the Sovereign Power to instruct or judge the populace, serve as integral components of the Commonwealth, aptly likened to the organs of voice within a natural body.
output: These properties of just and rationall Judicature considered, I cannot forbeare to observe the excellent constitution of the Courts of Justice, established both for Common, and also for Publique Pleas in England. By Common Pleas, I meane those, where both the Complaynant and Defendant are Subjects: and by Publique, (which are also called Pleas of the Crown) those, where the Complaynant is the Soveraign. For whereas there were two orders of men, whereof one was Lords, the other Commons; The Lords had this Priviledge, to have for Judges in all Capitall crimes, none but Lords; and of them, as many as would be present; which being ever acknowledged as a Priviledge of favour, their Judges were none but such as they had themselves desired. And in all controversies, every Subject (as also in civill controversies the Lords) had for Judges, men of the Country where the matter in controversie lay; against which he might make his exceptions, till at last Twelve men without exception being agreed on, they were Judged by those twelve. So that having his own Judges, there could be nothing alledged by the party, why the sentence should not be finall, These publique persons, with Authority from the Soveraign Power, either to Instruct, or Judge the people, are such members of the Common-wealth, as may fitly be compared to the organs of Voice in a Body naturall.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: In examining the nature and properties of the Tormenters, one encounters their designations, which are elucidated through the names of The Enemy, or Satan; The Accuser, or Diabolus; and The Destroyer, or Abbadon. These significant titles—Satan, Devil, Abbadon—do not denote an individual entity, as proper names typically do; rather, they signify a role or characteristic. Consequently, these terms are to be understood as appellatives, which should not have been left untranslated in the Latin and Modern Bibles. The failure to translate these names leads to the misconception that they refer to the proper names of demons, thus making individuals more susceptible to believing in the doctrine of devils. This doctrine was prevalent during a time when it constituted the religion of the Gentiles, standing in contrast to the beliefs espoused by Moses and Christ.
output: And first for the Tormenters, wee have their nature, and properties, exactly and properly delivered by the names of, The Enemy, or Satan; The Accuser, or Diabolus; The Destroyer, or Abbadon. Which significant names, Satan, Devill, Abbadon, set not forth to us any Individuall person, as proper names use to doe; but onely an office, or quality; and are therefore Appellatives; which ought not to have been left untranslated, as they are, in the Latine, and Modern Bibles; because thereby they seem to be the proper names of Daemons; and men are the more easily seduced to beleeve the doctrine of Devills; which at that time was the Religion of the Gentiles, and contrary to that of Moses, and of Christ.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Additionally, titles of honour, such as Duke, Count, Marquis, and Baron, are considered honourable inasmuch as they signify the value placed upon them by the sovereign power of the commonwealth. Furthermore, these titles were originally derived from offices and commands, with some originating from the Romans, others from the Germans, and others from the French. In essence, the titles of Duke, Count, and Marquis were initially associated with specific roles, with Dukes, or Duces in Latin, serving as generals in war, Counts, or Comites, accompanying generals out of friendship and governing and defending conquered and pacified places, and Marquises, or Marchiones, governing the marches or bounds of the empire. Moreover, these titles of Duke, Count, and Marquis were introduced into the empire around the time of Constantine the Great, originating from the customs of the German militia. It is worth noting that the title of Baron, on the other hand, appears to have originated from the Gauls, signifying a great man, such as the king's or prince's men, who were employed in war and attended to their persons, with the term being derived from the Gaulish language, where "vir" was equivalent to "ber" or "bar", and eventually led to the terms "Berones" and "Barones", and also "Varones" in Spanish. Moreover, for a more detailed understanding of the origin of titles of honour, one may consult Mr. Selden's excellent treatise on the subject, which has also informed the present discussion. In the course of time, these offices of honour, due to circumstances of trouble and the need for good and peaceful government, were transformed into mere titles, primarily serving to distinguish the precedence, place, and order of subjects in the commonwealth, with individuals being appointed as Dukes, Counts, Marquises, and Barons of places over which they had neither possession nor command, and other titles being devised to achieve the same end.
output: Titles of Honour, such as are Duke, Count, Marquis, and Baron, are Honourable; as signifying the value set upon them by the Soveraigne Power of the Common-wealth: Which Titles, were in old time titles of Office, and Command, derived some from the Romans, some from the Germans, and French. Dukes, in Latine Duces, being Generalls in War: Counts, Comites, such as bare the Generall company out of friendship; and were left to govern and defend places conquered, and pacified: Marquises, Marchiones, were Counts that governed the Marches, or bounds of the Empire. Which titles of Duke, Count, and Marquis, came into the Empire, about the time of Constantine the Great, from the customes of the German Militia. But Baron, seems to have been a Title of the Gaules, and signifies a Great man; such as were the Kings, or Princes men, whom they employed in war about their persons; and seems to be derived from Vir, to Ber, and Bar, that signified the same in the Language of the Gaules, that Vir in Latine; and thence to Bero, and Baro: so that such men were called Berones, and after Barones; and (in Spanish) Varones. But he that would know more particularly the originall of Titles of Honour, may find it, as I have done this, in Mr. Seldens most excellent Treatise of that subject. In processe of time these offices of Honour, by occasion of trouble, and for reasons of good and peacable government, were turned into meer Titles; serving for the most part, to distinguish the precedence, place, and order of subjects in the Common-wealth: and men were made Dukes, Counts, Marquises, and Barons of Places, wherein they had neither possession, nor command: and other Titles also, were devised to the same end.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input:
The Justice of Actions designates individuals as not merely Just, but rather Innocent; conversely, the Injustice of the same, referred to as Injury, categorizes them as Guilty. 

Furthermore, the Injustice of Manners represents the inclination or predisposition to commit Injury, existing as Injustice even prior to any actual act, and without necessarily implicating any specific individual as injured. However, the Injustice inherent in an Action, or Injury, presumes the existence of a specific individual who has been harmed, particularly the individual to whom a Covenant was made. Consequently, it is often the case that one person suffers an injury while the resulting damage impacts another. For example, when a Master instructs his servant to give money to a stranger, failure to execute this command results in Injury to the Master, the party to whom the obligation was previously established, while the damage ultimately affects the stranger, to whom the servant had no such obligation and thus could not inflict Injury. Similarly, within Commonwealths, private individuals may forgive one another for debts; however, they cannot overlook robberies or other acts of violence that result in damage, as the withholding of a debt constitutes an Injury to themselves, whereas Robbery and Violence represent Injuries to the Commonwealth as a whole.
output:
But the Justice of Actions denominates men, not Just, but Guiltlesse; and the Injustice of the same, (which is also called Injury,) gives them but the name of Guilty.

Again, the Injustice of Manners, is the disposition, or aptitude to do Injurie; and is Injustice before it proceed to Act; and without supposing any individuall person injured. But the Injustice of an Action, (that is to say Injury,) supposeth an individuall person Injured; namely him, to whom the Covenant was made: And therefore many times the injury is received by one man, when the dammage redoundeth to another. As when The Master commandeth his servant to give mony to a stranger; if it be not done, the Injury is done to the Master, whom he had before Covenanted to obey; but the dammage redoundeth to the stranger, to whom he had no Obligation; and therefore could not Injure him. And so also in Common-wealths, private men may remit to one another their debts; but not robberies or other violences, whereby they are endammaged; because the detaining of Debt, is an Injury to themselves; but Robbery and Violence, are Injuries to the Person of the Common-wealth.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Historically, there has never been a period in which individuals were constantly at war with one another. Nevertheless, kings and persons of sovereign authority have always been in a state of tension due to their independent nature. As a result, they maintain a perpetual state of readiness, similar to that of gladiators, with their attention focused on one another. This is evident in the fact that they have forts, garrisons, and guns positioned along the borders of their kingdoms, as well as spies continually monitoring their neighbors, which is essentially a wartime posture. However, because this state of affairs also serves to support the industry of their subjects, it does not necessarily lead to the same level of misery that can accompany the liberty of individual men. Additionally, this situation doesn became a necessary aspect of sovereign authority, as it allows kings to maintain power and control over their territories.
output: But though there had never been any time, wherein particular men were in a condition of warre one against another; yet in all times, Kings, and persons of Soveraigne authority, because of their Independency, are in continuall jealousies, and in the state and posture of Gladiators; having their weapons pointing, and their eyes fixed on one another; that is, their Forts, Garrisons, and Guns upon the Frontiers of their Kingdomes; and continuall Spyes upon their neighbours; which is a posture of War. But because they uphold thereby, the Industry of their Subjects; there does not follow from it, that misery, which accompanies the Liberty of particular men.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Reward is either a gift or something given by contract. When it is by contract, it is called salary or wages, which is a benefit owed for service performed or promised. When it is a gift, it is a benefit that comes from the grace of those who bestow it, intended to encourage or enable men to do them service. This suggests that when the sovereign of a commonwealth appoints a salary to any public office, the one who receives it is bound in justice to perform his office; otherwise, he is bound only in honor, to acknowledgment and an effort at repayment. For although men have no lawful remedy when they are commanded to leave their private business to serve the public without reward or salary, they are not bound to do so by the law of nature or by the institution of the commonwealth, unless the service cannot otherwise be done.
