This highlights that the sovereign is supposed to be able to make use of all their means, to the extent that even the most common soldier may demand the wages of his warfare as a debt.
output: REWARD, is either of Gift, or by Contract. When by Contract, it is called Salary, and Wages; which is benefit due for service performed, or promised. When of Gift, it is benefit proceeding from the Grace of them that bestow it, to encourage, or enable men to do them service. And therefore when the Soveraign of a Common-wealth appointeth a Salary to any publique Office, he that receiveth it, is bound in Justice to performe his office; otherwise, he is bound onely in honour, to acknowledgement, and an endeavour of requitall. For though men have no lawfull remedy, when they be commanded to quit their private businesse, to serve the publique, without Reward, or Salary; yet they are not bound thereto, by the Law of Nature, nor by the institution of the Common-wealth, unlesse the service cannot otherwise be done; because it is supposed the Soveraign may make use of all their means, insomuch as the most common Souldier, may demand the wages of his warrefare, as a debt.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: Additionally, it becomes apparent that an oath administered in accordance with any form or rite other than that which is recognized by the individual swearing is essentially invalid and devoid of significance. Furthermore, it is evident that swearing by any entity that is not regarded as divine by the swearer is without foundation. Moreover, although individuals have occasionally resorted to swearing by their monarchs, this has typically been motivated by fear or flattery, and it has been implied that such actions are undertaken with the intention of attributing divine honor to them. In essence, swearing unnecessarily in the name of God constitutes a form of profanation, whereas swearing by other entities, as is commonly practiced in everyday conversation, does not constitute genuine swearing, but rather an impious custom that has arisen as a result of excessive loquaciousness. It is worth noting that such behavior is ultimately a product of habitual and vehement speech patterns.
output: By this it appears, that an Oath taken according to any other Forme, or Rite, then his, that sweareth, is in vain; and no Oath: And there is no Swearing by any thing which the Swearer thinks not God. For though men have sometimes used to swear by their Kings, for feare, or flattery; yet they would have it thereby understood, they attributed to them Divine honour. And that Swearing unnecessarily by God, is but prophaning of his name: and Swearing by other things, as men do in common discourse, is not Swearing, but an impious Custome, gotten by too much vehemence of talking.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input:
The fairies do not engage in marriage, however, there are incubi among them that interact with humans in a physical manner. Additionally, the priests also refrain from marrying. 

The ecclesiastics acquire the majority of the land's resources through donations from individuals who hold them in high regard, as well as through tithes. Similarly, in fairy folklore, it is said that they enter dairy facilities and consume the cream that they skim from the milk. 

The type of currency used in the kingdom of fairies is not documented in the narrative. Nevertheless, the ecclesiastics accept the same form of money that is commonly used, when they are receiving payments. However, when they are required to make payments, they typically do so in the form of canonizations, indulgences, and masses.
output:
The Fairies marry not; but there be amongst them Incubi, that have copulation with flesh and bloud. The Priests also marry not.

The Ecclesiastiques take the Cream of the Land, by Donations of ignorant men, that stand in aw of them, and by Tythes: So also it is in the Fable of Fairies, that they enter into the Dairies, and Feast upon the Cream, which they skim from the Milk.

What kind of Money is currant in the Kingdome of Fairies, is not recorded in the Story. But the Ecclesiastiques in their Receipts accept of the same Money that we doe; though when they are to make any Payment, it is in Canonizations, Indulgences, and Masses.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: The Procreation, or Children of a Commonwealth, are what we call Plantations, or Colonies, which are groups of people sent out from the Commonwealth under a Conductor, or Governor, to inhabit a Foreign Country, either previously empty of inhabitants or made empty at that time by war. When a Colony is settled, it may either become a Commonwealth of its own, released from subjection to the Sovereign that sent it, as has been done by many Commonwealths in ancient times, in which case the Commonwealth from which they went was called their Metropolis, or Mother, and tends to require no more of them than fathers require of children whom they emancipate and free from their domestic government, which is Honor and Friendship; or else they may remain united to their Metropolis, as were the Colonies of the people of Rome, and in that case they are not Commonwealths themselves but Provinces and parts of the Commonwealth that sent them. Thus the Right of Colonies, apart from Honor and League with their Metropolis, depends wholly on their License, or Letters, by which their Sovereign authorized them to Plant.
output: The Procreation, or Children of a Common-wealth, are those we call Plantations, or Colonies; which are numbers of men sent out from the Common-wealth, under a Conductor, or Governour, to inhabit a Forraign Country, either formerly voyd of Inhabitants, or made voyd then, by warre. And when a Colony is setled, they are either a Common-wealth of themselves, discharged of their subjection to their Soveraign that sent them, (as hath been done by many Common-wealths of antient time,) in which case the Common-wealth from which they went was called their Metropolis, or Mother, and requires no more of them, then Fathers require of the Children, whom they emancipate, and make free from their domestique government, which is Honour, and Friendship; or else they remain united to their Metropolis, as were the Colonies of the people of Rome; and then they are no Common-wealths themselves, but Provinces, and parts of the Common-wealth that sent them. So that the Right of Colonies (saving Honour, and League with their Metropolis,) dependeth wholly on their Licence, or Letters, by which their Soveraign authorised them to Plant.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: This concludes the discussion of the Kingdom of God and ecclesiastical policy. I do not claim to advance any position of my own; rather, I intend only to show what consequences appear to me deducible from the principles of Christian politics, which are the Holy Scriptures, in confirmation of the power of civil sovereigns and the duty of their subjects. In citing Scripture, I have endeavored to avoid texts of obscure or disputed interpretation and to cite only those whose meaning is most plain and consistent with the harmony and scope of the whole Bible, which was written for the re-establishment of the Kingdom of God in Christ. It is not the bare words but the scope of the writer that gives the true light by which any writing is to be interpreted. Those who insist on single texts without considering the main design can derive nothing clearly from them; instead, by casting atoms of Scripture like dust before men's eyes, they make everything more obscure than it is. This is an ordinary artifice of those who seek not the truth but their own advantage.
output: And thus much shall suffice, concerning the Kingdome of God, and Policy Ecclesiasticall. Wherein I pretend not to advance any Position of my own, but onely to shew what are the Consequences that seem to me deducible from the Principles of Christian Politiques, (which are the holy Scriptures,) in confirmation of the Power of Civill Soveraigns, and the Duty of their Subjects. And in the allegation of Scripture, I have endeavoured to avoid such Texts as are of obscure, or controverted Interpretation; and to alledge none, but is such sense as is most plain, and agreeable to the harmony and scope of the whole Bible; which was written for the re-establishment of the Kingdome of God in Christ. For it is not the bare Words, but the Scope of the writer that giveth the true light, by which any writing is to bee interpreted; and they that insist upon single Texts, without considering the main Designe, can derive no thing from them cleerly; but rather by casting atomes of Scripture, as dust before mens eyes, make every thing more obscure than it is; an ordinary artifice of those that seek not the truth, but their own advantage.
title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes

input: If the silver coin were restored to its standard weight, similar to the gold coin, it is likely that a guinea would exchange for a greater amount of silver coin than it would purchase in silver bullion, based on the current proportion. This highlights a potential issue, as it would create a profit opportunity by melting down silver coins, selling the resulting bullion for gold coins, and then exchanging those gold coins for more silver coins to melt down, repeating the process. This suggests that the current system could be exploited for gain. Ultimately, adjusting the present proportion appears to be the only way to prevent this inconvenience from occurring.
output: Were the silver coin brought back as near to its standard weight as the gold, a guinea, it is probable, would, according to the present proportion, exchange for more silver in coin than it would purchase in bullion. The silver coin containing its full standard weight, there would in this case, be a profit in melting it down, in order, first to sell the bullion for gold coin, and afterwards to exchange this gold coin for silver coin, to be melted down in the same manner. Some alteration in the present proportion seems to be the only method of preventing this inconveniency.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: The output of all large-scale manufacturing intended for distant markets necessarily depends less on whether seasons in the producing countries are dear or cheap than on the conditions affecting demand in the countries where the goods are consumed—on peace or war, on the prosperity or decline of rival manufactures, and on the mood of the principal customers. This highlights that a considerable portion of the additional work likely performed during cheap years never appears in public records of manufacturing. Male servants who leave their masters become independent laborers. Women return to their parents and commonly spin in order to make clothes for themselves and their families. Even independent workmen do not always work for public sale, but are often employed by neighbors in manufacturing goods for family use. Ultimately, the output of their labor frequently goes unrecorded in those public registers, whose records are sometimes published with great fanfare and from which merchants and manufacturers often vainly claim to announce the prosperity or decline of the greatest empires.
output: The produce of all great manufactures for distant sale must necessarily depend, not so much upon the dearness or cheapness of the seasons in the countries where they are carried on, as upon the circumstances which affect the demand in the countries where they are consumed; upon peace or war, upon the prosperity or declension of other rival manufactures and upon the good or bad humour of their principal customers. A great part of the extraordinary work, besides, which is probably done in cheap years, never enters the public registers of manufactures. The men-servants, who leave their masters, become independent labourers. The women return to their parents, and commonly spin, in order to make clothes for themselves and their families. Even the independent workmen do not always work for public sale, but are employed by some of their neighbours in manufactures for family use. The produce of their labour, therefore, frequently makes no figure in those public registers, of which the records are sometimes published with so much parade, and from which our merchants and manufacturers would often vainly pretend to announce the prosperity or declension of the greatest empires.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input:
Observations about price fluctuations in commodities like corn may not have led many intelligent authors astray if they had not been influenced by a common belief. This belief holds that as a country's wealth and silver quantity increase, the value of silver decreases. This highlights a notion that appears to be without foundation. 

The quantity of precious metals in a country can increase due to two distinct factors. Firstly, it may be the result of an increase in the abundance of mines that supply these metals. Alternatively, it may stem from the increased wealth of the population, driven by a rise in the annual produce of their labor. The first cause is indeed linked to a decrease in the value of precious metals. However, the second cause does not have this effect. Ultimately, the relationship between the quantity and value of precious metals is more complex than the common notion suggests.
output:
Such slight observations, however, upon the prices either of corn or of other commodities, would not probably have misled so many intelligent authors, had they not been influenced at the same time by the popular notion, that as the quantity of silver naturally increases in every country with the increase of wealth, so its value diminishes as its quantity increases. This notion, however, seems to be altogether groundless.

The quantity of the precious metals may increase in any country from two different causes; either, first, from the increased abundance of the mines which supply it; or, secondly, from the increased wealth of the people, from the increased produce of their annual labour. The first of these causes is no doubt necessarily connected with the diminution of the value of the precious metals; but the second is not.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: The private interests and passions of individuals tend to guide their investment towards employments that are typically most beneficial to society. This highlights the natural inclination of individuals to allocate their resources in a way that aligns with the greater good. However, if this preference leads to an over-allocation of resources to certain employments, the resulting decrease in profit in those areas and increase in others will prompt individuals to adjust their distribution. This suggests that the market can self-correct without external intervention. Ultimately, the private interests and passions of individuals lead to a division and distribution of a society's stock among various employments, roughly in proportion to what is most beneficial for the society as a whole.
output: It is thus that the private interests and passions of individuals naturally dispose them to turn their stock towards the employments which in ordinary cases, are most advantageous to the society. But if from this natural preference they should turn too much of it towards those employments, the fall of profit in them, and the rise of it in all others, immediately dispose them to alter this faulty distribution. Without any intervention of law, therefore, the private interests and passions of men naturally lead them to divide and distribute the stock of every society among all the different employments carried on in it; as nearly as possible in the proportion which is most agreeable to the interest of the whole society.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input:
However, although the entire value of the annual produce of the land and labor of every country is divided among its different inhabitants and constitutes a revenue to them, we may nevertheless distinguish between gross revenue and net revenue in the revenue of all the inhabitants of a great country, just as we distinguish between gross rent and net rent in the rent of a private estate.

The gross rent of a private estate includes whatever is paid by the farmer, while the net rent is what remains free to the landlord after deducting the expense of management, of repairs, and all other necessary charges. It is also what he can afford to place in his stock reserved for immediate consumption, or to spend upon his table, equipage, the ornaments of his house and furniture, his private enjoyments and amusements, without hurting his estate. His real wealth is in proportion, not to his gross rent, but to his net rent.
output:
But though the whole value of the annual produce of the land and labour of every country, is thus divided among, and constitutes a revenue to, its different inhabitants; yet, as in the rent of a private estate, we distinguish between the gross rent and the neat rent, so may we likewise in the revenue of all the inhabitants of a great country.

The gross rent of a private estate comprehends whatever is paid by the farmer; the neat rent, what remains free to the landlord, after deducting the expense of management, of repairs, and all other necessary charges; or what, without hurting his estate, he can afford to place in his stock reserved for immediate consumption, or to spend upon his table, equipage, the ornaments of his house and furniture, his private enjoyments and amusements. His real wealth is in proportion, not to his gross, but to his neat rent.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input:
Since the initial discovery of America, the market for the output of its silver mines has been progressively expanding in scope. 

Additionally, the market in Europe has been steadily growing more extensive. Following the discovery of America, much of Europe has experienced significant improvement. Countries such as England, Holland, France, and Germany, as well as Sweden, Denmark, and Russia, have all made substantial advancements in both agriculture and manufacturing. It is worth noting that Italy does not appear to have regressed significantly; rather, its decline preceded the conquest of Peru, and it seems to have made a slight recovery since that time. Conversely, Spain and Portugal are often thought to have declined. However, it is important to recognize that Portugal constitutes only a minor part of Europe, and the decline of Spain may not be as pronounced as is commonly perceived. At the beginning of the sixteenth century, Spain was relatively impoverished compared to France, which has undergone considerable improvement since that period. The well-known observation of Emperor Charles V, who frequently traveled between both nations, highlighted that while France was abundant in resources, Spain lacked many essentials. The increasing agricultural output and manufacturing capabilities of Europe would necessarily have necessitated a gradual rise in the quantity of silver coin required for circulation. Furthermore, the growing number of affluent individuals would have similarly required an increase in their silver plate and other ornamental items.
output:
Since the first discovery of America, the market for the produce of its silver mines has been growing gradually more and more extensive.

First, the market of Europe has become gradually more and more extensive. Since the discovery of America, the greater part of Europe has been much improved. England, Holland, France, and Germany; even Sweden, Denmark, and Russia, have all advanced considerably, both in agriculture and in manufactures. Italy seems not to have gone backwards. The fall of Italy preceded the conquest of Peru. Since that time it seems rather to have recovered a little. Spain and Portugal, indeed, are supposed to have gone backwards. Portugal, however, is but a very small part of Europe, and the declension of Spain is not, perhaps, so great as is commonly imagined. In the beginning of the sixteenth century, Spain was a very poor country, even in comparison with France, which has been so much improved since that time. It was the well known remark of the emperor Charles V. who had travelled so frequently through both countries, that every thing abounded in France, but that every thing was wanting in Spain. The increasing produce of the agriculture and manufactures of Europe must necessarily have required a gradual increase in the quantity of silver coin to circulate it; and the increasing number of wealthy individuals must have required the like increase in the quantity of their plate and other ornaments of silver.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that merchants often express dissatisfaction with the elevated wages of labour in Britain, citing this factor as a primary reason for their manufactured goods being undersold in international markets. Furthermore, they tend to remain silent regarding the substantial profits accrued from stock ownership. Moreover, they frequently lament the excessive gains garnered by others, yet they refrain from commenting on their own gains. In essence, the high profits derived from British stock may, in numerous instances, contribute equally, and in certain cases perhaps even more significantly, to the increased price of British manufactured goods, as compared to the high wages of British labour.
output: Our merchants frequently complain of the high wages of British labour, as the cause of their manufactures being undersold in foreign markets; but they are silent about the high profits of stock. They complain of the extravagant gain of other people; but they say nothing of their own. The high profits of British stock, however, may contribute towards raising the price of British manufactures, in many cases, as much, and in some perhaps more, than the high wages of British labour.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: The construction and upkeep of public works that support commerce, such as roads, bridges, navigable canals, and harbors, require varying levels of expense at different stages of societal development. This necessity is clear and does not require further explanation. The costs associated with building and maintaining public roads in a country will naturally increase in tandem with the annual yield of its land and labor, or with the volume and weight of goods that need to be transported on those roads. Similarly, the design of a bridge must accommodate the anticipated number and weight of vehicles that will use it. Furthermore, the depth and water supply of a navigable canal must be aligned with the expected tonnage of the vessels that will transport goods on it. Likewise, the size of a harbor should correspond to the number of ships likely to seek refuge within its confines.
output:
ARTICLE I. - Of the public Works and Institutions for facilitating the Commerce of the Society.

That the erection and maintenance of the public works which facilitate the commerce of any country, such as good roads, bridges, navigable canals, harbours, etc. must require very different degrees of expense in the different periods of society, is evident without any proof. The expense of making and maintaining the public roads of any country must evidently increase with the annual produce of the land and labour of that country, or with the quantity and weight of the goods which it becomes necessary to fetch and carry upon those roads. The strength of a bridge must be suited to the number and weight of the carriages which are likely to pass over it. The depth and the supply of water for a navigable canal must be proportioned to the number and tonnage of the lighters which are likely to carry goods upon it; the extent of a harbour, to the number of the shipping which are likely to take shelter in it.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: When a civilized nation relies on a militia for its defense, it remains perpetually vulnerable to conquest by any barbarous nation that may reside in its vicinity. The frequent conquests of various civilized countries in Asia by the Tartars sufficiently illustrate the inherent superiority that the militia of a barbarous nation possesses over that of a civilized one. Furthermore, a well-regulated standing army is superior to any militia. Such an army, which can be effectively maintained by a wealthy and civilized nation, is uniquely capable of defending that nation against the incursions of a poor and barbarous neighbor. Therefore, it is only through the establishment of a standing army that the civilization of any country can be sustained or even preserved for a significant duration.
output: When a civilized nation depends for its defence upon a militia, it is at all times exposed to be conquered by any barbarous nation which happens to be in its neighbourhood. The frequent conquests of all the civilized countries in Asia by the Tartars, sufficiently demonstrates the natural superiority which the militia of a barbarous has over that of a civilized nation. A well regulated standing army is superior to every militia. Such an army, as it can best be maintained by an opulent and civilized nation, so it can alone defend such a nation against the invasion of a poor and barbarous neighbour. It is only by means of a standing army, therefore, that the civilization of any country can be perpetuated, or even preserved, for any considerable time.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: It is perhaps impossible to determine the proportion that the circulating money of any country bears to the total value of the annual produce circulated by means of it. Different authors have calculated this proportion as one-fifth, one-tenth, one-twentieth, or one-thirtieth of that value. However, no matter how small the proportion of circulating money may be relative to the total value of annual produce, since only a part, and often a small part, of that produce is ever used to maintain industry, the circulating money must always represent a very considerable proportion of that part. Therefore, when the substitution of paper reduces the gold and silver required for circulation to perhaps one-fifth of the former quantity, if the value of even the greater part of the other four-fifths is added to the funds used to maintain industry, it must create a very considerable increase in the quantity of that industry and, consequently, in the value of the annual produce of land and labor.
output: What is the proportion which the circulating money of any country bears to the whole value of the annual produce circulated by means of it, it is perhaps impossible to determine. It has been computed by different authors at a fifth, at a tenth, at a twentieth, and at a thirtieth, part of that value. But how small soever the proportion which the circulating money may bear to the whole value of the annual produce, as but a part, and frequently but a small part, of that produce, is ever destined for the maintenance of industry, it must always bear a very considerable proportion to that part. When, therefore, by the substitution of paper, the gold and silver necessary for circulation is reduced to, perhaps, a fifth part of the former quantity, if the value of only the greater part of the other four-fifths be added to the funds which are destined for the maintenance of industry, it must make a very considerable addition to the quantity of that industry, and, consequently, to the value of the annual produce of land and labour.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: The occasional and temporary fluctuations in the market price of any commodity fall chiefly upon those parts of its price which resolve themselves into wages and profit. Additionally, that part which resolves itself into rent is less affected by them. Furthermore, a rent certain in money is not in the least affected by them, either in its rate or in its value. Moreover, a rent which consists either in a certain proportion, or in a certain quantity, of the rude produce, is no doubt affected in its yearly value by all the occasional and temporary fluctuations in the market price of that rude produce; but it is seldom affected by them in its yearly rate. In essence, in settling the terms of the lease, the landlord and farmer endeavour, according to their best judgment, to adjust that rate, not to the temporary and occasional, but to the average and ordinary price of the produce.

input: Moreover, the bounty awarded to the white-herring fishery is a tonnage-based bounty, and its allocation is determined by the ship's burden, rather than its diligence or success in the fishery. It is worth noting that, unfortunately, it has been a relatively common practice for vessels to be outfitted primarily for the purpose of obtaining the bounty, rather than actually catching fish. Furthermore, in the year 1759, when the bounty amounted to fifty shillings per ton, the entire buss fishery of Scotland yielded a mere four barrels of sea-sticks. Additionally, it is notable that, in that year, the cost to the government, in terms of bounties alone, was substantial, with each barrel of sea-sticks costing £113:15s, and each barrel of merchantable herrings costing £159:7:6.
output: Secondly, The bounty to the white-herring fishery is a tonnage bounty, and is proportioned to the burden of the ship, not to her diligence or success in the fishery; and it has, I am afraid, been too common for the vessels to fit out for the sole purpose of catching, not the fish but the bounty. In the year 1759, when the bounty was at fifty shillings the ton, the whole buss fishery of Scotland brought in only four barrels of sea-sticks. In that year, each barrel of sea-sticks cost government, in bounties alone, £113:15s.; each barrel of merchantable herrings £159:7:6.

author: Adam Smith

input: The monopoly of the home market benefits merchants and manufacturers to the greatest extent. This highlights the fact that the prohibition of importing foreign cattle and salt provisions, as well as the high duties on foreign corn, do not greatly advantage the graziers and farmers of Great Britain compared to the benefits that merchants and manufacturers receive from similar regulations. Manufactures, particularly finer ones, can be transported more easily between countries than corn or cattle, which is why foreign trade is primarily focused on the transportation of manufactures. This suggests that even a small advantage can allow foreign manufacturers to undercut domestic workmen in the home market. Ultimately, a significant advantage would be required for foreign producers to undersell domestic producers in the market for raw agricultural products. If foreign manufactures were allowed to be imported freely, it is likely that some domestic manufactures would suffer, potentially leading to the decline of certain industries, and forcing a portion of the capital and labor currently invested in them to seek alternative employment. In contrast, the free importation of raw agricultural products would not have a comparable impact on the country's agriculture.
output: Merchants and manufacturers are the people who derive the greatest advantage from this monopoly of the home market. The prohibition of the importation of foreign cattle and of salt provisions, together with the high duties upon foreign corn, which in times of moderate plenty amount to a prohibition, are not near so advantageous to the graziers and farmers of Great Britain, as other regulations of the same kind are to its merchants and manufacturers. Manufactures, those of the finer kind especially, are more easily transported from one country to another than corn or cattle. It is in the fetching and carrying manufactures, accordingly, that foreign trade is chiefly employed. In manufactures, a very small advantage will enable foreigners to undersell our own workmen, even in the home market. It will require a very great one to enable them to do so in the rude produce of the soil. If the free importation of foreign manufactures were permitted, several of the home manufactures would probably suffer, and some of them perhaps go to ruin altogether, and a considerable part of the stock and industry at present employed in them, would be forced to find out some other employment. But the freest importation of the rude produce of the soil could have no such effect upon the agriculture of the country.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: Additionally, one may assert that the widespread ignorance and lack of understanding that, within a civilized society, frequently paralyze the comprehension of individuals in the lower social strata is noteworthy. A person who does not appropriately utilize their intellectual faculties is, if anything, even more contemptible than a coward, as they appear to be mutilated and deformed in a fundamental aspect of human character. Even if the state were to gain no tangible benefits from the education of the lower classes, it remains essential that they are not left entirely uneducated. However, it is important to note that the state does indeed derive significant advantages from their education. The more individuals are educated, the less susceptible they become to the delusions of enthusiasm and superstition, which, in societies characterized by ignorance, often lead to catastrophic disruptions. Furthermore, an educated and informed populace tends to exhibit greater decorum and order than one marked by ignorance and folly. This enhanced sense of respectability fosters a greater likelihood of earning the respect of their legitimate superiors, which, in turn, encourages a greater willingness to honor those superiors. Additionally, educated individuals are more inclined to scrutinize and are better equipped to discern the self-serving grievances of factions and sedition, making them less prone to being misled into unnecessary opposition against governmental measures. In free societies, where the stability of government relies significantly on the favorable assessments that citizens form regarding its actions, it is indeed of utmost importance that they avoid making hasty or arbitrary judgments about it.
output: The same thing may be said of the gross ignorance and stupidity which, in a civilized society, seem so frequently to benumb the understandings of all the inferior ranks of people. A man without the proper use of the intellectual faculties of a man, is, if possible, more contemptible than even a coward, and seems to be mutilated and deformed in a still more essential part of the character of human nature. Though the state was to derive no advantage from the instruction of the inferior ranks of people, it would still deserve its attention that they should not be altogether uninstructed. The state, however, derives no inconsiderable advantage from their instruction. The more they are instructed, the less liable they are to the delusions of enthusiasm and superstition, which, among ignorant nations frequently occasion the most dreadful disorders. An instructed and intelligent people, besides, are always more decent and orderly than an ignorant and stupid one. They feel themselves, each individually, more respectable, and more likely to obtain the respect of their lawful superiors, and they are, therefore, more disposed to respect those superiors. They are more disposed to examine, and more capable of seeing through, the interested complaints of faction and sedition; and they are, upon that account, less apt to be misled into any wanton or unnecessary opposition to the measures of government. In free countries, where the safety of government depends very much upon the favourable judgment which the people may form of its conduct, it must surely be of the highest importance, that they should not be disposed to judge rashly or capriciously concerning it.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: The historical policy in Europe aimed to manage agriculture, which was a significant sector, using principles distinct from those applied to manufacturing, which was primarily associated with urban areas. By restricting farmers to selling only to consumers or their immediate intermediaries, such as grain merchants and carriers, the policy sought to compel farmers to take on the roles of both producer and grain retailer. Conversely, in many instances, it restricted manufacturers from engaging in retail activities or selling their products directly to consumers. This approach aimed to serve the broader interest of the country, particularly by making grain more affordable, although the mechanisms for achieving this may not have been clearly understood. In contrast, the policy also aimed to protect the interests of shopkeepers, as it was believed that allowing manufacturers to sell directly would significantly undermine the shopkeeper's business, potentially leading to their decline.
output: The ancient policy of Europe endeavoured, in this manner, to regulate agriculture, the great trade of the country, by maxims quite different from those which it established with regard to manufactures, the great trade of the towns. By leaving a farmer no other customers but either the consumers or their immediate factors, the kidders and carriers of corn, it endeavoured to force him to exercise the trade, not only of a farmer, but of a corn merchant, or corn retailer. On the contrary, it, in many cases, prohibited the manufacturer from exercising the trade of a shopkeeper, or from selling his own goods by retail. It meant, by the one law, to promote the general interest of the country, or to render corn cheap, without, perhaps, its being well understood how this was to be done. By the other, it meant to promote that of a particular order of men, the shopkeepers, who would be so much undersold by the manufacturer, it was supposed, that their trade would be ruined, if he was allowed to retail at all.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: A similar observation applies to the drawbacks upon the re-exportation of imported foreign goods, which in Great Britain generally constitute by far the largest portion of the duty upon importation. Under the second of the rules annexed to the act of parliament that imposed what is now called the old subsidy, every merchant, whether English or foreign, was permitted to draw back half of that duty upon exportation. The English merchant could do so provided the exportation occurred within twelve months, while the foreign merchant was required to complete it within nine months. Wines, currants, and wrought silks were the only goods excluded from this rule, as they received other and more favorable allowances. At that time, the duties imposed by this act of parliament were the only duties upon the importation of foreign goods. The period within which this and all other drawbacks could be claimed was later extended to three years by 7 Geo. I. chap. 21. sect. 10.
output: The same thing may be said of the drawbacks upon the re-exportation of foreign goods imported, which, in Great Britain, generally amount to by much the largest part of the duty upon importation. By the second of the rules, annexed to the act of parliament, which imposed what is now called the old subsidy, every merchant, whether English or alien. was allowed to draw back half that duty upon exportation; the English merchant, provided the exportation took place within twelve months; the alien, provided it took place within nine months. Wines, currants, and wrought silks, were the only goods which did not fall within this rule, having other and more advantageous allowances. The duties imposed by this act of parliament were, at that time, the only duties upon the importation of foreign goods. The term within which this, and all other drawbacks could be claimed, was afterwards (by 7 Geo. I. chap. 21. sect. 10.) extended to three years.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input:
In the past, when large landed estates operated like principalities, the concept of entails may have seemed reasonable. Similar to the fundamental laws of certain monarchies, they could prevent the interests of many from being jeopardized by the whims or excesses of a single individual. However, in today's Europe, where both small and large estates find their security in national laws, the notion of entails appears entirely absurd. This idea is based on the flawed assumption that each subsequent generation does not possess an equal right to the land and its resources. Instead, it suggests that the property of the current generation should be governed by the preferences of those who may have died centuries ago.

Despite their absurdity, entails continue to be upheld across much of Europe, particularly in regions where noble birth is required for holding civil or military honors. They are regarded as essential for preserving the exclusive privileges of the nobility concerning high offices and honors. Given that this social class has already gained an unjust advantage over other citizens, it is deemed reasonable to grant them another to prevent their status from appearing ludicrous due to poverty. In England, the common law is said to reject perpetuities, resulting in stricter limitations compared to other European monarchies; nevertheless, England is not entirely free from them. In Scotland, it is estimated that more than one-fifth, and perhaps even more than one-third, of all land is currently subject to strict entail.
output: When great landed estates were a sort of principalities, entails might not be unreasonable. Like what are called the fundamental laws of some monarchies, they might frequently hinder the security of thousands from being endangered by the caprice or extravagance of one man. But in the present state of Europe, when small as well as great estates derive their security from the laws of their country, nothing can be more completely absurd. They are founded upon the most absurd of all suppositions, the supposition that every successive generation of men have not an equal right to the earth, and to all that it possesses; but that the property of the present generation should be restrained and regulated according to the fancy of those who died, perhaps five hundred years ago. Entails, however, are still respected, through the greater part of Europe; In those countries, particularly, in which noble birth is a necessary qualification for the enjoyment either of civil or military honours. Entails are thought necessary for maintaining this exclusive privilege of the nobility to the great offices and honours of their country; and that order having usurped one unjust advantage over the rest of their fellow-citizens, lest their poverty should render it ridiculous, it is thought reasonable that they should have another. The common law of England, indeed, is said to abhor perpetuities, and they are accordingly more restricted there than in any other European monarchy; though even England is not altogether without them. In Scotland, more than one fifth, perhaps more than one third part of the whole lands in the country, are at present supposed to be under strict entail.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: Successive reductions of the tax may not completely prevent the increase in the value of silver in the European market, but they are likely to slow it down to some extent. As a result of these tax reductions, it is possible that many mines can be operated that were previously unviable due to the older tax burden, and this could lead to an increase in the annual supply of silver. Consequently, the value of a given quantity of silver might be somewhat lower than it would have been otherwise. Following the reduction in 1736, the value of silver in the European market may not be lower than it was before, but it is likely at least ten percent lower than it would have been if Spain had maintained the old tax. Despite this reduction, I suspect that the value of silver has shown some signs of rising in the European market during this century, although my confidence in this observation is tentative. The increase, if it exists, has been so minimal that many might find it uncertain whether a rise has actually occurred or if the value might still be declining in the European market. In summary, the situation regarding the value of silver remains somewhat ambiguous.
output: Such successive reductions of the tax, however, though they may not prevent altogether, must certainly retard, more or less, the rise of the value of silver in the European market. In consequence of such reductions, many mines may be wrought which could not be wrought before, because they could not afford to pay the old tax; and the quantity of silver annually brought to market, must always be somewhat greater, and, therefore, the value of any given quantity somewhat less, than it otherwise would have been. In consequence of the reduction in 1736, the value of silver in the European market, though it may not at this day be lower than before that reduction, is, probably, at least ten per cent. lower than it would have been, had the court of Spain continued to exact the old tax. That, notwithstanding this reduction, the value of silver has, during the course of the present century, begun to rise somewhat in the European market, the facts and arguments which have been alleged above, dispose me to believe, or more properly to suspect and conjecture; for the best opinion which I can form upon this subject, scarce, perhaps, deserves the name of belief. The rise, indeed, supposing there has been any, has hitherto been so very small, that after all that has been said, it may, perhaps, appear to many people uncertain, not only whether this event has actually taken place, but whether the contrary may not have taken place, or whether the value of silver may not still continue to fall in the European market.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input:
The thirteenth statute of the current monarch, circa 43, appears to have instituted a new system concerning the corn laws, which is, in many respects, an improvement over the previous framework; however, in one or two aspects, it may not be entirely as favorable. 

By means of this legislation, the elevated duties imposed on the importation for domestic consumption are eliminated as soon as the price of middling wheat ascends to 48 shillings per quarter; the price for middling rye, peas, or beans reaches 32 shillings; the price for barley attains 24 shillings; and the price for oats rises to 16 shillings. In place of these high duties, a nominal duty of merely 6 pence per quarter is established for wheat, which is similarly applied to other grains in proportion. Consequently, concerning all varieties of grain, particularly wheat, the domestic market is effectively opened to foreign supplies at prices significantly lower than previously.
output:
The 13th of the present king, c. 43, seems to have established a new system with regard to the corn laws, in many respects better than the ancient one, but in one or two respects perhaps not quite so good.

By this statute, the high duties upon importation for home consumption are taken off, so soon as the price of middling wheat rises to 48s. the quarter; that of middling rye, pease, or beans, to 32s.; that of barley to 24s.; and that of oats to 16s.; and instead of them, a small duty is imposed of only 6d upon the quarter of wheat, and upon that or other grain in proportion. With regard to all those different sorts of grain, but particularly with regard to wheat, the home market is thus opened to foreign supplies, at prices considerably lower than before.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: Insofar as it is utilized in the second manner, it fosters industry; and although it enhances the consumption of society, it establishes a sustainable fund for sustaining that consumption. The individuals who engage in consumption regenerate, with a profit, the complete value of their annual consumption. The total revenue of society, which encompasses the annual output of both land and labor, is augmented by the entirety of the value that the labor of these workers contributes to the materials on which they are engaged. Furthermore, their net revenue is determined by the residual value that remains after accounting for the necessary expenses associated with maintaining the tools and instruments pertinent to their trade.
output: So far as it is employed in the second way, it promotes industry; and though it increases the consumption of the society, it provides a permanent fund for supporting that consumption; the people who consume reproducing, with a profit, the whole value of their annual consumption. The gross revenue of the society, the annual produce of their land and labour, is increased by the whole value which the labour of those workmen adds to the materials upon which they are employed, and their neat revenue by what remains of this value, after deducting what is necessary for supporting the tools and instruments of their trade.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: Old statutes from the reigns of Edward III, Henry VIII, and Edward VI prohibited the exportation of all metals. The only exceptions were lead and tin, likely due to the significant quantity of these metals available. At that time, a considerable portion of the kingdom's trade relied on their exportation. To support the mining industry, the 5th of William and Mary, chapter 17, lifted this prohibition for iron, copper, and mundic metal produced from British ore. Later, the 9th and 10th of William III, chapter 26, allowed the exportation of all types of copper bars, both foreign and British. However, the exportation of unmanufactured brass, gun-metal, bell-metal, and shroff metal remains prohibited. Conversely, brass products of all kinds may be exported without duty.
output: By some old statutes of Edward III, Henry VIII. and Edward VI. the exportation of all metals was prohibited. Lead and tin were alone excepted, probably on account of the great abundance of those metals; in the exportation of which a considerable part of the trade of the kingdom in those days consisted. For the encouragement of the mining trade, the 5th of William and Mary, chap.17, exempted from this prohibition iron, copper, and mundic metal made from British ore. The exportation of all sorts of copper bars, foreign as well as British, was afterwards permitted by the 9th and 10th of William III. chap 26. The exportation of unmanufactured brass, of what is called gun-metal, bell-metal, and shroff metal, still continues to be prohibited. Brass manufactures of all sorts may be exported duty free.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input:
Whatever factors may lead a certain number of students to attend a particular college or university, regardless of the merit or reputation of the teachers, can often tend to reduce the importance of that merit or reputation.

The privileges available to graduates in arts, law, medicine, and divinity, when they can be obtained only by residing for a certain number of years at certain universities, may necessarily compel a certain number of students to attend those universities, independent of the merit or reputation of the teachers. These graduate privileges can be seen as a kind of apprenticeship statute, and they have arguably contributed to the improvement of education in much the same way that other apprenticeship statutes have contributed to the improvement of arts and manufactures. In short, requirements and privileges that draw students to particular institutions regardless of teaching quality can tend to lessen the pressure on those institutions to earn their reputation through merit.
output:
Whatever forces a certain number of students to any college or university, independent of the merit or reputation of the teachers, tends more or less to diminish the necessity of that merit or reputation.

The privileges of graduates in arts, in law, physic, and divinity, when they can be obtained only by residing a certain number of years in certain universities, necessarily force a certain number of students to such universities, independent of the merit or reputation of the teachers. The privileges of graduates are a sort of statutes of apprenticeship, which have contributed to the improvement of education just as the other statutes of apprenticeship have to that of arts and manufactures.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: It may be necessary to allow towns that were permitted to manage their own revenues some form of compulsory jurisdiction to ensure that their citizens make payments. During those chaotic times, it could have been very inconvenient for them to pursue such justice through other tribunals. However, it is remarkable that the sovereigns of various European countries would agree to exchange a certain rent for a portion of their revenue that had the potential for natural growth without incurring additional costs or requiring their attention. Furthermore, they voluntarily established a kind of independent republic within their own territories.
output: It might, probably, be necessary to grant to such towns as were admitted to farm their own revenues, some sort of compulsive jurisdiction to oblige their own citizens to make payment. In those disorderly times, it might have been extremely inconvenient to have left them to seek this sort of justice from any other tribunal. But it must seem extraordinary, that the sovereigns of all the different countries of Europe should have exchanged in this manner for a rent certain, never more to be augmented, that branch of their revenue, which was, perhaps, of all others, the most likely to be improved by the natural course of things, without either expense or attention of their own; and that they should, besides, have in this manner voluntarily erected a sort of independent republics in the heart of their own dominions.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: It is rare for the individual who cultivates the land to have the necessary resources to support themselves until they gather the harvest. Typically, their maintenance is provided by a master, namely the farmer who hires them, who would not have a motivation to employ them unless they were to receive a portion of the produce of their labor. Additionally, the farmer's stock would need to be replenished with a profit, which is a key consideration. Moreover, this profit constitutes a secondary reduction from the produce of the labor that is utilized on the land.
output: It seldom happens that the person who tills the ground has wherewithal to maintain himself till he reaps the harvest. His maintenance is generally advanced to him from the stock of a master, the farmer who employs him, and who would have no interest to employ him, unless he was to share in the produce of his labour, or unless his stock was to be replaced to him with a profit. This profit makes a second deduction from the produce of the labour which is employed upon land.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

These prices are not recorded on account of their extraordinary dearness or cheapness, but are mentioned incidentally, as the prices actually paid for large quantities of grain consumed at a feast, which was famous for its magnificence.

In 1262, being the fifty-first year of Henry III, an ancient statute called the assize of bread and ale was revived, which, the king states in the preamble, had been made in the times of his progenitors, some time kings of England. It is probable, therefore, that it was at least as old as the time of his grandfather, Henry II, and it may have been as old as the Conquest. It regulates the price of bread according as the prices of wheat may happen to be, from one shilling to twenty shillings the quarter of the money of those times. However, statutes of this kind are generally presumed to provide with equal care for all deviations from the middle price, for those below it as well as for those above it. Ten shillings, therefore, containing six ounces of silver, Tower weight, and equal to about thirty shillings of our present money, must, upon this supposition, have been reckoned the middle price of the quarter of wheat when this statute was first enacted, and must have continued to be so in the fifty-first year of Henry III. We cannot, therefore, be very wrong in supposing that the middle price was not less than one-third of the highest price at which this statute regulates the price of bread, or than six shillings and eightpence of the money of those times, containing four ounces of silver, Tower weight.
