input: It is possible that if the parliament of Great Britain were to gain the right to tax the colonies without their consent, the significance of the colonial assemblies might be greatly diminished, which could, in turn, affect the influence of the leading men in British America. Many individuals tend to seek a role in managing public affairs because it can often provide them with a sense of importance. The stability of a system of free government may depend on the ability of leading men, who can be considered the natural aristocracy, to maintain or protect their own importance. In many countries, including America, leading men can be motivated to preserve their own influence, and they may perceive threats to their importance as a reason to take action. The leading men in America, like their counterparts elsewhere, may feel that if their assemblies were to become subordinate to the parliament of Great Britain, they would likely lose a significant amount of their own importance. As a result, they may have chosen to reject the proposal of being taxed by parliamentary requisition, opting instead to take a stronger stance in defense of their own influence. In summary, the potential loss of importance and influence for the leading men in British America may have been a key factor in their decision to resist parliamentary taxation.
output: Should the parliament of Great Britain, at the same time, be ever fully established in the right of taxing the colonies, even independent of the consent of their own assemblies, the importance of those assemblies would, from that moment, be at an end, and with it, that of all the leading men of British America. Men desire to have some share in the management of public affairs, chiefly on account of the importance which it gives them. Upon the power which the greater part of the leading men, the natural aristocracy of every country, have of preserving or defending their respective importance, depends the stability and duration of every system of free government. In the attacks which those leading men are continually making upon the importance of one another, and in the defence of their own, consists the whole play of domestic faction and ambition. The leading men of America, like those of all other countries, desire to preserve their own importance. They feel, or imagine, that if their assemblies, which they are fond of calling parliaments, and of considering as equal in authority to the parliament of Great Britain, should be so far degraded as to become the humble ministers and executive officers of that parliament, the greater part of their own importance would be at an end. They have rejected, therefore, the proposal of being taxed by parliamentary requisition, and, like other ambitious and high-spirited men, have rather chosen to draw the sword in defence of their own importance.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: In Holland, the taxes levied on male and female servants are based on expenses rather than on property. This structure makes them similar to taxes on consumable goods. Similarly, the recent tax of a guinea per man-servant introduced in Great Britain falls into this category. This tax disproportionately impacts the middle class. For instance, a person with an income of two hundred pounds per year may afford to employ one man-servant, while an individual with an income of ten thousand pounds per year is unlikely to hire fifty. This tax does not significantly affect those who are impoverished.
output: The taxes which in Holland are imposed upon men and maid servants, are taxes, not upon stock, but upon expense; and so far resemble the taxes upon consumable commodities. The tax of a guinea a-head for every man-servant, which has lately been imposed in Great Britain, is of the same kind. It falls heaviest upon the middling rank. A man of two hundred a-year may keep a single man-servant. A man of ten thousand a-year will not keep fifty. It does not affect the poor.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: Moreover, when infrastructure such as highways, bridges, and canals is constructed and maintained by the commercial activities that utilize them, it is likely that they will be established only in locations where they are necessitated by commerce, and, consequently, where their construction is warranted. Additionally, the expenditure, scale, and grandeur of these infrastructure projects must be commensurate with the financial resources that commerce can allocate to them. In essence, they must be designed and constructed in a manner that is appropriate, given the commercial context in which they operate. Furthermore, it is not feasible to construct a magnificent highway through a sparsely populated or desert region, where commercial activity is limited or nonexistent, merely to provide access to a provincial administrator's country estate or to curry favor with a prominent nobleman. It is worth noting that a substantial bridge cannot be built over a river at a location where there is minimal traffic or solely to enhance the aesthetic appeal of the surrounding landscape, as viewed from a nearby palace, which can occur in countries where such projects are funded by revenue sources unrelated to their own operational capabilities.
output: When high-roads, bridges, canals, etc. are in this manner made and supported by the commerce which is carried on by means of them, they can be made only where that commerce requires them, and, consequently, where it is proper to make them. Their expense, too, their grandeur and magnificence, must be suited to what that commerce can afford to pay. They must be made, consequently, as it is proper to make them. A magnificent high-road cannot be made through a desert country, where there is little or no commerce, or merely because it happens to lead to the country villa of the intendant of the province, or to that of some great lord, to whom the intendant finds it convenient to make his court. A great bridge cannot be thrown over a river at a place where nobody passes, or merely to embellish the view from the windows of a neighbouring palace; things which sometimes happen in countries, where works of this kind are carried on by any other revenue than that which they themselves are capable of affording.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: The expenditure on durable goods is beneficial not only for saving but also for self-discipline. If an individual overspends in this area, they can easily adjust their spending habits without attracting public scrutiny. However, significantly reducing one's household staff, shifting from lavish meals to simpler ones, or abandoning a previously established lifestyle are changes that are likely to be noticed by neighbors and may suggest previous financial mismanagement. Consequently, those who have previously overspent in these areas often lack the resolve to change until they face financial ruin or bankruptcy. In contrast, if an individual has overspent on items like construction, furnishings, books, or artwork, changing spending patterns does not imply imprudence. This is because existing investments in these areas can often negate the need for further expenditures. When a person decides to spend less, it appears to be a matter of personal preference rather than a reflection of financial limitations.
output: The expense, too, which is laid out in durable commodities, is favourable not only to accumulation, but to frugality. If a person should at any time exceed in it, he can easily reform without exposing himself to the censure of the public. To reduce very much the number of his servants, to reform his table from great profusion to great frugality, to lay down his equipage after he has once set it up, are changes which cannot escape the observation of his neighbours, and which are supposed to imply some acknowledgment of preceding bad conduct. Few, therefore, of those who have once been so unfortunate as to launch out too far into this sort of expense, have afterwards the courage to reform, till ruin and bankruptcy oblige them. But if a person has, at any time, been at too great an expense in building, in furniture, in books, or pictures, no imprudence can be inferred from his changing his conduct. These are things in which further expense is frequently rendered unnecessary by former expense; and when a person stops short, he appears to do so, not because he has exceeded his fortune, but because he has satisfied his fancy.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input:
Through such measures, the currency of, I believe, all nations has been progressively diminished in value, with the same nominal amount increasingly representing a lesser quantity of silver. 

Furthermore, nations have occasionally resorted to altering the quality of their coin in order to achieve similar objectives; this involves incorporating a higher proportion of alloy. For instance, if one pound of our silver currency contained, instead of the current standard of eighteen pennyweights, eight ounces of alloy, then a pound sterling, or twenty shillings of such currency, would hold a value not significantly exceeding six shillings and eightpence in our present monetary system. Consequently, the amount of silver represented by six shillings and eightpence would nearly align with the value of a pound sterling. The adulteration of the standard produces effects identical to what the French term an augmentation, or a direct increase in the denomination of the coin.
output:
By means of such expedients, the coin of, I believe, all nations, has been gradually reduced more and more below its original value, and the same nominal sum has been gradually brought to contain a smaller and a smaller quantity of silver.

Nations have sometimes, for the same purpose, adulterated the standard of their coin; that is, have mixed a greater quantity of alloy in it. If in the pound weight of our silver coin, for example, instead of eighteen penny-weight, according to the present standard, there were mixed eight ounces of alloy; a pound sterling, or twenty shillings of such coin, would be worth little more than six shillings and eightpence of our present money. The quantity of silver contained in six shillings and eightpence of our present money, would thus be raised very nearly to the denomination of a pound sterling. The adulteration of the standard has exactly the same effect with what the French call an augmentation, or a direct raising of the denomination of the coin.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: The occasional fluctuations in the market price of gold and silver bullion arise from the same causes as similar fluctuations in the price of all other commodities. In countries that possess no mines of their own, the frequent loss of these metals from various accidents by sea and by land, along with their continual waste in gilding and plating, in lace and embroidery, in the wear and tear of coin, and in that of plate, requires a continual importation to repair this loss and waste. We may believe that merchant importers, like all other merchants, endeavour as well as they can to suit their occasional importations to what they judge is likely to be the immediate demand. With all their attention, however, they sometimes overdo the business and sometimes underdo it. When they import more bullion than is wanted, rather than incur the risk and trouble of exporting it again, they are sometimes willing to sell a part of it for something less than the ordinary or average price. When, on the other hand, they import less than is wanted, they get something more than this price. But when, under all those occasional fluctuations, the market price of either gold or silver bullion continues for several years together steadily and constantly, either more or less above or more or less below the mint price, we may be assured that this steady and constant superiority or inferiority of price is the effect of something in the state of the coin which at that time renders a certain quantity of coin either of more value or of less value than the precise quantity of bullion it ought to contain. This highlights that the constancy and steadiness of the effect supposes a proportionable constancy and steadiness in the cause.
output: The occasional fluctuations in the market price of gold and silver bullion arise from the same causes as the like fluctuations in that of all other commodities. The frequent loss of those metals from various accidents by sea and by land, the continual waste of them in gilding and plating, in lace and embroidery, in the wear and tear of coin, and in that of plate, require, in all countries which possess no mines of their own, a continual importation, in order to repair this loss and this waste. The merchant importers, like all other merchants, we may believe, endeavour, as well as they can, to suit their occasional importations to what they judge is likely to be the immediate demand. With all their attention, however, they sometimes overdo the business, and sometimes underdo it. When they import more bullion than is wanted, rather than incur the risk and trouble of exporting it again, they are sometimes willing to sell a part of it for something less than the ordinary or average price. When, on the other hand, they import less than is wanted, they get something more than this price. But when, under all those occasional fluctuations, the market price either of gold or silver bullion continues for several years together steadily and constantly, either more or less above, or more or less below the mint price, we may be assured that this steady and constant, either superiority or inferiority of price, is the effect of something in the state of the coin, which, at that time, renders a certain quantity of coin either of more value or of less value than the precise quantity of bullion which it ought to contain. The constancy and steadiness of the effect supposes a proportionable constancy and steadiness in the cause.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: Additionally, when a fixed sum of money is paid in lieu of a proportion of the land's produce or the price of a certain portion, as full compensation for all tax or tythe, the tax in question assumes a nature identical to that of the land tax in England. Moreover, it neither increases nor decreases in conjunction with the rent of the land, and it neither promotes nor hinders improvement. In essence, the tythe in a significant number of parishes that pay a modus, in place of all other tythe, is a tax of this type. Furthermore, during the Mahometan government of Bengal, a modus, reportedly a moderate one, was established in a large portion of the districts or zemindaries, in lieu of the payment in kind of the fifth part of the produce. It is worth noting that some servants of the East India company, under the pretext of restoring the public revenue to its former value, have exchanged this modus for a payment in kind in certain provinces. Moreover, under their management, this alteration is likely to discourage cultivation and provide new opportunities for abuse in the collection of the public revenue, which has declined substantially from its initial value when it first came under the company's management. Additionally, while the servants of the company may have benefited from this change, it is probable that this has occurred at the expense of both their employers and the country as a whole.
output: When, instead either of a certain portion of the produce of land, or of the price of a certain portion, a certain sum of money is to be paid in full compensation for all tax or tythe; the tax becomes, in this case, exactly of the same nature with the land tax of England. It neither rises nor falls with the rent of the land. It neither encourages nor discourages improvement. The tythe in the greater part of those parishes which pay what is called a modus, in lieu of all other tythe is a tax of this kind. During the Mahometan government of Bengal, instead of the payment in kind of the fifth part of the produce, a modus, and, it is said, a very moderate one, was established in the greater part of the districts or zemindaries of the country. Some of the servants of the East India company, under pretence of restoring the public revenue to its proper value, have, in some provinces, exchanged this modus for a payment in kind. Under their management, this change is likely both to discourage cultivation, and to give new opportunities for abuse in the collection of the public revenue, which has fallen very much below what it was said to have been when it first fell under the management of the company. The servants of the company may, perhaps, have profited by the change, but at the expense, it is probable, both of their masters and of the country.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: Nations that are relatively advanced in skill, dexterity, and judgment in labor application have adopted various approaches to its overall management. These approaches have not all yielded equally favorable outcomes for productivity. The policies of some nations have provided significant support for national industry, while those of others have favored urban industry. Few nations have treated all forms of industry with equal fairness and impartiality. Since the fall of the Roman Empire, European policy has become more supportive of the arts, manufacturing, and commerce—reflecting a preference for urban industry over agriculture, which represents rural industry. The factors that appear to have led to this established policy are elaborated upon in the third book.
output: Nations tolerably well advanced as to skill, dexterity, and judgment, in the application of labour, have followed very different plans in the general conduct or direction of it; and those plans have not all been equally favourable to the greatness of its produce. The policy of some nations has given extraordinary encouragement to the industry of the country; that of others to the industry of towns. Scarce any nation has dealt equally and impartially with every sort of industry. Since the down-fall of the Roman empire, the policy of Europe has been more favourable to arts, manufactures, and commerce, the industry of towns, than to agriculture, the Industry of the country. The circumstances which seem to have introduced and established this policy are explained in the third book.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input:
His sacred royal majesty of Portugal pledges, both in his own name and on behalf of his successors, to permit the importation of woollen cloths and other woollen products from Britain into Portugal indefinitely, as was previously customary prior to their prohibition by law; however, this commitment is contingent upon the following condition:

In essence, her sacred royal majesty of Great Britain shall, in her own name and on behalf of her successors, be obligated, for all time henceforth, to allow the entry of wines produced in Portugal into Britain. Therefore, under no circumstances, whether at times of peace or conflict between Britain and France, shall there be any additional demands made for these wines, whether referred to as customs or duties, or by any other designation, either directly or indirectly. This stipulation applies whether the wines are imported into Great Britain in pipes, hogsheads, or other containers, and shall be limited to the same rate applied to a comparable quantity of French wine, with a deduction of one-third of the applicable customs or duties. Furthermore, should there be any attempt to hinder or infringe upon this stipulated deduction of customs at any point, it shall be deemed just and lawful for his sacred royal majesty of Portugal to reinstate the prohibition on woollen cloths and other woollen products from Britain.
output:
ART. I. His sacred royal majesty of Portugal promises, both in his own name and that of his successors, to admit for ever hereafter, into Portugal, the woollen cloths, and the rest of the woollen manufactures of the British, as was accustomed, till they were prohibited by the law; nevertheless upon this condition:

ART. II. That is to say, that her sacred royal majesty of Great Britain shall, in her own name, and that of her successors, be obliged, for ever hereafter, to admit the wines of the growth of Portugal into Britain; so that at no time, whether there shall be peace or war between the kingdoms of Britain and France, any thing more shall be demanded for these wines by the name of custom or duty, or by whatsoever other title, directly or indirectly, whether they shall be imported into Great Britain in pipes or hogsheads, or other casks, than what shall be demanded for the like quantity or measure of French wine, deducting or abating a third part of the custom or duty. But if, at any time, this deduction or abatement of customs, which is to be made as aforesaid, shall in any manner be attempted and prejudiced, it shall be just and lawful for his sacred royal majesty of Portugal, again to prohibit the woollen cloths, and the rest of the British woollen manufactures.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that the ordinary market price of land is dependent upon the ordinary market rate of interest. Furthermore, an individual who possesses a capital and desires to derive a revenue from it, without personally employing it, will consider whether to invest in land or lend it at interest. Moreover, the superior security associated with land, combined with other advantages that typically accompany this type of property, will generally lead the individual to be satisfied with a relatively smaller revenue from land compared to what could be obtained through lending money at interest. In essence, these advantages are sufficient to offset a certain difference in revenue, but they will only compensate for a limited difference. It is worth noting that if the rent of land were to fall short of the interest on money by a more significant difference, nobody would purchase land, which would subsequently lead to a reduction in its ordinary price. On the other hand, if the advantages were to more than compensate for the difference, everyone would buy land, resulting in an increase in its ordinary price. Moreover, historical data indicates that when interest rates were at ten percent, land was typically sold for ten or twelve years' purchase. As interest rates declined to six, five, and four percent, the price of land increased to twenty, twenty-five, and thirty years' purchase. Additionally, the market rate of interest is higher in France than in England, and consequently, the common price of land is lower in France. In England, land commonly sells for thirty years' purchase, whereas in France it sells for twenty years' purchase.
output: The ordinary market price of land, it is to be observed, depends everywhere upon the ordinary market rate of interest. The person who has a capital from which he wishes to derive a revenue, without taking the trouble to employ it himself, deliberates whether he should buy land with it, or lend it out at interest. The superior security of land, together with some other advantages which almost everywhere attend upon this species of property, will generally dispose him to content himself with a smaller revenue from land, than what he might have by lending out his money at interest. These advantages are sufficient to compensate a certain difference of revenue; but they will compensate a certain difference only; and if the rent of land should fall short of the interest of money by a greater difference, nobody would buy land, which would soon reduce its ordinary price. On the contrary, if the advantages should much more than compensate the difference, everybody would buy land, which again would soon raise its ordinary price. When interest was at ten per cent. land was commonly sold for ten or twelve years purchase. As interest sunk to six, five, and four per cent. the price of land rose to twenty, five-and-twenty, and thirty years purchase. The market rate of interest is higher in France than in England, and the common price of land is lower. In England it commonly sells at thirty, in France at twenty years purchase.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: In the province of Holland, according to the Memoires concernant les Droits, etc. (p. 223), every house is taxed at two and a half per cent of its value, without regard either to the rent it actually pays or to whether it is tenanted or untenanted. There can seem to be a hardship in requiring the proprietor to pay a tax on an untenanted house from which he can derive no revenue, especially when the tax is so heavy. In Holland, where the market rate of interest does not exceed three per cent, a tax of two and a half per cent on the whole value of the house may often amount to more than a third of the building rent, and perhaps of the whole rent. The valuation by which houses are rated, though it tends to be very unequal, is said always to be below the real value. When a house is rebuilt, improved, or enlarged, a new valuation is made and the tax is set accordingly. Overall, the tax appears to place a potentially significant burden on owners, particularly when a property is left untenanted.
output: In the province of Holland, {Memoires concernant les Droits, etc. p. 223.} every house is taxed at two and a-half per cent. of its value, without any regard, either to the rent which it actually pays, or to the circumstance of its being tenanted or untenanted. There seems to be a hardship in obliging the proprietor to pay a tax for an untenanted house, from which he can derive no revenue, especially so very heavy a tax. In Holland, where the market rate of interest does not exceed three per cent., two and a-half per cent. upon the whole value of the house must, in most cases, amount to more than a third of the building-rent, perhaps of the whole rent. The valuation, indeed, according to which the houses are rated, though very unequal, is said to be always below the real value. When a house is rebuilt, improved, or enlarged, there is a new valuation, and the tax is rated accordingly.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input:
In certain countries, additional taxes are imposed on the profits of stock, depending on the specific industry or sector in which they are utilized. Additionally, these taxes can be applied to agricultural activities. 

Examples of such taxes can be found in England, where taxes are levied on hawkers and pedlars, as well as on hackney-coaches and chairs. Furthermore, the keepers of ale-houses are required to pay a licence fee in order to retail ale and spiritous liquors. Meanwhile, during a recent period of conflict, a proposal was put forth for a similar tax on shops. The rationale behind this proposal was that the war was being fought, in part, to protect the country's trade interests, and therefore, the merchants who stood to benefit from it should contribute to its financial support.
output:
In some countries, extraordinary taxes are imposed upon the profits of stock; sometimes when employed in particular branches of trade, and sometimes when employed in agriculture.

Of the former kind, are in England, the tax upon hawkers and pedlars, that upon hackney-coaches and chairs, and that which the keepers of ale-houses pay for a licence to retail ale and spiritous liquors. During the late war, another tax of the same kind was proposed upon shops. The war having been undertaken, it was said, in defence of the trade of the country, the merchants, who were to profit by it, ought to contribute towards the support of it.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input:
Some ancient statutes of assize were inaccurately transcribed, leading to misunderstandings. This suggests that the careless work of some copyists, as well as potential errors in legislative composition, contributed to these misconceptions.

For example, in the statute regarding the price of bread from the 51st year of Henry III, the price of bread was supposed to vary based on wheat prices, which ranged from one shilling to twenty shillings per quarter. However, the manuscripts used to produce various editions of the statutes, prior to Mr. Ruffhead's edition, only recorded the price up to twelve shillings. Consequently, several authors, influenced by this incorrect transcription, mistakenly concluded that the average price of wheat during that period was six shillings per quarter, roughly equivalent to eighteen shillings today.
output:
Secondly, they have been misled by the slovenly manner in which some ancient statutes of assize had been sometimes transcribed by lazy copiers, and sometimes, perhaps, actually composed by the legislature.

Thus, in the assize of bread and ale, of the 51st of Henry III. the price of bread was regulated according to the different prices of wheat, from one shilling to twenty shillings the quarter of the money of those times. But in the manuscripts from which all the different editions of the statutes, preceding that of Mr Ruffhead, were printed, the copiers had never transcribed this regulation beyond the price of twelve shillings. Several writers, therefore, being misled by this faulty transcription, very naturally conclude that the middle price, or six shillings the quarter, equal to about eighteen shillings of our present money, was the ordinary or average price of wheat at that time.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input:
Joint-stock companies, established either by royal charter or by act of parliament, differ in several respects not only from regulated companies but also from private copartneries.

First, in a private copartnery, no partner may transfer a share to another person or introduce a new member without the consent of the company. Each member, however, may withdraw from the copartnery upon proper notice and demand payment of a share of the common stock. In a joint-stock company, by contrast, no member may demand payment of a share from the company, but each member may transfer a share to another person without consent and thereby introduce a new member. The value of a share in a joint stock is always the price it will bring in the market, and this price may be greater or less, in any proportion, than the sum for which its owner stands credited in the stock of the company.
output:
Joint-stock companies, established either by royal charter, or by act of parliament, are different in several respects, not only from regulated companies, but from private copartneries.

First, In a private copartnery, no partner without the consent of the company, can transfer his share to another person, or introduce a new member into the company. Each member, however, may, upon proper warning, withdraw from the copartnery, and demand payment from them of his share of the common stock. In a joint-stock company, on the contrary, no member can demand payment of his share from the company; but each member can, without their consent, transfer his share to another person, and thereby introduce a new member. The value of a share in a joint stock is always the price which it will bring in the market; and this may be either greater or less in any proportion, than the sum which its owner stands credited for in the stock of the company.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: The currency of a significant state, such as France or England, typically comprises almost entirely of its own coinage. If this currency becomes worn, clipped, or otherwise diminishes below its standard value, the state can effectively restore its currency through the reformation of its coinage. However, the currency of a smaller state, such as Genoa or Hamburg, rarely consists solely of its own coins, as it must largely incorporate coins from the neighboring states with which its residents engage in continuous commerce. Consequently, such a state may not always achieve currency reform through the reformation of its coinage. Furthermore, when foreign bills of exchange are settled using this currency, the inherent uncertainty surrounding the value of any amount, given its fundamentally unstable nature, will consistently disadvantage such a state, as its currency is invariably valued below its worth in all foreign territories.
output: The currency of a great state, such as France or England, generally consists almost entirely of its own coin. Should this currency, therefore, be at any time worn, clipt, or otherwise degraded below its standard value, the state, by a reformation of its coin, can effectually re-establish its currency. But the currency of a small state, such as Genoa or Hamburg, can seldom consist altogether in its own coin, but must be made up, in a great measure, of the coins of all the neighbouring states with which its inhabitants have a continual intercourse. Such a state, therefore, by reforming its coin, will not always be able to reform its currency. If foreign bills of exchange are paid in this currency, the uncertain value of any sum, of what is in its own nature so uncertain, must render the exchange always very much against such a state, its currency being in all foreign states necessarily valued even below what it is worth.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: The rent of land is often considered to be equivalent to a reasonable profit or interest for the capital invested by the landlord in its improvement. Nevertheless, this is only partially the case, as it can rarely be the sole factor. Additionally, the landlord typically requires a rent for unimproved land, and the perceived interest or profit from the cost of improvement is usually added to this initial rent. Furthermore, the improvements are not always financed by the landlord's capital, but sometimes by that of the tenant. Moreover, when the lease is renewed, the landlord generally demands an increase in rent, regardless of whether the improvements were made with his own capital or that of the tenant.
output: The rent of land, it may be thought, is frequently no more than a reasonable profit or interest for the stock laid out by the landlord upon its improvement. This, no doubt, may be partly the case upon some occasions; for it can scarce ever be more than partly the case. The landlord demands a rent even for unimproved land, and the supposed interest or profit upon the expense of improvement is generally an addition to this original rent. Those improvements, besides, are not always made by the stock of the landlord, but sometimes by that of the tenant. When the lease comes to be renewed, however, the landlord commonly demands the same augmentation of rent as if they had been all made by his own.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: Even during ordinary and quiet periods, holders of receipts benefit from lowering the agio. They can then buy bank money, and the bullion it allows them to withdraw, at a cheaper rate. Alternatively, they can sell their receipts at a higher price to those who hold bank money and wish to withdraw bullion. The price of a receipt generally equals the difference between the market price of bank money and that of the coin or bullion for which the receipt was issued. Conversely, owners of bank money benefit from raising the agio. They can then sell their bank money at a higher price or buy a receipt at a lower price. To prevent the speculative maneuvers that these opposing interests might sometimes cause, the bank in recent years resolved to sell bank money for currency at five percent agio at all times, and to buy it back at four percent agio. As a result of this resolution, the agio can never rise above five percent or fall below four percent. The proportion between the market price of bank money and that of current money is therefore kept very close to the proportion between their intrinsic values. Before this resolution was adopted, the market price of bank money sometimes rose as high as nine percent agio and sometimes fell as low as par, depending on which opposing interests happened to influence the market.
output: Even in ordinary and quiet times, it is the interest of the holders of receipts to depress the agio, in order either to buy bank money (and consequently the bullion which their receipts would then enable them to take out of the bank ) so much cheaper, or to sell their receipts to those who have bank money, and who want to take out bullion, so much dearer; the price of a receipt being generally equal to the difference between the market price of bank money and that of the coin or bullion for which the receipt had been granted. It is the interest of the owners of bank money, on the contrary, to raise the agio, in order either to sell their bank money so much dearer, or to buy a receipt so much cheaper. To prevent the stock-jobbing tricks which those opposite interests might sometimes occasion, the bank has of late years come to the resolution, to sell at all times bank money for currency at five per cent. agio, and to buy it in again at four per cent. agio. In consequence of this resolution, the agio can never either rise above five, or sink below four per cent.; and the proportion between the market price of bank and that of current money is kept at all times very near the proportion between their intrinsic values. Before this resolution was taken, the market price of bank money used sometimes to rise so high as nine per cent. agio, and sometimes to sink so low as par, according as opposite interests happened to influence the market.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: The knowledgeable author of the Tracts upon the Corn Trade has suggested that since the bounty on corn exports was first introduced, the price of exported corn, when assessed reasonably, tends to surpass that of imported corn, which is often valued quite highly, by a sum that may exceed the total amount of bounties paid during that time. He argues that, according to the principles of the mercantile system, this observation indicates that the regulated corn trade can be seen as advantageous to the nation, with the value of exports exceeding imports by a larger sum than the total extraordinary expenses incurred for exporting. However, he may overlook the fact that this extraordinary expense, or bounty, represents only a small fraction of the true costs associated with corn exportation. The capital invested by farmers in producing the corn should also be considered. If the selling price of corn in foreign markets does not cover not just the bounty, but also the capital and the usual profits of investment, then the society could potentially incur losses from the difference, leading to a reduction in national wealth. This concern is precisely why the bounty was initially deemed necessary, reflecting apprehensions about the adequacy of the price to cover these expenses.
output: The ingenious and well-informed author of the Tracts upon the Corn Trade has shown very clearly, that since the bounty upon the exportation of corn was first established, the price of the corn exported, valued moderately enough, has exceeded that of the corn imported, valued very high, by a much greater sum than the amount of the whole bounties which have been paid during that period. This, he imagines, upon the true principles of the mercantile system, is a clear proof that this forced corn trade is beneficial to the nation, the value of the exportation exceeding that of the importation by a much greater sum than the whole extraordinary expense which the public has been at in order to get it exported. He does not consider that this extraordinary expense, or the bounty, is the smallest part of the expense which the exportation of corn really costs the society. The capital which the farmer employed in raising it must likewise be taken into the account. Unless the price of the corn, when sold in the foreign markets, replaces not only the bounty, but this capital, together with the ordinary profits of stock, the society is a loser by the difference, or the national stock is so much diminished. But the very reason for which it has been thought necessary to grant a bounty, is the supposed insufficiency of the price to do this.
title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith

input: Additionally, the significant transformation brought about by the introduction of firearms in the art of war has further increased the expenditure associated with training and disciplining a given number of soldiers during peacetime, as well as the costs incurred when deploying them in wartime. Moreover, the expense of both the weapons and ammunition has risen considerably. In essence, a musket is a more costly device than a javelin or a bow and arrows, just as a cannon or a mortar is more expensive than a balista or a catapulta. Furthermore, the powder expended during modern military exercises is irretrievably lost, resulting in substantial additional costs. It is worth noting that the javelins and arrows utilized in ancient exercises could be easily recovered and were, moreover, of negligible value. The cannon and mortar are not only significantly more expensive, but also heavier, than the balista or catapulta, and require greater expenditure, both in preparation for deployment and in transportation to the field. Moreover, the considerable superiority of modern artillery over that of ancient times has made it substantially more difficult, and consequently more costly, to fortify a town in such a way as to withstand, even for a brief period, the onslaught of such superior artillery. In modern times, a variety of factors contribute to the increased expense of defending society. The inevitable consequences of the natural progression of improvement have, in this regard, been significantly exacerbated by a major revolution in the art of war, which appears to have been prompted by a mere accident, namely the invention of gunpowder.
output: The great change introduced into the art of war by the invention of fire-arms, has enhanced still further both the expense of exercising and disciplining any particular number of soldiers in time of peace, and that of employing them in time of war. Both their arms and their ammunition are become more expensive. A musket is a more expensive machine than a javelin or a bow and arrows; a cannon or a mortar, than a balista or a catapulta. The powder which is spent in a modern review is lost irrecoverably, and occasions a very considerable expense. The javelins and arrows which were thrown or shot in an ancient one, could easily be picked up again, and were, besides, of very little value. The cannon and the mortar are not only much dearer, but much heavier machines than the balista or catapulta; and require a greater expense, not only to prepare them for the field, but to carry them to it. I could not have endured the horrid screeching as the stake drove home; the plunging of writhing form, and lips of bloody foam. I should have fled in terror and left my work undone. But it is over! She did not begin visiting the churchyard until I came, and if she had not accompanied me there during the day, she would not have wandered there in her sleep. Your acquaintance and mine, Mr. Peter Hawkins, who resides beneath the grandeur of your magnificent cathedral in Exeter, which is situated quite far from London, procures my residence in London through your esteemed assistance. Furthermore, I wish to express candidly that you may find it unusual that I have chosen to engage the services of an individual situated so far from London rather than someone who resides there. My motivation for this choice was to ensure that no local interests would be prioritized other than my own. It is possible that a local resident might have personal interests or obligations to fulfill, which led me to seek an agent from a distance, one whose efforts would solely benefit my interests. Now, consider the scenario in which I, who am involved in various affairs, aim to ship goods to locations such as Newcastle, Durham, Harwich, or Dover. It stands to reason that it may be more efficient to entrust such shipping to an individual located in one of these ports. I acknowledged that this would indeed be the case; however, I explained that we solicitors operate under a system of mutual agency, which allows for local tasks to be managed by local practitioners under the guidance of any solicitor. Consequently, the client is able to place their trust in a single representative, who can execute their requests with minimal additional effort.
output: “I shall illustrate. Your friend and mine, Mr. Peter Hawkins, from under the shadow of your beautiful cathedral at Exeter, which is far from London, buys for me through your good self my place at London. Good! Now here let me say frankly, lest you should think it strange that I have sought the services of one so far off from London instead of some one resident there, that my motive was that no local interest might be served save my wish only; and as one of London residence might, perhaps, have some purpose of himself or friend to serve, I went thus afield to seek my agent, whose labours should be only to my interest. Now, suppose I, who have much of affairs, wish to ship goods, say, to Newcastle, or Durham, or Harwich, or Dover, might it not be that it could with more ease be done by consigning to one in these ports?” I answered that certainly it would be most easy, but that we solicitors had a system of agency one for the other, so that local work could be done locally on instruction from any solicitor, so that the client, simply placing himself in the hands of one man, could have his wishes carried out by him without further trouble.
title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker

input: When we locate the resting place of this man who was once alive, we can confine him to his coffin and eliminate him, provided we adhere to what we know. However, he is intelligent. I have requested my friend Arminius from Buda-Pesth University to document his history, and he will inform me about what he has been. It appears he must have been Voivode Dracula, who earned his name by fighting against the Turks near the great river on the border of Turkey. If this is true, he was no ordinary man; for during that time and for many years afterward, he was regarded as the most clever, cunning, and brave among the people of the 'land beyond the forest.' His formidable intellect and unwavering determination accompanied him to his grave and continue to oppose us today. According to Arminius, the Draculas were a prominent and noble lineage, although some members were occasionally believed by their contemporaries to have engaged in dealings with dark forces. They acquired forbidden knowledge in the Scholomance, located in the mountains above Lake Hermanstadt, where the devil claims one in every ten scholars. The records contain terms such as 'stregoica'—meaning witch, 'ordog'—meaning devil, and 'pokol'—meaning hell; in one manuscript, this very Dracula is referred to as 'wampyr,' a term we all recognize. From this individual have descended remarkable men and virtuous women, and their graves sanctify the ground that allows such malevolence to exist. It is particularly unsettling that this evil is deeply entwined with all that is good; it cannot find rest in barren soil devoid of sacred memories.
output: “Thus when we find the habitation of this man-that-was, we can confine him to his coffin and destroy him, if we obey what we know. But he is clever. I have asked my friend Arminius, of Buda-Pesth University, to make his record; and, from all the means that are, he tell me of what he has been. He must, indeed, have been that Voivode Dracula who won his name against the Turk, over the great river on the very frontier of Turkey-land. If it be so, then was he no common man; for in that time, and for centuries after, he was spoken of as the cleverest and the most cunning, as well as the bravest of the sons of the ‘land beyond the forest.’ That mighty brain and that iron resolution went with him to his grave, and are even now arrayed against us. The Draculas were, says Arminius, a great and noble race, though now and again were scions who were held by their coevals to have had dealings with the Evil One. They learned his secrets in the Scholomance, amongst the mountains over Lake Hermanstadt, where the devil claims the tenth scholar as his due. In the records are such words as ‘stregoica’ - witch, ‘ordog,’ and ‘pokol’ - Satan and hell; and in one manuscript this very Dracula is spoken of as ‘wampyr,’ which we all understand too well. There have been from the loins of this very one great men and good women, and their graves make sacred the earth where alone this foulness can dwell. For it is not the least of its terrors that this evil thing is rooted deep in all good; in soil barren of holy memories it cannot rest.”
title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker

input: He began to softly whisper, suggesting, "Rats, rats, rats! There may be hundreds, thousands, even millions of them, each one a life; there are also dogs and cats that may hunt them. All lives! All filled with red blood and potential years of life; and they are not merely buzzing flies!" I found myself laughing at him, as I was curious about what he might do next. At that moment, the dogs howled from beyond the dark trees surrounding his home. He gestured for me to approach the window. I stood up to look outside, and he raised his hands, appearing to call out silently. A dark mass began to spread over the grass, advancing like a flickering flame; then he parted the mist to reveal thousands of rats, their eyes glowing red—similar to his, yet smaller. He lifted his hand, and they all paused. I thought he seemed to imply, "I can offer you all these lives, and even many more and greater, across endless ages, if you will kneel and worship me!" Suddenly, a red cloud, reminiscent of blood, seemed to obscure my vision. Before I realized what I was doing, I found myself opening the window and inviting him in, saying, "Come in, Lord and Master!" Although the rats had vanished, he effortlessly entered the room through the narrow opening, much like the Moon, which can often slip through the tiniest crack to stand before me in all her majesty.
output: “Then he began to whisper: ‘Rats, rats, rats! Hundreds, thousands, millions of them, and every one a life; and dogs to eat them, and cats too. All lives! all red blood, with years of life in it; and not merely buzzing flies!’ I laughed at him, for I wanted to see what he could do. Then the dogs howled, away beyond the dark trees in His house. He beckoned me to the window. I got up and looked out, and He raised his hands, and seemed to call out without using any words. A dark mass spread over the grass, coming on like the shape of a flame of fire; and then He moved the mist to the right and left, and I could see that there were thousands of rats with their eyes blazing red - like His, only smaller. He held up his hand, and they all stopped; and I thought he seemed to be saying: ‘All these lives will I give you, ay, and many more and greater, through countless ages, if you will fall down and worship me!’ And then a red cloud, like the colour of blood, seemed to close over my eyes; and before I knew what I was doing, I found myself opening the sash and saying to Him: ‘Come in, Lord and Master!’ The rats were all gone, but He slid into the room through the sash, though it was only open an inch wide - just as the Moon herself has often come in through the tiniest crack and has stood before me in all her size and splendour.”
title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker

input:
After the man left, the three of us crossed the street and knocked on the door. Quincey Morris answered immediately, accompanied by Lord Godalming, who was lighting a cigar. Lord Godalming remarked on the foul smell inside, reminiscent of the old chapel at Carfax, which indicated that the Count had likely been using the space frequently. We began to explore the house, staying close together in case of an attack, aware that we were facing a clever and formidable enemy, and uncertain whether the Count was present.

In the dining room located at the back of the hall, we discovered eight boxes of earth, but we were still one box short of the nine we were searching for. This indicated that our task was incomplete, and we could not cease our efforts until we located the missing box. We first opened the shutters of a window overlooking a narrow stone-paved yard that faced a blank stable designed to resemble a small house. With no windows, we felt secure from being observed. We quickly began examining the boxes. Using the tools we had brought, we opened each one systematically, treating them as we had the previous boxes in the chapel. It became evident that the Count was not currently in the house, prompting us to continue our search for any of his belongings.
output:
When the man had fairly gone, we three crossed the street and knocked at the door. It was immediately opened by Quincey Morris, beside whom stood Lord Godalming lighting a cigar.

“The place smells so vilely,” said the latter as we came in. It did indeed smell vilely - like the old chapel at Carfax - and with our previous experience it was plain to us that the Count had been using the place pretty freely. We moved to explore the house, all keeping together in case of attack; for we knew we had a strong and wily enemy to deal with, and as yet we did not know whether the Count might not be in the house. In the dining-room, which lay at the back of the hall, we found eight boxes of earth. Eight boxes only out of the nine, which we sought! Our work was not over, and would never be until we should have found the missing box. First we opened the shutters of the window which looked out across a narrow stone-flagged yard at the blank face of a stable, pointed to look like the front of a miniature house. There were no windows in it, so we were not afraid of being over-looked. We did not lose any time in examining the chests. With the tools which we had brought with us we opened them, one by one, and treated them as we had treated those others in the old chapel. It was evident to us that the Count was not at present in the house, and we proceeded to search for any of his effects.

input: In the early morning, both individuals rose and headed to the harbor to check for any developments from the night before. The area was mostly deserted, and despite the bright sun and clear, fresh air, the large, imposing waves, which appeared dark with white foam resembling snow, surged through the narrow entrance of the harbor. This highlights a sense of turbulence and danger. One individual felt relieved that Jonathan had not been at sea the previous night, but uncertainty arose about his current whereabouts and condition. This suggests a growing concern and anxiety regarding Jonathan's safety. Ultimately, there was a desire for clarity and the ability to take action, reflecting feelings of helplessness.
output: Early in the morning we both got up and went down to the harbour to see if anything had happened in the night. There were very few people about, and though the sun was bright, and the air clear and fresh, the big, grim-looking waves, that seemed dark themselves because the foam that topped them was like snow, forced themselves in through the narrow mouth of the harbour - like a bullying man going through a crowd. Somehow I felt glad that Jonathan was not on the sea last night, but on land. But, oh, is he on land or sea? Where is he, and how? I am getting fearfully anxious about him. If I only knew what to do, and could do anything!

input:
It was time for us to begin our journey, and I bid farewell to Mina—a moment that may linger in our memories for the rest of our lives. Thus, we set off on our path.

I have come to a firm conclusion: if we discover that Mina may become a vampire, she shall not face that uncertain and frightening realm alone. It seems that historically, the fate of one vampire often implicated many; just as their unsettling forms could only find rest in consecrated ground, so too did the deepest love serve as a catalyst for their grim numbers. In summary, the bonds we share are significant, and I will stand by Mina through whatever may come.
output:
It was then time to start. So I said farewell to Mina, a parting which neither of us shall forget to our dying day; and we set out.

To one thing I have made up my mind: if we find out that Mina must be a vampire in the end, then she shall not go into that unknown and terrible land alone. I suppose it is thus that in old times one vampire meant many; just as their hideous bodies could only rest in sacred earth, so the holiest love was the recruiting sergeant for their ghastly ranks.

input:
The primary principle that emerges from the discussions presented in this text is the fundamental importance of human development in all its complexity. This concept is a crucial aspect of the work of Wilhelm von Humboldt, as seen in his book Sphere and Duties of Government. 

The topic of this essay is civil liberty, which refers to the nature and limits of the power that society can legitimately exercise over individuals. Meanwhile, the concept of liberty of the will, often mistakenly opposed to the idea of philosophical necessity, is not the focus of this discussion. Instead, the essay explores the question of social liberty, which is a topic that is rarely addressed in general terms, despite its significant influence on contemporary debates. Additionally, this issue is likely to become a critical concern in the future. 

This question is not a new one, as it has been a point of division among humans for centuries. However, as societies continue to progress, the issue presents itself in new ways, requiring a more comprehensive and nuanced approach. Consequently, it is necessary to reexamine this question in light of current conditions and to develop a more thorough understanding of its implications.
output:
The grand, leading principle, towards which every argument unfolded in these pages directly converges, is the absolute and essential importance of human development in its richest diversity. - WILHELM VON HUMBOLDT: Sphere and Duties of Government.

The subject of this Essay is not the so-called Liberty of the Will, so unfortunately opposed to the misnamed doctrine of Philosophical Necessity; but Civil, or Social Liberty: the nature and limits of the power which can be legitimately exercised by society over the individual. A question seldom stated, and hardly ever discussed, in general terms, but which profoundly influences the practical controversies of the age by its latent presence, and is likely soon to make itself recognised as the vital question of the future. It is so far from being new, that in a certain sense, it has divided mankind, almost from the remotest ages; but in the stage of progress into which the more civilised portions of the species have now entered, it presents itself under new conditions, and requires a different and more fundamental treatment.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: Having stated that individuality is identical to development, and that only the cultivation of individuality produces, or can produce, well-developed human beings, I might conclude the argument here. After all, what more or better can be said of any condition of human affairs than that it brings human beings closer to the best thing they can be? Likewise, what worse can be said of any obstruction to good than that it prevents this outcome? Doubtless, however, these considerations will not suffice to convince those who most need convincing. It is therefore necessary to demonstrate further that these developed human beings are of some use to the undeveloped. In particular, it must be shown to those who do not desire liberty and would not avail themselves of it that they may be rewarded in some intelligible manner for allowing other people to make use of it without hindrance.
output: Having said that Individuality is the same thing with development, and that it is only the cultivation of individuality which produces, or can produce, well-developed human beings, I might here close the argument: for what more or better can be said of any condition of human affairs, than that it brings human beings themselves nearer to the best thing they can be? or what worse can be said of any obstruction to good, than that it prevents this? Doubtless, however, these considerations will not suffice to convince those who most need convincing; and it is necessary further to show, that these developed human beings are of some use to the undeveloped - to point out to those who do not desire liberty, and would not avail themselves of it, that they may be in some intelligible manner rewarded for allowing other people to make use of it without hindrance.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: I insist, therefore, on the significance of genius and the necessity of allowing it to develop freely in both thought and action. I am acutely aware that, in theory, few would contest this viewpoint; however, I also recognize that, in practice, the majority exhibit a marked indifference to it. Individuals often regard genius as admirable when it facilitates the creation of an exhilarating poem or a remarkable painting. Nevertheless, in its truest form—characterized by originality in both thought and action—while no one openly disputes its value, most, at a fundamental level, believe they can manage quite adequately without it. Unfortunately, this perspective is understandable. Originality is a concept that unoriginal minds struggle to appreciate. They cannot comprehend its utility: how could they? If they were able to recognize its benefits, it would cease to be originality. The primary contribution that originality offers them is the act of enlightening their understanding; once this is achieved, they would possess the opportunity to become genuinely original. In the meantime, it is important to remember that nothing of significance has ever been accomplished without someone being the first to do so, and that all the worthwhile achievements we see today are the results of originality. Therefore, let them maintain the humility to believe that there remains much for originality to achieve, reassuring themselves that their need for originality is greatest when they remain unaware of that need.
output: I insist thus emphatically on the importance of genius, and the necessity of allowing it to unfold itself freely both in thought and in practice, being well aware that no one will deny the position in theory, but knowing also that almost every one, in reality, is totally indifferent to it. People think genius a fine thing if it enables a man to write an exciting poem, or paint a picture. But in its true sense, that of originality in thought and action, though no one says that it is not a thing to be admired, nearly all, at heart, think that they can do very well without it. Unhappily this is too natural to be wondered at. Originality is the one thing which unoriginal minds cannot feel the use of. They cannot see what it is to do for them: how should they? If they could see what it would do for them, it would not be originality. The first service which originality has to render them, is that of opening their eyes: which being once fully done, they would have a chance of being themselves original. Meanwhile, recollecting that nothing was ever yet done which some one was not the first to do, and that all good things which exist are the fruits of originality, let them be modest enough to believe that there is something still left for it to accomplish, and assure themselves that they are more in need of originality, the less they are conscious of the want.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: Seven years after the death of his wife, Mill was invited to stand for election in Westminster. His views on how elections should be conducted led him to decline any personal involvement in the campaign, and he expressed his political opinions quite openly, yet he was still elected by a large majority. He was not what one might call a conventional success in the House of Commons; as a speaker, he tended to lack a certain magnetism. Still, his influence could often be felt widely. "For the sake of the House of Commons at large," said Mr. Gladstone, "I rejoiced in his advent and deplored his disappearance. He did us all good." After only three years in Parliament, he was defeated at the next General Election by Mr. W. H. Smith. He then retired to Avignon, to the pleasant little house where he had spent the happiest years of his life in the company of his wife, and there he continued his disinterested labours. He completed his edition of his father's Analysis of the Mind and also produced, along with less important work, The Subjection of Women, in which he had the active cooperation of his step-daughter. A book on Socialism was under consideration, but, like an earlier study of Sociology, it was never written. He died in 1873, his last years being spent peacefully in the pleasant company of his step-daughter, from whose tender care and earnest intellectual sympathy he may have caught a far-off reflection of the light that had once illuminated his spiritual life. Overall, Mill's later years reflect a quiet but lasting commitment to his intellectual and personal ideals.
output: Seven years after the death of his wife, Mill was invited to contest Westminster. His feeling on the conduct of elections made him refuse to take any personal action in the matter, and he gave the frankest expression to his political views, but nevertheless he was elected by a large majority. He was not a conventional success in the House; as a speaker he lacked magnetism. But his influence was widely felt. "For the sake of the House of Commons at large," said Mr. Gladstone, "I rejoiced in his advent and deplored his disappearance. He did us all good." After only three years in Parliament, he was defeated at the next General Election by Mr. W. H. Smith. He retired to Avignon, to the pleasant little house where the happiest years of his life had been spent in the companionship of his wife, and continued his disinterested labours. He completed his edition of his father's Analysis of the Mind, and also produced, in addition to less important work, The Subjection of Women, in which he had the active co-operation of his step-daughter. A book on Socialism was under consideration, but, like an earlier study of Sociology, it never was written. He died in 1873, his last years being spent peacefully in the pleasant society of his step-daughter, from whose tender care and earnest intellectual sympathy he caught maybe a far-off reflection of the light which had irradiated his spiritual life.

input: The case of the Bombay Parsees serves as an intriguing example. When this industrious and enterprising community, descended from Persian fire-worshippers, fled their homeland in the face of the Caliphs, they arrived in Western India and were granted tolerance by the Hindu sovereigns, contingent upon their abstention from beef. Subsequently, when these regions came under the rule of Muslim conquerors, the Parsees secured a continuation of this indulgence, provided they refrained from consuming pork. What initially began as compliance with authority has evolved into a deeply ingrained practice, leading the Parsees to abstain from both beef and pork to this day. Although this dual abstinence is not mandated by their religious beliefs, it has become an established custom within their community; and in the context of Eastern culture, custom often holds a significance akin to religion.
output: The case of the Bombay Parsees is a curious instance in point. When this industrious and enterprising tribe, the descendants of the Persian fire-worshippers, flying from their native country before the Caliphs, arrived in Western India, they were admitted to toleration by the Hindoo sovereigns, on condition of not eating beef. When those regions afterwards fell under the dominion of Mahomedan conquerors, the Parsees obtained from them a continuance of indulgence, on condition of refraining from pork. What was at first obedience to authority became a second nature, and the Parsees to this day abstain both from beef and pork. Though not required by their religion, the double abstinence has had time to grow into a custom of their tribe; and custom, in the East, is a religion.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: To provide a more localized context, the majority of Spaniards perceive it as a significant offense, deeply disrespectful to the Supreme Being, to worship Him in any manner other than that of the Roman Catholic Church; thus, no other form of public worship is considered lawful on Spanish territory. Furthermore, the populations of Southern Europe view a married clergy as not only irreligious but also as unchaste, indecent, and thoroughly distasteful. It is worth noting that one must consider the perspective of Protestants regarding these deeply held convictions and the attempts to enforce them upon non-Catholics. Moreover, if humanity is justified in interfering with one another's liberties in matters that do not pertain to the interests of others, on what grounds can one consistently exclude these situations? Who can rightfully criticize individuals for wishing to eliminate what they perceive as a scandal in the eyes of both God and society? A more compelling argument can hardly be made for prohibiting any actions deemed as personal immorality than for suppressing practices viewed as impious; unless we are willing to adopt the rationale of persecutors and assert that we may oppress others because we are correct, while they must refrain from persecuting us because they are mistaken, we must be cautious about endorsing a principle that we would find profoundly unjust if applied to our own circumstances.
output: To come somewhat nearer home: the majority of Spaniards consider it a gross impiety, offensive in the highest degree to the Supreme Being, to worship him in any other manner than the Roman Catholic; and no other public worship is lawful on Spanish soil. The people of all Southern Europe look upon a married clergy as not only irreligious, but unchaste, indecent, gross, disgusting. What do Protestants think of these perfectly sincere feelings, and of the attempt to enforce them against non-Catholics? Yet, if mankind are justified in interfering with each other's liberty in things which do not concern the interests of others, on what principle is it possible consistently to exclude these cases? or who can blame people for desiring to suppress what they regard as a scandal in the sight of God and man? No stronger case can be shown for prohibiting anything which is regarded as a personal immorality, than is made out for suppressing these practices in the eyes of those who regard them as impieties; and unless we are willing to adopt the logic of persecutors, and to say that we may persecute others because we are right, and that they must not persecute us because they are wrong, we must beware of admitting a principle of which we should resent as a gross injustice the application to ourselves.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: I do not claim that the most unrestricted freedom to express all possible opinions would eliminate the problems of religious or philosophical sectarianism. Whenever people of limited understanding believe strongly in a particular truth, they will assert it, teach it, and often act on it as though no other truth exists, or at least none that could limit or qualify it. I recognize that the tendency of all opinions to become sectarian is not resolved by the freest discussion. Instead, it is often intensified by such discussion, because a truth that should have been acknowledged but was not is rejected all the more forcefully when it is proclaimed by those regarded as opponents. However, the beneficial effect of conflicting opinions is felt not by the passionate partisan but by the calmer and more impartial observer. The serious danger is not the violent conflict between different parts of the truth, but the quiet suppression of half of it. There is always hope when people are compelled to listen to both sides. It is when they attend to only one side that errors harden into prejudices, and truth itself loses its effect by being exaggerated into falsehood. Since the judicial faculty that can intelligently judge between two sides of a question is very rare, especially when only one side is represented by an advocate, truth has no chance unless every side of it, and every opinion that embodies any portion of the truth, not only finds advocates but is advocated in such a way that it is actually heard.
output: I do not pretend that the most unlimited use of the freedom of enunciating all possible opinions would put an end to the evils of religious or philosophical sectarianism. Every truth which men of narrow capacity are in earnest about, is sure to be asserted, inculcated, and in many ways even acted on, as if no other truth existed in the world, or at all events none that could limit or qualify the first. I acknowledge that the tendency of all opinions to become sectarian is not cured by the freest discussion, but is often heightened and exacerbated thereby; the truth which ought to have been, but was not, seen, being rejected all the more violently because proclaimed by persons regarded as opponents. But it is not on the impassioned partisan, it is on the calmer and more disinterested bystander, that this collision of opinions works its salutary effect. Not the violent conflict between parts of the truth, but the quiet suppression of half of it, is the formidable evil: there is always hope when people are forced to listen to both sides; it is when they attend only to one that errors harden into prejudices, and truth itself ceases to have the effect of truth, by being exaggerated into falsehood. And since there are few mental attributes more rare than that judicial faculty which can sit in intelligent judgment between two sides of a question, of which only one is represented by an advocate before it, truth has no chance but in proportion as every side of it, every opinion which embodies any fraction of the truth, not only finds advocates, but is so advocated as to be listened to.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input:
Objections to governmental involvement, as long as it does not infringe on individual liberties, may typically be categorized into three types. 

Firstly, one concern arises when it seems that individuals may be more capable of effectively managing certain tasks than the government. In many cases, those who have a personal stake in a matter may be best suited to handle it or decide how it should be managed. This idea often challenges the previous practices of legislative or governmental interference in everyday business activities. However, this aspect has been explored extensively by political economists and may not be directly relevant to the core principles discussed in this essay. In summary, while objections to government involvement can be understood in various ways, the notion of individual capability often emerges as a central concern.
output:
The objections to government interference, when it is not such as to involve infringement of liberty, may be of three kinds.

The first is, when the thing to be done is likely to be better done by individuals than by the government. Speaking generally, there is no one so fit to conduct any business, or to determine how or by whom it shall be conducted, as those who are personally interested in it. This principle condemns the interferences, once so common, of the legislature, or the officers of government, with the ordinary processes of industry. But this part of the subject has been sufficiently enlarged upon by political economists, and is not particularly related to the principles of this Essay.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: There is something both contemptible and frightful in the nature of the evidence upon which, in recent years, any individual may be judicially declared unfit for the management of his affairs, and after his death his disposal of his property may be set aside, provided there is enough of it to pay the expenses of litigation, which are charged upon the property itself. Furthermore, all the minute details of his daily life are pried into, and whatever is found which, seen through the medium of the perceiving and describing faculties of the lowest of the low, bears an appearance unlike absolute commonplace, is laid before the jury as evidence of insanity, and often with success, the jurors being little, if at all, less vulgar and ignorant than the witnesses. Moreover, the judges, with that extraordinary want of knowledge of human nature and life which continually astonishes us in English lawyers, often help to mislead them. It is worth noting that these trials speak volumes as to the state of feeling and opinion among the vulgar with regard to human liberty. In essence, so far from setting any value on individuality, so far from respecting the rights of each individual to act, in things indifferent, as seems good to his own judgment and inclinations, judges and juries cannot even conceive that a person in a state of sanity can desire such freedom. Additionally, in former days, when it was proposed to burn atheists, charitable people used to suggest putting them in a madhouse instead; it would be nothing surprising nowadays were we to see this done, and the doers applauding themselves, because, instead of persecuting for religion, they had adopted so humane and Christian a mode of treating these unfortunates, not without a silent satisfaction at their having thereby obtained their deserts.
