input: It's possible that someone who is skeptical of open discussion might argue that it's not necessarily essential for the general public to be aware of all the arguments for and against certain opinions, as presented by philosophers and theologians. They may suggest that it's not crucial for ordinary people to be able to identify and refute every misleading statement or flawed argument made by a skilled opponent. Instead, they might propose that it's sufficient to have experts who can respond to such claims, ensuring that no potentially misleading information goes unchallenged. In this view, individuals who are not experts can trust in the authority of those who have taught them the basic principles of a particular truth, and, acknowledging their own limitations, can be confident that any complex issues that arise have been or can be addressed by those with specialized knowledge and training. Overall, this perspective suggests that the public can rely on experts to handle complex debates and arguments, and that this can be a viable approach to navigating complex issues.
output: To abate the force of these considerations, an enemy of free discussion may be supposed to say, that there is no necessity for mankind in general to know and understand all that can be said against or for their opinions by philosophers and theologians. That it is not needful for common men to be able to expose all the misstatements or fallacies of an ingenious opponent. That it is enough if there is always somebody capable of answering them, so that nothing likely to mislead uninstructed persons remains unrefuted. That simple minds, having been taught the obvious grounds of the truths inculcated on them, may trust to authority for the rest, and being aware that they have neither knowledge nor talent to resolve every difficulty which can be raised, may repose in the assurance that all those which have been raised have been or can be answered, by those who are specially trained to the task.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: The tyranny of the majority, like other forms of tyranny, was initially and is still commonly feared mainly because it operates through the actions of public authorities. However, thoughtful individuals recognized that when society itself acts as the tyrant—society collectively exerting power over the separate individuals who make it up—its methods of oppression are not limited to the actions carried out by its political officials. Society can and does enforce its own demands, and when it issues wrong demands instead of right ones, or any demands at all in matters it should not interfere with, it practices a social tyranny more formidable than many kinds of political oppression. This is because, although it is not usually backed by such extreme penalties, it leaves fewer ways to escape, penetrating much more deeply into the details of life and enslaving the soul itself. This highlights that protection against the tyranny of the magistrate is not enough; there also needs to be protection against the tyranny of prevailing opinion and feeling, against society's tendency to impose its own ideas and practices as rules of conduct on those who dissent, by means other than civil penalties. This includes fettering the development of individuality and, if possible, preventing the formation of any individuality not in harmony with its ways, and compelling all characters to conform to its own model. Ultimately, there is a limit to the legitimate interference of collective opinion with individual independence, and finding and maintaining that limit against encroachment is as indispensable to a good condition of human affairs as protection against political despotism.
output: Like other tyrannies, the tyranny of the majority was at first, and is still vulgarly, held in dread, chiefly as operating through the acts of the public authorities. But reflecting persons perceived that when society is itself the tyrant - society collectively, over the separate individuals who compose it - its means of tyrannising are not restricted to the acts which it may do by the hands of its political functionaries. Society can and does execute its own mandates: and if it issues wrong mandates instead of right, or any mandates at all in things with which it ought not to meddle, it practises a social tyranny more formidable than many kinds of political oppression, since, though not usually upheld by such extreme penalties, it leaves fewer means of escape, penetrating much more deeply into the details of life, and enslaving the soul itself. Protection, therefore, against the tyranny of the magistrate is not enough: there needs protection also against the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling; against the tendency of society to impose, by other means than civil penalties, its own ideas and practices as rules of conduct on those who dissent from them; to fetter the development, and, if possible, prevent the formation, of any individuality not in harmony with its ways, and compel all characters to fashion themselves upon the model of its own. There is a limit to the legitimate interference of collective opinion with individual independence: and to find that limit, and maintain it against encroachment, is as indispensable to a good condition of human affairs, as protection against political despotism.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: In the eighteenth century, many educated individuals, as well as those who followed their lead, tended to admire what was referred to as civilisation, and they may have been impressed by the advancements in modern science, literature, and philosophy. At the same time, they can often be seen to have overestimated the differences between people in modern and ancient times, and may have believed that the differences were largely in their own favour. The ideas of Rousseau, which can be considered paradoxical, may have had a significant impact, potentially disrupting the prevailing one-sided opinions and forcing people to re-evaluate and recombine their ideas in a more nuanced way. It's worth noting that the current opinions of the time may not have been entirely inaccurate, and they may have contained more truth than Rousseau's ideas, with fewer errors. However, Rousseau's doctrine may have introduced some important truths that were lacking in popular opinion, and these ideas have continued to influence thought over time. The value of simplicity, the potential negative effects of artificial society, and the importance of authenticity are concepts that may have been highlighted by Rousseau's work, and they can often be seen to have had a lasting impact on cultivated minds, even if they still need to be reaffirmed and demonstrated through actions, as words alone may not be sufficient to bring about change. In summary, Rousseau's ideas may have played a significant role in shaping opinions and highlighting important truths, and their influence can still be seen today.
output: Thus, in the eighteenth century, when nearly all the instructed, and all those of the uninstructed who were led by them, were lost in admiration of what is called civilisation, and of the marvels of modern science, literature, and philosophy, and while greatly overrating the amount of unlikeness between the men of modern and those of ancient times, indulged the belief that the whole of the difference was in their own favour; with what a salutary shock did the paradoxes of Rousseau explode like bombshells in the midst, dislocating the compact mass of one-sided opinion, and forcing its elements to recombine in a better form and with additional ingredients. Not that the current opinions were on the whole farther from the truth than Rousseau's were; on the contrary, they were nearer to it; they contained more of positive truth, and very much less of error. Nevertheless there lay in Rousseau's doctrine, and has floated down the stream of opinion along with it, a considerable amount of exactly those truths which the popular opinion wanted; and these are the deposit which was left behind when the flood subsided. The superior worth of simplicity of life, the enervating and demoralising effect of the trammels and hypocrisies of artificial society, are ideas which have never been entirely absent from cultivated minds since Rousseau wrote; and they will in time produce their due effect, though at present needing to be asserted as much as ever, and to be asserted by deeds, for words, on this subject, have nearly exhausted their power.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: There is a particular characteristic of the current direction of public opinion that is especially calculated to render it intolerant of any notable manifestation of individuality. The general average of humanity is not only moderate in intellectual capacity, but also moderate in its inclinations; people possess no tastes or desires sufficiently strong to incline them toward unusual conduct, and consequently they do not comprehend those who do possess such tastes or desires, classifying all such persons among the wild and intemperate whom they are accustomed to regard with disdain. Furthermore, in addition to this general circumstance, one need only suppose that a powerful movement has commenced toward the improvement of morals, and it becomes evident what may be expected. In the present age, such a movement has indeed commenced; much has actually been accomplished in the way of increased regularity of conduct and the discouragement of excesses; and a philanthropic spirit prevails, for the exercise of which no more inviting field exists than the moral and prudential improvement of our fellow beings. Moreover, these tendencies of the times dispose the public more than at most former periods to prescribe general rules of conduct and to endeavor to make everyone conform to the approved standard. Additionally, that standard, whether expressed or tacit, is to desire nothing with intensity. Its ideal of character is to be devoid of any marked character; to impair by compression, like the foot of a Chinese lady, every part of human nature that stands out prominently and tends to render the individual markedly dissimilar in outline from commonplace humanity.
output: There is one characteristic of the present direction of public opinion, peculiarly calculated to make it intolerant of any marked demonstration of individuality. The general average of mankind are not only moderate in intellect, but also moderate in inclinations: they have no tastes or wishes strong enough to incline them to do anything unusual, and they consequently do not understand those who have, and class all such with the wild and intemperate whom they are accustomed to look down upon. Now, in addition to this fact which is general, we have only to suppose that a strong movement has set in towards the improvement of morals, and it is evident what we have to expect. In these days such a movement has set in; much has actually been effected in the way of increased regularity of conduct, and discouragement of excesses; and there is a philanthropic spirit abroad, for the exercise of which there is no more inviting field than the moral and prudential improvement of our fellow-creatures. These tendencies of the times cause the public to be more disposed than at most former periods to prescribe general rules of conduct, and endeavour to make every one conform to the approved standard. And that standard, express or tacit, is to desire nothing strongly. Its ideal of character is to be without any marked character; to maim by compression, like a Chinese lady's foot, every part of human nature which stands out prominently, and tends to make the person markedly dissimilar in outline to commonplace humanity.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: It is accurate to assert this perspective within the framework of Calvinistic theory. According to this theory, the predominant transgression of humanity is deemed to be self-will. The entirety of good that humanity can achieve is encapsulated in the concept of obedience. Individuals possess no choice in their actions; thus, they must act in a prescribed manner: any action that is not a duty is considered a sin. Given that human nature is fundamentally corrupt, there is no possibility of redemption for any individual until the corrupt aspects of human nature are eradicated from within. For those who adhere to this worldview, suppressing any of the human faculties, capacities, and sensibilities is not regarded as detrimental. Humanity requires no capacity beyond the ability to submit entirely to the divine will. Should individuals utilize any of their faculties for purposes other than fulfilling what is perceived as the divine will more effectively, it is argued that they would be better off without them. This encapsulates the essence of Calvinism; moreover, a modified interpretation of this theory is embraced by many who do not identify as Calvinists. This modification entails a less austere interpretation of the supposed will of God, positing that it is divine intent for humanity to indulge in certain inclinations. This indulgence is, of course, not to be pursued in the manner individuals may prefer but rather in obedience, adhering to directives established by authoritative sources, thereby imposing uniformity across all individuals in accordance with the requisite conditions of the case.
output: It is so, on the Calvinistic theory. According to that, the one great offence of man is Self-will. All the good of which humanity is capable, is comprised in Obedience. You have no choice; thus you must do, and no otherwise: "whatever is not a duty, is a sin." Human nature being radically corrupt, there is no redemption for any one until human nature is killed within him. To one holding this theory of life, crushing out any of the human faculties, capacities, and susceptibilities, is no evil: man needs no capacity, but that of surrendering himself to the will of God: and if he uses any of his faculties for any other purpose but to do that supposed will more effectually, he is better without them. That is the theory of Calvinism; and it is held, in a mitigated form, by many who do not consider themselves Calvinists; the mitigation consisting in giving a less ascetic interpretation to the alleged will of God; asserting it to be his will that mankind should gratify some of their inclinations; of course not in the manner they themselves prefer, but in the way of obedience, that is, in a way prescribed to them by authority; and, therefore, by the necessary conditions of the case, the same for all.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: If the absence of free discussion were to leave people unaware of the foundations of accepted opinions, it might be viewed as an intellectual issue rather than a moral one. Such a scenario could suggest that the value of these opinions remains intact, especially concerning their impact on character. However, the reality is that without discussion, individuals not only forget the basis of these opinions but often lose the very meaning of the opinions themselves. The words that express these ideas begin to lose their ability to convey thoughts, often communicating only a fraction of their original intent. Instead of fostering a clear understanding and genuine belief, only a few phrases may be memorized without comprehension, or merely the superficial elements of meaning may persist while the deeper significance is lost. This profound issue occupies a significant place in human history and deserves careful examination and reflection.
output: If, however, the mischievous operation of the absence of free discussion, when the received opinions are true, were confined to leaving men ignorant of the grounds of those opinions, it might be thought that this, if an intellectual, is no moral evil, and does not affect the worth of the opinions, regarded in their influence on the character. The fact, however, is, that not only the grounds of the opinion are forgotten in the absence of discussion, but too often the meaning of the opinion itself. The words which convey it, cease to suggest ideas, or suggest only a small portion of those they were originally employed to communicate. Instead of a vivid conception and a living belief, there remain only a few phrases retained by rote; or, if any part, the shell and husk only of the meaning is retained, the finer essence being lost. The great chapter in human history which this fact occupies and fills, cannot be too earnestly studied and meditated on.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: This volume is dedicated to the memory of a significant influence in the author's life, specifically the friend and wife who inspired much of his best work. Her strong sense of truth and justice served as a powerful motivation, and her approval was the author's primary reward. The author acknowledges that this work is as much hers as it is his, though it has not benefited as fully from her input as it could have, given that some critical parts were left for further review that will now not occur. The author expresses a desire to convey the profound thoughts and emotions that remain unspoken due to her passing, suggesting that achieving this would provide greater value to the world than his current writing can offer without her exceptional insight.
output: _To the beloved and deplored memory of her who was the inspirer, and in part the author, of all that is best in my writings - the friend and wife whose exalted sense of truth and right was my strongest incitement, and whose approbation was my chief reward - I dedicate this volume. Like all that I have written for many years, it belongs as much to her as to me; but the work as it stands has had, in a very insufficient degree, the inestimable advantage of her revision; some of the most important portions having been reserved for a more careful re-examination, which they are now never destined to receive. Were I but capable of interpreting to the world one-half the great thoughts and noble feelings which are buried in her grave, I should be the medium of a greater benefit to it than is ever likely to arise from anything that I can write, unprompted and unassisted by her all but unrivalled wisdom._
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: If the arguments presented in this chapter are valid, then the fullest liberty should exist for professing and discussing any doctrine as a matter of ethical conviction, regardless of how immoral that doctrine may be considered. It would therefore be irrelevant and inappropriate to examine here whether the doctrine of tyrannicide deserves that title. I will content myself with stating that this subject has always been one of the open questions of morals. The act of a private citizen in striking down a criminal who has placed himself above the law and beyond the reach of legal punishment or control has been regarded by whole nations, and by some of the best and wisest of men, not as a crime but as an act of exalted virtue. Whether right or wrong, it is not in the nature of assassination but of civil war. As such, I hold that instigation to it in a specific case may be a proper subject of punishment, but only if an overt act has followed and at least a probable connection can be established between the act and the instigation. Even then, it is not a foreign government but the very government assailed that alone, in the exercise of self-defence, can legitimately punish attacks directed against its own existence.
output: If the arguments of the present chapter are of any validity, there ought to exist the fullest liberty of professing and discussing, as a matter of ethical conviction, any doctrine, however immoral it may be considered. It would, therefore, be irrelevant and out of place to examine here, whether the doctrine of Tyrannicide deserves that title. I shall content myself with saying, that the subject has been at all times one of the open questions of morals; that the act of a private citizen in striking down a criminal, who, by raising himself above the law, has placed himself beyond the reach of legal punishment or control, has been accounted by whole nations, and by some of the best and wisest of men, not a crime, but an act of exalted virtue; and that, right or wrong, it is not of the nature of assassination, but of civil war. As such, I hold that the instigation to it, in a specific case, may be a proper subject of punishment, but only if an overt act has followed, and at least a probable connection can be established between the act and the instigation. Even then, it is not a foreign government, but the very government assailed, which alone, in the exercise of self-defence, can legitimately punish attacks directed against its own existence.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: It should not be assumed that because damage or the probability of damage to the interests of others is the only justification for social interference, such interference is therefore always justified. In many cases, an individual who pursues a legitimate goal necessarily and therefore legitimately causes pain or loss to others, or blocks a good that they had a reasonable hope of obtaining. Such conflicts of interest between individuals often arise from bad social institutions, but they are unavoidable as long as those institutions last. Some would be unavoidable under any institutions. Whoever succeeds in an overcrowded profession or in a competitive examination, or whoever is preferred to another in any contest for an object that both desire, gains benefit from the loss of others, from their wasted effort and their disappointment. However, it is generally agreed that the general interest of mankind is better served when people pursue their goals without being deterred by this kind of consequence. In other words, society recognizes no rights, whether legal or moral, for disappointed competitors to be immune from this kind of suffering. Society feels called on to interfere only when the means of success employed are those that it is contrary to the general interest to permit, namely fraud or treachery, and force.
output: In the first place, it must by no means be supposed, because damage, or probability of damage, to the interests of others, can alone justify the interference of society, that therefore it always does justify such interference. In many cases, an individual, in pursuing a legitimate object, necessarily and therefore legitimately causes pain or loss to others, or intercepts a good which they had a reasonable hope of obtaining. Such oppositions of interest between individuals often arise from bad social institutions, but are unavoidable while those institutions last; and some would be unavoidable under any institutions. Whoever succeeds in an overcrowded profession, or in a competitive examination; whoever is preferred to another in any contest for an object which both desire, reaps benefit from the loss of others, from their wasted exertion and their disappointment. But it is, by common admission, better for the general interest of mankind, that persons should pursue their objects undeterred by this sort of consequences. In other words, society admits no rights, either legal or moral, in the disappointed competitors, to immunity from this kind of suffering; and feels called on to interfere, only when means of success have been employed which it is contrary to the general interest to permit - namely, fraud or treachery, and force.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: Let us now move on to the second part of the argument. Setting aside the possibility that any of the accepted beliefs might be incorrect, we will assume their truth and explore how they are likely perceived when their validity is not openly discussed. Even someone who holds a strong opinion might find it challenging to accept that their viewpoint could be mistaken. However, they should consider that, regardless of its truth, if an opinion is not regularly and openly examined, it may come to be seen as a stagnant belief rather than a dynamic truth. In summary, continuous and open dialogue is essential for opinions to remain relevant and meaningful.
output: Let us now pass to the second division of the argument, and dismissing the supposition that any of the received opinions may be false, let us assume them to be true, and examine into the worth of the manner in which they are likely to be held, when their truth is not freely and openly canvassed. However unwillingly a person who has a strong opinion may admit the possibility that his opinion may be false, he ought to be moved by the consideration that however true it may be, if it is not fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed, it will be held as a dead dogma, not a living truth.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: This passage raises important questions about societal responsibility in guiding individuals who may lack the ability to govern themselves. It suggests that if society recognizes the need to protect children and minors from their own decisions, it should similarly extend that protection to adults who also demonstrate incapacity for self-governance. The text points out that behaviors such as gambling, alcoholism, promiscuity, idleness, and uncleanliness can be as detrimental to personal happiness and societal progress as many actions currently prohibited by law. This highlights the potential argument for law to address these issues within practical limits and social convenience. Furthermore, it proposes that public opinion should actively combat these vices and impose social penalties on those who engage in them. Importantly, the passage clarifies that the aim is not to restrict individual expression or stifle innovative ways of living, but rather to prevent the repetition of historically harmful behaviors that have proven unbeneficial. Ultimately, it asserts that after sufficient time and experience, certain moral or practical truths can be considered established, and society should strive to prevent future generations from repeating the mistakes of the past.
output: And even (it will be added) if the consequences of misconduct could be confined to the vicious or thoughtless individual, ought society to abandon to their own guidance those who are manifestly unfit for it? If protection against themselves is confessedly due to children and persons under age, is not society equally bound to afford it to persons of mature years who are equally incapable of self-government? If gambling, or drunkenness, or incontinence, or idleness, or uncleanliness, are as injurious to happiness, and as great a hindrance to improvement, as many or most of the acts prohibited by law, why (it may be asked) should not law, so far as is consistent with practicability and social convenience, endeavour to repress these also? And as a supplement to the unavoidable imperfections of law, ought not opinion at least to organise a powerful police against these vices, and visit rigidly with social penalties those who are known to practise them? There is no question here (it may be said) about restricting individuality, or impeding the trial of new and original experiments in living. The only things it is sought to prevent are things which have been tried and condemned from the beginning of the world until now; things which experience has shown not to be useful or suitable to any person's individuality. There must be some length of time and amount of experience, after which a moral or prudential truth may be regarded as established: and it is merely desired to prevent generation after generation from falling over the same precipice which has been fatal to their predecessors.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input:
It is worth noting that we have now recognized the necessity of freedom of opinion and freedom of expression for the mental well-being of humanity, which serves as the foundation for all other forms of well-being, on four distinct grounds. We will now briefly summarize these grounds.

Additionally, if any opinion is compelled to remain silent, that opinion may, to our best understanding, be true. To deny this possibility is to presume our own infallibility.

Furthermore, even if the silenced opinion represents an error, it may contain a fragment of truth, and in fact, this is often the case. Since the prevailing opinion on any subject is rarely, if ever, the complete truth, it is only through the confrontation of opposing opinions that the remaining aspects of truth have any opportunity to emerge.
output:
We have now recognised the necessity to the mental well-being of mankind (on which all their other well-being depends) of freedom of opinion, and freedom of the expression of opinion, on four distinct grounds; which we will now briefly recapitulate.

First, if any opinion is compelled to silence, that opinion may, for aught we can certainly know, be true. To deny this is to assume our own infallibility.

Secondly, though the silenced opinion be an error, it may, and very commonly does, contain a portion of truth; and since the general or prevailing opinion on any subject is rarely or never the whole truth, it is only by the collision of adverse opinions, that the remainder of the truth has any chance of being supplied.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: What Mill's wife truly meant to him is something we may never fully know. Yet there is abundant evidence that she was a real and vivid force in his life, one that awakened the latent enthusiasm within his nature. When she died at Avignon, his friends may have regained a companionship that had become somewhat distant, but on a personal level, Mill was the poorer for it. We cannot enter into the sorrow of that loss; we have no right or power to draw back the veil. It is enough to quote his simple words, so eloquent of an unspoken grief: "I can say nothing which could describe, even in the faintest manner, what that loss was and is. But because I know that she would have wished it, I endeavour to make the best of what life I have left, and to work for her purposes with such diminished strength as can be derived from thoughts of her, and communion with her memory." This highlights how deeply her presence shaped his life and purpose, and ultimately, how her memory became a sustaining force in his remaining years.
output: What his wife really was to Mill, we shall, perhaps, never know. But that she was an actual and vivid force, which roused the latent enthusiasm of his nature, we have abundant evidence. And when she died at Avignon, though his friends may have regained an almost estranged companionship, Mill was, personally, the poorer. Into the sorrow of that bereavement we cannot enter: we have no right or power to draw the veil. It is enough to quote the simple words, so eloquent of an unspoken grief - "I can say nothing which could describe, even in the faintest manner, what that loss was and is. But because I know that she would have wished it, I endeavour to make the best of what life I have left, and to work for her purposes with such diminished strength as can be derived from thoughts of her, and communion with her memory."
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: It is now necessary to assert that the situation was fundamentally different for the early Christians. Had the circumstances been otherwise, Christianity would not have evolved from a marginalized group of the disdained Hebrews into the dominant religion of the Roman Empire. When their adversaries remarked, "See how these Christians love one another," they undoubtedly possessed a much deeper understanding of their faith than has been observed in more recent times. This phenomenon likely accounts for the fact that Christianity currently experiences limited growth in its reach, remaining predominantly associated with Europeans and their descendants even after eighteen centuries. Furthermore, even among those who are fervent in their religious beliefs and ascribe significant meaning to their doctrines, it is frequently observed that the aspects of faith that actively engage their thoughts are those influenced by figures such as Calvin or Knox, individuals who are much closer to their own identities. The words of Christ tend to reside passively in their consciousness, exerting little influence beyond the gentle appeal of the language. There are certainly numerous explanations for why sect-specific doctrines maintain greater vitality than those shared across recognized sects and why educators make greater efforts to keep their significance alive; however, one clear reason is that these unique doctrines are more often subjected to scrutiny and must be defended against open challengers. In essence, both instructors and students tend to become complacent in their roles as soon as there is no opposition present.
output: Now we may be well assured that the case was not thus, but far otherwise, with the early Christians. Had it been thus, Christianity never would have expanded from an obscure sect of the despised Hebrews into the religion of the Roman empire. When their enemies said, "See how these Christians love one another" (a remark not likely to be made by anybody now), they assuredly had a much livelier feeling of the meaning of their creed than they have ever had since. And to this cause, probably, it is chiefly owing that Christianity now makes so little progress in extending its domain, and after eighteen centuries, is still nearly confined to Europeans and the descendants of Europeans. Even with the strictly religious, who are much in earnest about their doctrines, and attach a greater amount of meaning to many of them than people in general, it commonly happens that the part which is thus comparatively active in their minds is that which was made by Calvin, or Knox, or some such person much nearer in character to themselves. The sayings of Christ coexist passively in their minds, producing hardly any effect beyond what is caused by mere listening to words so amiable and bland. There are many reasons, doubtless, why doctrines which are the badge of a sect retain more of their vitality than those common to all recognised sects, and why more pains are taken by teachers to keep their meaning alive; but one reason certainly is, that the peculiar doctrines are more questioned, and have to be oftener defended against open gainsayers. Both teachers and learners go to sleep at their post, as soon as there is no enemy in the field.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: I do not affirm any such proposition. As humanity progresses, the number of doctrines that are no longer contested or doubted will continuously increase; the well-being of humanity can almost be quantified by the quantity and significance of the truths that have reached a state of being uncontested. The cessation of serious controversy concerning one question after another is an essential aspect of the consolidation of opinion, which is beneficial when it pertains to true opinions, while it can be perilous and harmful in the case of erroneous views. Furthermore, although this gradual reduction in the diversity of opinion is necessary in both respects, being simultaneously inevitable and essential, we are not compelled to conclude that all of its outcomes must be advantageous. The loss of such a crucial aid to the intelligent and dynamic comprehension of a truth, which is provided by the need to explain it to or defend it against opponents, although it does not outweigh the benefits of universal recognition, is neither insignificant nor negligible. Where this advantage can no longer be obtained, I must confess that I would appreciate witnessing the educators of humanity striving to offer a substitute; some method of presenting the complexities of the question as vividly to the learner's awareness as if they were being challenged by a dissenting advocate, keen to convert him.
output: I affirm no such thing. As mankind improve, the number of doctrines which are no longer disputed or doubted will be constantly on the increase: and the well-being of mankind may almost be measured by the number and gravity of the truths which have reached the point of being uncontested. The cessation, on one question after another, of serious controversy, is one of the necessary incidents of the consolidation of opinion; a consolidation as salutary in the case of true opinions, as it is dangerous and noxious when the opinions are erroneous. But though this gradual narrowing of the bounds of diversity of opinion is necessary in both senses of the term, being at once inevitable and indispensable, we are not therefore obliged to conclude that all its consequences must be beneficial. The loss of so important an aid to the intelligent and living apprehension of a truth, as is afforded by the necessity of explaining it to, or defending it against, opponents, though not sufficient to outweigh, is no trifling drawback from, the benefit of its universal recognition. Where this advantage can no longer be had, I confess I should like to see the teachers of mankind endeavouring to provide a substitute for it; some contrivance for making the difficulties of the question as present to the learner's consciousness, as if they were pressed upon him by a dissentient champion, eager for his conversion.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: The same principle generally applies to all traditional doctrines, including those pertaining to prudence, knowledge of life, as well as morals and religion. All languages and literatures are replete with overarching observations regarding life, encompassing both its nature and the appropriate manner in which to navigate it. These observations are widely acknowledged, frequently repeated, and often accepted without question; they are regarded as self-evident truths. However, it is worth noting that most individuals do not genuinely comprehend their significance until personal experience, often of a painful nature, has rendered them a reality. Frequently, when one is grappling with an unexpected misfortune or disappointment, they recall a proverb or common saying that has been familiar throughout their life. The significance of this saying, if it had been fully grasped prior to the present circumstance, might have prevented their misfortune. There are indeed various reasons for this phenomenon beyond the mere lack of discourse; many truths cannot be fully appreciated until they have been substantiated by personal experience. Moreover, a greater understanding of even these truths, along with a more profound mental imprint of what was understood, could have been achieved had individuals been accustomed to hearing them debated from multiple perspectives by those with a true understanding. The unfortunate tendency of humanity to cease contemplating a matter once it is no longer in doubt accounts for a significant portion of their errors. A contemporary author has aptly remarked upon "the deep slumber of a decided opinion."
output: The same thing holds true, generally speaking, of all traditional doctrines - those of prudence and knowledge of life, as well as of morals or religion. All languages and literatures are full of general observations on life, both as to what it is, and how to conduct oneself in it; observations which everybody knows, which everybody repeats, or hears with acquiescence, which are received as truisms, yet of which most people first truly learn the meaning, when experience, generally of a painful kind, has made it a reality to them. How often, when smarting under some unforeseen misfortune or disappointment, does a person call to mind some proverb or common saying, familiar to him all his life, the meaning of which, if he had ever before felt it as he does now, would have saved him from the calamity. There are indeed reasons for this, other than the absence of discussion: there are many truths of which the full meaning cannot be realised, until personal experience has brought it home. But much more of the meaning even of these would have been understood, and what was understood would have been far more deeply impressed on the mind, if the man had been accustomed to hear it argued pro and con by people who did understand it. The fatal tendency of mankind to leave off thinking about a thing when it is no longer doubtful, is the cause of half their errors. A contemporary author has well spoken of "the deep slumber of a decided opinion."
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: To frame the argument effectively, it is beneficial to first focus on a specific aspect of the broader thesis, particularly the Liberty of Thought. This aspect is inherently linked to the associated freedoms of speech and writing. While these liberties are recognized to varying degrees in the political morality of nations that uphold religious tolerance and democratic institutions, the underlying philosophical and practical foundations are not as widely understood or appreciated, even among influential figures. This suggests that a deeper understanding of these foundations extends beyond just this topic and is essential for addressing the broader issues at hand. Ultimately, for those familiar with the discourse surrounding this topic over the past three centuries, I ask for patience as I contribute to this ongoing discussion.
output: It will be convenient for the argument, if, instead of at once entering upon the general thesis, we confine ourselves in the first instance to a single branch of it, on which the principle here stated is, if not fully, yet to a certain point, recognised by the current opinions. This one branch is the Liberty of Thought: from which it is impossible to separate the cognate liberty of speaking and of writing. Although these liberties, to some considerable amount, form part of the political morality of all countries which profess religious toleration and free institutions, the grounds, both philosophical and practical, on which they rest, are perhaps not so familiar to the general mind, nor so thoroughly appreciated by many even of the leaders of opinion, as might have been expected. Those grounds, when rightly understood, are of much wider application than to only one division of the subject, and a thorough consideration of this part of the question will be found the best introduction to the remainder. Those to whom nothing which I am about to say will be new, may therefore, I hope, excuse me, if on a subject which for now three centuries has been so often discussed, I venture on one discussion more.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: Thirdly, even if a widely accepted opinion is entirely accurate, it is still important for it to be subjected to vigorous and earnest debate. This highlights the need for critical examination, as without it, most people will accept the opinion without fully understanding its underlying rationale, essentially holding it as a prejudice. Additionally, this suggests that the doctrine itself may be compromised, losing its original meaning and impact on an individual's character and behavior. Ultimately, if this occurs, the doctrine may become a mere formality, lacking the power to inspire positive change, while also occupying space and hindering the development of genuine, heartfelt convictions that arise from reason or personal experience.
output: Thirdly, even if the received opinion be not only true, but the whole truth; unless it is suffered to be, and actually is, vigorously and earnestly contested, it will, by most of those who receive it, be held in the manner of a prejudice, with little comprehension or feeling of its rational grounds. And not only this, but, fourthly, the meaning of the doctrine itself will be in danger of being lost, or enfeebled, and deprived of its vital effect on the character and conduct: the dogma becoming a mere formal profession, inefficacious for good, but cumbering the ground, and preventing the growth of any real and heartfelt conviction, from reason or personal experience.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: It can be challenging to defend the use of punishment to restrain irreligious opinions, as this approach may be difficult to justify without also condoning the actions of historical figures like Marcus Antoninus. When faced with criticism, opponents of religious freedom may acknowledge this potential consequence and argue, similarly to Dr. Johnson, that the persecutors of Christianity may have been justified in their actions. They tend to suggest that persecution can serve as a test of truth, which ultimately prevails, although legal penalties may sometimes be effective in suppressing harmful misconceptions. This line of reasoning in support of religious intolerance is noteworthy and may be worth considering. In summary, the debate surrounding religious freedom and tolerance is complex, and various arguments can be made, with some suggesting that persecution may have a role to play in testing the validity of certain beliefs.
output: Aware of the impossibility of defending the use of punishment for restraining irreligious opinions, by any argument which will not justify Marcus Antoninus, the enemies of religious freedom, when hard pressed, occasionally accept this consequence, and say, with Dr. Johnson, that the persecutors of Christianity were in the right; that persecution is an ordeal through which truth ought to pass, and always passes successfully, legal penalties being, in the end, powerless against truth, though sometimes beneficially effective against mischievous errors. This is a form of the argument for religious intolerance, sufficiently remarkable not to be passed without notice.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: It can be argued that a theory which suggests that truth may be justifiably persecuted because it may not be harmed by it, does not necessarily intend to be hostile to the acceptance of new truths. However, this theory may be seen as lacking in generosity towards the individuals who contribute to the discovery of these new truths. Discovering and sharing new information that is of significant importance to the world, and correcting previous misconceptions, can be a highly valuable service to humanity, as seen in the cases of the early Christians and the Reformers. In some instances, this can be considered one of the most significant contributions a person can make. Nevertheless, it may seem unfortunate that the individuals who make such significant contributions often face severe consequences, such as martyrdom, as a result of their actions. According to this theory, it may be seen as acceptable for the proponents of new ideas to face punishment, similar to the ancient Locrian law, where a person proposing a new law would face immediate punishment if their proposal was not accepted. It tends to be the case that people who support this approach may not place a high value on the benefits of new discoveries, and this view may be more commonly held by those who believe that new truths were once desirable, but are no longer necessary. In summary, this theory may be seen as having a limited perspective on the value of new truths and the treatment of those who discover them.
output: A theory which maintains that truth may justifiably be persecuted because persecution cannot possibly do it any harm, cannot be charged with being intentionally hostile to the reception of new truths; but we cannot commend the generosity of its dealing with the persons to whom mankind are indebted for them. To discover to the world something which deeply concerns it, and of which it was previously ignorant; to prove to it that it had been mistaken on some vital point of temporal or spiritual interest, is as important a service as a human being can render to his fellow-creatures, and in certain cases, as in those of the early Christians and of the Reformers, those who think with Dr. Johnson believe it to have been the most precious gift which could be bestowed on mankind. That the authors of such splendid benefits should be requited by martyrdom; that their reward should be to be dealt with as the vilest of criminals, is not, upon this theory, a deplorable error and misfortune, for which humanity should mourn in sackcloth and ashes, but the normal and justifiable state of things. The propounder of a new truth, according to this doctrine, should stand, as stood, in the legislation of the Locrians, the proposer of a new law, with a halter round his neck, to be instantly tightened if the public assembly did not, on hearing his reasons, then and there adopt his proposition. People who defend this mode of treating benefactors, cannot be supposed to set much value on the benefit; and I believe this view of the subject is mostly confined to the sort of persons who think that new truths may have been desirable once, but that we have had enough of them now.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: The issue highlighted here may not be merely theoretical; it might be reasonable to expect that I would identify specific cases where society today tends to impose its preferences as if they were moral laws. However, my intention is not to write a comprehensive essay on the shortcomings of current moral sentiments, as that topic may be too complex to address briefly and merely as an example. Nevertheless, I believe that providing instances is essential to demonstrate that the principle I am discussing is both significant and applicable in real life, rather than attempting to construct a defense against hypothetical concerns. It can often be observed through numerous examples that the tendency to broaden the scope of what might be viewed as moral authority, to the point where it infringes on the clearly legitimate freedoms of individuals, is a common trait among humans. In sum, this illustrates how societal influences can sometimes challenge personal liberties in the name of moral standards.
output: The evil here pointed out is not one which exists only in theory; and it may perhaps be expected that I should specify the instances in which the public of this age and country improperly invests its own preferences with the character of moral laws. I am not writing an essay on the aberrations of existing moral feeling. That is too weighty a subject to be discussed parenthetically, and by way of illustration. Yet examples are necessary, to show that the principle I maintain is of serious and practical moment, and that I am not endeavouring to erect a barrier against imaginary evils. And it is not difficult to show, by abundant instances, that to extend the bounds of what may be called moral police, until it encroaches on the most unquestionably legitimate liberty of the individual, is one of the most universal of all human propensities.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

input: This doctrine is intended to apply to human beings who have reached maturity and possess fully developed faculties. It does not pertain to children or young individuals who have not yet reached the age of adulthood as defined by law. Those who require care and protection from others must be safeguarded against their own actions and external harm. This highlights the need for protection and guidance during early stages of development. Similarly, in backward states of society where the population is not yet capable of spontaneous progress, the difficulties are so significant that there may be limited options for overcoming them. In such cases, a ruler who prioritizes improvement may be justified in using various means to achieve their goals, as long as the end result is the betterment of the society. This suggests that despotism can be a legitimate form of government when dealing with societies that are not yet developed, provided that the ultimate goal is improvement and the means used are effective in achieving that end. However, liberty as a principle only becomes applicable when a society has reached a stage where its members can be improved through free and equal discussion. Until that point, implicit obedience to a ruler may be necessary. Ultimately, once a society has reached the capacity for guided improvement through conviction or persuasion, compulsion is no longer justifiable as a means of achieving the greater good, except in cases where it is necessary for the security of others.
output: It is, perhaps, hardly necessary to say that this doctrine is meant to apply only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties. We are not speaking of children, or of young persons below the age which the law may fix as that of manhood or womanhood. Those who are still in a state to require being taken care of by others, must be protected against their own actions as well as against external injury. For the same reason, we may leave out of consideration those backward states of society in which the race itself may be considered as in its nonage. The early difficulties in the way of spontaneous progress are so great, that there is seldom any choice of means for overcoming them; and a ruler full of the spirit of improvement is warranted in the use of any expedients that will attain an end, perhaps otherwise unattainable. Despotism is a legitimate mode of government in dealing with barbarians, provided the end be their improvement, and the means justified by actually effecting that end. Liberty, as a principle, has no application to any state of things anterior to the time when mankind have become capable of being improved by free and equal discussion. Until then, there is nothing for them but implicit obedience to an Akbar or a Charlemagne, if they are so fortunate as to find one. But as soon as mankind have attained the capacity of being guided to their own improvement by conviction or persuasion (a period long since reached in all nations with whom we need here concern ourselves), compulsion, either in the direct form or in that of pains and penalties for non-compliance, is no longer admissible as a means to their own good, and justifiable only for the security of others.
title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill

output: The principles asserted in these pages must be more generally admitted as the basis for discussion of details, before a consistent application of them to all the various departments of government and morals can be attempted with any prospect of advantage. output:
“I think so,” murmured the Provincial Mayor; and, knitting his brows, he lapsed into an introspective state, his lips moving as one who repeats mystic words. “Yes, I think I see it now,” he said after some time, brightening in a quite transitory manner.

“Well, I do not mind telling you I have been at work upon this geometry of Four Dimensions for some time. Some of my results are curious. For instance, here is a portrait of a man at eight years old, another at fifteen, another at seventeen, another at twenty-three, and so on. All these are evidently sections, as it were, Three-Dimensional representations of his Four-Dimensioned being, which is a fixed and unalterable thing.”

input: She was greatly troubled, yet her unusual affection for me ultimately prevailed. For five nights during our acquaintance, including the final night, she rested her head on my arm while sleeping. However, as I recount my experiences with her, my thoughts begin to blur. It must have been the night before her rescue when I awoke just before dawn. I had been restless, plagued by a disturbing dream in which I was drowning, and sea anemones were brushing against my face with their soft tendrils. I suddenly woke up, harboring a strange notion that a greyish creature had darted out of the room. I attempted to fall asleep again, but I remained uneasy and restless. It was that dim, grey hour when shadows slowly recede from the darkness, creating a colorless and stark environment that felt unreal. I decided to rise and made my way down to the great hall, stepping out onto the flagstones in front of the palace. I thought I would turn my necessity into an opportunity and witness the sunrise.
output: “It troubled her greatly, but in the end her odd affection for me triumphed, and for five of the nights of our acquaintance, including the last night of all, she slept with her head pillowed on my arm. But my story slips away from me as I speak of her. It must have been the night before her rescue that I was awakened about dawn. I had been restless, dreaming most disagreeably that I was drowned, and that sea anemones were feeling over my face with their soft palps. I woke with a start, and with an odd fancy that some greyish animal had just rushed out of the chamber. I tried to get to sleep again, but I felt restless and uncomfortable. It was that dim grey hour when things are just creeping out of darkness, when everything is colourless and clear cut, and yet unreal. I got up, and went down into the great hall, and so out upon the flagstones in front of the palace. I thought I would make a virtue of necessity, and see the sunrise.

input: He set down his glass and moved toward the staircase door. I noticed once more his lameness and the soft sound of his footsteps. Rising from my seat, I caught a glimpse of his feet as he exited. He wore only a pair of tattered, blood-stained socks. Shortly after, the door closed behind him. I considered following him for a moment, but then I recalled his aversion to any fuss about himself. For a brief time, my thoughts wandered. Then I heard the Editor say, "Remarkable Behaviour of an Eminent Scientist," as he often thought in headlines. This pulled my attention back to the brightly lit dinner table.
output: He put down his glass, and walked towards the staircase door. Again I remarked his lameness and the soft padding sound of his footfall, and standing up in my place, I saw his feet as he went out. For a minute, perhaps, my mind was wool-gathering. Then, “Remarkable Behaviour of an Eminent Scientist,” I heard the Editor say, thinking (after his wont) in headlines. input: Additionally, it was not long before I found myself being grasped by multiple hands, and it was readily apparent that their intention was to pull me back. Furthermore, I ignited another light source and held it up to their faces, which were temporarily blinded by the illumination. Moreover, I did not linger to observe them further, instead opting to retreat once again, and when my second light source had burned out, I ignited my third. In essence, this third light source had nearly exhausted its fuel when I reached the entrance to the shaft. Moreover, I lay down at the edge of the opening, as the pulsating rhythm of the large pump below was causing me to feel lightheaded. Then, as I felt around for the protruding hooks, I experienced a sudden and violent tug on my feet from behind, as if someone was attempting to pull me backward. Nevertheless, I managed to ignite my final light source, although it was promptly extinguished. However, I had already gained a hold on the climbing bars, and by kicking vigorously, I was able to free myself from the grasp of the Morlocks, rapidly ascending the shaft while they remained below, peering and blinking up at me, with the exception of one small creature that pursued me for a short distance and nearly succeeded in seizing my boot as a prize.
output: “In a moment I was clutched by several hands, and there was no mistaking that they were trying to haul me back. I struck another light, and waved it in their dazzled faces. You can scarce imagine how nauseatingly inhuman they looked - those pale, chinless faces and great, lidless, pinkish-grey eyes! - as they stared in their blindness and bewilderment. But I did not stay to look, I promise you: I retreated again, and when my second match had ended, I struck my third. It had almost burnt through when I reached the opening into the shaft. I lay down on the edge, for the throb of the great pump below made me giddy. Then I felt sideways for the projecting hooks, and, as I did so, my feet were grasped from behind, and I was violently tugged backward. I lit my last match … and it incontinently went out. But I had my hand on the climbing bars now, and, kicking violently, I disengaged myself from the clutches of the Morlocks, and was speedily clambering up the shaft, while they stayed peering and blinking up at me: all but one little wretch who followed me for some way, and well-nigh secured my boot as a trophy.

input: I then tried to protect myself from the horror that was coming over me by viewing it as a strict punishment for human selfishness. People had been content to live in comfort and pleasure through the labor of others, had taken Necessity as their motto and excuse, and in time Necessity had come back to them. I even tried to feel a Carlyle-like scorn for this miserable aristocracy in decline. But this way of thinking was not possible for me. No matter how great their intellectual decline, the Eloi had retained too much of the human form not to earn my sympathy, and this tended to make me share, whether I wished it or not, in their decline and their fear. In the end, I found that I could not separate myself from the Eloi or regard their suffering as something they simply deserved.
output: “Then I tried to preserve myself from the horror that was coming upon me, by regarding it as a rigorous punishment of human selfishness. Man had been content to live in ease and delight upon the labours of his fellow-man, had taken Necessity as his watchword and excuse, and in the fullness of time Necessity had come home to him. I even tried a Carlyle-like scorn of this wretched aristocracy in decay. But this attitude of mind was impossible. However great their intellectual degradation, the Eloi had kept too much of the human form not to claim my sympathy, and to make me perforce a sharer in their degradation and their Fear.

input: Fruit, by the way, tended to be their entire diet. The fruits, though, were quite delightful; one in particular, which seemed to be in season the whole time I was there—a floury thing in a three-sided husk—was especially good, and I made it my staple. At first I was puzzled by all these strange fruits and by the strange flowers I saw, but later I began to understand their significance. input: After some time, I got up and started walking through the bushes toward the hill again, perhaps feeling a bit aimless. I reminded myself to be patient. If I wanted to retrieve my machine, it might be wise to leave the sphinx alone. If they intended to take my machine away, then damaging their bronze panels probably wouldn’t help, and if they didn’t, I would likely get it back as soon as I asked. Sitting amongst all those unfamiliar things, facing such a puzzle, may lead to a sense of hopelessness. It seems more beneficial to engage with this world, to observe its patterns, and to be cautious about making quick assumptions regarding its meaning. In time, I might uncover the clues I seek. Then, the humorous aspect of my situation struck me: I had dedicated years to studying and striving to enter this future age, and now I was anxiously eager to escape it. I had created what felt like an incredibly complex and inescapable trap for myself. Even as I recognized the irony, I found myself laughing.
output: “I got up after a time, and began walking aimlessly through the bushes towards the hill again. ‘Patience,’ said I to myself. ‘If you want your machine again you must leave that sphinx alone. If they mean to take your machine away, it’s little good your wrecking their bronze panels, and if they don’t, you will get it back as soon as you can ask for it. To sit among all those unknown things before a puzzle like that is hopeless. That way lies monomania. Face this world. Learn its ways, watch it, be careful of too hasty guesses at its meaning. In the end you will find clues to it all.’ Then suddenly the humour of the situation came into my mind: the thought of the years I had spent in study and toil to get into the future age, and now my passion of anxiety to get out of it. I had made myself the most complicated and the most hopeless trap that ever a man devised. Although it was at my own expense, I could not help myself. I laughed aloud.

author: H. G. Wells

input: Additionally, it is still my conviction that the fact that this box of matches had withstood the effects of time for an indefinite number of years was a highly unusual, and indeed fortunate, occurrence. Furthermore, I discovered a substance that was even more unlikely to have survived, namely camphor, which I found in a sealed jar that had, apparently by chance, been effectively hermetically sealed. Initially, I mistook it for paraffin wax and, as a result, broke the glass container, but the distinctive odour of camphor was readily identifiable. In the context of the widespread decay that surrounded me, it was remarkable that this volatile substance had managed to endure, possibly for thousands of centuries. Moreover, it brought to mind a sepia painting I had previously seen, which had been created using the ink of a fossilised Belemnite that must have perished and become fossilised millions of years ago. It is worth noting that I was on the verge of discarding the camphor, but I recalled that it was combustible and burned with a bright, intense flame, thereby rendering it a suitable substitute for a candle, and I consequently placed it in my pocket. Nevertheless, I did not find any explosives or means of breaching the bronze doors, and my iron crowbar remained the most useful item I had discovered up to that point. In essence, I departed from that gallery in a state of considerable elation.
output: “Now, I still think that for this box of matches to have escaped the wear of time for immemorial years was a most strange, as for me it was a most fortunate, thing. Yet, oddly enough, I found a far unlikelier substance, and that was camphor. I found it in a sealed jar, that by chance, I suppose, had been really hermetically sealed. I fancied at first that it was paraffin wax, and smashed the glass accordingly. But the odour of camphor was unmistakable. In the universal decay this volatile substance had chanced to survive, perhaps through many thousands of centuries. It reminded me of a sepia painting I had once seen done from the ink of a fossil Belemnite that must have perished and become fossilised millions of years ago. I was about to throw it away, but I remembered that it was inflammable and burnt with a good bright flame - was, in fact, an excellent candle - and I put it in my pocket. I found no explosives, however, nor any means of breaking down the bronze doors. As yet my iron crowbar was the most helpful thing I had chanced upon. Nevertheless I left that gallery greatly elated.

input: I found myself in a more precarious situation than before. Previously, I had maintained a sense of hope for eventual escape, despite the difficulties I faced, including the distressing loss of the Time Machine. However, this hope was shaken by my new discoveries. Until then, I had attributed my challenges to the simplistic nature of the little people and unknown forces that I believed I could overcome once I understood them. The Morlocks introduced a new and unsettling element, characterized by an inhuman and malevolent quality that instinctively evoked a strong sense of aversion. This highlights a significant shift in my perception, as I transitioned from feeling like a person who had fallen into a pit, focused on finding a way out, to feeling like a trapped animal, aware that a threatening entity would soon be upon me. Ultimately, my situation had become even more dire, with a heightened sense of vulnerability and urgency.
output: “Now, indeed, I seemed in a worse case than before. Hitherto, except during my night’s anguish at the loss of the Time Machine, I had felt a sustaining hope of ultimate escape, but that hope was staggered by these new discoveries. Hitherto I had merely thought myself impeded by the childish simplicity of the little people, and by some unknown forces which I had only to understand to overcome; but there was an altogether new element in the sickening quality of the Morlocks - a something inhuman and malign. Instinctively I loathed them. Before, I had felt as a man might feel who had fallen into a pit: my concern was with the pit and how to get out of it. Now I felt like a beast in a trap, whose enemy would come upon him soon.

author: H. G. Wells

input: I looked up once more at the crouching white shape, and the full temerity of my voyage came suddenly upon me. It is worth noting that I wondered what might appear when that hazy curtain was altogether withdrawn. Furthermore, I considered what might not have happened to men. Moreover, I asked myself what might occur if cruelty had grown into a common passion. In essence, I pondered what might have transpired if in this interval the race had lost its manliness and had developed into something inhuman, unsympathetic, and overwhelmingly powerful. Additionally, it seemed possible that I might appear as some old-world savage animal, only the more dreadful and disgusting for our common likeness, a foul creature to be incontinently slain.

input: I took Weena's hand. Subsequently, struck by a sudden idea, I released her grasp and turned towards a machine that featured a lever reminiscent of those found in a signal box. Ascending to the platform and firmly grasping this lever, I applied all of my weight to it sideways. At that moment, Weena, left alone in the central aisle, began to whimper. I had accurately assessed the strength of the lever, as it snapped after a minute of exertion, allowing me to rejoin her armed with a mace that I deemed more than sufficient for any Morlock skull I might encounter. It is worth noting that I felt a strong desire to confront and eliminate a Morlock or two. One might consider it inhumane to wish to harm one’s own descendants; however, it was extraordinarily difficult to sense any humanity within those creatures. Only my reluctance to abandon Weena and the belief that indulging my murderous impulses might jeopardize my Time Machine kept me from advancing down the gallery to confront the brutes I could hear.
output: “I took Weena’s hand. Then, struck with a sudden idea, I left her and turned to a machine from which projected a lever not unlike those in a signal-box. Clambering upon the stand, and grasping this lever in my hands, I put all my weight upon it sideways. Suddenly Weena, deserted in the central aisle, began to whimper. I had judged the strength of the lever pretty correctly, for it snapped after a minute’s strain, and I rejoined her with a mace in my hand more than sufficient, I judged, for any Morlock skull I might encounter. And I longed very much to kill a Morlock or so. Very inhuman, you may think, to want to go killing one’s own descendants! But it was impossible, somehow, to feel any humanity in the things. Only my disinclination to leave Weena, and a persuasion that if I began to slake my thirst for murder my Time Machine might suffer, restrained me from going straight down the gallery and killing the brutes I heard.

input: I had to climb down a shaft that was perhaps two hundred yards deep. The descent was made by means of metal bars projecting from the sides of the well. These bars were suited to a creature much smaller and lighter than myself, so I quickly became cramped and tired during the descent. I was not merely tired. One of the bars suddenly bent under my weight and nearly swung me off into the darkness below. For a moment I hung by one hand, and after that experience I did not dare to rest again. Although my arms and back soon became acutely painful, I continued climbing down the steep descent as quickly as possible. Looking upward, I saw the opening, a small blue disc in which a star was visible, while little Weena’s head appeared as a round black projection. The thudding sound of a machine below grew louder and more oppressive. Everything except that small disc above was profoundly dark, and when I looked up again Weena had disappeared.
output: “I had to clamber down a shaft of perhaps two hundred yards. The descent was effected by means of metallic bars projecting from the sides of the well, and these being adapted to the needs of a creature much smaller and lighter than myself, I was speedily cramped and fatigued by the descent. For a moment I hung by one hand, and after that experience I did not dare to rest again. Though my arms and back were presently acutely painful, I went on clambering down the sheer descent with as quick a motion as possible. Glancing upward, I saw the aperture, a small blue disc, in which a star was visible, while little Weena’s head showed as a round black projection. The thudding sound of a machine below grew louder and more oppressive. Everything save that little disc above was profoundly dark, and when I looked up again Weena had disappeared.

input: Additionally, as the sun was still partially visible above the horizon, we exited the Palace. Furthermore, I was resolute in my intention to arrive at the White Sphinx early the following morning, and thus, prior to dusk, I planned to navigate through the woods that had previously hindered my progress. In essence, my strategy was to proceed as far as possible during the night, and subsequently, having constructed a fire, to rest in the protective vicinity of its illumination. Moreover, as we journeyed on, I collected any sticks or dried grass that I encountered, and soon my arms were filled with such materials. It is worth noting that, thus encumbered, our advancement was slower than I had initially anticipated, and additionally, Weena was experiencing fatigue. Moreover, I also began to suffer from somnolence, such that it was completely dark before we reached the wood. Upon arriving at the shrubby hill that marked the edge of the wood, Weena would have halted, intimidated by the darkness that lay before us; however, a sense of impending disaster, which ought to have served as a warning, compelled me to continue onward. Additionally, having been without sleep for a period of one night and two days, I was in a state of feverishness and irritability, and I felt the onset of sleep, accompanied by the perceived presence of the Morlocks.
output: “We emerged from the Palace while the sun was still in part above the horizon. I was determined to reach the White Sphinx early the next morning, and ere the dusk I purposed pushing through the woods that had stopped me on the previous journey. My plan was to go as far as possible that night, and then, building a fire, to sleep in the protection of its glare. Accordingly, as we went along I gathered any sticks or dried grass I saw, and presently had my arms full of such litter. Thus loaded, our progress was slower than I had anticipated, and besides Weena was tired. And I, also, began to suffer from sleepiness too; so that it was full night before we reached the wood. Upon the shrubby hill of its edge Weena would have stopped, fearing the darkness before us; but a singular sense of impending calamity, that should indeed have served me as a warning, drove me onward. I had been without sleep for a night and two days, and I was feverish and irritable. I felt sleep coming upon me, and the Morlocks with it.

author: H. G. Wells

input: Additionally, it is worth noting that, at that particular point in time, none of us fully accepted the validity of the Time Machine. In essence, the Time Traveller was a individual who possessed a level of intellectual sophistication that made him difficult to comprehend; one never felt that they had a complete understanding of his character, as there was always a suspicion of a subtle reserve or a hidden motive behind his apparent frankness. Furthermore, had Filby presented the model and provided an explanation in his own words, we would have been less inclined to be sceptical, for we would have been able to discern his motivations, which would have been more readily apparent, given his more straightforward nature. Moreover, the Time Traveller's personality was characterized by a certain degree of unpredictability, which led us to be wary of him. It is a common phenomenon that individuals who accomplish tasks with ease are often viewed with a degree of suspicion, and in the case of the Time Traveller, his exceptional abilities only served to heighten our doubts. Consequently, those who took him seriously never felt entirely confident in their assessment of his behaviour, as they were aware that placing their trust in him was akin to entrusting delicate items to a vulnerable environment. Moreover, in the interval between that Thursday and the next, none of us engaged in extensive discussions about time travelling, although it is likely that the notion, with its inherent potentialities and paradoxes, remained a topic of consideration for many of us. In essence, the concept of time travelling, with its implausible yet intriguing possibilities, including the potential for anachronisms and confusion, was a subject that continued to occupy our thoughts. Additionally, I was particularly preoccupied with the mechanism of the model, and I recall discussing it with the Medical Man, whom I encountered on Friday at the Linnæan. He mentioned that he had seen a similar device at Tübingen and placed considerable emphasis on the extinguishing of the candle, although he was unable to provide a satisfactory explanation for the underlying principle of the trick.
output: I think that at that time none of us quite believed in the Time Machine. The fact is, the Time Traveller was one of those men who are too clever to be believed: you never felt that you saw all round him; you always suspected some subtle reserve, some ingenuity in ambush, behind his lucid frankness. Had Filby shown the model and explained the matter in the Time Traveller’s words, we should have shown him far less scepticism. For we should have perceived his motives: a pork-butcher could understand Filby. But the Time Traveller had more than a touch of whim among his elements, and we distrusted him. Things that would have made the fame of a less clever man seemed tricks in his hands. It is a mistake to do things too easily. The serious people who took him seriously never felt quite sure of his deportment; they were somehow aware that trusting their reputations for judgment with him was like furnishing a nursery with eggshell china. So I don’t think any of us said very much about time travelling in the interval between that Thursday and the next, though its odd potentialities ran, no doubt, in most of our minds: its plausibility, that is, its practical incredibleness, the curious possibilities of anachronism and of utter confusion it suggested. For my own part, I was particularly preoccupied with the trick of the model. That I remember discussing with the Medical Man, whom I met on Friday at the Linnæan. He said he had seen a similar thing at Tübingen, and laid considerable stress on the blowing-out of the candle. But how the trick was done he could not explain.
