author: H. G. Wells

input: The narrative describes a journey through time, marked by a fascination with the fate of Earth. Over the course of thirty million years, the sun appears to grow larger and duller in the western sky, while life on Earth diminishes. Eventually, the sun obscures a significant portion of the night sky. The observer notes the absence of crabs and a lifeless scene on the beach, which is now marked by sparse green liverworts and lichens, along with patches of white. A cold atmosphere prevails, accompanied by occasional falling snowflakes. To the northeast, a blanket of snow reflects starlight, revealing pinkish-white hills. The edges of the sea are lined with ice, while the main body of the ocean remains unfrozen, bathed in a reddish hue beneath the perpetual sunset. This suggests a stark transformation in the environment, highlighting a shift toward desolation.
output: “So I travelled, stopping ever and again, in great strides of a thousand years or more, drawn on by the mystery of the earth’s fate, watching with a strange fascination the sun grow larger and duller in the westward sky, and the life of the old earth ebb away. At last, more than thirty million years hence, the huge red-hot dome of the sun had come to obscure nearly a tenth part of the darkling heavens. Then I stopped once more, for the crawling multitude of crabs had disappeared, and the red beach, save for its livid green liverworts and lichens, seemed lifeless. And now it was flecked with white. A bitter cold assailed me. Rare white flakes ever and again came eddying down. To the north-eastward, the glare of snow lay under the starlight of the sable sky, and I could see an undulating crest of hillocks pinkish white. There were fringes of ice along the sea margin, with drifting masses farther out; but the main expanse of that salt ocean, all bloody under the eternal sunset, was still unfrozen.

input: With changes in our circumstances, there tend to be adaptations that follow. It can be worth considering the factors that contribute to human intelligence and vitality, which may include challenges and the presence of freedom. These conditions often favor the survival of the strong, active, and perceptive, while those who are weaker may struggle. Such environments tend to encourage the collaboration of capable individuals, emphasizing qualities such as self-discipline, patience, and decisiveness. The family unit, along with the emotions it evokes—such as intense jealousy, strong affection for children, and parental devotion—may find their basis in the potential threats faced by the young. However, one might observe that these looming dangers are becoming less pronounced, leading to a growing sentiment against traditional notions of marital jealousy, intense maternal instincts, and various forms of passion. These feelings may increasingly be viewed as unnecessary and uncomfortable remnants of a more primitive existence, creating tensions in a more refined and harmonious way of life. In summary, societal shifts may influence how we perceive and respond to familial emotions and relationships.
output: “But with this change in condition comes inevitably adaptations to the change. What, unless biological science is a mass of errors, is the cause of human intelligence and vigour? Hardship and freedom: conditions under which the active, strong, and subtle survive and the weaker go to the wall; conditions that put a premium upon the loyal alliance of capable men, upon self-restraint, patience, and decision. And the institution of the family, and the emotions that arise therein, the fierce jealousy, the tenderness for offspring, parental self-devotion, all found their justification and support in the imminent dangers of the young. Now, where are these imminent dangers? There is a sentiment arising, and it will grow, against connubial jealousy, against fierce maternity, against passion of all sorts; unnecessary things now, and things that make us uncomfortable, savage survivals, discords in a refined and pleasant life.

input: I returned after a period during which I might have been unaware while on the machine. The cycle of days and nights resumed, the sun appeared golden once more, and the sky was blue. I felt I could breathe more easily. The changing shapes of the land seemed to rise and fall. The hands on the dials appeared to move backward. Eventually, I recognized the faint outlines of houses, signs of human life in decline. These, too, transformed and were replaced by others. When the million dial reached zero, I gradually reduced my speed. I started to identify our familiar and charming architecture as the thousands hand reversed to its starting point, and the rhythm of night and day slowed down. Soon, I found myself surrounded by the old walls of the laboratory. With care, I began to slow the mechanism further. This experience suggests a return to familiarity and the gradual re-emergence of the known environment.
output: “So I came back. For a long time I must have been insensible upon the machine. The blinking succession of the days and nights was resumed, the sun got golden again, the sky blue. I breathed with greater freedom. The fluctuating contours of the land ebbed and flowed. The hands spun backward upon the dials. At last I saw again the dim shadows of houses, the evidences of decadent humanity. These, too, changed and passed, and others came. Presently, when the million dial was at zero, I slackened speed. I began to recognise our own pretty and familiar architecture, the thousands hand ran back to the starting-point, the night and day flapped slower and slower. Then the old walls of the laboratory came round me. Very gently, now, I slowed the mechanism down.

I proceeded out of the gallery and into another, which was even larger. At first glance, this new space resembled a military chapel adorned with tattered flags. However, upon closer inspection, I realized that the brown and charred rags hanging from the sides were actually the remnants of books. These books had deteriorated to the point where they had fallen apart, and all traces of print had disappeared. Nevertheless, the presence of warped boards and cracked metallic clasps still told a story. 

Meanwhile, the scene before me was a testament to the enormous amount of wasted labor. The sheer scale of the decay and rot was striking. As I took in the sight, I couldn't help but think of my own work, particularly the Philosophical Transactions and my seventeen papers on physical optics. Additionally, the thought of such a vast amount of knowledge and effort being reduced to nothing more than rotting paper was a sobering one. Furthermore, the experience had a profound impact on my perspective, and it led me to consider the broader implications of such a sombre wilderness of decay.
output: “Well, mace in one hand and Weena in the other, I went out of that gallery and into another and still larger one, which at the first glance reminded me of a military chapel hung with tattered flags. The brown and charred rags that hung from the sides of it, I presently recognised as the decaying vestiges of books. They had long since dropped to pieces, and every semblance of print had left them. But here and there were warped boards and cracked metallic clasps that told the tale well enough. Had I been a literary man I might, perhaps, have moralised upon the futility of all ambition. But as it was, the thing that struck me with keenest force was the enormous waste of labour to which this sombre wilderness of rotting paper testified. At the time I will confess that I thought chiefly of the Philosophical Transactions and my own seventeen papers upon physical optics.

input: As I stepped out of the large hall, the world was bathed in the gentle evening light, with the setting sun casting a warm glow over the scene. output: “The calm of evening was upon the world as I emerged from the great hall, and the scene was lit by the warm glow of the setting sun. At first things were very confusing. Everything was so entirely different from the world I had known - even the flowers. The big building I had left was situated on the slope of a broad river valley, but the Thames had shifted, perhaps, a mile from its present position. I resolved to mount to the summit of a crest, perhaps a mile and a half away, from which I could get a wider view of this our planet in the year Eight Hundred and Two Thousand Seven Hundred and One, A.D. For that, I should explain, was the date the little dials of my machine recorded.

input:
“I must admit,” the Editor remarked with a touch of humor, “these gentlemen here suggest you’ve been traveling into the middle of next week! Could you share your experiences with little Rosebery? I’m curious about what you might offer for it all.” 

The Time Traveller made his way to the designated spot without uttering a word. He smiled in his usual manner. “Where’s my mutton?” he inquired. “It’s quite a pleasure to have meat again!” 

“I would be willing to pay a shilling a line for a detailed account,” the Editor commented. The Time Traveller then nudged his glass toward the Silent Man and tapped it lightly with his fingernail, causing the Silent Man, who had been observing him intently, to jump and pour him some wine. The remainder of the dinner felt somewhat tense. Personally, I found myself grappling with many questions, and I suspect others did as well. The Journalist attempted to ease the atmosphere by sharing stories about Hettie Potter. Meanwhile, the Time Traveller focused on his meal, showing an appetite reminiscent of someone quite famished. The Medical Man leisurely smoked a cigarette, glancing at the Time Traveller from beneath his lashes. The Silent Man appeared somewhat awkward and eagerly drank champagne, perhaps to calm his nerves. Eventually, the Time Traveller set his plate aside and looked around at us. “I suppose I should apologize,” he said. “I was quite hungry. I’ve had an extraordinary experience.” He reached for a cigar and clipped the end. “However, let’s move to the smoking-room. It’s too lengthy a tale for this setting.” With that, he signaled for the bell and walked toward the adjoining room.
output:
“I say,” said the Editor hilariously, “these chaps here say you have been travelling into the middle of next week! Tell us all about little Rosebery, will you? What will you take for the lot?”

The Time Traveller came to the place reserved for him without a word. He smiled quietly, in his old way. “Where’s my mutton?” he said. “What a treat it is to stick a fork into meat again!”

“I’d give a shilling a line for a verbatim note,” said the Editor. The Time Traveller pushed his glass towards the Silent Man and rang it with his fingernail; at which the Silent Man, who had been staring at his face, started convulsively, and poured him wine. The rest of the dinner was uncomfortable. For my own part, sudden questions kept on rising to my lips, and I dare say it was the same with the others. The Journalist tried to relieve the tension by telling anecdotes of Hettie Potter. The Time Traveller devoted his attention to his dinner, and displayed the appetite of a tramp. The Medical Man smoked a cigarette, and watched the Time Traveller through his eyelashes. The Silent Man seemed even more clumsy than usual, and drank champagne with regularity and determination out of sheer nervousness. At last the Time Traveller pushed his plate away, and looked round us. “I suppose I must apologise,” he said. “I was simply starving. I’ve had a most amazing time.” He reached out his hand for a cigar, and cut the end. “But come into the smoking-room. It’s too long a story to tell over greasy plates.” And ringing the bell in passing, he led the way into the adjoining room.

input: Upon closer examination of their features, I observed additional peculiarities in their delicate appearance reminiscent of Dresden china. Their uniformly curly hair ended sharply at the neck and cheeks, with no trace of it on their faces. Their ears were notably small. The mouths were petite, adorned with bright red, thin lips, and their small chins tapered to a point. Their eyes were large and gentle; however, I could not help but feel that there was a certain absence of the interest I might have anticipated from them.
output: “And then, looking more nearly into their features, I saw some further peculiarities in their Dresden china type of prettiness. Their hair, which was uniformly curly, came to a sharp end at the neck and cheek; there was not the faintest suggestion of it on the face, and their ears were singularly minute. The mouths were small, with bright red, rather thin lips, and the little chins ran to a point. The eyes were large and mild; and - this may seem egotism on my part - I fancied even that there was a certain lack of the interest I might have expected in them.

It is worth noting that you have only just arrived. This situation is quite peculiar. He is unavoidably detained and has requested in this note that I initiate dinner at seven if he has not returned. He indicated that he would provide an explanation upon his arrival.

Furthermore, the Editor of a prominent daily publication remarked that it seemed unfortunate to allow the dinner to go to waste, and consequently, the Doctor rang the bell.

Additionally, the Psychologist was the only other individual present, besides the Doctor and myself, who had also attended the previous dinner. The other attendees included Blank, the aforementioned Editor, a particular journalist, and another individual—a reserved, timid man with a beard—whom I did not recognize, and who, based on my observations, remained silent throughout the evening. There was some speculation at the dinner table regarding the absence of the Time Traveller, to which I suggested the possibility of time travel in a rather light-hearted manner. The Editor requested clarification, and the Psychologist offered a somewhat wooden explanation of the "ingenious paradox and trick" we had observed the previous week. He was in the process of delivering his account when the door from the corridor opened slowly and silently. I was positioned to face the door and noticed it first. “Hello!” I exclaimed. “At last!” As the door opened wider, the Time Traveller appeared before us. I gasped in astonishment. “Good heavens! What has happened to you?” exclaimed the Medical Man, who was the next to see him. At this, the entire assembly turned to face the door.
output:
“You’ve just come? It’s rather odd. He’s unavoidably detained. He asks me in this note to lead off with dinner at seven if he’s not back. Says he’ll explain when he comes.”

“It seems a pity to let the dinner spoil,” said the Editor of a well-known daily paper; and thereupon the Doctor rang the bell.

The Psychologist was the only person besides the Doctor and myself who had attended the previous dinner. The other men were Blank, the Editor aforementioned, a certain journalist, and another - a quiet, shy man with a beard - whom I didn’t know, and who, as far as my observation went, never opened his mouth all the evening. There was some speculation at the dinner-table about the Time Traveller’s absence, and I suggested time travelling, in a half-jocular spirit. The Editor wanted that explained to him, and the Psychologist volunteered a wooden account of the “ingenious paradox and trick” we had witnessed that day week. He was in the midst of his exposition when the door from the corridor opened slowly and without noise. I was facing the door, and saw it first. “Hallo!” I said. “At last!” And the door opened wider, and the Time Traveller stood before us. I gave a cry of surprise. “Good heavens! man, what’s the matter?” cried the Medical Man, who saw him next. And the whole tableful turned towards the door.

output: “I was in an agony of discomfort. I had some thought of trying to go up the shaft again, and leave the Underworld alone. But even while I turned this over in my mind I continued to descend. At last, with intense relief, I saw dimly coming up, a foot to the right of me, a slender loophole in the wall. Swinging myself in, I found it was the aperture of a narrow horizontal tunnel in which I could lie down and rest. It was not too soon. My arms ached, my back was cramped, and I was trembling with the prolonged terror of a fall. Besides this, the unbroken darkness had had a distressing effect upon my eyes. The air was full of the throb and hum of machinery pumping air down the shaft.

input: The tendency of wealthier individuals, influenced by their advanced education and the widening divide from the harsh realities faced by the poor, is resulting in the restriction of significant portions of land for their benefit. In the vicinity of London, for example, nearly half of the more attractive countryside is effectively closed off to outsiders. This growing divide, stemming from the lengthy and costly nature of higher education along with the increased allure of refined living for the affluent, will likely diminish the interactions between social classes. The frequency of intermarriage, which currently serves to slow the fragmentation of society into distinct social strata, will become increasingly rare. Ultimately, society will consist of the Haves, who pursue pleasure, comfort, and beauty, and the Have-nots, the Workers, who will continuously adapt to their labor conditions. Once relegated underground, these individuals would likely have to pay rent for the ventilation of their living spaces. If they failed to do so, they would face starvation or suffocation due to unpaid dues. Those among them who were prone to despair and revolt would perish, leaving behind a stable population that would adapt to underground life, finding a semblance of happiness akin to that of the people above. The refined beauty of the upper classes and the pallor of the lower classes appear to follow this scenario quite naturally.
output: “Again, the exclusive tendency of richer people - due, no doubt, to the increasing refinement of their education, and the widening gulf between them and the rude violence of the poor - is already leading to the closing, in their interest, of considerable portions of the surface of the land. About London, for instance, perhaps half the prettier country is shut in against intrusion. And this same widening gulf - which is due to the length and expense of the higher educational process and the increased facilities for and temptations towards refined habits on the part of the rich - will make that exchange between class and class, that promotion by intermarriage which at present retards the splitting of our species along lines of social stratification, less and less frequent. So, in the end, above ground you must have the Haves, pursuing pleasure and comfort and beauty, and below ground the Have-nots, the Workers getting continually adapted to the conditions of their labour. Once they were there, they would no doubt have to pay rent, and not a little of it, for the ventilation of their caverns; and if they refused, they would starve or be suffocated for arrears. Such of them as were so constituted as to be miserable and rebellious would die; and, in the end, the balance being permanent, the survivors would become as well adapted to the conditions of underground life, and as happy in their way, as the Overworld people were to theirs. As it seemed to me, the refined beauty and the etiolated pallor followed naturally enough.

input: The narrator urgently ran through the dining hall, inadvertently knocking over someone while making their way outside into the moonlight. They heard cries of fear and the sound of small feet running in various directions. The events that transpired during the night are unclear, but it is suggested that the unexpected nature of their loss caused a deep sense of madness and isolation. The narrator experienced a feeling of being disconnected from their own kind, likening themselves to a strange creature in an unfamiliar environment. They raved about, expressing their anguish and despair towards God and Fate. As the night progressed, they felt an overwhelming fatigue and searched through the desolate landscape, encountering strange beings in the shadows. Eventually, they found themselves lying near a sphinx, consumed by feelings of misery and frustration over their lost strength. After this, the narrator fell asleep, and upon waking, it was daytime, with a couple of sparrows nearby on the grass.
output: “Abruptly, I dashed down the match, and knocking one of the people over in my course, went blundering across the big dining-hall again, out under the moonlight. I heard cries of terror and their little feet running and stumbling this way and that. I do not remember all I did as the moon crept up the sky. I suppose it was the unexpected nature of my loss that maddened me. I felt hopelessly cut off from my own kind - a strange animal in an unknown world. I must have raved to and fro, screaming and crying upon God and Fate. I have a memory of horrible fatigue, as the long night of despair wore away; of looking in this impossible place and that; of groping among moonlit ruins and touching strange creatures in the black shadows; at last, of lying on the ground near the sphinx and weeping with absolute wretchedness, even anger at the folly of leaving the machine having leaked away with my strength. I had nothing left but misery. Then I slept, and when I woke again it was full day, and a couple of sparrows were hopping round me on the turf within reach of my arm.

author: H. G. Wells

input: Weena drew close to my side, startling me in the process. This highlights the fact that, had she not been there, I may not have noticed the floor of the gallery sloping downward. It is possible that the slope was not a feature of the floor itself, but rather a result of the museum being built into the side of a hill. The entrance I had used was above ground level and received light through narrow, slit-like windows. As I made my way down the length of the gallery, the ground outside rose to meet these windows, eventually creating a pit-like area in front of each one, with only a thin line of daylight visible at the top. I proceeded slowly, preoccupied with the machines on display, and had not noticed the gradual decrease in light until Weena's growing unease caught my attention. Ultimately, I saw that the gallery extended into a region of thick darkness. Upon hesitation, I took stock of my surroundings and observed that the dust on the floor was less prevalent and its surface less uniform. Further ahead, toward the darker area, I noticed a series of small, narrow footprints disrupting the dust. This discovery renewed my awareness of the potential presence of the Morlocks. I realized that I was devoting too much time to examining the machinery and that my situation was becoming increasingly precarious. With the afternoon wearing on, I still lacked a weapon, a place of refuge, and a means of starting a fire. Then, from the distant darkness of the gallery, I heard a strange pattering sound, accompanied by the same unusual noises I had previously heard near the well.
output: “Suddenly Weena came very close to my side. So suddenly that she startled me. Had it not been for her I do not think I should have noticed that the floor of the gallery sloped at all. [Footnote: It may be, of course, that the floor did not slope, but that the museum was built into the side of a hill. - ED.] The end I had come in at was quite above ground, and was lit by rare slit-like windows. As you went down the length, the ground came up against these windows, until at last there was a pit like the ‘area‘ of a London house before each, and only a narrow line of daylight at the top. I went slowly along, puzzling about the machines, and had been too intent upon them to notice the gradual diminution of the light, until Weena’s increasing apprehensions drew my attention. Then I saw that the gallery ran down at last into a thick darkness. I hesitated, and then, as I looked round me, I saw that the dust was less abundant and its surface less even. Further away towards the dimness, it appeared to be broken by a number of small narrow footprints. My sense of the immediate presence of the Morlocks revived at that. I felt that I was wasting my time in this academic examination of machinery. I called to mind that it was already far advanced in the afternoon, and that I had still no weapon, no refuge, and no means of making a fire. And then down in the remote blackness of the gallery I heard a peculiar pattering, and the same odd noises I had heard down the well.

input: It appears that the lever was eventually fixed and pulled into position, which allowed me to break free from the restraining hands. As the darkness receded from my vision, I found myself once again in the same grey light and tumultuous environment that I had previously described. It's worth noting that time travelling can often be accompanied by a range of unpleasant symptoms, including sickness and confusion, which I had experienced before. On this particular occasion, I may not have been seated as securely in the saddle as I could have been, which may have contributed to the unstable sensation I felt as the machine swayed and vibrated. For a period of time, I clung to the machine, largely unaware of my surroundings, and when I finally checked the dials again, I was surprised to see where I had ended up. The machine's dials provide a range of measurements, including days, thousands of days, millions of days, and thousands of millions of days. It seems that, rather than reversing the levers, I had pulled them forward, which meant that I was now moving forward in time, and the indicators suggested that I was doing so at a rapid pace, with the thousands hand moving as quickly as the seconds hand of a watch. In summary, I had successfully activated the time machine and was now hurtling forward through time, albeit in a somewhat unpredictable and unstable manner.
output:
“But at last the lever was fixed and pulled over. The clinging hands slipped from me. The darkness presently fell from my eyes. I found myself in the same grey light and tumult I have already described.

“I have already told you of the sickness and confusion that comes with time travelling. And this time I was not seated properly in the saddle, but sideways and in an unstable fashion. For an indefinite time I clung to the machine as it swayed and vibrated, quite unheeding how I went, and when I brought myself to look at the dials again I was amazed to find where I had arrived. One dial records days, and another thousands of days, another millions of days, and another thousands of millions. Now, instead of reversing the levers, I had pulled them over so as to go forward with them, and when I came to look at these indicators I found that the thousands hand was sweeping round as fast as the seconds hand of a watch - into futurity.

author: H. G. Wells

input: I nodded and pointed to the sun, delivering a vivid imitation of a thunderclap that startled them. They stepped back and bowed. Then, one individual approached, laughing, and presented me with a chain of beautiful flowers that were entirely unfamiliar to me. This gesture was met with melodious applause, and soon they were all running around to gather more flowers, joyfully tossing them over me until I was nearly buried in blossoms. Those who have never witnessed such a spectacle can hardly imagine the delicate and extraordinary flowers that years of cultivation had produced. Then, someone proposed that their "plaything" be displayed in the nearest building, and I was guided past a white marble sphinx, which seemed to observe my astonishment with a knowing smile, toward a vast grey structure adorned with intricate stonework. As I walked with them, I recalled my earlier confident expectations of a profoundly serious and intellectual future, which brought me an irresistible sense of amusement.
output: “I nodded, pointed to the sun, and gave them such a vivid rendering of a thunderclap as startled them. They all withdrew a pace or so and bowed. Then came one laughing towards me, carrying a chain of beautiful flowers altogether new to me, and put it about my neck. The idea was received with melodious applause; and presently they were all running to and fro for flowers, and laughingly flinging them upon me until I was almost smothered with blossom. You who have never seen the like can scarcely imagine what delicate and wonderful flowers countless years of culture had created. Then someone suggested that their plaything should be exhibited in the nearest building, and so I was led past the sphinx of white marble, which had seemed to watch me all the while with a smile at my astonishment, towards a vast grey edifice of fretted stone. As I went with them the memory of my confident anticipations of a profoundly grave and intellectual posterity came, with irresistible merriment, to my mind.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input:
The Journalist asked what was going on, inquiring if the Time Traveller had been engaging in questionable behavior. I exchanged a glance with the Psychologist and saw my own interpretation reflected in his expression. I recalled the Time Traveller's noticeable lameness as he walked upstairs earlier, which seemed to have gone unnoticed by the others. 

This highlights the fact that the group was still trying to process the unexpected events unfolding before them. The Medical Man was the first to compose himself, ringing the bell for a hot plate, as the Time Traveller disliked having servants waiting during dinner. The Editor and the Silent Man then resumed eating, and the conversation became exclamatory, with periods of wonderment. Ultimately, the Editor's curiosity got the better of him, and he began to ask questions, suggesting that the Time Traveller might be supplementing his income in unusual ways. 

I took up the story, recounting the Psychologist's account of our previous meeting, which sparked incredulity among the new guests. The Editor raised objections, questioning the concept of time travel and suggesting that it was impossible for a person to become dusty simply by traveling through time. This suggests that the group was struggling to understand the idea of time travel, and the Editor, in particular, was skeptical. As the conversation continued, the Editor and the Journalist, both young and irreverent, began to ridicule the idea, with the Journalist even resorting to caricature, joking about the lack of clothes-brushes in the future. This tone prevailed until the Time Traveller returned, dressed in ordinary evening clothes, with only his haggard appearance remaining as a reminder of the earlier events.
output:
“What’s the game?” said the Journalist. “Has he been doing the Amateur Cadger? I don’t follow.” I met the eye of the Psychologist, and read my own interpretation in his face. I thought of the Time Traveller limping painfully upstairs. I don’t think anyone else had noticed his lameness.

The first to recover completely from this surprise was the Medical Man, who rang the bell - the Time Traveller hated to have servants waiting at dinner - for a hot plate. At that the Editor turned to his knife and fork with a grunt, and the Silent Man followed suit. The dinner was resumed. Conversation was exclamatory for a little while with gaps of wonderment; and then the Editor got fervent in his curiosity. “Does our friend eke out his modest income with a crossing? or has he his Nebuchadnezzar phases?” he inquired. “I feel assured it’s this business of the Time Machine,” I said, and took up the Psychologist’s account of our previous meeting. The new guests were frankly incredulous. The Editor raised objections. “What was this time travelling? A man couldn’t cover himself with dust by rolling in a paradox, could he?” And then, as the idea came home to him, he resorted to caricature. Hadn’t they any clothes-brushes in the Future? The Journalist too, would not believe at any price, and joined the Editor in the easy work of heaping ridicule on the whole thing. They were both the new kind of journalist - very joyous, irreverent young men. “Our Special Correspondent in the Day after Tomorrow reports,” the Journalist was saying - or rather shouting - when the Time Traveller came back. He was dressed in ordinary evening clothes, and nothing save his haggard look remained of the change that had startled me.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: The narrator expresses determination despite facing obstacles. They strike the bronze panels with their fist, initially believing they might have heard a sound from within, possibly a chuckle, although they later doubt this perception. To make an impact, they pick up a pebble from the river and begin hammering, eventually flattening part of the decorative design and causing the verdigris to flake away. It is suggested that the nearby delicate figures could hear the hammering from a distance, yet they do not respond. Observing a group of these figures watching from the slopes, the narrator eventually sits down to monitor the area. However, they find it difficult to remain still, indicating a preference for active engagement over passive waiting, which they feel is challenging.
output: “But I was not beaten yet. I banged with my fist at the bronze panels. I thought I heard something stir inside - to be explicit, I thought I heard a sound like a chuckle - but I must have been mistaken. Then I got a big pebble from the river, and came and hammered till I had flattened a coil in the decorations, and the verdigris came off in powdery flakes. The delicate little people must have heard me hammering in gusty outbreaks a mile away on either hand, but nothing came of it. I saw a crowd of them upon the slopes, looking furtively at me. At last, hot and tired, I sat down to watch the place. But I was too restless to watch long; I am too Occidental for a long vigil. I could work at a problem for years, but to wait inactive for twenty-four hours - that is another matter.

author: H. G. Wells

input: This occurred in the morning. Later in the afternoon, I encountered a woman, whom I believe was significant to me, as I returned from an exploration. She greeted me with visible joy and offered me a large garland of flowers that appeared to be meant specifically for me. This gesture captured my imagination and likely alleviated feelings of desolation I had been experiencing. I made an effort to show my gratitude for the gift. We soon found ourselves sitting together in a small stone arbour, engaged in conversation that consisted mainly of smiles. Her warmth affected me in a manner similar to that of a child’s affection. We exchanged flowers, and she kissed my hands, which I reciprocated. When I attempted to communicate further, I learned her name was Weena. Although I was unsure of its meaning, it felt fitting. This marked the beginning of a unique friendship that lasted for a week, concluding in a manner I will describe later.
output: “This happened in the morning. In the afternoon I met my little woman, as I believe it was, as I was returning towards my centre from an exploration, and she received me with cries of delight and presented me with a big garland of flowers - evidently made for me and me alone. The thing took my imagination. Very possibly I had been feeling desolate. At any rate I did my best to display my appreciation of the gift. We were soon seated together in a little stone arbour, engaged in conversation, chiefly of smiles. The creature’s friendliness affected me exactly as a child’s might have done. We passed each other flowers, and she kissed my hands. I did the same to hers. Then I tried talk, and found that her name was Weena, which, though I don’t know what it meant, somehow seemed appropriate enough. That was the beginning of a queer friendship which lasted a week, and ended - as I will tell you!
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: A young man attempted to relight his cigar while expressing his agreement. He remarked that the concept being discussed was very clear. The Time Traveller then noted that it is quite remarkable how often this concept is overlooked. He explained that what is referred to as the Fourth Dimension is essentially another perspective on Time. The distinction between Time and the three dimensions of Space lies in the way our consciousness navigates through them. However, some individuals have misunderstood this notion. He inquired whether those present were familiar with the various interpretations surrounding the Fourth Dimension.
output:
“That,” said a very young man, making spasmodic efforts to relight his cigar over the lamp; “that... very clear indeed.”

“Now, it is very remarkable that this is so extensively overlooked,” continued the Time Traveller, with a slight accession of cheerfulness. “Really this is what is meant by the Fourth Dimension, though some people who talk about the Fourth Dimension do not know they mean it. It is only another way of looking at Time. There is no difference between Time and any of the three dimensions of Space except that our consciousness moves along it. But some foolish people have got hold of the wrong side of that idea. You have all heard what they have to say about this Fourth Dimension?”
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: From her, too, I learned that fear had not yet left the world. In daylight she was fearless enough, and she had the strangest confidence in me; once, in a foolish moment, I made threatening faces at her, and she simply laughed. But she dreaded the dark, dreaded shadows, dreaded black things. Darkness was, to her, the one thing that inspired dread. It was a remarkably intense emotion, and it prompted me to think and observe. I discovered then, among other things, that these small people gathered in the great houses after dark and slept in crowds. To enter one of these houses without a light threw them into a turmoil of fear. I never found one of them outdoors after dark, nor one sleeping alone indoors. Yet I was still foolish enough to miss the lesson of that fear, and despite Weena's distress, I insisted on sleeping apart from those slumbering crowds.
output: “It was from her, too, that I learnt that fear had not yet left the world. She was fearless enough in the daylight, and she had the oddest confidence in me; for once, in a foolish moment, I made threatening grimaces at her, and she simply laughed at them. But she dreaded the dark, dreaded shadows, dreaded black things. Darkness to her was the one thing dreadful. It was a singularly passionate emotion, and it set me thinking and observing. I discovered then, among other things, that these little people gathered into the great houses after dark, and slept in droves. To enter upon them without a light was to put them into a tumult of apprehension. I never found one out of doors, or one sleeping alone within doors, after dark. Yet I was still such a blockhead that I missed the lesson of that fear, and in spite of Weena’s distress, I insisted upon sleeping away from these slumbering multitudes.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: Upon observing the ease and security with which these individuals lived, it became apparent that the close resemblance between the sexes was a natural consequence. The traditional characteristics of men and women, the structure of the family unit, and the division of labor are largely driven by the demands of a society reliant on physical force. However, in a population that is balanced and abundant, excessive childbearing can become a burden rather than a benefit to the state. Furthermore, in an environment where violence is rare and offspring are safe, the need for a traditional family structure diminishes, and the specialization of roles based on childrearing responsibilities becomes less relevant. Meanwhile, it is worth noting that similar trends are emerging in our own era, and in this future society, they had become fully realized. At the time, this was my interpretation of the situation, although I would later come to realize that it did not entirely capture the complexity of the reality. Subsequently, my understanding would undergo significant refinement as I gained a deeper appreciation for the actual circumstances.
output: “Seeing the ease and security in which these people were living, I felt that this close resemblance of the sexes was after all what one would expect; for the strength of a man and the softness of a woman, the institution of the family, and the differentiation of occupations are mere militant necessities of an age of physical force. Where population is balanced and abundant, much childbearing becomes an evil rather than a blessing to the State; where violence comes but rarely and offspring are secure, there is less necessity - indeed there is no necessity - for an efficient family, and the specialisation of the sexes with reference to their children’s needs disappears. We see some beginnings of this even in our own time, and in this future age it was complete. This, I must remind you, was my speculation at the time. Later, I was to appreciate how far it fell short of the reality.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: Before balloons, aside from some occasional jumping and the unevenness of the ground, people generally did not have much freedom of vertical movement. Also, it may seem that you cannot move in Time at all, and that you cannot get away from the present moment. But, my dear sir, that is perhaps where you are mistaken, and it may be where the whole world has tended to go wrong. We are, in fact, always moving away from the present moment. Our mental lives, which are immaterial and have no dimensions, tend to pass along the Time Dimension at a steady pace from birth to death, much as we would travel downward if we began our existence fifty miles above the earth’s surface. In short, movement through Time appears to be a constant part of human existence, even if we do not usually notice it.
output:
“But before the balloons, save for spasmodic jumping and the inequalities of the surface, man had no freedom of vertical movement.”

“And you cannot move at all in Time, you cannot get away from the present moment.”

“My dear sir, that is just where you are wrong. That is just where the whole world has gone wrong. We are always getting away from the present moment. Our mental existences, which are immaterial and have no dimensions, are passing along the Time-Dimension with a uniform velocity from the cradle to the grave. Just as we should travel down if we began our existence fifty miles above the earth’s surface.”

author: H. G. Wells

input:
Then I halted the machine and observed once more the familiar surroundings of my laboratory, with my tools and appliances precisely as I had left them. I dismounted from the apparatus unsteadily and seated myself on my workbench. For several minutes, I experienced intense trembling. Subsequently, I attained a state of greater calmness. Surrounding me was my old workshop, unchanged from its previous state. I could have easily believed that I had simply slept there and that the entire experience had been a mere dream.

Furthermore, it is essential to note that the machine had originated from the south-eastern corner of the laboratory. It had come to a rest in the north-west corner, against the wall where you observed it. This detail provides the exact distance from my small lawn to the pedestal of the White Sphinx, to which the Morlocks had transported my machine.
output:
“Then I stopped the machine, and saw about me again the old familiar laboratory, my tools, my appliances just as I had left them. I got off the thing very shakily, and sat down upon my bench. For several minutes I trembled violently. Then I became calmer. Around me was my old workshop again, exactly as it had been. I might have slept there, and the whole thing have been a dream.

“And yet, not exactly! The thing had started from the south-east corner of the laboratory. It had come to rest again in the north-west, against the wall where you saw it. That gives you the exact distance from my little lawn to the pedestal of the White Sphinx, into which the Morlocks had carried my machine.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: Additionally, I must acknowledge that I acquired very little knowledge regarding drains, bells, modes of transportation, and similar conveniences during my time in this actual future. Furthermore, in certain visions of utopias and forthcoming eras that I have encountered, there exists a considerable amount of detail concerning construction, social arrangements, and related matters. Moreover, while such details are readily obtainable when the entire world is contained within one's imagination, they remain entirely inaccessible to an actual traveler amid the realities I encountered here. It is worth noting that one might conceive of the account of London that an individual from Central Africa would bring back to their community. In essence, what would such a person know of railway companies, social movements, telephone and telegraph wires, the Parcels Delivery Company, postal orders, and the like? Yet we, at least, would be sufficiently willing to explain these matters to them. Furthermore, even regarding what such a person did know, how much could they enable an untraveled acquaintance to comprehend or accept? Then consider how narrow the gap between an individual from Central Africa and a white man of our own era, and how wide the interval between myself and those of the Golden Age. I was aware of much that was unseen and that contributed to my comfort; however, apart from a general impression of automatic organization, I fear I can convey very little of the difference to your mind.
output: “And here I must admit that I learnt very little of drains and bells and modes of conveyance, and the like conveniences, during my time in this real future. In some of these visions of Utopias and coming times which I have read, there is a vast amount of detail about building, and social arrangements, and so forth. But while such details are easy enough to obtain when the whole world is contained in one’s imagination, they are altogether inaccessible to a real traveller amid such realities as I found here. Conceive the tale of London which a negro, fresh from Central Africa, would take back to his tribe! What would he know of railway companies, of social movements, of telephone and telegraph wires, of the Parcels Delivery Company, and postal orders and the like? Yet we, at least, should be willing enough to explain these things to him! And even of what he knew, how much could he make his untravelled friend either apprehend or believe? Then, think how narrow the gap between a negro and a white man of our own times, and how wide the interval between myself and these of the Golden Age! I was sensible of much which was unseen, and which contributed to my comfort; but save for a general impression of automatic organisation, I fear I can convey very little of the difference to your mind.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: On the following Thursday, I returned to Richmond, and it appears I had become a frequent visitor to the Time Traveller's residence. Upon arriving late, I found that four or five men had already gathered in the drawing-room. The Medical Man was standing by the fire, holding a sheet of paper in one hand and his watch in the other. As I looked around for the Time Traveller, the Medical Man remarked, "It's half-past seven now," which prompted him to suggest, "I suppose we'd better have dinner." This highlights the informal nature of the gathering, and the group's decision to proceed with dinner in the Time Traveller's absence. Ultimately, the evening was underway, despite the host's tardiness.
output: The next Thursday I went again to Richmond - I suppose I was one of the Time Traveller’s most constant guests - and, arriving late, found four or five men already assembled in his drawing-room. The Medical Man was standing before the fire with a sheet of paper in one hand and his watch in the other. I looked round for the Time Traveller, and - “It’s half-past seven now,” said the Medical Man. “I suppose we’d better have dinner?”
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input:
The Time Traveller directed his attention to us and then to the mechanism. The Psychologist inquired about the situation. 
The Time Traveller began to explain the device, resting his elbows on the table and clasping his hands together above the apparatus. He stated that this particular device was only a model, representing his plan for a machine that would facilitate travel through time. Additionally, he noted that the model appeared somewhat irregular in shape, and a certain bar exhibited a peculiar sparkling effect, giving it an almost intangible quality. Furthermore, he indicated specific components of the model, pointing out a small white lever and another similar one nearby.
output:
The Time Traveller looked at us, and then at the mechanism. “Well?” said the Psychologist.

“This little affair,” said the Time Traveller, resting his elbows upon the table and pressing his hands together above the apparatus, “is only a model. It is my plan for a machine to travel through time. You will notice that it looks singularly askew, and that there is an odd twinkling appearance about this bar, as though it was in some way unreal.” He pointed to the part with his finger. “Also, here is one little white lever, and here is another.”
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: Last Thursday, I shared with some of you the principles behind the Time Machine and presented the incomplete model from the workshop. It is now somewhat worn, with one ivory bar cracked and a brass rail bent; however, the rest remains structurally sound. I anticipated completing it on Friday, but encountered an issue while assembling it. One of the nickel bars was found to be precisely one inch too short, which required a replacement. As a result, the machine was not fully assembled until this morning. At ten o'clock today, the first Time Machine commenced its operation. I made a final adjustment, checked all the screws, added a drop of oil to the quartz rod, and positioned myself in the saddle. At that moment, I experienced a sense of wonder akin to that of a person contemplating a significant decision. With the starting lever in one hand and the stopping lever in the other, I pressed the start button and almost immediately the stop button. I felt disoriented, experiencing a sensation reminiscent of falling, and upon looking around, I observed the laboratory as it had been. I questioned whether anything had occurred. For a brief moment, I wondered if my mind had deceived me. Then, I glanced at the clock. A moment earlier, it had read just past ten o'clock, and now it indicated nearly half-past three.
output: “I told some of you last Thursday of the principles of the Time Machine, and showed you the actual thing itself, incomplete in the workshop. There it is now, a little travel-worn, truly; and one of the ivory bars is cracked, and a brass rail bent; but the rest of it’s sound enough. I expected to finish it on Friday; but on Friday, when the putting together was nearly done, I found that one of the nickel bars was exactly one inch too short, and this I had to get remade; so that the thing was not complete until this morning. It was at ten o’clock today that the first of all Time Machines began its career. I gave it a last tap, tried all the screws again, put one more drop of oil on the quartz rod, and sat myself in the saddle. I suppose a suicide who holds a pistol to his skull feels much the same wonder at what will come next as I felt then. I took the starting lever in one hand and the stopping one in the other, pressed the first, and almost immediately the second. I seemed to reel; I felt a nightmare sensation of falling; and, looking round, I saw the laboratory exactly as before. Had anything happened? For a moment I suspected that my intellect had tricked me. Then I noted the clock. A moment before, as it seemed, it had stood at a minute or so past ten; now it was nearly half-past three!
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: I experienced what may often be described as a strange sense of exultation that tends to accompany hard fighting. I knew that both Weena and I were likely lost, but I decided to make the Morlocks pay for their meat. I stood with my back against a tree, swinging the iron bar in front of me. The whole wood seemed filled with their stirring and cries. A minute passed. Their voices seemed to rise to a higher pitch of excitement, and their movements became faster. Yet none came within reach. I stood glaring into the darkness. Then suddenly hope came. What if the Morlocks were afraid? Close behind that thought came something strange. The darkness seemed to grow luminous. Very dimly I began to see the Morlocks around me—three battered at my feet—and then I recognized, with incredulous surprise, that the others were running in what seemed an incessant stream from behind me and away through the wood in front. Their backs no longer seemed white, but reddish. As I stood open-mouthed, I saw a little red spark drift across a gap of starlight between the branches and vanish. At that I understood the smell of burning wood, the slumbrous murmur that was now growing into a gusty roar, the red glow, and the Morlocks’ flight.
output: “The strange exultation that so often seems to accompany hard fighting came upon me. I knew that both I and Weena were lost, but I determined to make the Morlocks pay for their meat. I stood with my back to a tree, swinging the iron bar before me. The whole wood was full of the stir and cries of them. A minute passed. Their voices seemed to rise to a higher pitch of excitement, and their movements grew faster. Yet none came within reach. I stood glaring at the blackness. Then suddenly came hope. What if the Morlocks were afraid? And close on the heels of that came a strange thing. The darkness seemed to grow luminous. Very dimly I began to see the Morlocks about me - three battered at my feet - and then I recognised, with incredulous surprise, that the others were running, in an incessant stream, as it seemed, from behind me, and away through the wood in front. And their backs seemed no longer white, but reddish. As I stood agape, I saw a little red spark go drifting across a gap of starlight between the branches, and vanish. And at that I understood the smell of burning wood, the slumbrous murmur that was growing now into a gusty roar, the red glow, and the Morlocks’ flight.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input:
As I sat on the machine, I heard a loud scream in the distance, up the barren slope. The sound was followed by the sight of a large white object that resembled a butterfly, moving erratically upwards and eventually disappearing over a nearby series of hills. The scream had a profoundly unsettling effect on me, causing me to shiver and adjust my position on the machine. Consequently, I took a closer look at my surroundings and noticed a reddish mass that I had initially thought was a rock, but was actually moving slowly towards me.

Upon closer inspection, I realized that the object was a massive creature that resembled a crab, with numerous legs that moved slowly and uncertainly. Furthermore, it had large claws that swayed back and forth, as well as long antennae that waved and felt its way through the environment. The creature's eyes, which were positioned on either side of its metallic front, gleamed as it moved. Additionally, its back was covered in ridges and uneven bumps, and it had a greenish coating in various spots. As the creature moved, the many parts of its complex mouth flickered and felt its way through the environment, creating a disturbing image.
output: “Far away up the desolate slope I heard a harsh scream, and saw a thing like a huge white butterfly go slanting and fluttering up into the sky and, circling, disappear over some low hillocks beyond. The sound of its voice was so dismal that I shivered and seated myself more firmly upon the machine. Looking round me again, I saw that, quite near, what I had taken to be a reddish mass of rock was moving slowly towards me. Then I saw the thing was really a monstrous crab-like creature. Can you imagine a crab as large as yonder table, with its many legs moving slowly and uncertainly, its big claws swaying, its long antennæ, like carters’ whips, waving and feeling, and its stalked eyes gleaming at you on either side of its metallic front? Its back was corrugated and ornamented with ungainly bosses, and a greenish incrustation blotched it here and there. I could see the many palps of its complicated mouth flickering and feeling as it moved.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: There was a pause of perhaps a minute. The Psychologist appeared as though he were about to address me, but then he altered his intention. Subsequently, the Time Traveller extended his finger towards the lever. "No," he said abruptly. "Lend me your hand." Additionally, turning to the Psychologist, he took that individual's hand in his own and instructed him to extend his forefinger. Thus, it was the Psychologist himself who dispatched the model Time Machine upon its endless journey. Furthermore, we all observed the lever turn. I am entirely certain that there was no deception. There was a movement of air, and the flame of the lamp flickered. Moreover, one of the candles upon the mantel was extinguished, and the small machine suddenly rotated, became indistinct, and was perceived as a spectral form for perhaps a second, as a swirling mass of faintly luminous brass and ivory; and then it was gone—vanished. In essence, apart from the lamp, the table was unoccupied.
output: There was a minute’s pause perhaps. The Psychologist seemed about to speak to me, but changed his mind. Then the Time Traveller put forth his finger towards the lever. “No,” he said suddenly. “Lend me your hand.” And turning to the Psychologist, he took that individual’s hand in his own and told him to put out his forefinger. So that it was the Psychologist himself who sent forth the model Time Machine on its interminable voyage. We all saw the lever turn. I am absolutely certain there was no trickery. There was a breath of wind, and the lamp flame jumped. One of the candles on the mantel was blown out, and the little machine suddenly swung round, became indistinct, was seen as a ghost for a second perhaps, as an eddy of faintly glittering brass and ivory; and it was gone - vanished! Save for the lamp the table was bare.
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: The Time Traveller continued, allowing a moment for consideration of this concept, that scientists may be aware that time can often be viewed as a form of space. To illustrate this idea, a common tool used in science is a weather record, which can provide a visual representation of changes over time. For example, if we look at a graph of a barometer's movement, we can see that the line tracing its progress may show a high reading yesterday, a drop overnight, and then a gradual increase this morning. It's unlikely that the mercury's movement would be visible in the traditional dimensions of space, but it does appear to follow a path, which we can conclude may be along a dimension related to time. In summary, the Time Traveller's explanation suggests that time and space may be more closely linked than they initially seem.
output: “Scientific people,” proceeded the Time Traveller, after the pause required for the proper assimilation of this, “know very well that Time is only a kind of Space. Here is a popular scientific diagram, a weather record. This line I trace with my finger shows the movement of the barometer. Yesterday it was so high, yesterday night it fell, then this morning it rose again, and so gently upward to here. Surely the mercury did not trace this line in any of the dimensions of Space generally recognised? But certainly it traced such a line, and that line, therefore, we must conclude, was along the Time-Dimension.”
title: The Time Machine
author: H. G. Wells

input: It is worth noting that an alternative account of these events suggests that on Sunday morning, the entirety of London was profoundly impacted by the news emanating from Woking. Furthermore, a more nuanced examination of the situation reveals that there was no substantial basis for such an exaggerated assertion. Additionally, a significant proportion of London's population remained unaware of the Martian presence until the onset of panic on Monday morning. Moreover, those individuals who were informed of the events via the hastily composed telegrams published in the Sunday papers required a considerable amount of time to fully comprehend the implications of the information conveyed. In essence, the majority of London's inhabitants do not regularly peruse Sunday publications, which contributed to the delayed dissemination of news regarding the Martian presence.
output: I have read, in another account of these events, that on Sunday morning “all London was electrified by the news from Woking.” As a matter of fact, there was nothing to justify that very extravagant phrase. Plenty of Londoners did not hear of the Martians until the panic of Monday morning. Those who did took some time to realise all that the hastily worded telegrams in the Sunday papers conveyed. The majority of people in London do not read Sunday papers.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: In this location, surrounded by young pine trees and furze bushes, I stopped to catch my breath and awaited further events. The common area near the sand-pits was populated with individuals who, like myself, were frozen in a state of half-fascinated terror, gazing at the creatures or, more specifically, at the piled gravel at the edge of the pit where they were located. This highlights the intense fear that had taken hold of the onlookers. Then, a renewed sense of horror struck me as I saw a round, black object bobbing up and down at the edge of the pit. This was the head of the shopman who had fallen in, visible as a small, dark shape against the bright western sun. The shopman managed to lift his shoulder and knee out of the pit, but then appeared to slip back, leaving only his head visible. Ultimately, he disappeared from view, and I thought I might have heard a faint shriek. This suggests that the shopman's situation was increasingly dire. I experienced a brief impulse to return and assist him, but my fears ultimately proved overwhelming.
output: There, among some young pine trees and furze bushes, I stopped, panting, and waited further developments. The common round the sand-pits was dotted with people, standing like myself in a half-fascinated terror, staring at these creatures, or rather at the heaped gravel at the edge of the pit in which they lay. And then, with a renewed horror, I saw a round, black object bobbing up and down on the edge of the pit. It was the head of the shopman who had fallen in, but showing as a little black object against the hot western sun. Now he got his shoulder and knee up, and again he seemed to slip back until only his head was visible. Suddenly he vanished, and I could have fancied a faint shriek had reached me. I had a momentary impulse to go back and help him that my fears overruled.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
It appeared to me that the pit had grown larger, and repeatedly puffs of vivid green vapor rose from it toward the brightening dawn, rising, whirling, breaking, and vanishing.

Beyond it stood the pillars of fire near Chobham. At the first touch of daylight, they turned into pillars of bloodshot smoke.

As the dawn became brighter, we withdrew from the window where we had watched the Martians and went quietly downstairs.

The artilleryman agreed with me that the house was not a safe place to remain. He said he intended to make his way toward London and then rejoin his battery, No. 12 of the Horse Artillery. My plan was to return immediately to Leatherhead. The strength of the Martians had impressed me so greatly that I had decided to take my wife to Newhaven and leave the country with her at once. I already clearly perceived that the area around London would inevitably become the scene of a disastrous struggle before creatures such as these could be destroyed.
output:
It seemed to me that the pit had been enlarged, and ever and again puffs of vivid green vapour streamed up and out of it towards the brightening dawn - streamed up, whirled, broke, and vanished.

Beyond were the pillars of fire about Chobham. They became pillars of bloodshot smoke at the first touch of day.

As the dawn grew brighter we withdrew from the window from which we had watched the Martians, and went very quietly downstairs.

The artilleryman agreed with me that the house was no place to stay in. He proposed, he said, to make his way Londonward, and thence rejoin his battery - No. 12, of the Horse Artillery. My plan was to return at once to Leatherhead; and so greatly had the strength of the Martians impressed me that I had determined to take my wife to Newhaven, and go with her out of the country forthwith. For I already perceived clearly that the country about London must inevitably be the scene of a disastrous struggle before such creatures as these could be destroyed.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
For a time I stood unsteadily on the mound, disregarding my own safety. Inside that foul den from which I had just come, I had thought only narrowly of our immediate survival. I had not understood what was happening to the world, nor expected this startling sight of unfamiliar things. I had thought I would see Sheen in ruins; instead, around me lay a landscape strange and lurid, like that of another planet.

In that moment I felt an emotion beyond the ordinary range of human experience, yet one that the unfortunate creatures we dominate know very well. I felt as a rabbit might feel returning to its burrow and suddenly finding a dozen busy laborers digging the foundations of a house. I felt the first hint of something that soon became clear in my mind and weighed on me for many days: a sense of being dethroned, a conviction that I was no longer a master but an animal among animals, under Martian rule. It would be with us as with them: to lurk and watch, to run and hide. The fear and empire of man had passed away.
output:
For some time I stood tottering on the mound regardless of my safety. Within that noisome den from which I had emerged I had thought with a narrow intensity only of our immediate security. I had not realised what had been happening to the world, had not anticipated this startling vision of unfamiliar things. I had expected to see Sheen in ruins - I found about me the landscape, weird and lurid, of another planet.

For that moment I touched an emotion beyond the common range of men, yet one that the poor brutes we dominate know only too well. I felt as a rabbit might feel returning to his burrow and suddenly confronted by the work of a dozen busy navvies digging the foundations of a house. I felt the first inkling of a thing that presently grew quite clear in my mind, that oppressed me for many days, a sense of dethronement, a persuasion that I was no longer a master, but an animal among the animals, under the Martian heel. With us it would be as with them, to lurk and watch, to run and hide; the fear and empire of man had passed away.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
It is worth noting that I uttered the opinion that they had acted imprudently. Furthermore, I believed that they posed a significant threat, largely due to the fact that they were likely driven by extreme fear. Moreover, it is possible that they had anticipated encountering no living organisms, and certainly not any intelligent beings.

Additionally, the intense nature of the events that had transpired had undoubtedly left my faculties of perception in a heightened state of sensitivity. In essence, my recollection of the dinner table remains remarkably vivid, even at this point in time. Moreover, the image of my wife's anxious face, illuminated by the pink lamp shade, as well as the white tablecloth adorned with silver and glassware, is etched in my memory with great clarity. It is also worth noting that the deep crimson-purple hue of the wine in my glass is similarly well-defined. Ultimately, I sat at the end of the table, smoking a cigarette and cracking nuts, while also reflecting on the impulsive behavior of Ogilvy and criticizing the shortsighted caution exhibited by the Martians.
output:
“They have done a foolish thing,” said I, fingering my wineglass. “They are dangerous because, no doubt, they are mad with terror. Perhaps they expected to find no living things - certainly no intelligent living things.”

The intense excitement of the events had no doubt left my perceptive powers in a state of erethism. I remember that dinner table with extraordinary vividness even now. My dear wife’s sweet anxious face peering at me from under the pink lamp shade, the white cloth with its silver and glass table furniture - for in those days even philosophical writers had many little luxuries - the crimson-purple wine in my glass, are photographically distinct. At the end of it I sat, tempering nuts with a cigarette, regretting Ogilvy’s rashness, and denouncing the short-sighted timidity of the Martians.

author: H. G. Wells

input:
By midnight, the illuminated trees on the slopes of Richmond Park and the bright lights from Kingston Hill may have cast their glow over a vast area of dark smoke, which likely obscured the entire valley of the Thames and stretched as far as the eye could see. Amidst this scene, two Martians slowly made their way, directing their hissing steam jets in various directions.

They appeared to be cautious with the use of the Heat-Ray that evening, possibly due to a limited supply of the materials needed for its production or perhaps a desire to avoid total destruction of the area while aiming to suppress and intimidate the opposition they had stirred up. In this effort, they seemed to achieve success. Sunday night marked the end of organized resistance to their movements, as the task of standing against them began to feel insurmountable. Even the crews of the torpedo boats and destroyers that had brought their rapid-fire weapons up the Thames reportedly refused to engage, choosing to mutiny instead and retreat. Following that night, the only actions taken by men in response were the frantic and sporadic preparations of mines and traps. In summary, the situation had shifted significantly in favor of the Martians, diminishing human resistance considerably.
output:
By midnight the blazing trees along the slopes of Richmond Park and the glare of Kingston Hill threw their light upon a network of black smoke, blotting out the whole valley of the Thames and extending as far as the eye could reach. And through this two Martians slowly waded, and turned their hissing steam jets this way and that.

They were sparing of the Heat-Ray that night, either because they had but a limited supply of material for its production or because they did not wish to destroy the country but only to crush and overawe the opposition they had aroused. In the latter aim they certainly succeeded. Sunday night was the end of the organised opposition to their movements. After that no body of men would stand against them, so hopeless was the enterprise. Even the crews of the torpedo-boats and destroyers that had brought their quick-firers up the Thames refused to stop, mutinied, and went down again. The only offensive operation men ventured upon after that night was the preparation of mines and pitfalls, and even in that their energies were frantic and spasmodic.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: I stayed on the roof for a very long time, astonished by the strange transformations the day had brought. I thought back over my mental states, from the midnight prayer to the foolish card-playing. A violent revulsion of feeling came over me. I remember throwing away the cigar with a kind of wasteful symbolism. My folly appeared to me in glaring exaggeration. I felt I had betrayed my wife and my kind, and I was filled with remorse. I resolved to leave this strange, undisciplined dreamer of great things to his drink and gluttony, and to go on into London. There, it seemed to me, I had the best chance of learning what the Martians and my fellow men were doing. I was still on the roof when the late moon rose.
output: I remained a very long time upon the roof, wondering at the grotesque changes of the day. I recalled my mental states from the midnight prayer to the foolish card-playing. I had a violent revulsion of feeling. I remember I flung away the cigar with a certain wasteful symbolism. My folly came to me with glaring exaggeration. I seemed a traitor to my wife and to my kind; I was filled with remorse. I resolved to leave this strange undisciplined dreamer of great things to his drink and gluttony, and to go on into London. There, it seemed to me, I had the best chance of learning what the Martians and my fellowmen were doing. I was still upon the roof when the late moon rose.

input: The Martians had been repulsed, showing that they were not invulnerable. They had withdrawn once more to their triangle of cylinders, within the circle around Woking. From all directions, signallers with heliographs were advancing toward them. Guns were being moved rapidly from Windsor, Portsmouth, Aldershot, and Woolwich, and even from the north; among them were long wire-guns of ninety-five tons from Woolwich. In total, one hundred and sixteen guns were either in position or being hastily placed, mainly to cover London. This highlights that never before in England had there been such a vast or rapid concentration of military material.
output: The Martians had been repulsed; they were not invulnerable. They had retreated to their triangle of cylinders again, in the circle about Woking. Signallers with heliographs were pushing forward upon them from all sides. Guns were in rapid transit from Windsor, Portsmouth, Aldershot, Woolwich - even from the north; among others, long wire-guns of ninety-five tons from Woolwich. Altogether one hundred and sixteen were in position or being hastily placed, chiefly covering London. Never before in England had there been such a vast or rapid concentration of military material.

input:
At that time, there was a widespread perception among the public that the authorities were responsible for their inability to effectively manage the invasion, resulting in significant inconvenience. This highlights the level of frustration and discontent among the population. 

Around eight o'clock, a loud noise of heavy firing could be heard clearly throughout the southern part of London. Although the sound was obscured by traffic in the main streets, it became distinct when heard from the quieter back streets near the river. This suggests that the conflict was escalating and becoming more intense.

My brother walked from Westminster to his residence near Regent's Park at around two o'clock. He was increasingly concerned about my well-being and was troubled by the apparent scale of the disturbance. Ultimately, his thoughts turned to the military aspects of the situation, much like mine had on Saturday. He pondered the presence of silent, expectant guns and the rapid changes in the countryside, and he attempted to visualize the appearance of "boilers on stilts" that were reportedly a hundred feet high.
output:
At that time there was a strong feeling in the streets that the authorities were to blame for their incapacity to dispose of the invaders without all this inconvenience.

About eight o’clock a noise of heavy firing was distinctly audible all over the south of London. My brother could not hear it for the traffic in the main thoroughfares, but by striking through the quiet back streets to the river he was able to distinguish it quite plainly.

He walked from Westminster to his apartments near Regent’s Park, about two. He was now very anxious on my account, and disturbed at the evident magnitude of the trouble. His mind was inclined to run, even as mine had run on Saturday, on military details. He thought of all those silent, expectant guns, of the suddenly nomadic countryside; he tried to imagine “boilers on stilts” a hundred feet high.

input: Additionally, the railway line on the London side of Woking station was still in the process of being repaired, which necessitated my disembarking at Byfleet station and proceeding along the road to Maybury. Furthermore, my route took me past the location where the artilleryman and I had previously engaged in conversation with the hussars, and subsequently by the area where I had encountered the Martian during the thunderstorm. Moreover, it is worth noting that my curiosity prompted me to deviate from my course in order to investigate a nearby thicket, where I discovered the remnants of a damaged vehicle, surrounded by a tangled mass of foliage, and the skeletal remains of a horse, which had been scattered and partially consumed. In essence, I paused for a time to contemplate these remnants, reflecting on the circumstances that had led to their present state.
output: The line on the London side of Woking station was still undergoing repair, so I descended at Byfleet station and took the road to Maybury, past the place where I and the artilleryman had talked to the hussars, and on by the spot where the Martian had appeared to me in the thunderstorm. Here, moved by curiosity, I turned aside to find, among a tangle of red fronds, the warped and broken dog cart with the whitened bones of the horse scattered and gnawed. For a time I stood regarding these vestiges....
