input: As he observed Miss Elphinstone covering her eyes, he also noticed a young child staring with wide eyes at a lifeless, crushed object under the wheels of a vehicle. This highlights the child's limited ability to comprehend the severity of the situation. The man shouted, "Let us go back!" and began to turn the pony around, stating that they could not proceed through the chaotic scene. Ultimately, they retreated about a hundred yards in the direction they had come from, until the violent crowd was out of sight. As they rounded the bend in the lane, my brother caught a glimpse of a dying man's face in the ditch beneath the privet, which was deathly pale and slick with sweat. This suggests that the situation was extremely dire. The two women remained silent, huddled together in their seat and shivering, clearly shaken by what they had witnessed.
output: He saw Miss Elphinstone covering her eyes, and a little child, with all a child’s want of sympathetic imagination, staring with dilated eyes at a dusty something that lay black and still, ground and crushed under the rolling wheels. “Let us go back!” he shouted, and began turning the pony round. “We cannot cross this - hell,” he said and they went back a hundred yards the way they had come, until the fighting crowd was hidden. As they passed the bend in the lane my brother saw the face of the dying man in the ditch under the privet, deadly white and drawn, and shining with perspiration. The two women sat silent, crouching in their seat and shivering.

input: Everyone anticipated the emergence of a man—perhaps one who was somewhat different from humans, but fundamentally a man. I certainly did. However, as I observed, I soon noticed something moving in the shadows. There were greyish, billowing motions, one atop the other, followed by two glowing disks that resembled eyes. Then, something that looked like a small grey snake, roughly the thickness of a walking stick, coiled out from the writhing center and slithered through the air toward me. Shortly thereafter, I saw another one.
output: I think everyone expected to see a man emerge - possibly something a little unlike us terrestrial men, but in all essentials a man. I know I did. But, looking, I presently saw something stirring within the shadow: greyish billowy movements, one above another, and then two luminous disks - like eyes. Then something resembling a little grey snake, about the thickness of a walking stick, coiled up out of the writhing middle, and wriggled in the air towards me - and then another.

input: The prevailing thought among many individuals, including myself, was the question of how much the opposing forces understood about us. This highlights the possibility that they may have recognized our organization, discipline, and collaborative efforts as a collective. Alternatively, they might have interpreted our sudden bursts of fire and consistent shelling of their encampment as a chaotic assault, similar to how one might view an agitated beehive. This raises further questions about their intentions; did they believe they could eliminate us entirely? At that moment, our specific needs, including food requirements, remained unknown to them. Numerous questions occupied my mind as I observed the imposing figure before me. Additionally, I was aware of the significant and unseen forces in London. This suggests the possibility that they might have set traps for us. Were the powder mills at Hounslow prepared as a potential obstacle? Would the residents of London have the resolve to transform their vast city into a fortified stronghold?
output: No doubt the thought that was uppermost in a thousand of those vigilant minds, even as it was uppermost in mine, was the riddle - how much they understood of us. Did they grasp that we in our millions were organized, disciplined, working together? Or did they interpret our spurts of fire, the sudden stinging of our shells, our steady investment of their encampment, as we should the furious unanimity of onslaught in a disturbed hive of bees? Did they dream they might exterminate us? (At that time no one knew what food they needed.) A hundred such questions struggled together in my mind as I watched that vast sentinel shape. And in the back of my mind was the sense of all the huge unknown and hidden forces Londonward. Had they prepared pitfalls? Were the powder mills at Hounslow ready as a snare? Would the Londoners have the heart and courage to make a greater Moscow of their mighty province of houses?
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
As the sunset gave way to a golden haze, the sound of gunfire and the movement of dark shapes became apparent. Consequently, all passengers rushed to the steamer's rail and gazed out into the intense western light, but it was impossible to discern any clear details. Meanwhile, a large cloud of smoke rose at an angle, obscuring the sun's face. The steamboat continued on its course, surrounded by an atmosphere of prolonged uncertainty.

As the sun dipped below the grey clouds, the sky underwent a rapid transformation, changing from a flushed tone to a darker hue. Furthermore, the evening star became visible, twinkling faintly. It was during this deep twilight period that the captain suddenly cried out and pointed to something in the distance. My brother strained his eyes to see what had caught the captain's attention. At that moment, a large, flat object emerged from the grey surroundings, rising swiftly and diagonally into the clear sky above the western clouds. The object described a vast curve, gradually decreasing in size as it sank slowly and eventually disappeared into the night's darkness. As it flew overhead, it seemed to cast a shadow of darkness over the land.
output:
Then suddenly out of the golden haze of the sunset came the vibration of guns, and a form of black shadows moving. Everyone struggled to the rail of the steamer and peered into the blinding furnace of the west, but nothing was to be distinguished clearly. A mass of smoke rose slanting and barred the face of the sun. The steamboat throbbed on its way through an interminable suspense.

The sun sank into grey clouds, the sky flushed and darkened, the evening star trembled into sight. It was deep twilight when the captain cried out and pointed. My brother strained his eyes. Something rushed up into the sky out of the greyness - rushed slantingly upward and very swiftly into the luminous clearness above the clouds in the western sky; something flat and broad, and very large, that swept round in a vast curve, grew smaller, sank slowly, and vanished again into the grey mystery of the night. And as it flew it rained down darkness upon the land.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
An intense determination consumed me. I contemplated ending my life but decided against that, choosing instead to confront the Titan directly. As I approached, I noticed a large number of black birds circling around the hood. This sudden sight caused a surge of energy within me, prompting me to run along the road.

I hurried through the dense red weed that obstructed St. Edmund’s Terrace, wading through a torrent of water flowing from the waterworks toward Albert Road, and emerged onto the grass just before dawn. Large mounds had been constructed at the top of the hill, forming a significant fortification that was the largest structure created by the Martians. Thin smoke rose from behind these mounds into the sky. An eager dog ran by and disappeared against the skyline. The thought that had briefly crossed my mind became more tangible and believable. I experienced no fear, only a wild, trembling exhilaration as I ascended the hill toward the still Titan. Hanging from the hood were long, thin strips of brown, which the ravenous birds began to peck at and tear.
output:
An insane resolve possessed me. I would die and end it. And I would save myself even the trouble of killing myself. I marched on recklessly towards this Titan, and then, as I drew nearer and the light grew, I saw that a multitude of black birds was circling and clustering about the hood. At that my heart gave a bound, and I began running along the road.

I hurried through the red weed that choked St. Edmund’s Terrace (I waded breast-high across a torrent of water that was rushing down from the waterworks towards the Albert Road), and emerged upon the grass before the rising of the sun. Great mounds had been heaped about the crest of the hill, making a huge redoubt of it - it was the final and largest place the Martians had made - and from behind these heaps there rose a thin smoke against the sky. Against the sky line an eager dog ran and disappeared. The thought that had flashed into my mind grew real, grew credible. I felt no fear, only a wild, trembling exultation, as I ran up the hill towards the motionless monster. Out of the hood hung lank shreds of brown, at which the hungry birds pecked and tore.

author: H. G. Wells

input: Thus, the state of affairs on Friday night was as follows. In the center, a cylinder was embedded in the surface of our old planet Earth like a poisoned dart. However, the poison was barely taking effect at that point. Surrounding it was a patch of silent common, smoldering in certain places, with a few dark, dimly visible objects lying in contorted positions here and there. In various spots, there was a burning bush or tree. Beyond this area was a fringe of excitement, and the inflammation had not yet spread farther than that boundary. In the rest of the world, the stream of life continued to flow as it had for countless years. The fever of war, which would soon clog veins and arteries, deaden nerves, and destroy the brain, had yet to develop.
output: So you have the state of things on Friday night. In the centre, sticking into the skin of our old planet Earth like a poisoned dart, was this cylinder. But the poison was scarcely working yet. Around it was a patch of silent common, smouldering in places, and with a few dark, dimly seen objects lying in contorted attitudes here and there. Here and there was a burning bush or tree. Beyond was a fringe of excitement, and farther than that fringe the inflammation had not crept as yet. In the rest of the world the stream of life still flowed as it had flowed for immemorial years. The fever of war that would presently clog vein and artery, deaden nerve and destroy brain, had still to develop.

author: H. G. Wells

input: After a lengthy and unsuccessful attempt to board a North-Western train at Chalk Farm, my brother proceeded to the Chalk Farm road. The scene at the train station had been chaotic, with trains loaded in the goods yard moving forward and pushing through crowds of people, while a group of strong men struggled to protect the driver from being crushed against the furnace. Meanwhile, my brother managed to dodge through a large number of vehicles that were moving quickly through the area. Fortunately, he was able to gain access to a cycle shop and acquire a bicycle, although the front tire was damaged as he pulled it through the window. Nevertheless, he was able to begin his journey, suffering only a minor cut to his wrist. As he rode, he encountered an obstacle at the foot of Haverstock Hill, where several horses had been overturned, making it impossible to pass. Therefore, my brother decided to take an alternative route and turned into Belsize Road.
output: After a fruitless struggle to get aboard a North-Western train at Chalk Farm - the engines of the trains that had loaded in the goods yard there ploughed through shrieking people, and a dozen stalwart men fought to keep the crowd from crushing the driver against his furnace - my brother emerged upon the Chalk Farm road, dodged across through a hurrying swarm of vehicles, and had the luck to be foremost in the sack of a cycle shop. The front tire of the machine he got was punctured in dragging it through the window, but he got up and off, notwithstanding, with no further injury than a cut wrist. The steep foot of Haverstock Hill was impassable owing to several overturned horses, and my brother struck into Belsize Road.

author: H. G. Wells

input:
They encountered significant challenges in getting her to the beach, but eventually, my brother managed to catch the attention of some crew members from a paddle steamer on the Thames. They arranged for a boat to come to shore and negotiated a fare of thirty-six pounds for the three of them. The crew indicated that the steamer was headed to Ostend.

Around two o'clock, after paying their fares at the gangway, my brother found himself safely on board the steamboat with the two others. Although the prices for food were notably high, they managed to have a meal together on one of the forward seats.
output:
It was with the greatest difficulty they could get her down to the beach, where presently my brother succeeded in attracting the attention of some men on a paddle steamer from the Thames. They sent a boat and drove a bargain for thirty-six pounds for the three. The steamer was going, these men said, to Ostend.

It was about two o’clock when my brother, having paid their fares at the gangway, found himself safely aboard the steamboat with his charges. There was food aboard, albeit at exorbitant prices, and the three of them contrived to eat a meal on one of the seats forward.

input: He managed to escape the intense panic and, avoiding the Edgware Road, arrived in Edgware around seven, exhausted and hungry, but ahead of the crowd. This highlights the chaos that was unfolding. Along the way, people stood in the road, curious and wondering what was happening. He was overtaken by several cyclists, horsemen, and two motor cars, which suggests that many people were fleeing the area. About a mile from Edgware, the wheel of his machine broke, rendering it unusable. He abandoned it by the side of the road and continued on foot through the village. In the main street, shops were partially open, and people gathered on the pavement, in doorways, and at windows, staring in astonishment at the growing number of fugitives. Ultimately, he was able to obtain some food at a local inn, which helped to alleviate his hunger and fatigue.
output: So he got out of the fury of the panic, and, skirting the Edgware Road, reached Edgware about seven, fasting and wearied, but well ahead of the crowd. Along the road people were standing in the roadway, curious, wondering. He was passed by a number of cyclists, some horsemen, and two motor cars. A mile from Edgware the rim of the wheel broke, and the machine became unridable. He left it by the roadside and trudged through the village. There were shops half opened in the main street of the place, and people crowded on the pavement and in the doorways and windows, staring astonished at this extraordinary procession of fugitives that was beginning. He succeeded in getting some food at an inn.

author: H. G. Wells

input: In London, no one had a clear understanding of the armored Martians, and there was a prevailing notion that these creatures must be slow. Descriptions such as "crawling" and "creeping painfully" appeared in nearly all early reports. None of the telegrams seemed to originate from eyewitnesses who had seen their advance. The Sunday papers published special editions as new information became available, some even doing so in the absence of actual updates. However, there was little more to report until late in the afternoon when authorities finally shared the news they had. It was announced that residents of Walton, Weybridge, and the surrounding areas were fleeing along the roads toward London, and that was all the information available at that time.
output: No one in London knew positively of the nature of the armoured Martians, and there was still a fixed idea that these monsters must be sluggish: “crawling,” “creeping painfully” - such expressions occurred in almost all the earlier reports. None of the telegrams could have been written by an eyewitness of their advance. The Sunday papers printed separate editions as further news came to hand, some even in default of it. But there was practically nothing more to tell people until late in the afternoon, when the authorities gave the press agencies the news in their possession. It was stated that the people of Walton and Weybridge, and all the district were pouring along the roads Londonward, and that was all.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: The area was completely obscured from view, concealed by the deep pit and the large mound of sand that had been created by the cylinder's fall. Meanwhile, individuals traveling along the road from Chobham or Woking would have been astonished by the scene before them. A sizable crowd of approximately one hundred people or more was gathered in a large, irregular circle, with some standing in ditches, others behind bushes, and still others behind gates and hedges. Additionally, the onlookers were speaking very little to one another, and when they did, it was in brief, excited shouts. Furthermore, they were staring intently at several large heaps of sand. Nearby, a barrow of ginger beer stood abandoned, its dark color starkly visible against the bright sky. Moreover, a row of deserted vehicles was situated in the sand-pits, with their horses either eating from nosebags or pawing at the ground.
output: Everything was then quite invisible, hidden by the deep pit and the heap of sand that the fall of the cylinder had made. Anyone coming along the road from Chobham or Woking would have been amazed at the sight - a dwindling multitude of perhaps a hundred people or more standing in a great irregular circle, in ditches, behind bushes, behind gates and hedges, saying little to one another and that in short, excited shouts, and staring, staring hard at a few heaps of sand. The barrow of ginger beer stood, a queer derelict, black against the burning sky, and in the sand-pits was a row of deserted vehicles with their horses feeding out of nosebags or pawing the ground.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: The Martians could have easily destroyed the entire population of London on Monday, given the slow and disorganized manner in which the population was spreading throughout the home counties. Meanwhile, a massive exodus was underway, with people fleeing not only along the road through Barnet, but also through Edgware and Waltham Abbey, as well as along the roads leading eastward to Southend and Shoeburyness, and south of the Thames to Deal and Broadstairs. Additionally, if one were to have observed the scene from a balloon above London on that June morning, it would have been clear that every road leading out of the city was filled with people, each one representing a individual experiencing intense fear and physical distress. As previously described in the last chapter, my brother's account of the road through Chipping Barnet provides a detailed illustration of what this scene would have looked like to one of the people involved. Furthermore, it is worth noting that this event was unprecedented in human history, with a larger number of people affected than in any previous conflict, including the massive armies of Goths and Huns that had been seen in Asia. Moreover, this was not a organized or disciplined movement, but rather a chaotic and terrifying stampede, with approximately six million unarmed and unprovisioned people fleeing without a clear goal or direction. Ultimately, this event marked the beginning of the end of civilization as it was known, and the start of a massive and devastating massacre of humanity.
output: Had the Martians aimed only at destruction, they might on Monday have annihilated the entire population of London, as it spread itself slowly through the home counties. Not only along the road through Barnet, but also through Edgware and Waltham Abbey, and along the roads eastward to Southend and Shoeburyness, and south of the Thames to Deal and Broadstairs, poured the same frantic rout. If one could have hung that June morning in a balloon in the blazing blue above London every northward and eastward road running out of the tangled maze of streets would have seemed stippled black with the streaming fugitives, each dot a human agony of terror and physical distress. I have set forth at length in the last chapter my brother’s account of the road through Chipping Barnet, in order that my readers may realise how that swarming of black dots appeared to one of those concerned. Never before in the history of the world had such a mass of human beings moved and suffered together. The legendary hosts of Goths and Huns, the hugest armies Asia has ever seen, would have been but a drop in that current. And this was no disciplined march; it was a stampede - a stampede gigantic and terrible - without order and without a goal, six million people unarmed and unprovisioned, driving headlong. It was the beginning of the rout of civilisation, of the massacre of mankind.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
In that case, the cylinder might be destroyed by means of dynamite or artillery before it had cooled sufficiently for the Martians to emerge, or they might be slaughtered by means of firearms as soon as the screw was opened. It appears to me that they have lost a considerable advantage through the failure of their initial surprise. It is possible that they perceive the matter in the same manner.

Furthermore, Lessing has advanced excellent reasons for supposing that the Martians have in fact succeeded in effecting a landing upon the planet Venus. It is worth noting that seven months ago, Venus and Mars were in alignment with the sun; that is to say, Mars was in opposition from the perspective of an observer situated upon Venus. Subsequently, a peculiar luminous and sinuous marking appeared upon the unillumined half of the inner planet, and almost simultaneously a faint dark mark of a similar sinuous character was detected upon a photograph of the Martian disk. In essence, one needs to observe the drawings of these appearances in order to appreciate fully their remarkable resemblance in character.
output:
In that case the cylinder might be destroyed with dynamite or artillery before it was sufficiently cool for the Martians to emerge, or they might be butchered by means of guns so soon as the screw opened. It seems to me that they have lost a vast advantage in the failure of their first surprise. Possibly they see it in the same light.

Lessing has advanced excellent reasons for supposing that the Martians have actually succeeded in effecting a landing on the planet Venus. Seven months ago now, Venus and Mars were in alignment with the sun; that is to say, Mars was in opposition from the point of view of an observer on Venus. Subsequently a peculiar luminous and sinuous marking appeared on the unillumined half of the inner planet, and almost simultaneously a faint dark mark of a similar sinuous character was detected upon a photograph of the Martian disk. One needs to see the drawings of these appearances in order to appreciate fully their remarkable resemblance in character.

input: Between our location and Leatherhead, the third cylinder was situated, accompanied by its guarding giants. This highlights the potential danger of the direct route. Had I been traveling alone, I might have attempted to cross the countryside, taking a risk to reach my destination. However, the artilleryman advised against this, suggesting that it would be irresponsible to put my life in jeopardy and potentially leave a spouse a widow. This suggests that he was considering the potential consequences of my actions. Ultimately, I decided to accompany him, traveling northward under the cover of the woods as far as Street Cobham, before parting ways. From there, I planned to make a significant detour via Epsom to reach Leatherhead, avoiding the direct route and its associated risks.
output: Between us and Leatherhead, however, lay the third cylinder, with its guarding giants. Had I been alone, I think I should have taken my chance and struck across country. But the artilleryman dissuaded me: “It’s no kindness to the right sort of wife,” he said, “to make her a widow;” and in the end I agreed to go with him, under cover of the woods, northward as far as Street Cobham before I parted with him. Thence I would make a big detour by Epsom to reach Leatherhead.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
As soon as the cab had passed, he threw himself, with both hands extended, upon the pile of coins and began to thrust handfuls into his pocket. A horse approached him closely, and in an instant, as he was half rising, he was knocked down beneath the horse's hooves. 

"Stop!" my brother screamed, and, pushing a woman aside, he attempted to grasp the reins of the horse. 

Before he could reach them, he heard a scream beneath the wheels and, through the dust, he witnessed the rim passing over the unfortunate individual's back. The driver of the cart lashed his whip in my brother's direction, prompting him to run around behind the cart. The multitude of voices surrounding him created a cacophony that confused his senses. The man was writhing in the dust amid his scattered money, unable to rise due to a broken back, leaving his lower limbs limp and lifeless. My brother stood up and called out to the next driver, and a man on a black horse came to provide assistance.
output:
So soon as the cab had passed, he flung himself, with both hands open, upon the heap of coins, and began thrusting handfuls in his pocket. A horse rose close upon him, and in another moment, half rising, he had been borne down under the horse’s hoofs.

“Stop!” screamed my brother, and pushing a woman out of his way, tried to clutch the bit of the horse.

Before he could get to it, he heard a scream under the wheels, and saw through the dust the rim passing over the poor wretch’s back. The driver of the cart slashed his whip at my brother, who ran round behind the cart. The multitudinous shouting confused his ears. The man was writhing in the dust among his scattered money, unable to rise, for the wheel had broken his back, and his lower limbs lay limp and dead. My brother stood up and yelled at the next driver, and a man on a black horse came to his assistance.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: The concept of personal security is deeply ingrained in the mindset of Londoners, allowing them to read alarming news with a sense of detachment. For instance, a report detailed that at around seven o'clock the previous evening, Martians emerged from their cylinder, causing significant destruction at Woking station and killing an entire battalion of the Cardigan Regiment. The report stated that no further details were available, noting the ineffectiveness of machine guns against the Martians' armor and the disabling of field artillery. Troops were seen rushing towards Chertsey, while the Martians appeared to be advancing slowly in the direction of Chertsey or Windsor. This situation generated considerable concern in West Surrey, prompting the construction of earthworks to halt the approach towards London. The Sunday Sun conveyed this information, and another article in the Referee likened the events to a menagerie being released in a village.
output: The habit of personal security, moreover, is so deeply fixed in the Londoner’s mind, and startling intelligence so much a matter of course in the papers, that they could read without any personal tremors: “About seven o’clock last night the Martians came out of the cylinder, and, moving about under an armour of metallic shields, have completely wrecked Woking station with the adjacent houses, and massacred an entire battalion of the Cardigan Regiment. No details are known. Maxims have been absolutely useless against their armour; the field guns have been disabled by them. Flying hussars have been galloping into Chertsey. The Martians appear to be moving slowly towards Chertsey or Windsor. Great anxiety prevails in West Surrey, and earthworks are being thrown up to check the advance Londonward.” That was how the Sunday Sun put it, and a clever and remarkably prompt “handbook” article in the Referee compared the affair to a menagerie suddenly let loose in a village.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: As the day progressed and with engine drivers and stokers seemingly unwilling to return to London, the urgency of the situation may have caused a growing crowd to move away from the stations and along the roads heading north. By midday, a Martian was reportedly sighted in Barnes, while a slow-moving plume of black vapor drifted along the Thames and across the flatlands of Lambeth, potentially obstructing escape routes over the bridges in its gradual approach. Another bank of vapor appeared over Ealing, encircling a small group of survivors on Castle Hill, who were alive but found themselves unable to flee. This situation illustrates the increasing tension and danger faced by the populace during this crisis.
output: And as the day advanced and the engine drivers and stokers refused to return to London, the pressure of the flight drove the people in an ever-thickening multitude away from the stations and along the northward-running roads. By midday a Martian had been seen at Barnes, and a cloud of slowly sinking black vapour drove along the Thames and across the flats of Lambeth, cutting off all escape over the bridges in its sluggish advance. Another bank drove over Ealing, and surrounded a little island of survivors on Castle Hill, alive, but unable to escape.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
He heard their screams and, hurrying around the corner, observed a pair of men attempting to extract them from the small pony-chaise in which they had been traveling, while a third man struggled to hold the frightened pony's head. One of the women, a short figure attired in white, was simply screaming; the other, a dark and slender silhouette, struck at the man who grasped her arm with a whip that she held in her free hand. 

My brother immediately comprehended the situation, shouted, and proceeded toward the altercation. One of the men ceased his efforts and turned towards him, and my brother, recognizing from the expression on his adversary's face that a confrontation was inevitable, and being an expert boxer, engaged him without hesitation and sent him crashing against the wheel of the chaise.
output:
He heard their screams, and, hurrying round the corner, saw a couple of men struggling to drag them out of the little pony-chaise in which they had been driving, while a third with difficulty held the frightened pony’s head. One of the ladies, a short woman dressed in white, was simply screaming; the other, a dark, slender figure, slashed at the man who gripped her arm with a whip she held in her disengaged hand.

My brother immediately grasped the situation, shouted, and hurried towards the struggle. One of the men desisted and turned towards him, and my brother, realising from his antagonist’s face that a fight was unavoidable, and being an expert boxer, went into him forthwith and sent him down against the wheel of the chaise.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: The period of suffering has concluded, and healing is set to commence on that very day. The survivors, dispersed across the nation and lacking leadership, order, and resources, will start to return. This highlights a resurgence of life in the once deserted streets and vacant squares. Despite the extensive destruction, the forces of devastation have been halted. The remnants of buildings, now mere shells, will soon be filled with the sounds of those working to restore them. At this prospect, there is a sense of gratitude and hope. Ultimately, one envisions a significant transformation within a year.
output: The torment was over. Even that day the healing would begin. The survivors of the people scattered over the country - leaderless, lawless, foodless, like sheep without a shepherd - the thousands who had fled by sea, would begin to return; the pulse of life, growing stronger and stronger, would beat again in the empty streets and pour across the vacant squares. Whatever destruction was done, the hand of the destroyer was stayed. All the gaunt wrecks, the blackened skeletons of houses that stared so dismally at the sunlit grass of the hill, would presently be echoing with the hammers of the restorers and ringing with the tapping of their trowels. At the thought I extended my hands towards the sky and began thanking God. In a year, thought I - in a year....
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: Several farm wagons and carts were moving creakily along the road to Addlestone. Suddenly, through the gate of a field, we saw six twelve-pounders standing neatly at equal distances across a stretch of flat meadow, pointing toward Woking. The gunners stood by the guns waiting, and the ammunition wagons were positioned at a practical distance. The men stood almost as if under inspection. Farther on toward Weybridge, just over the bridge, a number of men in white fatigue jackets were throwing up a long rampart, with more guns behind them.
output:
Several farm waggons and carts were moving creakily along the road to Addlestone, and suddenly through the gate of a field we saw, across a stretch of flat meadow, six twelve-pounders standing neatly at equal distances pointing towards Woking. The gunners stood by the guns waiting, and the ammunition waggons were at a business-like distance. The men stood almost as if under inspection.

Farther on towards Weybridge, just over the bridge, there were a number of men in white fatigue jackets throwing up a long rampart, and more guns behind.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: The small steamer was making its way eastward past the large crescent of ships, and the low Essex coast appeared to be becoming blue and hazy. At that moment, a Martian could be seen in the distance, small and faint, moving along the muddy shoreline from the direction of Foulness. The captain on the bridge may have reacted with a mix of fear and frustration at his own delay, expressing his emotions quite loudly. The paddles seemed to reflect his anxiety. Crew members and passengers stood at the bulwarks or on the seats of the steamer, gazing at that distant figure, which appeared taller than the trees or church towers inland and was moving with a slow imitation of a human walk. Overall, the scene evoked a sense of tension and curiosity among those on board.
output: The little steamer was already flapping her way eastward of the big crescent of shipping, and the low Essex coast was growing blue and hazy, when a Martian appeared, small and faint in the remote distance, advancing along the muddy coast from the direction of Foulness. At that the captain on the bridge swore at the top of his voice with fear and anger at his own delay, and the paddles seemed infected with his terror. Every soul aboard stood at the bulwarks or on the seats of the steamer and stared at that distant shape, higher than the trees or church towers inland, and advancing with a leisurely parody of a human stride.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: The sounds of howling and gunfire that we had heard at Upper Halliford were originating from Ripley and St. George's Hill. The artillery volunteers stationed at Ripley were inexperienced and hadn't received adequate training, which made them ill-equipped to handle such a situation. Consequently, they fired a single, poorly aimed volley and then rapidly retreated from the area, fleeing on horseback and on foot through the empty village. Meanwhile, the Martian proceeded calmly towards their position, carefully avoiding the abandoned guns as it walked by. Additionally, the Martian moved past the guns and continued on to Painshill Park, where it encountered and destroyed the guns that were located there.
output: It was this howling and firing of the guns at Ripley and St. George’s Hill that we had heard at Upper Halliford. The Ripley gunners, unseasoned artillery volunteers who ought never to have been placed in such a position, fired one wild, premature, ineffectual volley, and bolted on horse and foot through the deserted village, while the Martian, without using his Heat-Ray, walked serenely over their guns, stepped gingerly among them, passed in front of them, and so came unexpectedly upon the guns in Painshill Park, which he destroyed.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: The crescent shape was visible in numerous locations, including Staines, Hounslow, Ditton, Esher, and Ockham, as well as behind hills and woods to the south of the river and across the flat grass meadows to the north. Additionally, the guns were positioned wherever a cluster of trees or village houses provided sufficient cover. Meanwhile, the signal rockets burst and rained their sparks through the night, subsequently vanishing from sight. As a result, the spirit of all those watching batteries rose to a state of tense expectation. Consequently, the Martians simply had to advance into the line of fire, and immediately those motionless black forms of men, along with the guns that glittered so darkly in the early night, would erupt into a fierce and thunderous fury of battle.
output: But facing that crescent everywhere - at Staines, Hounslow, Ditton, Esher, Ockham, behind hills and woods south of the river, and across the flat grass meadows to the north of it, wherever a cluster of trees or village houses gave sufficient cover - the guns were waiting. The signal rockets burst and rained their sparks through the night and vanished, and the spirit of all those watching batteries rose to a tense expectation. The Martians had but to advance into the line of fire, and instantly those motionless black forms of men, those guns glittering so darkly in the early night, would explode into a thunderous fury of battle.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
Upon seeing this, the curate let out a soft sound and began to run. However, I understood that escaping from a Martian was likely futile, so I chose to move aside and carefully made my way through the damp nettles and thorny brambles into the wide ditch beside the road. He glanced back, noticed my actions, and decided to join me. 

We both paused, with the one closer to us standing and facing Sunbury, while the one further away appeared as a vague shape against the evening star, in the direction of Staines. In summary, we found ourselves in a moment of stillness amidst the unfolding situation.
output:
At this sight the curate cried faintly in his throat, and began running; but I knew it was no good running from a Martian, and I turned aside and crawled through dewy nettles and brambles into the broad ditch by the side of the road. He looked back, saw what I was doing, and turned to join me.

The two halted, the nearer to us standing and facing Sunbury, the remoter being a grey indistinctness towards the evening star, away towards Staines.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: On the sixth day of our imprisonment, I looked out for the last time and soon found myself alone. The curate had gone back into the scullery instead of staying close to me and trying to force me away from the slit. A sudden thought struck me. I returned quickly and quietly to the scullery. In the darkness, I heard the curate drinking. I reached out in the darkness, and my fingers closed around a bottle of burgundy.
output: It was on the sixth day of our imprisonment that I peeped for the last time, and presently found myself alone. Instead of keeping close to me and trying to oust me from the slit, the curate had gone back into the scullery. I was struck by a sudden thought. I went back quickly and quietly into the scullery. In the darkness I heard the curate drinking. I snatched in the darkness, and my fingers caught a bottle of burgundy.

author: H. G. Wells

input:
I must admit that the sight of all the armaments and preparations filled me with excitement. My imagination turned aggressive, envisioning various scenarios in which I defeated the invaders in impressive ways. Memories of my youthful dreams of battle and heroism resurfaced. At that moment, it seemed to me that the conflict was not a fair one. The invaders appeared vulnerable in their confined position.

Around three o'clock, I began to hear the rhythmic thud of a gun from either Chertsey or Addlestone. I discovered that the smoldering pine forest, where the second cylinder had landed, was being shelled in an attempt to destroy it before it opened. However, it was not until approximately five o'clock that a field gun arrived in Chobham for use against the first group of Martians.
output:
I must confess the sight of all this armament, all this preparation, greatly excited me. My imagination became belligerent, and defeated the invaders in a dozen striking ways; something of my schoolboy dreams of battle and heroism came back. It hardly seemed a fair fight to me at that time. They seemed very helpless in that pit of theirs.

About three o’clock there began the thud of a gun at measured intervals from Chertsey or Addlestone. I learned that the smouldering pine wood into which the second cylinder had fallen was being shelled, in the hope of destroying that object before it opened. It was only about five, however, that a field gun reached Chobham for use against the first body of Martians.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
A moment later, the huge wave, which was almost at the boiling point, rushed over me. I screamed out loud, and scalded, half blinded, and in great pain, I staggered through the leaping, hissing water toward the shore. If my foot had stumbled, it would likely have been the end. I fell helplessly, in full view of the Martians, onto the broad, bare gravelly spit that runs down to mark the angle of the Wey and Thames. I expected nothing but death.

I have a vague memory of the foot of a Martian coming down within about twenty yards of my head, driving straight into the loose gravel, whirling it this way and that and lifting again; of a long suspense, and then of the four carrying the debris of their companion between them, now clear and then faint through a veil of smoke, receding endlessly, it seemed to me, across a vast space of river and meadow. And then, very slowly, I realized that by a miracle I had escaped.
output:
In another moment the huge wave, well-nigh at the boiling-point had rushed upon me. I screamed aloud, and scalded, half blinded, agonised, I staggered through the leaping, hissing water towards the shore. Had my foot stumbled, it would have been the end. I fell helplessly, in full sight of the Martians, upon the broad, bare gravelly spit that runs down to mark the angle of the Wey and Thames. I expected nothing but death.

I have a dim memory of the foot of a Martian coming down within a score of yards of my head, driving straight into the loose gravel, whirling it this way and that and lifting again; of a long suspense, and then of the four carrying the debris of their comrade between them, now clear and then presently faint through a veil of smoke, receding interminably, as it seemed to me, across a vast space of river and meadow. And then, very slowly, I realised that by a miracle I had escaped.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
On the fourteenth day, I entered the kitchen and was taken aback to see that the fronds of the red weed had spread across the hole in the wall. This growth transformed the dim light in the room into a deep crimson hue. 

Early on the fifteenth day, I heard an unusual yet familiar series of sounds coming from the kitchen. As I listened closely, I recognized the snuffing and scratching of a dog. Upon entering the kitchen, I noticed a dog's nose peeking through a gap in the vibrant fronds. This sight surprised me greatly. When he caught my scent, he let out a brief bark.
output:
On the fourteenth day I went into the kitchen, and I was surprised to find that the fronds of the red weed had grown right across the hole in the wall, turning the half-light of the place into a crimson-coloured obscurity.

It was early on the fifteenth day that I heard a curious, familiar sequence of sounds in the kitchen, and, listening, identified it as the snuffing and scratching of a dog. Going into the kitchen, I saw a dog’s nose peering in through a break among the ruddy fronds. This greatly surprised me. At the scent of me he barked shortly.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input:
I have formed in my mind a dim and wonderful vision of life spreading slowly from this small seed bed of the solar system throughout the inanimate vastness of sidereal space. However, that is a remote dream. On the other hand, it may be that the destruction of the Martians is only a reprieve. Perhaps the future is ordained for them, and not for us.

I must confess that the stress and danger of the time have left an abiding sense of doubt and insecurity in my mind. I sit in my study writing by lamplight, and suddenly I see again the healing valley below set with writhing flames, and I feel the house behind and about me empty and desolate. I go out into the Byfleet Road, and vehicles pass me, a butcher boy in a cart, a cabful of visitors, a workman on a bicycle, children going to school, and suddenly they become vague and unreal, and I hurry again with the artilleryman through the hot, brooding silence. At night I see the black powder darkening the silent streets, and the contorted bodies shrouded in that layer; they rise upon me tattered and dog-bitten. They gibber and grow fiercer, paler, uglier, mad distortions of humanity at last, and I wake, cold and wretched, in the darkness of the night.
output:
Dim and wonderful is the vision I have conjured up in my mind of life spreading slowly from this little seed bed of the solar system throughout the inanimate vastness of sidereal space. But that is a remote dream. It may be, on the other hand, that the destruction of the Martians is only a reprieve. To them, and not to us, perhaps, is the future ordained.

I sit in my study writing by lamplight, and suddenly I see again the healing valley below set with writhing flames, and feel the house behind and about me empty and desolate. I go out into the Byfleet Road, and vehicles pass me, a butcher boy in a cart, a cabful of visitors, a workman on a bicycle, children going to school, and suddenly they become vague and unreal, and I hurry again with the artilleryman through the hot, brooding silence. Of a night I see the black powder darkening the silent streets, and the contorted bodies shrouded in that layer; they rise upon me tattered and dog-bitten. They gibber and grow fiercer, paler, uglier, mad distortions of humanity at last, and I wake, cold and wretched, in the darkness of the night.

input: During this period, I thought often of the curate and the manner of his death, though my thoughts were rambling and inconclusive. On the thirteenth day I drank more water and drifted in and out of sleep, thinking disjointedly about eating and about vague, impossible plans of escape. Whenever I dozed, I dreamt of horrible phantoms, of the curate's death, or of lavish dinners; but whether asleep or awake, I felt a sharp pain that drove me to drink again and again. The light entering the scullery was no longer grey but red. To my disordered imagination, it seemed the colour of blood. This highlights how hunger, thirst, and fear had begun to distort my perception of even the simplest things.
output:
During these days, in a rambling, inconclusive way, I thought much of the curate and of the manner of his death.

On the thirteenth day I drank some more water, and dozed and thought disjointedly of eating and of vague impossible plans of escape. Whenever I dozed I dreamt of horrible phantasms, of the death of the curate, or of sumptuous dinners; but, asleep or awake, I felt a keen pain that urged me to drink again and again. The light that came into the scullery was no longer grey, but red. To my disordered imagination it seemed the colour of blood.

author: H. G. Wells

input:
Additionally, during the initial period, my mouth and throat were exceedingly dry, and my overall strength decreased noticeably. Furthermore, I sat in the darkness of the scullery, experiencing a profound sense of despair and despondency. Moreover, my mind became preoccupied with the idea of consuming food. It is worth noting that I thought I had lost my hearing, as the sounds of movement that I had previously been accustomed to hearing from the pit had stopped completely. In essence, I did not possess sufficient strength to quietly make my way to the peephole, otherwise I would have done so.

Moreover, by the twelfth day, my throat had become so painful that, despite the risk of alerting the Martians, I decided to operate the creaking rain-water pump located near the sink, and I managed to obtain a couple of glassfuls of contaminated and discolored rain water. Additionally, I was significantly revitalized by this, and my confidence was boosted by the fact that no investigative tentacle emerged in response to the noise generated by my pumping action.
output:
At first my mouth and throat were parched, and my strength ebbed sensibly. I sat about in the darkness of the scullery, in a state of despondent wretchedness. My mind ran on eating. I thought I had become deaf, for the noises of movement I had been accustomed to hear from the pit had ceased absolutely. I did not feel strong enough to crawl noiselessly to the peephole, or I would have gone there.

On the twelfth day my throat was so painful that, taking the chance of alarming the Martians, I attacked the creaking rain-water pump that stood by the sink, and got a couple of glassfuls of blackened and tainted rain water. I was greatly refreshed by this, and emboldened by the fact that no enquiring tentacle followed the noise of my pumping.
title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells

input: The Freedmen's Bureau achieved its greatest success in establishing free schools for African Americans and promoting the concept of free elementary education for all classes in the South. This highlights the Bureau's efforts to recruit teachers through benevolent agencies and construct schoolhouses. The organization also played a key role in identifying and supporting educators such as Edmund Ware, Samuel Armstrong, and Erastus Cravath, who were dedicated to promoting human culture. Initially, the South resisted the idea of Negro education, with opposition manifesting in violent and hostile forms, including destruction of property, verbal abuse, and physical harm. This suggests that the South viewed educated African Americans as a potential threat. Ultimately, education has always had the potential to inspire dissatisfaction and discontent among individuals, which can lead to social change. Nevertheless, the desire for knowledge is a fundamental human aspiration. The Freedmen's Bureau's work in this area helped to alleviate some of the opposition to education, although remnants of this resistance still exist in the South today. This period also saw the founding of institutions such as Fisk, Atlanta, Howard, and Hampton, with approximately six million dollars spent on educational initiatives, including $750,000 contributed by the freedmen themselves despite their limited financial resources.
output: The greatest success of the Freedmen’s Bureau lay in the planting of the free school among Negroes, and the idea of free elementary education among all classes in the South. It not only called the school-mistresses through the benevolent agencies and built them schoolhouses, but it helped discover and support such apostles of human culture as Edmund Ware, Samuel Armstrong, and Erastus Cravath. The opposition to Negro education in the South was at first bitter, and showed itself in ashes, insult, and blood; for the South believed an educated Negro to be a dangerous Negro. And the South was not wholly wrong; for education among all kinds of men always has had, and always will have, an element of danger and revolution, of dissatisfaction and discontent. Nevertheless, men strive to know. Perhaps some inkling of this paradox, even in the unquiet days of the Bureau, helped the bayonets allay an opposition to human training which still to-day lies smouldering in the South, but not flaming. Fisk, Atlanta, Howard, and Hampton were founded in these days, and six million dollars were expended for educational work, seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars of which the freedmen themselves gave of their poverty.
title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois

input: Alexander Crummell emerged from his struggles. He overcame the temptations of hate and the pain of despair. He triumphed over doubt and became resilient through sacrifice, returning home across the waters with a sense of humility and strength. He faced the ridicule and prejudices, along with the hatred and discrimination, with a rare courtesy that protected his pure spirit. He contended with those around him, including the lowly, the greedy, and the immoral, wielding an unwavering righteousness that served as his weapon. He remained steadfast and rarely voiced complaints; instead, he dedicated himself to hard work. He inspired the young, admonished the elderly, supported the weak, and guided the strong.
output: But Alexander Crummell it gave back. Out of the temptation of Hate, and burned by the fire of Despair, triumphant over Doubt, and steeled by Sacrifice against Humiliation, he turned at last home across the waters, humble and strong, gentle and determined. He bent to all the gibes and prejudices, to all hatred and discrimination, with that rare courtesy which is the armor of pure souls. He fought among his own, the low, the grasping, and the wicked, with that unbending righteousness which is the sword of the just. He never faltered, he seldom complained; he simply worked, inspiring the young, rebuking the old, helping the weak, guiding the strong.
title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois

input:
It may have surprised the nation to hear a Black individual advocating such a program after many years of significant grievances; this response may have startled and garnered the approval of the South while also piquing the interest and admiration of the North. Following some initial murmurs of dissent, it may have ultimately quieted, if not convinced, the Black community itself. 

Mr. Washington's primary challenge was to gain the support and collaboration of the diverse groups within the white South, which, at the time of Tuskegee's establishment, seemed quite challenging for a Black man. However, a decade later, he successfully articulated his vision at Atlanta, suggesting that "in all things purely social we can be as separate as the five fingers, and yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress." This “Atlanta Compromise” is arguably the most significant achievement of Mr. Washington’s career. The South interpreted this agreement in various ways: radicals viewed it as a complete concession on the pursuit of civil and political equality, while conservatives saw it as a well-thought-out foundation for mutual understanding. Both groups found merit in it, and today, its author is regarded as one of the most prominent Southerners since Jefferson Davis, enjoying a substantial personal following.
output:
It startled the nation to hear a Negro advocating such a programme after many decades of bitter complaint; it startled and won the applause of the South, it interested and won the admiration of the North; and after a confused murmur of protest, it silenced if it did not convert the Negroes themselves.

To gain the sympathy and cooperation of the various elements comprising the white South was Mr. Washington’s first task; and this, at the time Tuskegee was founded, seemed, for a black man, well-nigh impossible. And yet ten years later it was done in the word spoken at Atlanta: “In all things purely social we can be as separate as the five fingers, and yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress.” This “Atlanta Compromise” is by all odds the most notable thing in Mr. Washington’s career. The South interpreted it in different ways: the radicals received it as a complete surrender of the demand for civil and political equality; the conservatives, as a generously conceived working basis for mutual understanding. So both approved it, and to-day its author is certainly the most distinguished Southerner since Jefferson Davis, and the one with the largest personal following.
title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois

input: "Perhaps," said John, settling himself on the train, "perhaps I am to blame for struggling against my manifest destiny simply because it appears difficult and unpleasant. My duty to Altamaha lies plainly before me. Perhaps they will allow me to help address the Negro problems there, and perhaps they will not. 'I will go in to the King, which is not according to the law; and if I perish, I perish.'" He then mused and dreamed, and planned a life's work, while the train sped south.
output: “Perhaps,” said John, as he settled himself on the train, “perhaps I am to blame myself in struggling against my manifest destiny simply because it looks hard and unpleasant. Here is my duty to Altamaha plain before me; perhaps they’ll let me help settle the Negro problems there, - perhaps they won’t. ‘I will go in to the King, which is not according to the law; and if I perish, I perish.’” And then he mused and dreamed, and planned a life-work; and the train flew south.
title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois

input: It is worth noting that I should be the last to deny the evident weaknesses and shortcomings of the Negro people, and I should likewise be the last to withhold sympathy from the white South in its efforts to address its complex social problems. Furthermore, I freely acknowledge that it is possible, and at times preferable, that a partially developed people should be governed by the best of their stronger and more advanced neighbors for their own benefit, until such time as they are able to contend independently in the world's struggles. Moreover, I have already indicated how greatly the emancipated Negro required such economic and spiritual guidance, and I am entirely willing to concede that if the representatives of the best white Southern public opinion were the governing and directing forces in the South today, the conditions described would be reasonably well satisfied. However, the point I have maintained and now emphasize again is that the best opinion of the South today is not the governing opinion. In essence, to leave the Negro helpless and without a ballot today is to leave him not to the guidance of the best, but rather to the exploitation and corruption of the worst. Additionally, this is no more true of the South than of the North, nor of the North than of Europe: in any land, in any country under modern free competition, to place any class of weak and despised people, whether white, black, or otherwise, at the political mercy of their stronger, wealthier, and more resourceful fellows, constitutes a temptation that human nature has seldom withstood and seldom will withstand.
output: I should be the last one to deny the patent weaknesses and shortcomings of the Negro people; I should be the last to withhold sympathy from the white South in its efforts to solve its intricate social problems. I freely acknowledged that it is possible, and sometimes best, that a partially undeveloped people should be ruled by the best of their stronger and better neighbors for their own good, until such time as they can start and fight the world’s battles alone. I have already pointed out how sorely in need of such economic and spiritual guidance the emancipated Negro was, and I am quite willing to admit that if the representatives of the best white Southern public opinion were the ruling and guiding powers in the South to-day the conditions indicated would be fairly well fulfilled. But the point I have insisted upon and now emphasize again, is that the best opinion of the South to-day is not the ruling opinion. That to leave the Negro helpless and without a ballot to-day is to leave him not to the guidance of the best, but rather to the exploitation and debauchment of the worst; that this is no truer of the South than of the North, - of the North than of Europe: in any land, in any country under modern free competition, to lay any class of weak and despised people, be they white, black, or blue, at the political mercy of their stronger, richer, and more resourceful fellows, is a temptation which human nature seldom has withstood and seldom will withstand.
title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois

input: In this community, there appears to be little room for a leisure class. It is often overlooked that in the United States, a significant portion of youth and adults may not be engaged in income-generating activities, as they might instead be focused on building homes, gaining knowledge about the world, or resting after their struggles. However, here, a striking ninety-six percent of individuals seem to be engaged in labor; few have the opportunity to transform a simple, stark cabin into a home, and there may be no elderly family members to share stories and traditions by the fire. This environment may offer limited space for carefree childhoods or reflective youth. The repetitive nature of daily work is occasionally interrupted by moments of lightheartedness or the weekly journey to town. The labor, much like farm work elsewhere, tends to be dull and unvaried, and the lack of machinery and tools may make the tasks feel even more burdensome. Nonetheless, this work takes place in the open air, which is a notable benefit in an age when fresh air can often be hard to come by. Overall, while the conditions may be challenging, the opportunity to work outdoors remains a significant aspect of their experience.
output: Among this people there is no leisure class. We often forget that in the United States over half the youth and adults are not in the world earning incomes, but are making homes, learning of the world, or resting after the heat of the strife. But here ninety-six per cent are toiling; no one with leisure to turn the bare and cheerless cabin into a home, no old folks to sit beside the fire and hand down traditions of the past; little of careless happy childhood and dreaming youth. The dull monotony of daily toil is broken only by the gayety of the thoughtless and the Saturday trip to town. The toil, like all farm toil, is monotonous, and here there are little machinery and few tools to relieve its burdensome drudgery. But with all this, it is work in the pure open air, and this is something in a day when fresh air is scarce.
title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois

input:
Mr. Washington deserves significant criticism for his failure to recognize and convey this important point. His doctrine has led white individuals, both in the North and the South, to shift the responsibility of the Negro problem onto the shoulders of the Negro population. They have become critical and rather pessimistic observers, neglecting their own roles in addressing these issues. In reality, the burden belongs to the entire nation, and none of us are innocent if we do not dedicate our efforts to rectify these significant injustices.

The South should be encouraged, through open and honest criticism, to embrace its better self and fulfill its obligations to the race it has wronged so severely and continues to wrong. The North, which shares in this guilt, cannot alleviate its conscience by simply applying superficial solutions. We cannot resolve this issue through diplomacy and charm or through policy alone. Ultimately, if the situation worsens, can the moral integrity of this country endure the gradual destruction and suffering of nine million individuals?
output:
In his failure to realize and impress this last point, Mr. Washington is especially to be criticised. His doctrine has tended to make the whites, North and South, shift the burden of the Negro problem to the Negro’s shoulders and stand aside as critical and rather pessimistic spectators; when in fact the burden belongs to the nation, and the hands of none of us are clean if we bend not our energies to righting these great wrongs.

The South ought to be led, by candid and honest criticism, to assert her better self and do her full duty to the race she has cruelly wronged and is still wronging. The North - her co-partner in guilt - cannot salve her conscience by plastering it with gold. We cannot settle this problem by diplomacy and suaveness, by “policy” alone. If worse come to worst, can the moral fibre of this country survive the slow throttling and murder of nine millions of men?
title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois

input: First, black men have a duty to judge the South with discernment. The current generation of Southerners is not responsible for the past, and they should not be hated or blamed blindly for it. Moreover, no group finds the indiscriminate endorsement of the South's recent treatment of Negroes more distasteful than the South's best thinkers do. The South is not "solid"; it is a region in the ferment of social change, where forces of all kinds compete for supremacy. To praise the evil the South currently commits is just as wrong as to condemn the good. What the South needs is discerning, broad-minded criticism. It needs this for the sake of its own white sons and daughters, and to ensure robust, healthy mental and moral development.
output: First, it is the duty of black men to judge the South discriminatingly. The present generation of Southerners are not responsible for the past, and they should not be blindly hated or blamed for it. Furthermore, to no class is the indiscriminate endorsement of the recent course of the South toward Negroes more nauseating than to the best thought of the South. The South is not “solid”; it is a land in the ferment of social change, wherein forces of all kinds are fighting for supremacy; and to praise the ill the South is today perpetrating is just as wrong as to condemn the good. Discriminating and broad-minded criticism is what the South needs, - needs it for the sake of her own white sons and daughters, and for the insurance of robust, healthy mental and moral development.
title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois

input:
The agents that the Bureau could command varied widely, ranging from unselfish philanthropists to narrow-minded busybodies and thieves. And even though it may be true that the average was far better than the worst, it was the occasional bad apple that tended to spoil the barrel.

Meanwhile, amid all this, the freed slave often found himself crouched in bewilderment between friend and foe. He had emerged from slavery—not the worst slavery in the world, not one that made all of life unbearable, but rather one that here and there had something of kindliness, fidelity, and happiness—yet it was still slavery, which, as far as human aspiration and worth were concerned, classed the black man and the ox together. And the Negro knew full well that, whatever their deeper convictions may have been, Southern men had fought with desperate energy to perpetuate this slavery, under which the black masses, with half-articulate thought, had writhed and shivered. They welcomed freedom with a cry. They shrank from the master who still strove to put them back in chains; they fled to the friends who had freed them, even though those friends stood ready to use them as a club for driving the recalcitrant South back into loyalty. So the cleft between the white and black South tended to grow. It is idle to say it never should have happened; it was as inevitable as its results were pitiable. Curiously incongruous elements were left arrayed against each other—on one side, the North, the government, the carpet-bagger, and the slave; and on the other, all the South that was white, whether gentleman or vagabond, honest man or rascal, lawless murderer or martyr to duty.

In the end, the period left a fractured and deeply divided society, in which formerly enslaved people had to navigate a precarious space between those who had freed them and those who still sought to keep them in bondage.
output:
The agents that the Bureau could command varied all the way from unselfish philanthropists to narrow-minded busybodies and thieves; and even though it be true that the average was far better than the worst, it was the occasional fly that helped spoil the ointment.

Then amid all crouched the freed slave, bewildered between friend and foe. He had emerged from slavery, - not the worst slavery in the world, not a slavery that made all life unbearable, rather a slavery that had here and there something of kindliness, fidelity, and happiness, - but withal slavery, which, so far as human aspiration and desert were concerned, classed the black man and the ox together. And the Negro knew full well that, whatever their deeper convictions may have been, Southern men had fought with desperate energy to perpetuate this slavery under which the black masses, with half-articulate thought, had writhed and shivered. They welcomed freedom with a cry. They shrank from the master who still strove for their chains; they fled to the friends that had freed them, even though those friends stood ready to use them as a club for driving the recalcitrant South back into loyalty. So the cleft between the white and black South grew. Idle to say it never should have been; it was as inevitable as its results were pitiable. Curiously incongruous elements were left arrayed against each other, - the North, the government, the carpet-bagger, and the slave, here; and there, all the South that was white, whether gentleman or vagabond, honest man or rascal, lawless murderer or martyr to duty.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois

input: I first saw Alexander Crummell at a Wilberforce commencement season, amid all its bustle and crush. He stood there tall, frail, and black, with a simple dignity and an unmistakable air of good breeding. I spoke with him apart, where the noise of the vigorous young orators could not reach us. I addressed him politely at first, then with curiosity, and finally with eagerness, as I began to sense the fineness of his character: his calm courtesy, the sweetness of his strength, and his balanced blending of hope and truth in life. Instinctively I bowed before this man, as one bows before the prophets of the world. He seemed to me a kind of seer, one who came not from the crimson Past or the gray To-come, but from the pulsing Now—that mocking world that seemed to me at once so light and dark, so splendid and sordid. For eighty years he had wandered in this same world of mine, within the Veil.
output: I saw Alexander Crummell first at a Wilberforce commencement season, amid its bustle and crush. Tall, frail, and black he stood, with simple dignity and an unmistakable air of good breeding. I talked with him apart, where the storming of the lusty young orators could not harm us. I spoke to him politely, then curiously, then eagerly, as I began to feel the fineness of his character, - his calm courtesy, the sweetness of his strength, and his fair blending of the hope and truth of life. Instinctively I bowed before this man, as one bows before the prophets of the world. Some seer he seemed, that came not from the crimson Past or the gray To-come, but from the pulsing Now, - that mocking world which seemed to me at once so light and dark, so splendid and sordid. Fourscore years had he wandered in this same world of mine, within the Veil.
title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois

input: When night falls on the City of a Hundred Hills, a wind rises from the seas and moves westward with a murmuring sound. At its prompting, the smoke from the drowsy factories drifts down over the great city and covers it like a pall, while over at the University the stars twinkle above Stone Hall. It is said that the gray mist there is the tunic of Atalanta as she pauses over her golden apples. Fly, my maiden, fly, for Hippomenes is coming. This highlights how the scene blends the industrial city with a classical myth. If the Soul can cast the Dust aside and ride naked on the Air of Heaven, would it not be a shame, would it not be a shame, for him to remain crippled in this clay carcass? This suggests a longing for release from the body, and ultimately it frames that longing as a moral reproach.
output:
When night falls on the City of a Hundred Hills, a wind gathers itself from the seas and comes murmuring westward. And at its bidding, the smoke of the drowsy factories sweeps down upon the mighty city and covers it like a pall, while yonder at the University the stars twinkle above Stone Hall. And they say that yon gray mist is the tunic of Atalanta pausing over her golden apples. Fly, my maiden, fly, for yonder comes Hippomenes!

Why, if the Soul can fling the Dust aside, And naked on the Air of Heaven ride, Were’t not a Shame - were’t not a Shame for him In this clay carcase crippled to abide?
title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois

input:
A sense of calling and purpose led him to pursue the priesthood—to serve, perhaps, as a guide for those who felt excluded or oppressed. He saw a restless, struggling crowd turning toward him, and he reached out eagerly to help. Yet even as he did so, a feeling of despair suddenly came over him.

These were not bad people. The challenges of life are not simply about good versus evil. They were calm, well-meaning men, bishops in the church, who tried to do what was right. They explained slowly that his desire was understandable and even admirable, but that the seminary could not admit a Black student. When he continued to seek entrance, they gently and somewhat regretfully told him that they understood his feelings, but that it was simply not possible—or at least, not yet. They expressed hope that such distinctions would someday disappear, but for now, the world was as it was.

In the end, even sincere and well-intentioned people can sometimes uphold unfair barriers, and progress often comes more slowly than we might hope.
output:
A voice and vision called him to be a priest, - a seer to lead the uncalled out of the house of bondage. He saw the headless host turn toward him like the whirling of mad waters, - he stretched forth his hands eagerly, and then, even as he stretched them, suddenly there swept across the vision the temptation of Despair.

They were not wicked men, - the problem of life is not the problem of the wicked, - they were calm, good men, Bishops of the Apostolic Church of God, and strove toward righteousness. They said slowly, “It is all very natural - it is even commendable; but the General Theological Seminary of the Episcopal Church cannot admit a Negro.” And when that thin, half-grotesque figure still haunted their doors, they put their hands kindly, half sorrowfully, on his shoulders, and said, “Now, - of course, we - we know how you feel about it; but you see it is impossible, - that is - well - it is premature. Sometime, we trust - sincerely trust - all such distinctions will fade away; but now the world is as it is.”
title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W. E. B. Du Bois

input: Such churches function essentially as governments of men, and therefore even a little investigation reveals a curious fact: in the South, at least, practically every American Negro is a church member. Some, it is true, are not regularly enrolled, and a few do not habitually attend services; but a proscribed people must have a social center, and for this people that center is the Negro church. The census of 1890 showed nearly twenty-four thousand Negro churches in the country, with a total enrolled membership of over two and a half million, or ten actual church members to every twenty-eight persons, and in some Southern States one in every two persons. Besides these, there is a large number who, while not enrolled as members, attend and take part in many of the activities of the church. This suggests that there is an organized Negro church for every sixty black families in the nation, and in some States for every forty families, owning, on average, a thousand dollars' worth of property each, or nearly twenty-six million dollars in all.
output: Such churches are really governments of men, and consequently a little investigation reveals the curious fact that, in the South, at least, practically every American Negro is a church member. Some, to be sure, are not regularly enrolled, and a few do not habitually attend services; but, practically, a proscribed people must have a social centre, and that centre for this people is the Negro church. The census of 1890 showed nearly twenty-four thousand Negro churches in the country, with a total enrolled membership of over two and a half millions, or ten actual church members to every twenty-eight persons, and in some Southern States one in every two persons. Besides these there is the large number who, while not enrolled as members, attend and take part in many of the activities of the church. There is an organized Negro church for every sixty black families in the nation, and in some States for every forty families, owning, on an average, a thousand dollars’ worth of property each, or nearly twenty-six million dollars in all.
