input: In regard to probable opinion, one can derive significant assistance from coherence, which we have dismissed as a definition of truth, yet may often function as a useful criterion. A collection of individually probable opinions, when they exhibit mutual coherence, becomes more probable than any single opinion would be on its own. It is through this mechanism that many scientific hypotheses attain their probability. These hypotheses integrate into a coherent framework of probable opinions, thereby elevating their likelihood compared to when they are considered in isolation. The same principle applies to general philosophical hypotheses. In particular instances, such hypotheses may initially appear highly questionable; however, upon evaluating the order and coherence they introduce into a collection of probable opinions, they may approach a state of near certainty. This is especially relevant to distinctions between dreams and waking life. If our dreams, night after night, demonstrated the same coherence as our daytime experiences, we would find it difficult to determine whether to trust our dreams or our waking life. As it stands, the coherence test discredits the dreams and validates the waking experience. Nevertheless, while this test enhances probability when it is successful, it does not yield absolute certainty unless there is already some certainty present within the coherent system. Consequently, the mere organization of probable opinion cannot, in isolation, transform it into indubitable knowledge.
output: In regard to probable opinion, we can derive great assistance from coherence, which we rejected as the definition of truth, but may often use as a criterion. A body of individually probable opinions, if they are mutually coherent, become more probable than any one of them would be individually. It is in this way that many scientific hypotheses acquire their probability. They fit into a coherent system of probable opinions, and thus become more probable than they would be in isolation. The same thing applies to general philosophical hypotheses. Often in a single case such hypotheses may seem highly doubtful, while yet, when we consider the order and coherence which they introduce into a mass of probable opinion, they become pretty nearly certain. This applies, in particular, to such matters as the distinction between dreams and waking life. If our dreams, night after night, were as coherent one with another as our days, we should hardly know whether to believe the dreams or the waking life. As it is, the test of coherence condemns the dreams and confirms the waking life. But this test, though it increases probability where it is successful, never gives absolute certainty, unless there is certainty already at some point in the coherent system. Thus the mere organization of probable opinion will never, by itself, transform it into indubitable knowledge.

input: The manner in which simplicity is introduced through the supposition that physical objects truly exist can be readily observed. If the cat appears at one moment in one part of the room and at another moment in a different part, it is natural to suppose that it has moved from the one location to the other, traversing a series of intermediate positions. However, if it is merely a collection of sense-data, it cannot have been in any place where I did not perceive it; consequently, we must suppose that it did not exist at all during the intervals when I was not observing it, but instead suddenly came into being in a new location. Furthermore, if the cat exists regardless of whether I see it, we can understand from our own experience how it becomes hungry between one meal and the next; but if it does not exist when I am not seeing it, it appears peculiar that appetite should increase during non-existence as rapidly as during existence. Moreover, if the cat consists only of sense-data, it cannot be hungry, since no hunger other than my own can constitute a sense-datum for me. In essence, the behaviour of the sense-data that represent the cat to me, though it appears quite natural when regarded as an expression of hunger, becomes entirely inexplicable when regarded as mere movements and changes of coloured patches, which are as incapable of hunger as a triangle is of playing football.
output: The way in which simplicity comes in from supposing that there really are physical objects is easily seen. If the cat appears at one moment in one part of the room, and at another in another part, it is natural to suppose that it has moved from the one to the other, passing over a series of intermediate positions. But if it is merely a set of sense-data, it cannot have ever been in any place where I did not see it; thus we shall have to suppose that it did not exist at all while I was not looking, but suddenly sprang into being in a new place. If the cat exists whether I see it or not, we can understand from our own experience how it gets hungry between one meal and the next; but if it does not exist when I am not seeing it, it seems odd that appetite should grow during non-existence as fast as during existence. And if the cat consists only of sense-data, it cannot be hungry, since no hunger but my own can be a sense-datum to me. Thus the behaviour of the sense-data which represent the cat to me, though it seems quite natural when regarded as an expression of hunger, becomes utterly inexplicable when regarded as mere movements and changes of patches of colour, which are as incapable of hunger as a triangle is of playing football.

input: It appears that we have tentatively agreed that physical objects may not be entirely like our sense-data, but can often be viewed as the cause of our sensations. These physical objects are situated in the space of science, which may be referred to as 'physical' space. It is worth noting that, if our sensations are to be caused by physical objects, it is likely that there must be a physical space that contains both these objects and our sense-organs, nerves, and brain. We tend to experience a sensation of touch from an object when we are in close proximity to it, which means that some part of our body occupies a nearby location in physical space. Generally speaking, we see an object when there is no opaque object between the object and our eyes in physical space. Similarly, we can usually only hear, smell, or taste an object when we are sufficiently close to it, or when it comes into contact with our tongue, or is positioned in a suitable location in physical space relative to our body. Unless we consider the object and our body to be in the same physical space, it may be challenging to predict what sensations we will derive from a given object under different circumstances, as the relative positions of the object and our body tend to play a significant role in determining the sensations we experience. In summary, our understanding of physical objects and sensations suggests that they are interconnected and can be understood in the context of physical space.
output: We agreed provisionally that physical objects cannot be quite like our sense-data, but may be regarded as causing our sensations. These physical objects are in the space of science, which we may call 'physical' space. It is important to notice that, if our sensations are to be caused by physical objects, there must be a physical space containing these objects and our sense-organs and nerves and brain. We get a sensation of touch from an object when we are in contact with it; that is to say, when some part of our body occupies a place in physical space quite close to the space occupied by the object. We see an object (roughly speaking) when no opaque body is between the object and our eyes in physical space. Similarly, we only hear or smell or taste an object when we are sufficiently near to it, or when it touches the tongue, or has some suitable position in physical space relatively to our body. We cannot begin to state what different sensations we shall derive from a given object under different circumstances unless we regard the object and our body as both in one physical space, for it is mainly the relative positions of the object and our body that determine what sensations we shall derive from the object.

author: Bertrand Russell

input: It appears that there may be two types of self-evident truths of perception, which can often be distinguished, although they may ultimately be interconnected. Initially, there is the type that merely confirms the existence of a sense-datum without examining it in detail. For instance, when we see a patch of red, we can form the judgement 'there is a patch of red' or, more precisely, 'that exists'; this tends to be a basic intuitive judgement of perception. On the other hand, a different type of judgement emerges when the object of our senses is complex and we break it down to some extent. If, for example, we see a round patch of red, we may conclude 'that patch of red is round'; this is also a judgement of perception, but it differs from the first type. In this case, we have a single sense-datum with both colour and shape, where the colour is red and the shape is round, and our judgement separates the datum into colour and shape before combining them again to state that the red colour has a round shape. A similar example of this type of judgement is 'this is to the right of that', where 'this' and 'that' are seen at the same time, and the sense-datum contains elements that have a particular relationship to each other, which the judgement then affirms. In summary, these two types of judgements of perception can be distinguished by the level of analysis involved, with one confirming existence and the other examining and combining the components of a sense-datum.
output: It would seem that there are two kinds of self-evident truths of perception, though perhaps in the last analysis the two kinds may coalesce. First, there is the kind which simply asserts the existence of the sense-datum, without in any way analysing it. We see a patch of red, and we judge 'there is such-and-such a patch of red', or more strictly 'there is that'; this is one kind of intuitive judgement of perception. The other kind arises when the object of sense is complex, and we subject it to some degree of analysis. If, for instance, we see a round patch of red, we may judge 'that patch of red is round'. This is again a judgement of perception, but it differs from our previous kind. In our present kind we have a single sense-datum which has both colour and shape: the colour is red and the shape is round. Our judgement analyses the datum into colour and shape, and then recombines them by stating that the red colour is round in shape. Another example of this kind of judgement is 'this is to the right of that', where 'this' and 'that' are seen simultaneously. In this kind of judgement the sense-datum contains constituents which have some relation to each other, and the judgement asserts that these constituents have this relation.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input: Kant's position is that our experiences consist of two distinct elements: one attributed to the object itself, and the other to our own nature. As previously discussed, the physical object differs from its associated sense-data, which arise from the interaction between the object and ourselves. This highlights the complex relationship between the object and our perception of it. Kant's unique perspective lies in how he allocates the contributions of the object and ourselves. He argues that the raw sensory data, such as color and hardness, originates from the object, while our mind supplies the spatial and temporal framework, as well as the relationships between sense-data that emerge from comparison or causal reasoning. This suggests that our understanding of space, time, causality, and comparison is rooted in our own cognitive nature. Ultimately, Kant's reasoning is based on the idea that we possess a priori knowledge of these concepts, but not of the raw sensory material. He asserts that any experience we have will necessarily conform to the characteristics defined by our a priori knowledge, as these characteristics are inherent to our own nature and therefore inescapable in our experience of the world.
output: What Kant maintained was that in all our experience there are two elements to be distinguished, the one due to the object (i.e. to what we have called the 'physical object'), the other due to our own nature. We saw, in discussing matter and sense-data, that the physical object is different from the associated sense-data, and that the sense-data are to be regarded as resulting from an interaction between the physical object and ourselves. So far, we are in agreement with Kant. But what is distinctive of Kant is the way in which he apportions the shares of ourselves and the physical object respectively. He considers that the crude material given in sensation - the colour, hardness, etc. - is due to the object, and that what we supply is the arrangement in space and time, and all the relations between sense-data which result from comparison or from considering one as the cause of the other or in any other way. His chief reason in favour of this view is that we seem to have a priori knowledge as to space and time and causality and comparison, but not as to the actual crude material of sensation. We can be sure, he says, that anything we shall ever experience must show the characteristics affirmed of it in our a priori knowledge, because these characteristics are due to our own nature, and therefore nothing can ever come into our experience without acquiring these characteristics.
title: The Problems of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell

input:
When we state that a particular entity exists, we imply that there is only one object that possesses the specified characteristics. The statement that an individual is a specific entity means that this individual has the corresponding property, and no other entity possesses it. For instance, if we say that Mr. A is the Unionist candidate for a particular constituency, it means that Mr. A is a Unionist candidate for that constituency, and no one else holds this position. Similarly, the existence of the Unionist candidate for a constituency implies that someone is a Unionist candidate for that constituency, and no one else is.

Furthermore, when we are familiar with an object that is a specific entity, we are aware that this entity exists. However, it is also possible to know that a specific entity exists without being acquainted with any object that we know to be that entity. Additionally, we may know that a specific entity exists even when we are not familiar with any object that actually is that entity.
output: When we say 'the so-and-so exists', we mean that there is just one object which is the so-and-so. The proposition 'a is the so-and-so' means that a has the property so-and-so, and nothing else has. 'Mr. A. is the Unionist candidate for this constituency' means 'Mr. A. is a Unionist candidate for this constituency, and no one else is'. 'The Unionist candidate for this constituency exists' means 'some one is a Unionist candidate for this constituency, and no one else is'. Thus, when we are acquainted with an object which is the so-and-so, we know that the so-and-so exists; but we may know that the so-and-so exists when we are not acquainted with any object which we know to be the so-and-so, and even when we are not acquainted with any object which, in fact, is the so-and-so.

input: In a neighborhood beyond Dockhead in the Borough of Southwark, Jacob's Island stands surrounded by a muddy ditch. This ditch is six or eight feet deep and fifteen or twenty wide when the tide is in. It was once called Mill Pond, but in the days of this story it is known as Folly Ditch. It is a creek or inlet from the Thames and can always be filled at high water by opening the sluices at the Lead Mills, from which it took its old name. At such times, a stranger looking from one of the wooden bridges across it at Mill Lane will see the inhabitants of the houses on either side lowering buckets, pails, and domestic utensils of all kinds from their back doors and windows to haul the water up. When his eye turns from these operations to the houses themselves, his utmost astonishment will be excited by the scene before him. Crazy wooden galleries are common to the backs of half a dozen houses, with holes from which to look upon the slime beneath. Windows are broken and patched, with poles thrust out on which to dry linen that is never there. Rooms are so small, so filthy, and so confined that the air would seem too tainted even for the dirt and squalor they shelter. Wooden chambers thrust themselves out above the mud and threaten to fall into it, as some have done. Dirt-besmeared walls and decaying foundations are present. Every repulsive lineament of poverty and every loathsome indication of filth, rot, and garbage ornament the banks of Folly Ditch.

“So I mean to be a gentleman,” said Mr. Claypole, kicking out his legs, and continuing a conversation, the commencement of which Fagin had arrived too late to hear. “No more jolly old coffins, Charlotte, but a gentleman’s life for me: and, if yer like, yer shall be a lady.”

When he finally approached Jim Hollis, he was met with the reminder of the supposed blessing of his recent bout with measles, which served as a warning. Each boy he encountered contributed to the weight of his despair. Ultimately, in a moment of desperation, he sought solace in the companionship of Huckleberry Finn, only to be greeted with a Scriptural quotation. At that moment, his heart shattered, and he retreated home to his bed, fully aware that he was the sole individual in the town who was irredeemably lost, forever and ever.
output:
The dreadful secret of the murder was a chronic misery. It was a very cancer for permanency and pain.

He hunted up Jim Hollis, who called his attention to the precious blessing of his late measles as a warning. Every boy he encountered added another ton to his depression; and when, in desperation, he flew for refuge at last to the bosom of Huckleberry Finn and was received with a Scriptural quotation, his heart broke and he crept home and to bed realizing that he alone of all the town was lost, forever and forever.

When I finally made it to the shore and climbed up the bank, my visibility was limited, but I began to navigate the uneven terrain for about a quarter of a mile. Eventually, I stumbled upon an old double log house, but I almost passed by it. Just then, a group of dogs surged out, barking and howling at me, which made me realize it was wise to stay put. 

In summary, I found myself navigating a challenging situation with unexpected encounters along the way.
output:
I sung out for Jim about a dozen times, but I didn’t get any answer; so I grabbed a plank that touched me while I was “treading water,” and struck out for shore, shoving it ahead of me. But I made out to see that the drift of the current was towards the left-hand shore, which meant that I was in a crossing; so I changed off and went that way.

It was one of these long, slanting, two-mile crossings; so I was a good long time in getting over. I made a safe landing, and clumb up the bank. I couldn’t see but a little ways, but I went poking along over rough ground for a quarter of a mile or more, and then I run across a big old-fashioned double log-house before I noticed it. I was going to rush by and get away, but a lot of dogs jumped out and went to howling and barking at me, and I knowed better than to move another peg.

output:

Thinks I, it won’t do to paddle; first I know I’ll run into the bank or a tow-head or something; I got to set still and float, and yet it’s mighty fidgety business to have to hold your hands still at such a time. Hindley tends to be too careless to choose his friends wisely; he doesn’t bother to consider why he might not trust someone he has treated badly. He also hopes that I will have more chances to see him there than I would if he settled in Gimmerton. He intends to pay generously for permission to stay at the Heights, and my brother’s greed will likely lead him to accept the offer, since he has always been greedy—though what he gains with one hand, he often throws away with the other.”

He means to offer liberal payment for permission to lodge at the Heights; and doubtless my brother’s covetousness will prompt him to accept the terms: he was always greedy; though what he grasps with one hand he flings away with the other.”

I led my young lady out: she was too glad of her escape to resist; the other followed, and Mr. Heathcliff had the room to himself till dinner. The two new friends established themselves in the house during his absence; where I heard Hareton sternly check his cousin, on her offering a revelation of her father-in-law’s conduct to his father. He said he wouldn’t suffer a word to be uttered in his disparagement: if he were the devil, it didn’t signify; he would stand by him; and he’d rather she would abuse himself, as she used to, than begin on Mr. Heathcliff. Catherine was waxing cross at this; but he found means to make her hold her tongue, by asking how she would like him to speak ill of her father? Then she comprehended that Earnshaw took the master’s reputation home to himself; and was attached by ties stronger than reason could break - chains, forged by habit, which it would be cruel to attempt to loosen. She showed a good heart, thenceforth, in avoiding both complaints and expressions of antipathy concerning Heathcliff; and confessed to me her sorrow that she had endeavoured to raise a bad spirit between him and Hareton: indeed, I don’t believe she has ever breathed a syllable, in the latter’s hearing, against her oppressor since.

It is worth noting that her affection for her father must have been deeply rooted, given the considerable attention and care she bestowed upon me. Moreover, although I stated that her days were divided between us, the master would often retire early, and I generally required no further assistance after six o'clock, thereby leaving the evening hours at her disposal. Additionally, I must admit that I never gave much consideration to how she occupied herself after tea, and although I frequently observed a healthy complexion and a subtle flush on her fingers when she came to bid me good-night, I attributed this to the warmth of the library fire rather than any other possible explanation.
output: My little mistress behaved like an angel in coming to wait on me, and cheer my solitude; the confinement brought me exceedingly low. It is wearisome, to a stirring active body: but few have slighter reasons for complaint than I had. The moment Catherine left Mr. Linton’s room she appeared at my bedside. Her day was divided between us; no amusement usurped a minute: she neglected her meals, her studies, and her play; and she was the fondest nurse that ever watched. She must have had a warm heart, when she loved her father so, to give so much to me. I said her days were divided between us; but the master retired early, and I generally needed nothing after six o’clock, thus the evening was her own. Poor thing! I never considered what she did with herself after tea. And though frequently, when she looked in to bid me good-night, I remarked a fresh colour in her cheeks and a pinkness over her slender fingers, instead of fancying the hue borrowed from a cold ride across the moors, I laid it to the charge of a hot fire in the library.

Yet, she spoke untruths, did she not? Mr. Heathcliff is not a monster; he possesses an honorable and genuine spirit, or how could he retain memories of her?”

Moreover, she responded, “You are aligned with the others, Ellen! I shall not heed your defamatory remarks. What malice must you harbor to attempt to persuade me that there is no joy to be found in the world!”
output:
“For shame! for shame!” she repeated, angrily. “You are worse than twenty foes, you poisonous friend!”

“And I must suffer for her egotism!” she sobbed, as Mrs. Linton left the room. “All, all is against me: she has blighted my single consolation. But she uttered falsehoods, didn’t she? Mr. Heathcliff is not a fiend: he has an honourable soul, and a true one, or how could he remember her?”

“You are leagued with the rest, Ellen!” she replied. “I’ll not listen to your slanders. What malevolence you must have to wish to convince me that there is no happiness in the world!”

output: Yesterday afternoon set in misty and cold. I had half a mind to spend it by my study fire, instead of wading through heath and mud to Wuthering Heights. On coming up from dinner, however, (N.B. - I dine between twelve and one o’clock; the housekeeper, a matronly lady, taken as a fixture along with the house, could not, or would not, comprehend my request that I might be served at five) - on mounting the stairs with this lazy intention, and stepping into the room, I saw a servant-girl on her knees surrounded by brushes and coal-scuttles, and raising an infernal dust as she extinguished the flames with heaps of cinders. This spectacle drove me back immediately; I took my hat, and, after a four-miles’ walk, arrived at Heathcliff’s garden-gate just in time to escape the first feathery flakes of a snow shower.

input: Cathy may have been a significant support at home, and together they eventually convinced my master to agree to allow them to take a ride or a walk together about once a week, with me overseeing their outings on the moors near the Grange. By June, he was still not improving. Although he had consistently set aside part of his income for my young lady’s future, he naturally hoped that she might stay—or perhaps return soon—to her ancestral home. He believed her best chance of achieving this was through a union with his heir. Little did he know that the heir was deteriorating almost as quickly as he was. As far as I know, no doctor ever visited the Heights, and no one seemed to check on Master Heathcliff’s condition among us. Personally, I began to worry that my concerns were unfounded and that he might actually be recovering when he talked about riding and walking on the moors and appeared so determined to pursue this goal. It was difficult for me to imagine a father treating a sick child as harshly and cruelly as I later discovered Heathcliff had treated him, all in an effort to drive this seemingly eager pursuit; his determination seemed to increase as his greedy and unfeeling plans faced the threat of failure due to death. Overall, this situation reflects the complexities of their relationships amid challenging circumstances.
output: Cathy was a powerful ally at home; and between them they at length persuaded my master to acquiesce in their having a ride or a walk together about once a week, under my guardianship, and on the moors nearest the Grange: for June found him still declining. Though he had set aside yearly a portion of his income for my young lady’s fortune, he had a natural desire that she might retain - or at least return in a short time to - the house of her ancestors; and he considered her only prospect of doing that was by a union with his heir; he had no idea that the latter was failing almost as fast as himself; nor had any one, I believe: no doctor visited the Heights, and no one saw Master Heathcliff to make report of his condition among us. I, for my part, began to fancy my forebodings were false, and that he must be actually rallying, when he mentioned riding and walking on the moors, and seemed so earnest in pursuing his object. I could not picture a father treating a dying child as tyrannically and wickedly as I afterwards learned Heathcliff had treated him, to compel this apparent eagerness: his efforts redoubling the more imminently his avaricious and unfeeling plans were threatened with defeat by death.

I set my burden on the house-steps by the kitchen-door, and lingered to rest, and drew in a few more breaths of the soft, sweet air; my eyes were on the moon, and my back to the entrance, when I heard a voice behind me say, - “Nelly, is that you?”

input: The next morning was bright and cheerful outside. Soft light filtered through the blinds of the quiet room, casting a warm glow over the couch and its occupant. Edgar Linton lay with his head on the pillow, his eyes closed. His youthful and fair features appeared almost lifeless, resembling the form beside him, yet his expression reflected the stillness of exhausted anguish, while hers conveyed perfect peace. Her brow was smooth, her eyelids closed, and a gentle smile graced her lips. No angel in heaven could appear more beautiful than she did in that moment. As I observed her serene image, I felt enveloped by an infinite calm. My thoughts were never more pure than while I gazed upon her tranquil form. I instinctively recalled her words from just a few hours earlier: “Incomparably beyond and above us all! Whether still on earth or now in heaven, her spirit is at home with God!”

It seems quite possible that, rooted in the woods of France and Norway, there were trees already growing when that sufferer was put to death, trees that may have been marked by the Woodman, Fate, to be cut down and sawn into boards, in order to make a certain movable framework with a sack and a knife in it, one that tends to be remembered as terrible in history. It also seems quite possible that in the rough outhouses of some tillers of the heavy lands near Paris, there were sheltered from the weather on that very day rude carts, splattered with rustic mire, sniffed at by pigs, and used as roosts by poultry, which the Farmer, Death, had already set apart to serve as his tumbrils of the Revolution. But that Woodman and that Farmer, though they may work unceasingly, tend to work silently, and no one heard them as they went about with muffled tread, especially since to entertain any suspicion that they were awake could be considered atheistical and traitorous. In short, these quiet forces of fate and death were already at work, even if no one around them was willing or able to notice.

The door closed, and Carton was left alone. Straining his powers of listening to the utmost, he listened for any sound that might denote suspicion or alarm. There was none. Keys turned, doors clashed, footsteps passed along distant passages: no cry was raised, or hurry made, that seemed unusual. Breathing more freely in a little while, he sat down at the table, and listened again until the clock struck Two.

Sounds that he was not afraid of, for he divined their meaning, then began to be audible. Several doors were opened in succession, and finally his own. A gaoler, with a list in his hand, looked in, merely saying, “Follow me, Evrémonde!” and he followed into a large dark room, at a distance. It was a dark winter day, and what with the shadows within, and what with the shadows without, he could but dimly discern the others who were brought there to have their arms bound. Some were standing; some seated. Some were lamenting, and in restless motion; but, these were few. The great majority were silent and still, looking fixedly at the ground.

Having taken some refreshment during her journey, Miss Manette did not require anything else at that moment and was very keen to see the gentleman as soon as it was convenient for him. 

The gentleman from Tellson's felt he had no choice but to finish his drink with a sense of resignation, adjust his unusual flaxen wig, and follow the waiter to Miss Manette's room. This room was spacious and dark, furnished in a somber style with black horsehair and heavy dark tables. The tables had been polished repeatedly, causing the reflections of the two tall candles in the center to appear dim and foreboding, as if they were entombed in deep, dark graves of mahogany, offering little hope of light until they were liberated.
output:
In a very few minutes the waiter came in to announce that Miss Manette had arrived from London, and would be happy to see the gentleman from Tellson’s.

Miss Manette had taken some refreshment on the road, and required none then, and was extremely anxious to see the gentleman from Tellson’s immediately, if it suited his pleasure and convenience.

The gentleman from Tellson’s had nothing left for it but to empty his glass with an air of stolid desperation, settle his odd little flaxen wig at the ears, and follow the waiter to Miss Manette’s apartment. It was a large, dark room, furnished in a funereal manner with black horsehair, and loaded with heavy dark tables. These had been oiled and oiled, until the two tall candles on the table in the middle of the room were gloomily reflected on every leaf; as if they were buried, in deep graves of black mahogany, and no light to speak of could be expected from them until they were dug out.

He distributed orders, allocated weapons, pushed one individual backward, pulled another forward, disarmed one person to equip another, and labored amidst the thick of the uproar. 

“Stay close to me, Jacques Three,” Defarge exclaimed. “Furthermore, Jacques One and Two, you should separate and lead as many of these patriots as you can. Where is my wife?”
output:

“Keep near to me, Jacques Three,” cried Defarge; “and do you, Jacques One and Two, separate and put yourselves at the head of as many of these patriots as you can. Where is my wife?”

As long as a servant was present, no other words passed between them. When coffee had been served and they were alone together, the nephew looked at the uncle and met the eyes of the face that was like a fine mask, and then began a conversation.

As we have been traveling, I have been pondering a particular idea, and it remains on my mind now as I gaze at your supportive face. If the Republic truly benefits the poor and improves their overall well-being, it may have a long and enduring existence. Consequently, it is possible that the Republic will survive for a considerable period of time.

Meanwhile, I turn to you and ask: do you think that the wait will seem lengthy to you as you await the Republic's potential longevity in the afterlife, where I hope that both of us will find refuge? Your eyes, which have endured so much, begin to fill with tears, and your lips tremble slightly as you consider this question.
output:
“What I have been thinking as we came along, and what I am still thinking now, as I look into your kind strong face which gives me so much support, is this: - If the Republic really does good to the poor, and they come to be less hungry, and in all ways to suffer less, she may live a long time: she may even live to be old.”

“Do you think:” the uncomplaining eyes in which there is so much endurance, fill with tears, and the lips part a little more and tremble: “that it will seem long to me, while I wait for her in the better land where I trust both you and I will be mercifully sheltered?”
title: A Tale of Two Cities

The precaution that had been initiated provided significant relief to Miss Pross. Additionally, the need to arrange her appearance to avoid attracting attention in the streets was another source of comfort. She glanced at her watch and noted that it was twenty minutes past two. She realized she had no time to waste and needed to prepare immediately.

In her heightened state of anxiety, Miss Pross felt uneasy in the empty rooms, haunted by the thought of imaginary figures lurking behind every open door. To alleviate her discomfort, she filled a basin with cold water and began to wash her swollen, red eyes. However, her feverish worries prevented her from allowing the water to obscure her vision for even a moment. She frequently paused to check that no one was observing her. During one of these interruptions, she gasped and recoiled in fear, for she noticed a figure standing in the room.
output:
The having originated a precaution which was already in course of execution, was a great relief to Miss Pross. The necessity of composing her appearance so that it should attract no special notice in the streets, was another relief. She looked at her watch, and it was twenty minutes past two. She had no time to lose, but must get ready at once.

Afraid, in her extreme perturbation, of the loneliness of the deserted rooms, and of half-imagined faces peeping from behind every open door in them, Miss Pross got a basin of cold water and began laving her eyes, which were swollen and red. Haunted by her feverish apprehensions, she could not bear to have her sight obscured for a minute at a time by the dripping water, but constantly paused and looked round to see that there was no one watching her. In one of those pauses she recoiled and cried out, for she saw a figure standing in the room.

It is evident, I believe, why he may be in such a state. The memory is indeed a dreadful one. Additionally, his loss of self-identity is a direct consequence of this experience. Lacking an understanding of how he lost his sense of self, or how he was able to regain it, he may perpetually remain uncertain about the possibility of losing himself again. That uncertainty alone, I would contend, renders the subject rather unappealing.

Furthermore, this was a more profound observation than Mr. Lorry had anticipated. "Indeed," he remarked, "and it is a frightening concept to contemplate. However, a lingering doubt persists in my mind, Miss Pross, regarding whether it is beneficial for Doctor Manette to continuously harbor that repression within him. In fact, it is this doubt, along with the discomfort it occasionally induces in me, that has prompted me to share our current confidence."
output:
“It’s plain enough, I should think, why he may be. It’s a dreadful remembrance. Besides that, his loss of himself grew out of it. Not knowing how he lost himself, or how he recovered himself, he may never feel certain of not losing himself again. That alone wouldn’t make the subject pleasant, I should think.”

It was a profounder remark than Mr. Lorry had looked for. “True,” said he, “and fearful to reflect upon. Yet, a doubt lurks in my mind, Miss Pross, whether it is good for Doctor Manette to have that suppression always shut up within him. Indeed, it is this doubt and the uneasiness it sometimes causes me that has led me to our present confidence.”

The hungry man may have nibbled on one of his fingers while glancing at the other three, and his finger could have trembled with the intense desire he felt. 

Following a period of silent reflection, the first Jacques remarked, “Good! You have acted and shared your account honestly. Would you please wait for us just outside the door?”

“Of course,” replied the mender of roads, who was then escorted by Defarge to the top of the stairs. After leaving him seated there, Defarge returned. 

When he arrived back at the garret, the three had stood up, and their heads were close together in conversation.
output:
The hungry man gnawed one of his fingers as he looked at the other three, and his finger quivered with the craving that was on him.

After a gloomy silence, the first Jacques said, “Good! You have acted and recounted faithfully. Will you wait for us a little, outside the door?”

“Very willingly,” said the mender of roads. Whom Defarge escorted to the top of the stairs, and, leaving seated there, returned.

The three had risen, and their heads were together when he came back to the garret.

Young Jerry, still in his closet, may have stirred from a troubled sleep after dawn but before the sun had fully risen, alerted by the presence of his father in the family room. It seemed that something was amiss with him; at least, that was the impression Young Jerry formed from observing his father grasping Mrs. Cruncher by the ears and striking the back of her head against the bed's headboard. 

“You are standing in the way of the business's success,” Jerry expressed, “and my partners and I are feeling the effects. You promised to honor and obey; why aren’t you doing so?” 

In this way, the tension within the family dynamic is highlighted, reflecting the struggles they face.
output:
From his oppressed slumber, Young Jerry in his closet was awakened after daybreak and before sunrise, by the presence of his father in the family room. Something had gone wrong with him; at least, so Young Jerry inferred, from the circumstance of his holding Mrs. Cruncher by the ears, and knocking the back of her head against the head-board of the bed.

“You oppose yourself to the profit of the business,” said Jerry, “and me and my partners suffer. You was to honour and obey; why the devil don’t you?”
